## The Granularity Benchmark

Professional investment analysis is defined by **specificity**, not length. A 200-page report that uses vague language is worse than a 50-page report where every claim has a number attached. The following standards are non-negotiable:

### Numbers Must Be Precise
- ❌ "approximately 45%" → ✅ "43.1373%" or "43.1%" (state source and confidence)
- ❌ "hundreds of patents" → ✅ "69 granted patents + 12 pending across US/CN/EP"
- ❌ "founded in 2023" → ✅ "2023-10-15" or "2023-10"
- ❌ "raised several hundred million" → ✅ "$75M Series B at $450M pre-money (2025-03-15)"
- ❌ "large facility" → ✅ "16,000 m², including GMP plants for Class II and III active medical devices"

### People Must Be Traceable
- ❌ "graduated from a well-known university" → ✅ "BS, University of Science and Technology of China, mechatronic engineering; MS, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, software engineering"
- ❌ "has worked at several companies" → ✅ each role: company + title + dates + specific achievements
- ❌ "industry veteran" → ✅ "69 peer-reviewed papers; previously head of clinical partnerships at Neuralink"
- Every founder bio must trace from undergraduate through highest degree
- Every key hire must have: institution + degree + year + prior employer + role + achievements

### Events Must Be Dated
- ❌ "recently completed funding" → ✅ "on 2026-06-26, phase 1 of the super factory was completed and began operating"
- ❌ "has partnerships with hospitals" → ✅ "joint laboratories with Huashan Hospital (Shanghai), Shanghai Mental Health Center and West China Hospital"
- ❌ "attended by investors" → ✅ "the ribbon cutting was attended by Ji Wei of Huaying Capital, Zhang Song of Qingsong Capital, Tang Qibo of Gobi Partners and Gu Jie of Fourier"

### If Data Is Unavailable
- State EXACTLY what is missing (e.g., "registered capital not disclosed" not "insufficient information")
- Explain how material the gap is to the investment decision
- List what source would resolve it (e.g., "needs the business registration file")
- NEVER fill the gap with vague language that sounds informative but conveys no data

{"url":"https://www.therobotreport.com/abundant-robotics-shuts-down-fruit-harvesting-business/","title":"Abundant Robotics shuts down fruit harvesting business","text":"Abundant Robotics’ apple-picking robot.
Abundant Robotics, a Hayward, Calif.-based agricultural robotics company founded in 2016, has shut down. According to a memo about Abundant’s liquidation obtained by The Robot Report, the company “was unable to develop the market traction necessary to support its business during the pandemic.”
On June 29, 2021, Abundant put up for sale all of its intellectual property and assets. Abundant said it has a “host of IP, including a large body of vacuum manipulation patents (and patent applications), a patented sensory system to allow the vacuum to navigate obstruction, a patented world-class vision system for identifying fruits and their quality, and several software patents for the machine’s automated operations (including a solution to solve for “doubles” that enables the machine to pick multiple fruit at once.”
You can read the liquidation memo here to learn more about the available assets and the market opportunity. Abundant also failed to raise another round of funding. It raised a total of $12 million, according to Crunchbase, but its $10 million Series A closed back in May 2017. It raised a $2 million Seed Round from SRI Ventures in 2016.
Abundant developed a harvesting robot that initially targeted apples. The system combined computer vision and a vacuum end-effector to select and pick ripe fruit, transferring it into a bin. The company estimated its machine could reach between 50-90% of fruit on trees. The system is designed to augment human labor and could allegedly pick apples every two seconds. Abundant said it was targeting a pick rate of 1.5 seconds for the commercialized version of the robot. The company planned to broaden the type of fruit it picked in the future.
According to the memo, Abundant partnered with one of New Zealand’s largest apple growers, T&G Global, to test the apple harvesting robot in small-scale commercial trials. Abundant said it also conducted similar small-scale trials in the U.S with multiple customers. According to the memo, the market for orchard fruit production is about $200 billion, about $40-60 billion of which is specific to apple production.
Abundant said some of its competitors include FFRobotics (Israel), Ripe Robotics (Australia) and Tevel (Israel). Tevel won a 2021 RBR50 Robotics Innovation Award, produced by our sister publication Robotics Business Review, for its tethered drone that uses vision and an attached robotic arm and gripper to pick ripe fruit.

Abundant was planning to use a robotics as a service (RaaS) model. It would own, maintain, transport, and operate the robots in exchange for contract payments from farms, focusing on two 90-day harvest seasons: August-November in the Northern Hemisphere and February-May in the Southern Hemisphere. The company claimed to have developed a “strong, $100M+ business development pipeline through four years of co-development with industry leaders across the U.S., European and Oceania regions.” Abundant projected it would be cash flow positive “as early as Q2 2024, representing revenues at that time of less than 2% of the total available market.”
Despite this shutdown, the agricultural robotics market has seen a variety of acquisitions and investments in 2021. Most notably, Somerville, Mass.-based startup Root AI was acquired by AppHarvest for $60 million in April. Root AI was developing the Virgo harvesting robot for indoor farms. The robot can identify and harvest multiple crops, including tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers and more. Its tomato dataset, for example, allows it to identify more than 50 varieties of the fruit.
Abundant spun out of SRI International and was co-founded by Michael Eriksen, Curt Salisbury and Dan Steere.","truncated":false}

CNH Industrial N.V. (NYSE: CNHI / MI: CNHI) today announced that it has entered into an agreement to acquire 100% of the capital stock of Raven Industries, Inc. (NASDAQ: RAVN), a US-based leader in precision agriculture technology for US$58 per share, representing a 33.6% premium to the Raven Industries 4-week volume-weighted average stock price, and US$2.1 billion Enterprise Value. The transaction will be funded with available cash on hand of CNH Industrial. Closing is expected to occur in the fourth quarter of 2021, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions, including approval of Raven shareholders and receipt of regulatory approvals.

The acquisition builds upon a long partnership between the two companies and will further enhance CNH Industrial’s position in the global agriculture equipment market by adding strong innovation capabilities in autonomous and precision agriculture technology.

“Precision agriculture and autonomy are critical components of our strategy to help our agricultural customers reach the next level of productivity and to unlock the true potential of their operations,” said Scott Wine, Chief Executive Officer, CNH Industrial. “Raven has been a pioneer in precision agriculture for decades, and their deep product experience, customer driven software expertise and engineering acumen offer a significant boost to our capabilities. This acquisition emphasizes our commitment to enhance our precision farming portfolio and aligns with our digital transformation strategy. The combination of Raven’s technologies and CNH Industrial’s strong current and new product portfolio will provide our customers with novel, connected technologies, allowing them to be more productive and efficient.”
“Our Board and Management are excited about this partnership and what it means for our future,” said Dan Rykhus, President & Chief Executive Officer for Raven Industries. “For 65 years, our company has been committed to solving great challenges. Part of that commitment includes delivering groundbreaking innovation by developing and investing in our core capabilities and technology. By coming together with CNH Industrial, we believe we will further accelerate that path as well as bring tremendous opportunities and value to our customers — once again fulfilling our purpose to solve great challenges. Our relationship with CNH Industrial has expanded over decades, and we have a deep respect for one another and a shared commitment to transform agriculture practices across the world. We look forward to CNH Industrial leveraging the Raven talent and culture, as well as the Sioux Falls community, as part of their vision and future success.”
“Raven Industries’ capabilities, innovation culture, entrepreneurial spirit and engineering talent are impressive and will continue to thrive as part of the CNH Industrial family. Sioux Falls is and will continue to be a true center of excellence,” added Wine. “We are incredibly excited to collaborate in bringing our customers more integrated precision and autonomous solutions, not only to improve productivity and profitability, but also promote more sustainable solutions and environmental stewardship. Together, our teams will create a stronger business for our employees, dealer network, and customers, enabling us to shape the future of agriculture, augment our world-leading sustainability credentials, and maximize our growth opportunities.”
Headquartered in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, Raven Industries is organized into three business divisions: Applied Technology (precision agriculture), Engineered Films (highperformance specialty films) and Aerostar (aerospace) with consolidated net sales of US$ 348.4 million for the twelve months ended January 31, 2021. The company is a global technology partner for key strategic OEMs, agriculture retailers and dealers. The transaction is expected to generate approximately US$400 million of run-rate revenue synergies by calendar year 2025, resulting in US$150 million of incremental EBITDA from synergies.
The Engineered Films and Aerostar segments are industry leaders in the high performance specialty films and stratospheric platform industries, respectively, and CNH Industrial believes they represent attractive independent businesses with excellent near and long-term potential. Accordingly, CNH Industrial plans to undertake a strategic review of each business to best position them for future success and maximize shareholder value.
CNH Industrial does not expect the proposed acquisition will have any impact on its guidance for 2021. The acquisition is expected to be funded with Group consolidated cash1 not affecting third party debt of industrial activities2 . Cash consideration for the transaction is not included in the free cash flow definition, and consequently it will not affect its free cash flow guidance for the FY 2021E.
Barclays and Goldman Sachs acted as financial advisors to CNH Industrial

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"DEERE & CO 10-K for the period ending 2025-11-02, filed 2025-12-18 (accession 0001104659-25-122321): Item 1 (Business), paragraphs mentioning autonom, robotic, acquisition, precision. Page 1 of 1 (7,489 characters).

John Deere has manufactured agricultural equipment since 1837. Deere & Company was incorporated under the laws of Delaware in 1958. Our business is managed through the following four business segments: Production & Precision Agriculture (PPA), Small Agriculture & Turf (SAT), Construction & Forestry (CF), and Financial Services (John Deere Financial or FS).
PRODUCTION & PRECISION AGRICULTURE
Technology Stack . Investments in technology, as well as research and development, which deliver intelligent solutions to our customers through hardware and devices, embedded software, connectivity, data platforms, and applications. The technology stack leverages these core technologies across the enterprise, including digital capabilities, automation and machine learning, and autonomy. The stack has the potential to unlock economic and sustainable value for customers by optimizing jobs, strengthening decision-making, and better connecting the steps of a production system.
Lifecycle Solutions . The enterprise integration of our aftermarket and support capabilities to more effectively manage customer equipment, service, and technology needs across the full lifetime of a John Deere product, and with a specific lifecycle solution focus on the ownership experience. This integrated support seeks to enhance customer value through proactive and reactive support, easy access to parts, value-add services, and precision upgrades, regardless of when a customer purchases our equipment.
Our refined Ambitions feature long-term financial and operational goals, emphasizing the use of our differentiated equipment and service solutions, including automation, autonomy, digitalization, lifecycle solutions, and Solutions as a Service (SaaS). Utilization of these solutions is currently measured through various performance indicators. Our refined Ambitions and their timelines may be updated from time to time. In addition, we may not be able to achieve these goals for a variety of reasons, some of which may be beyond our control. See Item 1A Risk Factors, “Strategic Risks— We may not realize the anticipated benefits of our Smart Industrial Operating Model and Leap Ambitions.”
Production & Precision Agriculture
We continue to invest in the development and production of advanced technology through integrated agricultural solutions and precision technologies across our portfolio of equipment. We believe our investments in precision technology will transform our farmers’ equipment into smarter, more efficient machines.
Aftermarket and Precision Upgrades
SAT is committed to meeting the needs of our customers through defining, developing, and delivering global equipment and technology solutions for dairy and livestock producers, high-value crop and small acre crop producers, and turf and utility customers. The segment works to provide product leadership while extending integrated agricultural solutions and precision technologies across its portfolio of equipment.
In the small agriculture market, we are developing autonomous solutions, connectivity capabilities, and a path to electrifying our future by delivering a portfolio that helps current customers meet sustainability goals while finding innovative ways to serve new customers and unlock new markets for mechanization at scale.
Aftermarket and Precision Updates
We believe innovations in machinery and technology may influence purchases of agricultural equipment, especially when the agricultural environment is challenging. For example, larger, more productive equipment is well accepted where farmers are striving for more efficiency in their operations to increase profits. Large, cost-efficient, highly mechanized agricultural operations account for an important share of worldwide farm output. These customers are increasingly adopting and integrating precision agricultural technologies like guidance, telematics, automation, and data-driven management in their operations. The large-size agricultural equipment used on such farms has been particularly important to us. A large proportion of the equipment operations’ total agricultural equipment sales in the U.S. and Canada, as well as in many countries outside the U.S. and Canada, are comprised of (1) tractors over 100 horsepower, (2) self-propelled combines, cotton pickers, forage harvesters, and sprayers, and (3) seeding equipment.
To address these challenges, we have delivered a portfolio of construction, roadbuilding, and forestry products with precision technology solutions. Our smart solutions such as SmartWeigh™, Smart Grade™, machine and system automation, and the John Deere Operations Center™, are designed to allow customers to complete more functions with fewer inputs, reduce rework and guesswork, and transform data into insights to allow for better decisions. Obstacle detection solutions such as SmartDetect™ supplement operator visibility on the jobsite through a combination of cameras, radar, and machine learning. Additionally, we plan to deliver hybrid-electric and battery electric equipment solutions to help customers reduce tailpipe emissions without sacrificing power and performance.
In forestry, our primary products include skidders, wheeled and tracked feller bunchers, forwarders, knuckleboom loaders, wheeled and tracked harvesters, swing machines, and precision forestry technology solutions such as Intelligent Boom Control, TimberMatic™ maps, and TimberManager™ —a web-based solution allowing customers to follow progress on the jobsite . These solutions allow customers to closely track jobsite progress and provide visibility into fleet location, utilization, performance, and maintenance information.
Our precision technology is integrated into our equipment as well as offered as aftermarket parts of retrofit solutions through our dealer network and owner support tools sold through our e-commerce John Deere Store. We support our connected machines, which integrate technology with our equipment through our John Deere Operations Center™ with service alerts, operator insights, and predictive repairs and maintenance.
Considerable effort is being dedicated to manufacturing cost optimization through improvements in process, optimization of factories, including product line relocation, product design, advanced manufacturing technology, and supply management and logistics, as well as compensation incentives related to productivity and organizational structure. We are also integrating emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence driven analytics and advanced robotics into our manufacturing processes where appropriate.
We offer our employees upskill training, career planning, and leadership development to better prepare our employees for future career opportunities at Deere. We have tools and solutions for continuous learning and career development, along with training programs that are tailored to different geographic regions and job functions. Examples of such training include technical operation of equipment, robotics, automation, equipment assembly, and interpersonal skills for establishing relationships with customers and dealers.

Decision question: Is Orrin a legally clean, properly capitalised Delaware parent that actually owns the fleet contracts and the IP, and what do the entities and cap table imply for a new lead investor?

A. Entity structure:
- Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. (Delaware, formed 2021-09-14), parent and Series A issuer; employs US staff; holds patent applications and Calder license. 100% owner of Fleet Services; 99% of Mexico; Fleet holds 1% of Mexico.
- Orrin Fleet Services LLC (California, 2023-11-02): owns robot fleet; signs grower contracts; borrower under Kestrel equipment facility. 100% subsidiary.
- Orrin Fieldworks Mexico S. de R.L. de C.V. (Jalisco, 2024-07-19): assembly; 7 staff; 99/1.

Asset/contract mismatch analysis: The fleet entity signs grower contracts and owns the fleet that generates RaaS revenue; the parent holds IP/license and is the issuer. The equipment lender (Kestrel) lends to Fleet Services, secured on the fleet. This is a standard asset-backed structure. But risks:
- The parent's Series A proceeds: investors put $18M into the parent. If the parent must fund Fleet's robot build, it needs intercompany arrangements. If Fleet is the borrower and the revenue counterparty, the parent's claim on Fleet cash flows is via equity, but a lender with a security interest in the fleet ranks ahead. If Fleet defaults, the parent's principal asset (fleet) can be seized; grower contracts may be assigned to lender as collateral (not disclosed). Deck doesn't disclose whether Kestrel has a first lien on grower receivables/contracts or a negative pledge; not disclosed.
- Series A investors buy parent preferred; their liquidation preference is at the parent. Value depends on parent's equity in Fleet after $2.5M facility. The parent has 100% equity, so okay, but the debt is structurally senior to the preferred at the operating subsidiary. Post-money $90M; $2.5M facility (=$1.6M drawn) small relative.
- The 1% Mexico stake held by Fleet Services creates a minority holder at the Mexican opco (the Fleet LLC itself), not an outside person. But under Mexican law, S. de R.L. de C.V. requires at least two partners; 99/1 split is common. Fine. However, the parent's indirect economic interest is 100% (100% of Fleet × 1% + 99%), so no leakage. Good.
- IP: held at parent, licensed from Calder. Patent applications are owned by parent. But the Calder license is "exclusive for agricultural harvesting" and includes two patent families from Castellano's university work. License becomes non-exclusive if <100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31. That's a key asset test: if Orrin fails to reach 100 commercial robots by end-2027, exclusivity is lost, which weakens IP moat and could allow competitors (including Tallis?) to license the same core perception tech. rows.weakens: Smaller rounds at lower valuations are normal at Series A; Advanced Farm's $25M Series B shows a strawberry-robot leader raising a similar amount, which makes Orrin's $18M round size unremarkable even if its price is not.
rows.implication: The comp set supports the round size but not the price; a lead should underwrite Orrin as the smallest, least-funded player in a category where the leader has 13x the capital.
rows.confidence: medium: round amounts are disclosed, valuations are not; Tortuga and Harvest CROO figures are aggregator data
rows.follow_up: What post-money valuations did Carbon's and Monarch's last rounds clear at, and what revenue multiples are secondary buyers quoting for ag-robotics positions in 2026?

rows.finding: The round dilutes existing holders by 30.8%: founders fall from 47.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7%, granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%, and the unallocated pool rises from 9.0% to 12.0%; the 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M-$39.3M (Series A $18M + A-1 $7.77M + Seed $11.0M, plus the $2.5M pre-seed SAFEs if they converted into the Seed preference), equal to 41-44% of the $90M post-money.
rows.mechanism: A 1x non-participating preference converts only when the exit value per share exceeds the preference; with a $36.8M-$39.3M stack, common receives nothing below that value and the Series A receives only its money back until the exit clears about $90M, where conversion value equals its $18M preference.
rows.benchmark: The preference stack is 41-44% of post-money, high for a Series A because three preferred classes stack at 1x; the Kestrel equipment facility ($1.6M drawn at 11.5%, secured on the fleet, $1.5M minimum cash covenant) ranks ahead of the preferred on the fleet assets.
rows.weakens: 1x non-participating is the most company-favourable preference and is common at Series A, so the stack protects the investor's downside better than a participating structure would; the real problem is the entry price, not the preference.
rows.implication: At a $40M exit the common is wiped out and Meridian recovers roughly $12.1M (about 1.01x) on its $12M; the preference does not rescue a 1x return if the price is wrong.
rows.confidence: high on the cap table; medium on the seed preference because the pre-seed SAFE conversion terms are not in the deck
rows.follow_up: Do the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs sit inside the $11.0M Series Seed preference, and is the preference senior to or pari passu with the Kestrel facility?

rows.finding: Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, 13.33% of the $90M post-money. At exit values of $150M, $250M, $300M and $500M in 2029-2031 it returns 1.67x, 2.78x, 3.33x and 5.56x with no further dilution, or 1.33x, 2.22x, 2.67x and 4.44x after a 20% Series B dilution.
rows.mechanism: Return depends on ownership at exit and exit equity value, both of which the entry price fixes: a 3x on $12M needs a $36M exit stake, which at 13.33% is a $270M company and at 10.67% (after 20% dilution) is $337.5M.
rows.benchmark: The plan's 2031 strawberry revenue ceiling is about $35.4M (15% of the company's $236M US strawberry robot market), so a $270M-$337.5M exit is 7.6x-9.5x that revenue, above CNH's 6.0x for Raven and far above the 2.7x listed median.
rows.weakens: A strategic buyer paying for the perception model, the Calder licence and the harvest dataset could pay $250M-$305M pre-scale, as Deere did for Blue River and Bear Flag; that is the one path that makes the current price work.
rows.implication: The round only earns a venture return through an OEM technology premium or revenue well beyond the 2031 plan; a 3x is not achievable on a 4x-sales exit of the planned business.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; low-medium on exit values, which are scenarios
rows.follow_up: What exit value does the company's own Series B model assume, and what ownership does it model for the Series A after the next round?

rows.finding: The terms are conventional on preference (1x non-participating, equal rank), anti-dilution (broad-based weighted average) and dividends (8% non-cumulative, if declared), but the board is 5 seats with only 1 independent, and the deck discloses no pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching, information rights or related-party approval protection for the lead.
rows.mechanism: Board control sits with the common and Seed bloc (2 common + 1 Seed + 1 independent agreed by both = 3 of 5 on most votes), so the Series A director cannot block budgets, debt, related-party contracts or a sale process without protective provisions; Tallis holds an observer seat while also being noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer, v4 contract manufacturer and $1.0M investor.
rows.benchmark: Tallis's five roles and Vashti Harvest Services' $310,000 of related-party payments are exactly the transactions a lead's protective provisions and independent-director approval should cover.
rows.weakens: The deck is a summary, not the definitive documents; pro-rata and protective provisions may exist in the term sheet even if not listed.
rows.implication: Meridian should require a second board seat or a listed-veto package, a related-party approval majority including the Series A director, pro-rata and pay-to-play, monthly KPI information rights, and tranching tied to the 2027 season milestones.
rows.confidence: medium: terms are as disclosed in a summary deck; definitive documents not reviewed
rows.follow_up: What do the definitive documents say on pro-rata, drag-along, protective provisions, related-party approval and the Tallis manufacturing agreement's IP and tooling ownership?

rows.finding: The $18M is sized to a $9.9M robot build (300 robots at $33,000 average unit cost) plus $4.5M R&D and $3.6M sales and field operations; at the $12M minimum close the robot budget alone consumes 83% of the round, and the company's $3.7M cash at $410,000 monthly net burn runs to about 2027-06.
rows.mechanism: The 2027 season starts in April 2027 and needs 360 robots in service; a $12M close funds the fleet but not the service organization or the R&D that the v4 cost target depends on, so the round size and the plan are coupled.
rows.benchmark: Cash runway of about 9 months from 2026-09-30 against a target close of 2026-12-15 leaves roughly six months of buffer before the 2027 season; a missed close forces a bridge or a down round.
rows.weakens: A lower close might be paired with a slower build (fewer than 300 robots), which could still hit a smaller revenue base; the deck does not model that case.
rows.implication: The lead should size its check to the plan it believes, not to the $18M headline; $12M at a $72M pre funds a plan that needs $18M, so either the price falls or the plan shrinks.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the unit-cost quote, which is a Tallis bill-of-materials quote from Aug 2026
rows.follow_up: What is the minimum robot count for the 2027 season that keeps the Calder 100-robot test and the $8M ARR milestone in reach?

rows.finding: The failure base rate is real: Abundant Robotics raised $12M, ran commercial apple trials under a RaaS model with a claimed $100M+ pipeline, and sold its IP and assets in liquidation on 2021-06-29 after failing to raise another round; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 and remains at seed stage.
rows.mechanism: Harvesting robotics fails on market traction and follow-on capital, not only on technology: field trials and a pipeline did not convert into a fundable revenue base before the cash ran out.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's $2.6M of 2026E revenue and $3.2M company ARR are ahead of Abundant's at shutdown, but its $18M round and $72M pre assume a funding market that Abundant never reached.
rows.weakens: Abundant's apple market and 2017-2021 capital environment differ from 2026; Carbon's $232M and Monarch's $220M+ show the category leaders can still raise, so capital is available for leaders, not for the field.
rows.implication: A lead should price the downside as a liquidation or a flat-round recapitalization, not as a protected 1x; the preference only helps if there is an exit above $36.8M-$39.3M.
rows.confidence: high on the facts; medium on their transferability to Orrin
rows.follow_up: What is Orrin's liquidation waterfall if the 2027 season fails and the fleet is sold to a grower or a competitor?

plan.decision_question: Is $72M pre-money defensible against comparable rounds and precedent transactions, and what must be true for a Series A investor to earn a venture return?
plan.thesis_sentence: At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x 2026E revenue and 101x its actual 2026 RaaS revenue, so the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M-$338M; the price asks the Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not yet shown.
plan.why_different: This section prices the round: what the investor pays, how the cap table and preference stack convert that price into ownership, and what exit value the price therefore requires. It does not re-argue the technology or the market.
plan.mechanism: Price paid sets ownership; ownership plus exit equity value sets the return. A 27.7x forward-revenue entry with a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack leaves a 13.33% Series A stake needing a $270M exit for 3x, which is 7.6x the plan's 2031 revenue.
plan.comparison_set: Private ag-robotics rounds (Carbon $232M raised, Monarch $220M+, Advanced Farm $25M Series B, Harvest CROO $10M, Abundant $12M then liquidation); listed ag equipment and precision ag (Deere 4.0x, Trimble 4.3x, AGCO 1.0x EV/Sales, median 2.7x); strategic M&A (Raven 6.0x sales, Blue River $305M, Bear Flag $250M).
plan.counter_evidence: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag before scale; if Orrin's 2027 milestones land, a $72M pre is 9x the $8M ARR target and an OEM could pay $250M+, making the price look cheap. The 2027 plan itself ($5.6M revenue, $8M ARR) would put the post-money at 16.1x forward revenue, inside the range of venture-priced hardware growth rounds.
plan.visual: Valuation methods table (method, inputs, value, source) plus a peer-multiples table and a return-sensitivity table at $150M-$500M exits with and without 20% Series B dilution.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong team; well positioned; clear business model; fierce competition; risks are manageable; about; many; recently; internal tool, record or bot names; review or request IDs

arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.4x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it actually billed in 2026, so the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M; the price asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not yet shown [S53].

The terms are clean but the headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which at the round price transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value before the new money arrives; strip both out and the operating business is being sold at roughly $64-66M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck, so the bridge's full cost cannot be checked.

Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus the $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and it enters the round with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, about nine months of runway from 2026-09-30. The comparable private set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation visibility it offers: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, including a $70M Series D in October 2024 and a further $20M Series D in October 2025; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US company to commercialize a robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S55, S119]. None of those rounds discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated directly against a peer's multiple; what the set does establish is that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital and that the category leader needed roughly 13 times Orrin's round to build a fleet in five countries.

On revenue the price is at the top of any observable range. The $72M pre is 27.7x 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 34.6x on the $90M post, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR and 101.4x the $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue (75 robot-seasons at $9,500); on the 2027 plan it falls to 12.9x pre and 16.1x post, and on 2028 to 5.5x and 6.8x. The $3.2M ARR is not recurring revenue: it adds $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of letters of intent. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA (Deere 4.0x sales, Trimble 4.3x, AGCO 1.0x), and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S8, S12, S14]. On a 4.0x exit multiple, the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M the company projects.

The cap table makes the downside starker than the price alone. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2% of the company: founders from 47.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7% and granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M), or $39.3M if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference, equal to 41-44% of the $90M post-money. Ahead of the preferred on the fleet sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt at 11.5% with a $1.5M minimum-cash covenant [S53]. At a $40M exit the common receives nothing and Meridian recovers roughly $12.1M, about 1.01x its $12M, which is the definition of a preference that protects the money but does not produce a venture return.

Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, or 13.33% of the $90M post-money. The terms are conventional where they are disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture, and the 8% dividend is cosmetic because it is payable only if declared. The board is not: five seats with two for common, one for Seed, one for Series A and one independent agreed by both, which leaves Meridian with one of five votes and no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package; Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor, and Vashti Harvest Services has received $310,000 of related-party payments. For a $12M lead check, the minimum package is a second board seat or a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilization, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost a robot-season, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true for the price to work is specific: the 2027 season must reach 360 robots and $8M of real ARR by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence must stay exclusive by clearing its 100-robot test on that date, unit cost must fall below $36,000, and an OEM or a revenue base of $67.5M-$84M at a 4x multiple must arrive by 2029-2031. The counter-evidence is that OEMs do pay strategic prices before scale — Deere paid $305M for Blue River in September 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in August 2021 — so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy; the failure case is equally documented, with Abundant Robotics raising $12M, running commercial apple trials under a RaaS model and selling its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 after failing to raise again [S53, S91]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on the 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment. At a $50M pre-money Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post-money, which returns 3.7x at a $250M exit and 2.9x at $200M.

Let me reason with horticulture: strawberries are non-climacteric; bruised tissue loses firmness and is highly susceptible to Botrytis (S110 genomic prediction of postharvest decay; S112 Botrytis). arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.4x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it actually billed in 2026, so the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M; the price asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not yet shown [S53].

The terms are clean but the headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which at the round price transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value before the new money arrives; strip both out and the operating business is being sold at roughly $64-66M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck, so the bridge's full cost cannot be checked.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2024-09 to 2026 | USDA SBIR Phase II grant | $0.65M | n/a | USDA | S53 |
| 2025-02-10 | Convertible notes | $7.0M ($7.77M with interest at conversion) | 80% of the Series A price, $3.7716 a share | Granary $3.5M; Tallis $2.5M; others $1.0M | S53 |
| 2025-06-16 | Equipment facility (debt) | $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 11.5% | n/a | Kestrel Equipment Finance | S53 |
| 2026-12-15 (target) | Series A | $18.0M | $72M pre / $90M post | Granary $3.0M; Tallis $1.0M; Meridian proposed $12.0M; $2.0M open | S53 |

Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus the $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and it enters the round with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, about nine months of runway from 2026-09-30. The comparable private set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation visibility it offers: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, including a $70M Series D in October 2024 and a further $20M Series D in October 2025; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US company to commercialize a robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S55, S119]. None of those rounds discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated directly against a peer's multiple; what the set does establish is that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital and that the category leader needed roughly 13 times Orrin's round to build a fleet in five countries.

On revenue the price is at the top of any observable range. The $72M pre is 27.7x 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 34.6x on the $90M post, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR and 101.4x the $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue (75 robot-seasons at $9,500); on the 2027 plan it falls to 12.9x pre and 16.1x post, and on 2028 to 5.5x and 6.8x. The $3.2M ARR is not recurring revenue: it adds $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of letters of intent. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA (Deere 4.0x sales, Trimble 4.3x, AGCO 1.0x), and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S8, S12, S14]. On a 4.0x exit multiple, the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M the company projects.

The cap table makes the downside starker than the price alone. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2% of the company: founders from 47.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7% and granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M), or $39.3M if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference, equal to 41-44% of the $90M post-money. Ahead of the preferred on the fleet sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt at 11.5% with a $1.5M minimum-cash covenant [S53]. At a $40M exit the common receives nothing and Meridian recovers roughly $12.1M, about 1.01x its $12M: a preference that protects the money but produces no venture return.

Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, or 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $270M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. Against the plan's 2031 strawberry revenue ceiling of about $35.4M (15% of the company's $236M US strawberry robot market), those exits are 7.6x-9.5x sales, above CNH's 6.0x for Raven and nearly three times the listed median. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years); at $300M it is 3.33x (27.2% a year); at $500M it is 5.56x (40.9% a year) [S53].

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture, and the dividend is cosmetic because it is payable only if declared. The board is not: five seats with two for common, one for Seed, one for Series A and one independent agreed by both, which leaves Meridian one of five votes and no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package; Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor, and Vashti Harvest Services has received $310,000 of related-party payments. For a $12M lead, the minimum package is a second board seat or a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilization, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost a robot-season, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true for the price to work is specific: the 2027 season must reach 360 robots and $8M of real ARR by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence must stay exclusive by clearing its 100-robot test on that date, unit cost must fall below $36,000, and an OEM or a revenue base of $67.5M-$84M at a 4x multiple must arrive by 2029-2031. The counter-evidence is that OEMs do pay strategic prices before scale — Deere paid $305M for Blue River in September 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in August 2021 — so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy; the failure case is equally documented, with Abundant Robotics raising $12M, running commercial apple trials under a RaaS model and selling its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 after failing to raise again [S53, S91]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on the 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment. At a $50M pre-money Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post-money, which returns 3.7x at a $250M exit and 2.9x at $200M.

arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.4x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it actually billed in 2026, so the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M; the price asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not yet shown [S53].

The terms are clean but the headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which at the round price transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value before the new money arrives; strip both out and the operating business is being sold at roughly $64-66M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck, so the bridge's full cost cannot be checked.

| Date | Round | Amount | Valuation | Investors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022-04 | Pre-seed SAFEs | $2.5M | not disclosed | Furrowline Angels (lead) | S53 |
| 2023-03-08 | Series Seed | $11.0M | not disclosed | Granary Ventures (lead); pre-seed SAFEs converted | S53 |
| 2024-09 to 2026 | USDA SBIR Phase II grant | $0.65M | n/a | USDA | S53 |
| 2025-02-10 | Convertible notes | $7.0M ($7.77M with interest at conversion) | 80% of the Series A price, $3.7716 a share | Granary $3.5M; Tallis $2.5M; others $1.0M | S53 |
| 2025-06-16 | Equipment facility (debt) | $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 11.5% | n/a | Kestrel Equipment Finance | S53 |
| 2026-12-15 (target) | Series A | $18.0M | $72M pre / $90M post | Granary $3.0M; Tallis $1.0M; Meridian proposed $12.0M; $2.0M open | S53 |

Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus the $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and it enters the round with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, about nine months of runway from 2026-09-30. The comparable private set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation visibility it offers: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, including a $70M Series D in October 2024 and a further $20M Series D in October 2025; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US company to commercialize a robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S55, S119]. None of those rounds discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated directly against a peer's multiple; what the set does establish is that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital and that the category leader needed roughly 13 times Orrin's round to build a fleet in five countries.

On revenue the price is at the top of any observable range. The $72M pre is 27.7x 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 34.6x on the $90M post, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR and 101.4x the $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue (75 robot-seasons at $9,500); on the 2027 plan it falls to 12.9x pre and 16.1x post, and on 2028 to 5.5x and 6.8x. The $3.2M ARR is not recurring revenue: it adds $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of letters of intent. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA (Deere 4.0x sales, Trimble 4.3x, AGCO 1.0x), and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S8, S12, S14]. On a 4.0x exit multiple, the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M the company projects.

The cap table makes the downside starker than the price alone. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2% of the company: founders from 47.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7% and granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M), or $39.3M if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference, equal to 41-44% of the $90M post-money. Ahead of the preferred on the fleet sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt at 11.5% with a $1.5M minimum-cash covenant [S53]. At a $40M exit the common receives nothing and Meridian recovers $12.1M, about 1.01x its $12M: a preference that protects the money but produces no venture return.

Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, or 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $270M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. Against the plan's 2031 strawberry revenue ceiling of about $35.4M (15% of the company's $236M US strawberry robot market), those exits are 7.6x-9.5x sales, above CNH's 6.0x for Raven and nearly three times the listed median. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years); at $300M it is 3.33x (27.2% a year); at $500M it is 5.56x (40.9% a year) [S53].

| Exit value, 2029-2031 | Meridian at 13.33%, no dilution | MOIC | Meridian at 10.67%, after 20% Series B dilution | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $150M | $20.0M | 1.67x | $16.0M | 1.33x | S53 |
| $250M | $33.3M | 2.78x | $26.7M | 2.22x | S53 |
| $300M | $40.0M | 3.33x | $32.0M | 2.67x | S53 |
| $500M | $66.7M | 5.56x | $53.3M | 4.44x | S53 |

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture, and the dividend is cosmetic because it is payable only if declared. The board is not: five seats with two for common, one for Seed, one for Series A and one independent agreed by both, which leaves Meridian one of five votes and no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package; Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor, and Vashti Harvest Services has received $310,000 of related-party payments. For a $12M lead, the minimum package is a second board seat or a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilization, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost a robot-season, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true for the price to work is specific: the 2027 season must reach 360 robots and $8M of real ARR by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence must stay exclusive by clearing its 100-robot test on that date, unit cost must fall below $36,000, and an OEM or a revenue base of $67.5M-$84M at a 4x multiple must arrive by 2029-2031. The counter-evidence is that OEMs do pay strategic prices before scale — Deere paid $305M for Blue River in September 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in August 2021 — so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy; the failure case is equally documented, with Abundant Robotics raising $12M, running commercial apple trials under a RaaS model and selling its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 after failing to raise again [S53, S91]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on the 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment. At a $50M pre-money Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post-money, which returns 3.7x at a $250M exit and 2.9x at $200M.

rows.implication: Price the round as a service business, not an IP monopoly; require a patent prosecution plan and a Calder licence amendment before close.
rows.confidence: medium-low — the deck discloses the rejection but USPTO records were not retrievable
rows.follow_up: Were the PCT national-phase fees paid by 2026-10-30, and can the Calder licence be made exclusive regardless of the 100-robot test?

rows.benchmark: Market lead terms usually give new money seniority or a stronger ratchet; broad-based weighted average anti-dilution is standard.

arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.4x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it actually billed in 2026, so the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M; the price asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not yet shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which at the round price transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value before the new money arrives; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters the round with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, 9.0 months of runway from 2026-09-30. The comparable set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation it discloses: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, including $70M in October 2024 and $20M in October 2025; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US company to commercialize a strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S53, S55, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple; the set does show that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital, and that the category leader needed 12.9 times Orrin's round. All cap-table, round and financial figures taken from the company's October 2026 deck are company-provided and unaudited (unverified), and the 2027-2028 figures are management projections.

On revenue the price is at the top of any observable range. The $72M pre is 27.7x 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 34.6x on the $90M post, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR and 101.4x the $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue (75 robot-seasons at $9,500); on the 2027 plan it falls to 12.9x pre and 16.1x post, and on 2028 to 5.5x and 6.8x. The $3.2M ARR is not recurring revenue: it adds $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of letters of intent. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA (Deere 4.0x sales, Trimble 4.3x, AGCO 1.0x), and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S53, S8, S12, S14]. On a 4.0x exit multiple, the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M the company projects.

The cap table makes the downside starker than the price alone. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2% of the company: founders from 47.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7% and granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M), or $39.3M if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference, equal to 41-44% of the $90M post-money. Ahead of the preferred on the fleet sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt at 11.5% with a $1.5M minimum-cash covenant [S53]. At a $40M exit the common receives nothing and Meridian recovers $12.1M, 1.01x its $12M: a preference that protects the money but not the return.

Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, or 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $270M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. Against the plan's 2031 strawberry revenue ceiling of $35.4M (15% of the company's $236M US strawberry robot market), those exits are 7.6x-9.5x sales, above CNH's 6.0x for Raven and nearly three times the listed median. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years); at $300M it is 3.33x (27.2% a year); at $500M it is 5.56x (40.9% a year) [S53].

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture. arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.4x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it actually billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. The price asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not yet shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, 9.0 months of runway. The comparable set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation it discloses: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S53, S55, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple; the set does show that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital, and that the category leader needed 12.9 times Orrin's round. All cap-table, round and financial figures taken from the company's October 2026 deck are company-provided and unaudited (unverified), and the 2027-2028 figures are management projections.

plan.decision_question: Does the per-robot-season RaaS contract earn a positive contribution after fleet depreciation at any price the market will pay, and can the model scale?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin's RaaS contract loses about $8,100 per robot-season at its 2026 price once the fleet is depreciated, is only marginally positive at the 2027 renewal price and $31,000 target cost, and becomes attractive only at the unproven $16,500 list price, so this is a capital-intensive fleet rental whose economics depend on a price increase the company has not yet sold.
plan.why_different: Section 6 is the only place that rebuilds the contract-level cash flow and prices the fleet asset itself; the market section sizes demand, the technology section tests field performance, and the financial section aggregates the P&L.
plan.mechanism: Depreciation is a real cost of a four-season asset; excluding it from gross margin turns a negative contribution into a 41% margin and hides a 12-season payback against a four-season life. Price, unit cost and service cost jointly decide whether a robot-season creates or destroys cash.
plan.comparison_set: Orrin's own 2026 actuals, 2027 renewal and list prices and $31,000 target cost; peer capital raised (Monarch >$220M, Carbon $157M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest CROO ~$10M) and Abundant Robotics' 2021 shutdown.

arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.4x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, 9.0 months of runway. The comparable set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation it discloses: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S53, S55, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple; the set does show that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital, and that the category leader needed 12.9 times Orrin's round. All cap-table, round and financial figures taken from the company's October 2026 deck are company-provided and unaudited (unverified), and the 2027-2028 figures are management projections.

| 2022-04 | Pre-seed SAFEs | $2.5M | not disclosed | Furrowline Angels (lead) | S53 unverified |
| 2023-03-08 | Series Seed | $11.0M | not disclosed | Granary Ventures (lead); pre-seed SAFEs converted | S53 unverified |
| 2024-09 to 2026 | USDA SBIR Phase II grant | $0.65M | n/a | USDA | S53 unverified |
| 2025-02-10 | Convertible notes | $7.0M ($7.77M with interest at conversion) | 80% of the Series A price, $3.7716 a share | Granary $3.5M; Tallis $2.5M; others $1.0M | S53 unverified |
| 2025-06-16 | Equipment facility (debt) | $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 11.5% | n/a | Kestrel Equipment Finance | S53 unverified |
| 2026-12-15 (target) | Series A | $18.0M | $72M pre / $90M post | Granary $3.0M; Tallis $1.0M; Meridian proposed $12.0M; $2.0M open | S53 unverified |

On revenue the price is at the top of any observable range. The $72M pre is 27.7x 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 34.6x on the $90M post, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR and 101.4x the $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue (75 robot-seasons at $9,500); on the 2027 plan it falls to 12.9x pre and 16.1x post, and on 2028 to 5.5x and 6.8x. The $3.2M ARR is not recurring revenue: it adds $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of letters of intent. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA (Deere 4.0x sales, Trimble 4.3x, AGCO 1.0x), and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S53, S8, S12, S14]. On a 4.0x exit multiple, the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M the company projects.

The cap table makes the downside starker than the price alone. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2% of the company: founders from 47.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7% and granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M), or $39.3M if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference, equal to 41-44% of the $90M post-money. Ahead of the preferred sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt at 11.5% with a $1.5M minimum-cash covenant [S53]. At a $40M exit the common receives nothing and Meridian recovers $12.1M, 1.01x its $12M: a preference that protects the money but not the return.

Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, or 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $270M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. Against the plan's 2031 strawberry revenue ceiling of $35.4M (15% of the company's $236M US strawberry robot market), those exits are 7.6x-9.5x sales, above CNH's 6.0x for Raven and nearly three times the listed median. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years); at $300M it is 3.33x (27.2% a year); at $500M it is 5.56x (40.9% a year) [S53].

| Exit value, 2029-2031 | Meridian at 13.33%, no dilution | MOIC | Meridian at 10.67%, after 20% Series B dilution | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $150M | $20.0M | 1.67x | $16.0M | 1.33x | S53 unverified |
| $250M | $33.3M | 2.78x | $26.7M | 2.22x | S53 unverified |
| $300M | $40.0M | 3.33x | $32.0M | 2.67x | S53 unverified |
| $500M | $66.7M | 5.56x | $53.3M | 4.44x | S53 unverified |

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture. The board is not: five seats with two for common, one for Seed, one for Series A and one independent agreed by both, leaving Meridian one of five votes and no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package; Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor, and Vashti Harvest Services has received $310,000 of related-party payments (company deck, S53; unverified). For a $12M lead the minimum package is a second board seat or a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilization, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost a robot-season, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true is specific: the 2027 season must reach 360 robots and $8M of real ARR by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence must stay exclusive by clearing its 100-robot test on that date, unit cost must fall below $36,000, and an OEM or a revenue base of $67.5M-$84M at a 4x multiple must arrive by 2029-2031. OEMs do pay strategic prices before scale — Deere paid $305M for Blue River in September 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in August 2021 — so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy; the failure case is equally documented, with Abundant Robotics raising $12M, running apple trials under a RaaS model and selling its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 after failing to raise again [S53, S91]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on the 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment. At a $50M pre-money Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post-money, which returns 3.7x at a $250M exit and 2.9x at $200M.

Let me write it.

plan.comparison_set: Capital and exit precedents: Advanced Farm raised $25M and closed in 2025; Tortuga raised $47.7M and sold its IP to Oishii in 2025; Harvest CROO raised about $10M over 14 rounds and is still private; Monarch raised $133M Series C and Carbon Robotics $70M Series D to scale hardware, so the capital bar for fleet scale is well above $18M. OEM exits: Deere-Bear Flag $250M (2021), Deere-Blue River $305M (2017), CNH-Raven $2.1B (2021).
plan.counter_evidence: The rental model removes grower capex, which is a real difference from the equipment-sale peers that failed; and 110 contracted robots plus 50 letters of intent show demand exists. But the largest revenue line is a related-party engineering contract that expires 2027-06-30, the round is $2M short of its own $18M target, and service labour at the claimed 1:8 supervision ratio exceeds the target service cost several times over.
plan.decision_question: Is the RaaS plus engineering-services plus grant revenue mix a coherent path to a Series B, and what must the 2027 plan deliver operationally for the next round to be financeable?
plan.mechanism: Engineering services and grants pay the bills while the robot fleet is sub-scale, but neither scales with robots; the Series A must convert a services business into a rental fleet within one season, and the fleet only earns its cost of capital at a price 74% above today's contract price with a unit cost 35% lower - three simultaneous step changes whose failure modes all land in the same four-month build window.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong pipeline', 'well positioned for growth', 'clear path to profitability', 'strategic partnerships' without scope and dates, no 'Series B is achievable' without the conditions, no unqualified ARR figure without its composition.
plan.thesis_sentence: The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business - engineering services and grants were two-thirds of FY2025 revenue and both end by mid-2027 - so the Series A is really a one-season bet that 360 robots can be built, serviced and repriced before the current cash runs out, and the capital, headcount and unit economics in the plan do not yet reconcile.
plan.visual: Milestone table with target dates and current status, plus the partner table showing that every counterparty with real leverage over the plan is also an investor, lender or related party.
plan.why_different: This section tests the plan against resources and time - what must happen, by when, with whose money and people - while section 3 tests the machine and section 6 tests the market. It is the only place the 2027 operating plan, the round arithmetic and the exit routes are put on one timeline.
