### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season (3.7-season payback). At $16,500 with current service cost the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 seasons at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback ($31,000 divided by $14,750) omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost [S53]. The 110 contracted 2027 renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book, not the strongest.

| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | S53 |

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The customer counts are partially verified: the deck's grower table sums to 75, matching the stated total. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 and has contracted 20 for 2027, and Grower E ended its Plant City pilot in June 2026 over fruit bruising, the one customer-side data point that contradicts the 3.8% bruising claim. For 2027 Orrin shows 110 contracted robots (Marisol 40, Pajaro 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20) and 50 LOI robots from eight other pilots: 160 of the 360 planned, or 44%, with 200 uncontracted. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Those ties are disclosed and not disqualifying, but they mean the 53% concentration and the cost of field service are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many robots were idle or deployed on unpaid pilots. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot could serve Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $19,000 at the 782 seasons implied by FY2028 revenue. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

Strawberry harvesting has absorbed well over $100M of venture capital without a scaled commercial winner: Monarch Tractor has raised more than $220M, Carbon Robotics $157M and Advanced Farm Technologies a $25M Series B, while Harvest CROO, the closest US strawberry peer, had raised $10M across 14 rounds and was still announcing commercial-viability demonstrations in April 2025; Abundant Robotics shut down its fruit-harvesting business in 2021 [S54, S55, S91, S93, S94]. Orrin's $18M is small against that record, and its own numbers say why: the 2026 contract destroys $8,100 a season, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The investor implication is to wait for 2027 field data, or to structure the $12M as tranches tied to at least 160 contracted robots at $16,500 or more and a v4 unit cost at or below $33,000; at current unit economics, more robots destroy more capital.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown that the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower and measured differently: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at about 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit; an earlier platform ranged from 50% to 97.1% with occlusion. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is about 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, roughly 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

:::

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking and the deck offers no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature now quantifies bruise area at pixel level with hyperspectral imaging and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate at all, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers matter because the winter season carries part of the 2027 plan. A 3.8% average that co-exists with a lost Florida customer is a distribution, not a specification, and the deck does not say how many farms sit above it.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Eighty-six per cent uptime across a 20-hour day is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot per day; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is about $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin on price, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. What would settle whether price can rise is the grower's hand-harvest cost per acre, which the deck does not disclose.

### The IP is one rejected application and two rented families

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and academic slip sensing has been dense since 2020, including force-and-slip sensing on compliant fingers in 2025. A first-action rejection is routine and not by itself fatal, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered. Harvest CROO, an operating competitor, holds 13 patents in strawberry harvesting.

### The moat is service, not science

A funded 50-person team with the published literature could match v3 picking performance in about 24 months — the perception stack is documented and the gripper art is crowded — but matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step at which the best-funded peer failed. arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at about 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit; an earlier platform ranged from 50% to 97.1% with occlusion. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is about 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, roughly 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

::: data
| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53, S56, S42, S57 |
| Detection | not disclosed | 80% average | S56 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | about 20 s per berry | S53, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53, S42, S56 |
| Uptime and cover | 86% of 20 h/day; 1.5 acres per 24 h | not reported | S53 |
:::

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking and the deck offers no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature now quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate at all, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers matter because the winter season carries part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Eighty-six per cent uptime over a 20-hour day is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is about $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. What would settle whether price can rise is the grower's hand-harvest cost per acre, which the deck does not disclose.

### The IP is one rejected application and two rented families

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and academic slip sensing has been dense since 2020, including force-and-slip sensing on compliant fingers in 2025. A first-action rejection is routine and not by itself fatal, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered.

| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 |

| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 fingers | 2026-07-08; unpublished | Cost-reduced design | S53 |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling | 2026-04-17; convert by 2027-04-17 | Service moat | S53 |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive under 100 robots at 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented | S53 |
:::

### The moat is service, not science

A funded 50-person team with the published literature could match v3 picking performance in about 24 months — the perception stack is documented and the gripper art is crowded — but matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step at which the best-funded peer failed. Advanced Farm, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH minority investment, then ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025, whose robots were rated for tunnels and tabletop beds rather than open fields. Orrin's durable assets are its field-service organisation, its grower relationships and its night-operation data, none of which appears in the patent table.

| **Composite** | **4/10** | Operations are the barrier, not patents | **24-30 months to a comparable machine** |
:::

| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-selected rows, not a field harvest rate, and it is the only performance number this round can be underwritten on.**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit and the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025), 83-87% on detected and pluckable fruit (*Journal of Field Robotics*, 2025) and 50-97.1% by occlusion (2019); adjusted for detection, Orrin's harvest recovery is about 75-80%, and its bruise rate has no published comparator while one paying grower has already left over bruising. [S57]
:::

### What the round should test before it closes

1. The vision system's detection rate on the same 212 rows, and the share of 2027 target acreage under tunnels or above 4% slope.
2. A 7-10 day cold-chain trial against a hand-picked control, with bruising scored at outturn.
3. The examiner's grounds for US 17/902,118 and whether the PCT national phase was entered by 2026-10-30.
4. A second, arm's-length contract-manufacturing quote for the v4 bill of materials.

At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, 9.0 months of runway. The comparable set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation it discloses: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S53, S55, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple; the set does show that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital, and that the category leader needed 12.9 times Orrin's round. All cap-table, round and financial figures taken from the company's October 2026 deck are company-provided and unaudited (unverified), and the 2027-2028 figures are management projections.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is secured to a lender and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE or offshore holdco and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: US staff, five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company with seven staff holds the Guadalajara operation. That is conventional, but the parent's value in a sale or default is its equity in Fleet after Kestrel is repaid. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts as well as robots, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility that is small in dollars but senior in priority [S53].

The IP estate is thinner than a deep-tech round normally carries. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is in-licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at a 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum, but exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised soft grippers (US20220134579A1, 2022) and slip-sensing grippers (US4605354A, 1986) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. The fully diluted count is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead would not rank ahead of $18.8M of seed and note money [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, while carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer through 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, which is vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility [S53].

Against the peer set, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch Tractor has raised a $133M Series C and more than $220M; Advanced Farm closed a $25M Series B in 2021-09; Harvest Croo had raised about $10M across 14 rounds by 2026-10; Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage ag-robotics companies, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at about 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is about 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, roughly 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

::: data
| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53, S56, S42, S57 |
| Detection | not disclosed | 80% average | S56 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | about 20 s per berry | S53, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53, S42, S56 |
| Uptime and cover | 86% of 20 h/day; 1.5 acres per 24 h | not reported | S53 |
:::

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature now quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers matter because the winter season carries part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Eighty-six per cent uptime over a 20-hour day is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is about $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. The deck discloses no hand-harvest cost per acre, which is what would settle whether the price can rise.

### The IP is one rejected application and two rented families

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and academic slip sensing has been dense since 2020, including force-and-slip sensing on compliant fingers in 2025. A first-action rejection is routine and not by itself fatal, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered.

### The moat is service, not science

A funded 50-person team with the published literature could match v3 picking performance in about 24 months — the perception stack is documented and the gripper art is crowded — but matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step at which the best-funded peer failed. Advanced Farm, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH minority investment, then ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. Orrin's durable assets are its field-service organisation, its grower relationships and its night-operation data, none of which appears in the patent table.

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The customer counts are partially verified: the deck's grower table sums to 75, matching the stated total, but the contracts themselves are unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 and has contracted 20 for 2027, and Grower E ended its Plant City pilot in June 2026 over fruit bruising, the one customer-side data point that contradicts the 3.8% bruising claim. For 2027 Orrin shows 110 contracted robots (Marisol 40, Pajaro 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20) and 50 LOI robots from eight other pilots: 160 of the 360 planned, or 44%, with 200 uncontracted. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Those ties are disclosed and not disqualifying, but they mean the 53% concentration and the cost of field service are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many robots were idle or deployed on unpaid pilots. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot could serve Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $19,000 at the 782 seasons implied by FY2028 revenue. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025 | S54 |
| Carbon Robotics | $70M Series D; $157M in total | Private, 2024 | S55 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Private, 2021 | S93 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; commercial-viability demonstration 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and one shutdown: strawberry harvesting has absorbed well over $100M of venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. Orrin's ask is small against that record, and its own numbers say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The investor implication is to wait for 2027 field data, or to structure the $12M as tranches tied to the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 unit cost at or below target; at current unit economics, more robots destroy more capital.

At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, 9.0 months of runway. The comparable set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation it discloses: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S53, S55, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple; the set does show that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital, and that the category leader needed 12.9 times Orrin's round. The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture. The board is not: five seats with two for common, one for Seed, one for Series A and one independent agreed by both, leaving Meridian one of five votes and no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package; Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor, and Vashti Harvest Services has received $310,000 of related-party payments (company deck, S53; unverified). What must be true is specific: the 2027 season must reach 360 robots and $8M of real ARR by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence must stay exclusive by clearing its 100-robot test on that date, unit cost must fall below $36,000, and an OEM or a revenue base of $67.5M-$84M at a 4x multiple must arrive by 2029-2031. At a $50M pre-money Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post-money, which returns 3.7x at a $250M exit and 2.9x at $200M.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is secured to a lender and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: US staff, five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company with seven staff runs Guadalajara. That is conventional, but the parent's value in a sale or default is its equity in Fleet after Kestrel is repaid. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts as well as robots, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility that is small in dollars but senior in priority [S53].

The IP estate is thinner than a deep-tech round normally carries. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at a 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum, but exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised soft grippers (US20220134579A1, 2022) and slip-sensing grippers (US4605354A, 1986) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead would not rank ahead of $18.8M of seed and note money [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer through 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility [S53].

Against the peer set, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch Tractor has raised a $133M Series C and more than $220M; Advanced Farm closed a $25M Series B in 2021-09; Harvest Croo had raised about $10M across 14 rounds by 2026-10; Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at about 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price it covers 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost, with a 24% cushion. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season (April-October) and a three-month Florida season (December-March), at $9,500 per robot per season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. The product is sold one season at a time; payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not publicly disclosed, which matters because a collection after the harvest would put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts in this paragraph are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. At a six-season life, depreciation would be $8,000 and contribution still -$4,100. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season (3.7-season payback). At $16,500 with current service cost the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 seasons at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback ($31,000 divided by $14,750) omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted 2027 renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book, not the strongest. Prices are company-reported and unverified; the recomputation is verified [S53].

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The customer counts are partially verified: the deck's grower table sums to 75, matching the stated total, but the contracts themselves are unverified. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many robots were idle or deployed on unpaid pilots. If each robot could serve Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $19,000 at the 782 seasons implied by FY2028 revenue. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |

| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025 | S54 |
| Carbon Robotics | $70M Series D; $157M in total | Private, 2024 | S55 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Private, 2021 | S93 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; commercial-viability demonstration 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and one shutdown: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. Orrin's ask is small against that record, and its own numbers say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The investor implication is to wait for 2027 field data, or to structure the $12M as tranches tied to the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 unit cost at or below target; at current unit economics, more robots destroy more capital.

At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck. The comparable set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation it discloses: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S53, S55, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple; the set does show that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital, and that the category leader needed 12.9 times Orrin's round. arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at about 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is about 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, roughly 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53, S56, S42, S57 |
| Detection | not disclosed | 80% average | S56 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | about 20 s per berry | S53, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53, S42, S56 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature now quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Eighty-six per cent uptime over a 20-hour day is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is about $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. The deck discloses no hand-harvest cost per acre, which is what would settle whether the price can rise.

### The IP is one rejected application and two rented families

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and academic slip sensing has been dense since 2020, including force-and-slip sensing on compliant fingers in 2025. A first-action rejection is routine and not by itself fatal, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered.

| Application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected in first action, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 |

### The moat is service, not science

A funded 50-person team with the published literature could match v3 picking performance in about 24 months — the perception stack is documented and the gripper art is crowded — but matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step at which the best-funded peer failed. Advanced Farm, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH minority investment, then ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. | Product | Stage and launch | 2026E revenue | Margin | Next milestone |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-selected rows, not a field harvest rate, and it is the only performance number this round can be underwritten on.**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit and the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected and pluckable fruit (JFR, 2025); adjusted for detection, harvest recovery is about 75-80%, and the bruise rate has no published comparator while one paying grower has left over bruising. Two questions would settle the gap between this technology and the round: the vision system's detection rate on the same 212 rows, and a cold-chain trial against a hand-picked control with bruising scored at outturn.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price it covers 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost, with a 24% cushion. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season (April-October) and a three-month Florida season (December-March), at $9,500 per robot per season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. The product is sold one season at a time; payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not publicly disclosed, which matters because a collection after the harvest would put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts in this paragraph are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. At a six-season life, depreciation would be $8,000 and contribution still -$4,100. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $9,500 | $31,000 (v4 target) | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$3,850 | 8.0 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 | +$4,500 | 2.5 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season (3.7-season payback). At $16,500 with current service cost the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 seasons at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback ($31,000 divided by $14,750) omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted 2027 renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book, not the strongest. Prices are company-reported and unverified; the recomputation is verified [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list, target service | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $12,000 | 138% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The customer counts are partially verified: the deck's grower table sums to 75, matching the stated total, but the contracts themselves are unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 and has contracted 20 for 2027, and Grower E ended its Plant City pilot in June 2026 over fruit bruising, the one customer-side data point that contradicts the 3.8% bruising claim. For 2027 Orrin shows 110 contracted robots (Marisol 40, Pajaro 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20) and 50 LOI robots from eight other pilots: 160 of the 360 planned, or 44%, with 200 uncontracted. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Those ties are disclosed and not disqualifying, but they mean the 53% concentration and the cost of field service are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many robots were idle or deployed on unpaid pilots. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot could serve Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $19,000 at the 782 seasons implied by FY2028 revenue. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025 | S54 |
| Carbon Robotics | $70M Series D; $157M in total | Private, 2024 | S55 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Private, 2021 | S93 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; commercial-viability demonstration 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and one shutdown: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. Orrin's ask is small against that record, and the economics above say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The investor implication is to wait for field data, or to structure the lead check as tranches tied to the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 unit cost at or below target; at current unit economics, more robots destroy more capital.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding. All company-specific facts below are unverified company material unless marked otherwise [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: US staff, five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts as well as robots, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at a 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum, but exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against the peer set, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm closed a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo had raised about $10M across 14 rounds, and Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding. All company-specific facts below are unverified company material unless marked otherwise [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against the peer set, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo about $10M, and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].
