arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Every performance figure below is company-reported and unverified: no independent trial of this machine exists in this review.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 company, S56, S42, S57 |
| Detection | not disclosed | 80% average | S56 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 company, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53 company, S42, S56 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Eighty-six per cent uptime over a 20-hour day is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. The deck discloses no hand-harvest cost per acre, which is what would settle whether the price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and the academic field has been crowded since 2020. A first-action rejection is routine, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking performance in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step where the best-funded peer failed. Advanced Farm, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH minority investment, then ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. At $72M pre-money the buyer is paying for that service organisation, so the price should rest on renewal evidence and service cost per robot-season, not on the patent table.

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected in first action, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 company, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation, unverified | S53 company |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | Platform copying, unverified | S53 company |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 fingers | 2026-07-08; unpublished | Cost-reduced design, unverified | S53 company |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling | 2026-04-17; convert by 2027-04-17 | Service moat, unverified | S53 company |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive under 100 robots at 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented; terms company-reported | S53 company |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perception and labelled data | 5 | 1.9M images, but core families are licensed and published | 2 years | S53, S56 |

| Dimension | Orrin Picker v3 | Harvest CROO | Advanced Farm / Tortuga | Academic open-field | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Performance | 94% of detected; 5.6 s/berry | "on par with human harvesting", no rate | not disclosed | 74% of ripe at 20 s/berry; 83-87% | S53, S1, S56, S42 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | not disclosed | not disclosed | not reported | S53 |
| Status 2026-10 | 64 robots, 5 growers | Operating, 13 patents | Ceased 2025; IP sold 2025 | Research | S53, S1, S114, S115 |

| Product | Stage and launch | 2026E revenue | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robots-as-a-Service | Commercial, 5 growers, 2025 season | $0.71M | 41% before fleet depreciation | 360 robots in 2027 | S53 |
| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-selected rows, not a field harvest rate, and it is the only performance number this round can be underwritten on.**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit and the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected and pluckable fruit (JFR, 2025); adjusted for detection, harvest recovery is 75-80%, and the bruise rate has no comparator while one paying grower has left over bruising. [S57]
:::

The two numbers that would settle the gap are the detection rate on the same 212 rows and a cold-chain bruise trial against a hand-picked control.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding. All company-specific facts below are unverified company material unless marked otherwise [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against the peer set, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo about $10M, and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Every performance figure below is company-reported and unverified: no independent trial of this machine exists in this review.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53 unverified, S42, S56 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not reported | S53 unverified |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (company measurement, unverified) over a 20-hour day, which is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. The deck discloses no hand-harvest cost per acre, which is what would settle whether the price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and the academic field has been crowded since 2020. A first-action rejection is routine, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking performance in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step where the best-funded peer failed. Advanced Farm, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH minority investment, then ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. For an investor that argues for conditioning the cheque on renewal evidence at $12,700 or more and a service cost below $2,500 a robot-season, rather than paying for the patent estate.

A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Every figure below is company-reported and unverified: no independent trial of this machine exists.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53 unverified, S42, S56 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not reported | S53 unverified |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (company measurement, unverified) over a 20-hour day, which is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. The deck discloses no hand-harvest cost per acre, which is what would settle whether the price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and the field has been crowded since 2020. A first-action rejection is routine, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking performance in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step where the best-funded peer failed. Advanced Farm, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH minority investment, then ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. For an investor that argues for conditioning the cheque on renewal evidence at $12,700 or more and a service cost below $2,500 a robot-season, rather than paying for the patent estate.

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected in first action, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 unverified, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation, unverified | S53 unverified |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | Platform copying, unverified | S53 unverified |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 fingers | 2026-07-08; unpublished | Cost-reduced design, unverified | S53 unverified |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling | 2026-04-17; convert by 2027-04-17 | Service moat, unverified | S53 unverified |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive under 100 robots at 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented, unverified | S53 unverified |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perception and labelled data | 5 | 1.9M images, but core families are licensed and published | 2 years | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Gripper and slip sensing | 3 | Crowded art back to 1986; no allowed claim | 1 year | S130 |
| Field service at 1:8 | 6 | Seasonal crews in two states, parts network | 3-4 years | S53 unverified |
| Unit cost $31,000-$33,000 | 6 | Volume, new design, no competitive bid | 2-3 years | S53 unverified |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | Operations are the barrier, not patents | **24-30 months to a comparable machine** | S53, S114 |

| Dimension | Orrin Picker v3 | Harvest CROO | Advanced Farm / Tortuga | Academic open-field | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Performance | 94% of detected; 5.6 s/berry | "on par with human harvesting", no rate | not disclosed | 74% of ripe at 20 s/berry; 83-87% | S53 unverified, S1, S56, S42 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | not disclosed | not disclosed | not reported | S53 unverified |
| Status 2026-10 | 64 robots, 5 growers | Operating, 13 patents | Ceased 2025; IP sold 2025 | Research | S53 unverified, S1, S114, S115 |

| Product | Stage and launch | 2026E revenue | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robots-as-a-Service | Commercial, 5 growers, 2025 season | $0.71M | 41% before fleet depreciation | 360 robots in 2027 | S53 unverified |
| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 unverified |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-selected rows, not a field harvest rate, and it is the only performance number this round can be underwritten on. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit and the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected and pluckable fruit (JFR, 2025); adjusted for detection, harvest recovery is 75-80%, and the bruise rate has no comparator while one paying grower has left over bruising. [S57]
:::

The two numbers that would settle the gap are the detection rate on the same 212 rows and a cold-chain bruise trial against a hand-picked control (S53, S56).

**Paragraph 1 — revenue mix and P&L reconstruction.**

"The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 the services line was 50% of $1.9M and grants 16%. RaaS revenue grew from $0.38M in FY2025 to $0.71M in FY2026E, which is 75 seasons at $9,500, and is the only line that scales with the fleet. The largest revenue line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026; both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS rather than on the services line. The reported history is unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so the FY2023-FY2026 figures should be treated as management accounts [S53]."

Table follows.

**Paragraph 2 — margin quality and opex.**

"Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but the composition flatters it. Stripping the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at about 51%; the RaaS line's own 41% is calculated before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the RaaS contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65× revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at the 360 robots planned for 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8× the $16,500 list price and 2.4× the $12,700 renewal. Even FY2028's $14.9M over the 782 seasons implied by $12.9M of RaaS is $19,000 per season, above the gross profit per season at either price. The plan never reaches operating leverage: every projected year loses money, and FY2028 still loses $6.9M [S53]."

**Paragraph 3 — ARR and projection consistency.**

"The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate that ends 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts, against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5× the headline ARR but 51× the contracted robot revenue. The projections also do not use the list price: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M divided by 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal and 23% below the $16,500 list, while a mix of 110 renewals at $12,700 and 250 new robots at $16,500 would produce $5.5M. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M requires 782 seasons at $16,500 or 1,016 at $12,700, which is 2.2-2.8× the 2027 fleet; the deck does not say whether that comes from ~$14M of unfunded robot capex or from an unstated two-season-per-robot assumption [S53]."

Check: 782/360 = 2.17; 1,016/360 = 2.82. Good. The ~$14M: 422 extra robots × $33,000 = $13.9M. Yes.

**Paragraph 4 — cash and financing.**

"The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 and $410k of monthly net burn give the advertised nine months, but the Kestrel facility requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, so usable cash is $2.2M, or 5.4 months to about 2027-03-15; the $1.6M drawn at 11.5% costs $184k a year and is secured on the fleet. The $18M round plus ~$2.5M of year-end cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is ~$7.1M after ~$0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes into working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027, of which $1.5M is the covenant. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The full round therefore buys one season and a Series B that must close in the first half of 2028, before the 2028 season proves anything. Burn multiple is ~7.0× in FY2026 ($4.9M burn ÷ $0.7M net new revenue) and ~5.9× in FY2027 (($7.9M loss + $9.9M capex) ÷ $3.0M net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E [S53]."

Note the 2025 notes: "$7.0M principal converts at $7.77M with interest into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716 (80% of the $4.7145 price), so the pre-money includes the note discount and the option-pool top-up to 12%; the effective price for existing holders is lower than the headline $72M." This is from the note N1. Include in paragraph 4 or a separate sentence. It adds ~250 chars. Important for financial section. Add: "The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M with interest into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 Series A price; the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the option pool's increase to 12% of post-money." Good. Source S53.

**Paragraph 5 — returns, working capital, accounting quality.** Table + prose.

"Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield, contribution after depreciation divided by robot cost, is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, all before the $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill, interest cover and net debt cannot be calculated: the only balance-sheet facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn on the facility, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital has to be estimated: 360 robot-seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M of season costs before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; the deck discloses none of the grower payment terms or the Tallis prepayment schedule. The $310,000 paid to the COO's Vashti Harvest Services in 2025-2026 is the only related-party cost disclosed. Warranty accrual, robot capitalization and revenue recognition across the season are not disclosed, and the head of finance is part-time [S53, S7]."

**Paragraph 6 — scenarios and the one variable.**

"Three cases bracket the 2027 outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots; with $7.9M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex, the covenant is breached by mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert at $12,700-16,500, producing ~$2.2M of RaaS and ~$3.2M of total revenue against a $5.6M plan; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots at the $16,500 list, the $31,000 cost and the $1,750 service target produce $5.9M of RaaS and $4.5M of contribution, but $10.8M of opex still leaves a ~$6.3M operating loss. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation, robot-seasons per robot per year, because it divides $10.8M of opex and $7,750 of depreciation: 360 seasons carry $30,000 of opex each, 720 carry $15,000 and 1,000 carry $10,800, while each $1,000 of price on 360 robots is only $0.36M. The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and evidence of Florida-to-California redeployment, not the number of robots built. Until then, the $18M funds a fleet whose unit economics are unproven, and the investor should price and stage accordingly [S53]."

Check upside: 360 × $16,500 = $5.94M; contribution per season at target service, $31k = $4,500 × 360 = $1.62M, not $4.5M! I made an error: $4,500 per season × 360 = $1.62M. Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at about 51%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over the 782 seasons implied by $12.9M of RaaS is $19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The reported figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. arguments.markdown:
The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university page, patent inventorship record, employer reference, licensing-board entry or corporate filing for any named individual could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential on the team: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year as a controls engineer at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist and lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab from 2016 to 2021. She is a named inventor on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university, of which Orrin licenses two families; the other nine are unlicensed. Her fit is the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: she has no disclosed operating role outside academia and a one-year machinery job, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners from 2006 to 2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms from 2014 to 2021 — 15 years running crews for large berry growers. The evidence that this converts is the customer list: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months and no search or interim appointment is described. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design across two countries. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor, and the company has not shown which one he is (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant hardware CV, but she has no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West) after a 2004 economics degree from Ridgemont State; she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, head of finance part-time since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — about $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, about 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context cuts both ways: Monarch has raised over $220M and Advanced Farm a $25M Series B; Harvest Croo raised about $10M and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, so under-capitalised harvest robotics fails; Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08, so a strategic exit exists for proven autonomy. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

::: evidence
**The founders have shipped a real product, but the bench behind them has never run a fleet at the scale the plan requires.** The deck shows 64 robots at 14 farms, 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and two pilot-to-paid conversions, built by 38 employees on about $20.5M raised [S53]. It also shows a CTO seat vacant since 2023-08-31, nine field-operations staff for a planned 5.6x fleet increase, a part-time finance head and no disclosed prior exit for any of the five leaders [S53].

arguments.markdown:
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services and grants supplied $1.25M of $1.9M of revenue, and both stop by mid-2027 [S53]. What the Series A must therefore prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers the capital, the headcount and the unit economics do not yet reconcile. The plan is not implausible — 110 robots are contracted for 2027 and 50 more are under letters of intent — but it asks for four step changes at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window.

### Services and grants pay the bills; neither survives 2027

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M comprised $0.95M of engineering services for Tallis, $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent [S53]. On the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is about $1.4M, which at a $72M pre-money is 51x rather than the 22x the headline figure implies. The services line was rational while the fleet was sub-scale; it becomes a valuation problem the moment the round is priced on recurring revenue.

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 [S53]. Against $3.7M of cash on 2026-09-30 and $410,000 of monthly net burn the company has nine months of runway before the round lands, while the Kestrel facility — $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5%, secured on the fleet — requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, a covenant that binds hardest during the build. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need about 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the entire fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage. Either supervision reaches roughly 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the projected 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer. The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. The governance picture compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but it means neither the revenue nor the cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition rather than an intention.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established pattern in this category is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries. Deere's 2025 annual report describes autonomy, machine learning and Solutions-as-a-Service as core to a small-agriculture strategy serving high-value and small-acreage crops, which is precisely where a berry picker would fit. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, which is exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. A standalone rental fleet at 360 robots has no precedent in this review: Harvest CROO has raised about $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, and Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B [S117, S8, S114, S115]. For Meridian the implication is structural — the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with the fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed, not a bet on a rental business reaching escape velocity alone.

Uptime above 92% and a technician ratio near 1:20 shown in telemetry rather than in a slide. An independent harvest-level trial above 85% on blocks the company did not choose. The Calder milestone of 100 robots on 2027-12-31 should be cleared by a wide margin under any credible plan, which makes it an early-warning indicator rather than a live risk: a company that cannot show 100 robots by then will have failed the demand test, the licence and the round together [S53]. Confidence in the arithmetic above is high, because every input is disclosed in the deck; confidence in the demand read-through is medium, because the 110 contracted robots sit with four growers, two of them related to the team, and the Florida season has already lost one customer.

arguments.markdown:
The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university page, patent inventorship record, employer reference or corporate filing for any named individual could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year as a controls engineer at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist and lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab from 2016 to 2021. She is a named inventor on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university, of which Orrin licenses two families; the other nine are unlicensed. Her fit is the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: she has no disclosed operating role outside academia and a one-year machinery job, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners from 2006 to 2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms from 2014 to 2021 — 15 years running crews for large berry growers. The evidence that this converts is the customer list: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months and no search or interim appointment is described. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design across two countries. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor, and the company has not said which (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but she has no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West) after a 2004 economics degree from Ridgemont State; she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, head of finance part-time since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — about $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, about 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context cuts both ways: Monarch has raised over $220M and Advanced Farm a $25M Series B; Harvest Croo raised about $10M and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, so under-capitalised harvest robotics fails; Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08, so a strategic exit exists. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

::: evidence
**The founders have shipped a real product, but the bench behind them has never run a fleet at the scale the plan requires.** The deck shows 64 robots at 14 farms, 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and two pilot-to-paid conversions, built by 38 employees on about $20.5M raised [S53]. It also shows a CTO seat vacant since 2023-08-31, nine field-operations staff for a planned 5.6x fleet increase, a part-time finance head and no disclosed prior exit for any of the five leaders [S53].
:::

arguments.markdown:
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services and grants supplied $1.25M of $1.9M of revenue, and both stop by mid-2027 [S53]. What the Series A must therefore prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all of them company-reported and unverified in this review — the capital, the headcount and the unit economics do not yet reconcile. The plan is not implausible: 110 robots are contracted for 2027 and 50 more are under letters of intent. It asks for four step changes at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window.

### Services and grants pay the bills; neither survives 2027

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M (company-reported, unverified) comprised $0.95M of engineering services for Tallis, $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent [S53]. On the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, which at a $72M pre-money is 51x rather than the 22x the headline figure implies. The services line was rational while the fleet was sub-scale; it becomes a valuation problem the moment the round is priced on recurring revenue.

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified) [S53]. Against $3.7M of cash on 2026-09-30 and $410,000 of monthly net burn the company has nine months of runway before the round lands, while the Kestrel facility — $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5%, secured on the fleet — requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, a covenant that binds hardest during the build. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the entire fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage. Either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the projected 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. The governance picture compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but it means neither the revenue nor the cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition rather than an intention.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established pattern in this category is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries. Deere's 2025 annual report describes autonomy, machine learning and Solutions-as-a-Service as core to a small-agriculture strategy serving high-value and small-acreage crops, which is precisely where a berry picker would fit. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, which is exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. A standalone rental fleet at 360 robots has no precedent in this review: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, and Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B [S117, S8, S114, S115]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed, not a bet on a rental business reaching escape velocity alone.

The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%). RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 should be read as management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over the 782 seasons implied by $12.9M of RaaS is $19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The reported figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate that ends 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The projections do not use the list price: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M divided by 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal and 23% below the $16,500 list. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M requires 782 seasons at $16,500 or 1,016 at $12,700, 2.2-2.8 times the 2027 fleet; the deck does not say whether that needs $13.9M of unfunded robot capex or an unstated two-season-per-robot assumption. The ARR composition is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months.** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M of year-end cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season and a Series B by mid-2028. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. These are company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield, contribution after depreciation divided by robot cost, is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the only balance-sheet facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital has to be estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. arguments.markdown:
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services and grants supplied $1.25M of $1.9M of revenue, and both stop by mid-2027 [S53]. What the Series A must therefore prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all of them company-reported and unverified in this review — the capital, the headcount and the unit economics do not yet reconcile. The plan is not implausible: 110 robots are contracted for 2027 and 50 more are under letters of intent. It asks for four step changes at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window.

### Services and grants pay the bills; neither survives 2027

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M (company-reported, unverified) comprised $0.95M of engineering services for Tallis, $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent [S53]. On the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, which at a $72M pre-money is 51x rather than the 22x the headline figure implies. The services line was rational while the fleet was sub-scale; it becomes a valuation problem the moment the round is priced on recurring revenue.

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified) [S53]. Against $3.7M of cash on 2026-09-30 and $410,000 of monthly net burn the company has nine months of runway before the round lands, while the Kestrel facility — $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5%, secured on the fleet — requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, a covenant that binds hardest during the build. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the entire fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage. Either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the projected 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. The governance picture compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but it means neither the revenue nor the cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition rather than an intention.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established pattern in this category is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries. Deere's 2025 annual report describes autonomy, machine learning and Solutions-as-a-Service as core to a small-agriculture strategy serving high-value and small-acreage crops, which is precisely where a berry picker would fit. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, which is exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. A standalone rental fleet at 360 robots has no precedent in this review: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, and Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B [S117, S8, S114, S115]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed, not a bet on a rental business reaching escape velocity alone.

### What must be true twelve months from closing

Five signposts, all company-reported and unverified until they appear in telemetry, decide whether a Series B is financeable. A 20-unit v4 pilot build before February 2027, with unit cost measured rather than quoted. At least 200 robots working by May 2027 rather than 360 announced. Renewals signed at $12,700 or more instead of the $9,500 of 2026. Uptime above 92% and a technician ratio near 1:20 shown in telemetry rather than in a slide. An independent harvest-level trial above 85% on blocks the company did not choose. The Calder milestone of 100 robots on 2027-12-31 should be cleared by a wide margin under any credible plan, which makes it an early-warning indicator rather than a live risk: a company that cannot show 100 robots by then will have failed the demand test, the licence and the round together [S53]. Confidence in the arithmetic above is high, because every input is disclosed in the deck; confidence in the demand read-through is medium, because the 110 contracted robots sit with four growers, two of them related to the team, and the Florida season has already lost one customer.

arguments.claims: Cal/OSHA Standards Board published an overview of safety standards and practices for autonomous agricultural machinery, mapping ISO 18497, an Australian code of practice and EU Regulation 2023/1230, indicating the regulator is studying a framework for autonomous field machinery rather than leaving it unaddressed.
arguments.claims_weakened: A presentation, not a rule; no California-specific mandatory standard for autonomous harvesters was identified, so the exposure is prospective and certification-based.
arguments.title: Cal/OSHA Standards Board — Overview of safety standards and practices for autonomous agricultural machinery

arguments.claims: The FDA Produce Safety Rule (21 CFR 112) sets science-based minimum standards for growing, harvesting, packing and holding produce, including requirements for equipment, tools, buildings and sanitation, and inspection of food-contact and non-food-contact surfaces of equipment.
arguments.claims_weakened: The rule binds the grower, not the equipment maker; Orrin's exposure is contractual and reputational through grower audits and sanitation instructions, not direct FDA registration.
arguments.title: FDA — FSMA Final Rule on Produce Safety (21 CFR Part 112)

arguments.claims_weakened: Advisory-firm summary rather than the Ley Federal del Trabajo text; the subsidiary's 7 staff make absolute cost small, but the obligations are mandatory and PTU is a profit-linked liability.

arguments.claims: USMCA rules of origin for machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally require regional value content of 60% under the transaction-value method or 50% under the net-cost method, with tariff-shift rules for some categories; origin must be documented to claim 0% duty.
arguments.claims_weakened: Consultancy summary; the product-specific rule for heading 8433 harvesting machinery was not read from the USMCA text, so Orrin's qualification for its robots is unverified.

arguments.markdown:
The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university, patent, employer or corporate record for any named individual could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist to lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab, 2016-2021. She is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university; Orrin licenses two families, the other nine are unlicensed. Her fit is the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: no disclosed operating role outside academia and a one-year machinery job, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014-2021 — 15 years running crews for large berry growers. The customer list shows the conversion: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months and no search or interim appointment is described. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor, and the company has not said which (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West) after a 2004 economics degree from Ridgemont State; she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, while Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

Meridian should make a CTO and full-time CFO search a closing condition and tranche part of the $12M against those hires.

::: evidence
**The founders have shipped a real product, but the bench behind them has never run a fleet at the scale the plan requires.** The deck shows 64 robots at 14 farms, 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and two pilot-to-paid conversions, built by 38 employees on $20.5M raised (company-provided, unverified). It also shows a CTO seat vacant since 2023-08-31, nine field-operations staff for a planned 5.6x fleet increase, a part-time finance head and no disclosed prior exit for any of the five leaders (company-provided, unverified).
:::

The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%). RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 should be read as management accounts [S53].
