Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over the 782 seasons implied by $12.9M of RaaS is $19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The reported figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate that ends 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The projections do not use the list price: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M divided by 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal and 23% below the $16,500 list. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M requires 782 seasons at $16,500 or 1,016 at $12,700, 2.2-2.8 times the 2027 fleet; the deck does not say whether that needs $13.9M of unfunded robot capex or an unstated two-season-per-robot assumption. The ARR composition is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months (company-reported, unverified).** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M of year-end cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season and a Series B by mid-2028. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. These are company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield, contribution after depreciation divided by robot cost, is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the only balance-sheet facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital has to be estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. The company figures are unverified; the yield and working-capital figures are derived estimates [S53, S7].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex exhaust the round and breach the covenant by mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation: $10.8M of opex divided by 360 seasons is $30,000 per season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet. Price matters less: $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and evidence of Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. These are analyst estimates, not company guidance, based on company-reported figures [S53].

The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university, patent, employer or corporate record could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist to lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab, 2016-2021. She is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university; Orrin licenses two families, the other nine are unlicensed. Her career fits the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: no disclosed operating role outside academia and a one-year machinery job, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014-2021 — 15 years running crews for large berry growers. The customer list shows the conversion: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months and no search or interim appointment is described. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West) after a 2004 economics degree from Ridgemont State; she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, while Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93]. We would not lead at $72M pre-money without those hires and a Kestrel estoppel (S53).

arguments.markdown:
The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university, patent, employer or corporate record could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist to lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab, 2016-2021. She is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university; Orrin licenses two families, the other nine are unlicensed. Her career fits the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: no disclosed operating role outside academia, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014-2021 — 15 years running crews for berry growers. The customer list shows the conversion: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West); she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, while Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

We would not lead at $72M pre-money without those hires and a Kestrel estoppel; a smaller check at a lower price, tranched against the 2027 fleet, is the investable structure (S53).

arguments.markdown:
The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 should be read as management accounts [S53].

| Grants | 0.07 | 0.08 | 0.30 | 0.35 | 0.0 | 0.0 | Unverified | S53 |
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | Unverified | S53 |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | Unverified | S53 |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | Unverified | S53 |
| Operating loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | Unverified | S53 |
| RaaS gross margin | n/a | n/a | 22% | 41% | 52% | 61% | Unverified | S53 |

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over the 782 seasons implied by $12.9M of RaaS is $19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The reported figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate that ends 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The projections do not use the list price: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M divided by 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal and 23% below the $16,500 list. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M requires 782 seasons at $16,500 or 1,016 at $12,700, 2.2-2.8 times the 2027 fleet; the deck does not say whether that needs $13.9M of unfunded robot capex or an unstated two-season-per-robot assumption. The ARR composition is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months (company-reported, unverified).** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M of year-end cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season and a Series B by mid-2028. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. These are company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield, contribution after depreciation divided by robot cost, is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the only balance-sheet facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital has to be estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. The company figures are unverified; the yield and working-capital figures are derived estimates [S53, S7].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex exhaust the round and breach the covenant by mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation: $10.8M of opex divided by 360 seasons is $30,000 per season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet. Price matters less: $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and evidence of Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. These are analyst estimates, not company guidance, based on company-reported figures [S53].

rows.finding: California's agricultural wage floor is $16.90/hour from 2026-01-01, with overtime at 1.5x after 8 hours/day and 40 hours/week since 2022 (26+ employees) or 2025 (25 or fewer) and double time after 12 hours; the 2026 California H-2A AEWR is reported at $19.97/hour and AB 2646 sets a $19.75/hour floor for non-resident agricultural employees.
rows.mechanism: Rising hourly floors and overtime make the hand crew more expensive per tray each season, widening the gap between hand-pick cost and Orrin's $9,500 robot-season price and pulling growers toward mechanisation.
rows.benchmark: 2026 general minimum $16.90 vs the $19.97 H-2A floor and $19.75 AB 2646 floor; 2027 minimum scheduled at $17.40.
rows.weakens: AEWR and AB 2646 figures come from secondary summaries, not the DOL table or chaptered bill; a freeze or cut in the AEWR would narrow the gap.
rows.implication: Demand tailwind is real and policy-driven; underwrite adoption as a function of the wage floor, not as a permanent moat.
rows.confidence: high on minimum and overtime (DIR), medium on AEWR and AB 2646 (secondary)
rows.follow_up: Obtain OFLC H-2A disclosure data and the 2026 AEWR table (request U9).

rows.finding: USMCA-qualifying Mexican goods enter the US at 0% duty, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content (transaction value) or 50% (net cost) and documented origin. Sources conflict on whether a 25% IEEPA surtax or a 10% Section 122 charge applies to non-qualifying goods.
rows.mechanism: If the Guadalajara-assembled robots or subassemblies fail origin, roughly 10% of the $33,000 v4 unit cost (about $3,300 a robot) lands on Orrin, against a 41% 2026 gross margin and a $9,500 selling price.
rows.benchmark: $33,000 average v4 unit cost in the deck's $9.9M robot budget; 10% duty equals about $3,300 per robot.
rows.weakens: Orrin may already qualify; a shift to US assembly removes the duty; the tariff stack itself is inconsistent across secondary sources and may change at the 2027 review.
rows.implication: Make a USMCA certification or CBP ruling a closing condition; do not underwrite Mexican assembly without it.
rows.confidence: low to medium: no primary customs notice could be opened in this run
rows.follow_up: Obtain Orrin's USMCA certification and the HTS 8433 product-specific rule (request U10).

rows.finding: No Orrin product-safety certification, recall or enforcement record is disclosed; the machine works at night around harvest crews, had 3.8% bruising and 2.1% mistaken unripe picks in 2025 pilots, and one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the design-safety standard for autonomous agricultural machinery and Cal/OSHA has published a framework review of such standards; the FDA Produce Safety Rule imposes equipment and food-contact-surface sanitation on the grower.
rows.mechanism: An injury or a pathogen event traced to machine contact would trigger strict product liability, grower indemnity claims and reputational damage, and could force design changes or certification before fleet scale; bruising also raises decay and rejection risk that growers price into renewal.
rows.benchmark: ISO 18497-1:2024 as the design benchmark; 3.8% bruising vs the deck's own ~5% acceptability threshold; the Grower E exit as a realised quality failure.
rows.weakens: No California rule specifically mandates ISO 18497; the standard is voluntary; FDA requirements fall on growers, not directly on Orrin, and no incident is public.
rows.implication: Price product-liability exposure and make insurance limits, exclusions and incident logs diligence conditions.
rows.confidence: medium to high on the standards, low on Orrin's compliance because it is undisclosed
rows.follow_up: Obtain insurance certificates, autonomous-machinery exclusions, OSHA 300 logs and incident reports (request U11, U12).

rows.finding: Orrin's Mexican subsidiary has 7 staff and must comply with IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing; dismissal without cause costs at least three months' salary plus seniority premium.
rows.mechanism: The absolute cost is small at 7 employees, but PTU is a profit-linked liability, IMSS/INFONAVIT add mandatory payroll cost, and a subsidiary with its own payroll and profit-sharing obligations needs separate governance and transfer-pricing discipline.
rows.benchmark: 7 of 38 employees in Mexico (18%); $650,000 SBIR and $1.9M FY2025 revenue set the scale against which any labour liability is immaterial.
rows.weakens: No evidence of non-compliance; the subsidiary is an assembly operation, not a maquila shelter, so exposure is routine rather than structural.
rows.implication: Not a valuation driver, but a governance and reporting item; require Mexican payroll and PTU compliance evidence.
rows.confidence: medium: advisory summaries, not the statute text
rows.follow_up: Confirm IMSS/INFONAVIT registration and PTU provision in the data room.

rows.finding: The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award (2024-2026) brings Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference for products embodying subject inventions under 35 U.S.C. 204, and audit exposure; a recent executive order pushes agencies toward taking title and requiring domestic manufacturing.
rows.mechanism: If any Orrin invention was made under the award and is assembled in Guadalajara, the US-manufacturing preference could require a waiver or reshoring, and an audit or title dispute would cloud the IP that the Calder licence and the patent portfolio depend on.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 6 by Valuation Analyst, 8,974 characters)
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 ($2.5M pre-seed, $11.0M seed, $7.0M notes, $18.0M Series A) plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash and a $410,000 monthly net burn, 9.0 months of runway. The comparable set shows how capital-hungry the category is and how little valuation it discloses: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds; Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C in 2025 and reports over $220M raised; Advanced Farm Technologies, the first US robotic strawberry harvester, raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor participating; Tortuga AgTech has raised a reported $47.7M; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 [S53, S55, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple; the set does show that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital, and that the category leader needed 12.9 times Orrin's round. The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture. The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university, patent, employer or corporate record could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist to lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab, 2016-2021. She is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university; Orrin licenses two families, the other nine are unlicensed. Her career fits the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: no disclosed operating role outside academia, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014-2021 — 15 years running crews for berry growers. The customer list shows the conversion: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West); she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, while Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,980 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Every figure below is company-reported and unverified: no independent trial of this machine exists.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53 unverified, S42, S56 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not reported | S53 unverified |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (company measurement, unverified) over a 20-hour day, which is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. The deck discloses no hand-harvest cost per acre, which is what would settle whether the price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and the field has been crowded since 2020. A first-action rejection is routine, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking performance in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step where the best-funded peer failed. Advanced Farm, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH minority investment, then ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. For an investor that argues for conditioning the cheque on renewal evidence at $12,700 or more and a service cost below $2,500 a robot-season, rather than paying for the patent estate.

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0%. The 2025 bridge was raised in February 2025 from Granary ($3.5M), Tallis Agricultural Machinery ($2.5M) and others ($1.0M); its caps and maturity are not in the deck. None discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple; the set does show that Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's lifetime capital, and that the category leader needed 12.9 times Orrin's round. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.

The $18M round plus $2.47M of year-end cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price it covers 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost, with a 24% cushion. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season (April-October) and a three-month Florida season (December-March), at $9,500 per robot per season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. The product is sold one season at a time; payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not publicly disclosed, which matters because a collection after the harvest would put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts in this paragraph are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. At a six-season life, depreciation would be $8,000 and contribution still -$4,100. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season (3.7-season payback). At $16,500 with current service cost the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 seasons at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback ($31,000 divided by $14,750) omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted 2027 renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book, not the strongest. Prices are company-reported and unverified; the recomputation is verified [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list, target service | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $12,000 | 138% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The customer counts are partially verified: the deck's grower table sums to 75, matching the stated total, but the contracts themselves are unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 and has contracted 20 for 2027, and Grower E ended its Plant City pilot in June 2026 over fruit bruising, the one customer-side data point that contradicts the 3.8% bruising claim. For 2027 Orrin shows 110 contracted robots (Marisol 40, Pajaro 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20) and 50 LOI robots from eight other pilots: 160 of the 360 planned, or 44%, with 200 uncontracted. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Those ties are disclosed and not disqualifying, but they mean the 53% concentration and the cost of field service are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many robots were idle or deployed on unpaid pilots. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot could serve Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $19,000 at the 782 seasons implied by FY2028 revenue. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025 | S54 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; commercial-viability demonstration 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. Orrin's ask is small against that record, and the economics above say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The investor implication is to wait for field data, or to structure the lead check as tranches tied to the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 unit cost at or below target; at current unit economics, more robots destroy more capital.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,980 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Every figure below is company-reported and unverified: no independent trial of this machine exists.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53 unverified, S42, S56 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not reported | S53 unverified |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (company measurement, unverified) over a 20-hour day, which is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. The deck discloses no hand-harvest cost per acre, which is what would settle whether the price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and the field has been crowded since 2020. A first-action rejection is routine, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. arguments.markdown:
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that is real yet reversible, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around night crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor with little control. At $1.9M of FY2025 revenue and $2.6M expected for FY2026, Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor of the crews it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly, and its own safety and related-party terms [S144].

### The labour-policy tailwind is real but reversible

California's minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 and is scheduled at $17.40 for 2027; agricultural overtime has applied at 1.5 times the regular rate after eight hours a day and 40 hours a week since 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and since 2025-01-01 for smaller ones, with double time after 12 hours [S141, S142, S143, S146, S157]. The H-2A floor is higher: the 2026 California adverse effect wage rate is reported at $19.97 an hour, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor for non-resident agricultural employees. A grower weighs Orrin's $9,500 robot-season on 2026 contracts, or $16,500 list and $12,700 average renewal for 2027, against a hand crew whose marginal hour gets more expensive every January. H-2A is the escape valve: expansion, an AEWR freeze or a methodology change would lower hand-pick cost and slow conversion. Florida is a second brake, because a three-to-four-month season buys less utilisation for the same price than California's seven months; one Plant City grower paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and another ended its pilot over bruising. Confidence is high on the wage rules and medium on the two $19-plus floors.

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's Jalisco subsidiary performs gripper and wiring-harness assembly with seven staff, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost, with documented origin [S148, S149, S152, S156]. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, about $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build and 10% of the $9.9M robot budget [S144]. The evidence is weaker than the policy: one tracker says a 25% IEEPA surtax still applies to non-qualifying Mexican goods, another reports the Supreme Court terminated it on 2026-02-20 and replaced it with a 10% Section 122 charge from 2026-02-24; both agree only that USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no published outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was found [S150]. The implication is a closing condition: Orrin's USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the Tallis v4 build, whose location the deck does not disclose.

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs about 20 hours a day, day and night, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8%, picked 2.1% unripe berries, ran at 86% uptime and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising [S151, S153, S154]. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires equipment and food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so a machine that cuts stems and carries clamshells adds a surface to the grower's sanitation audit. Safety is standards-led: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, and the Cal/OSHA Standards Board has reviewed ISO 18497, an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230, so a California framework is foreseeable even though no robot-specific rule was found. Liability is ordinary California strict product liability plus grower premises and indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, autonomous-operation exclusions, additional-insured cover and incident logs.

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The related-party record is more decision-relevant than any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor [S144]. Two of five board seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action with a response filed in 2026-05, and the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30, the day before this assessment, while the October 2026 deck still called it not yet decided. Whether those entries were filed is a data-room question. None of this is wrongdoing; it is reason to require an independent director, a related-party approval committee, monthly field and safety KPIs and a right to inspect incident and related-party ledgers.

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium [S155, S158, S159]. At seven people the absolute cost is immaterial against $1.9M of FY2025 revenue, but PTU is profit-linked and the subsidiary needs its own payroll and transfer-pricing discipline. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with a presidential executive order reported by counsel pushing agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver, so a Bayh-Dole opinion should precede closing. No mandatory climate or ESG reporting regime was identified that binds a private company of Orrin's size; institutional LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint on this round, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions.

### ESG issues that carry financial weight

| ESG issue | Why material | Evidence | Rating impact | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Governance and related parties | Insider cash flows; conflicts over the v4 build | $310,000 to the COO's company, 16% of FY2025 revenue; Tallis holds five roles | Negative; require an independent director | S144 |
| Product safety | An injury at night could exceed the balance sheet | 20-hour duty cycle; 3.8% bruising; one pilot exit; no certification disclosed | Negative; price insurance and certification | S144, S151, S154 |
| Food safety | Grower audits cover the machine's surfaces | FDA 21 CFR 112 equipment and food-contact standards | Neutral to negative; cleaning validation | S153 |
| Labour practices | Technicians and Mexican staff; displacement narrative | 38 staff, 7 in Mexico; related-party night-shift contractor | Neutral; confirm licensing and payroll | S144, S155 |
| Environment | Lithium fire and transport risk; soil compaction | Swappable packs, 20-hour duty cycle, no permit disclosed | Low; diligence item | S144 |
| ESG disclosure | Investor reporting burden | Private company, $1.9M FY2025 revenue | Not decision-changing | S144 |

### Regulatory record

| Regulator or registry | Record | Date | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DOL OFLC / FLAG | H-2A AEWR notice for non-range occupations (91 FR 48946); California rate reported at $19.97/hour | 2026-08-03 | In force; primary table not read | S145, S147, S143 |
| California DIR | Minimum wage $16.90; overtime after 8 hours/day and 40 hours/week; double time after 12 | 2026-01-01; overtime 2022/2025 | In force | S141, S142 |
| California Legislature | AB 2646, $19.75/hour floor for non-resident agricultural employees | 2026 | Enacted; operative date to confirm | S146 |
| USTR | Consultation for the 2027 USMCA review; comments due 2027-01-12 | 2026-10-02 | Open | S148, S150 |
| CBP / USTR tariff | 10% Section 301-type duty on non-USMCA Mexico-origin goods; qualifying goods 0% | 2026-07-24 | In force; rate stack contested in secondary sources | S152, S149 |
| Cal/OSHA Standards Board | Review of autonomous agricultural machinery standards, including ISO 18497 | Retrieved 2026-10-31 | Guidance only; no robot-specific rule found | S154 |
| FDA | Produce Safety Rule, 21 CFR 112, equipment and food-contact sanitation | In force | Binds growers, not Orrin directly | S153 |
| USDA SBIR | Phase II award $650,000, 2024-2026; Bayh-Dole terms | 2024-2026 | Active to award end; US-manufacturing preference | S144, S158 |

### Policy impact matrix

| Factor | Exposure | Probability | Impact on company | Mitigant | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California wage floor and overtime | California revenue; hand-pick cost | High, in force | Positive demand: $16.90 rising to $17.40 | 2027 list price $16,500 | S141, S142, S157 |
| H-2A AEWR and AB 2646 | California labour cost | High | Positive demand: $19.97 and $19.75 floors | Monitor only | S143, S146 |
| H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze | All US revenue | Low to medium | Negative: narrows the robot's saving | Multi-year contracts; 360 robots planned for 2027 | S147, S144 |
| USMCA origin failure | Guadalajara assembly | Low to medium | Negative: $3,300 per robot, about $0.99M on 300 robots | USMCA certification; US dual assembly | S152, S156, S144 |
| USMCA 2027 review | Mexican assembly and pricing | Medium | Uncertainty; rules could tighten | Diversify assembly; comment by 2027-01-12 | S148, S150 |
| Cal/OSHA and ISO 18497 | Product design and certification | Medium | Cost and delay; weaker liability defence if uncertified | Design to ISO 18497-1:2024 | S151, S154 |
| FDA produce-safety audits | California and Florida sales | High, baseline | Cleaning validation and audit cost | Cleanable design; sanitation procedure | S153 |
| Bayh-Dole US-manufacturing preference | IP and Mexican assembly | Low to medium | Waiver or reshoring requirement | Legal opinion; US assembly option | S158, S159 |

California's minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 and is scheduled at $17.40 for 2027; agricultural overtime has applied at 1.5 times the regular rate after eight hours a day and 40 hours a week since 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and since 2025-01-01 for smaller ones, with double time after 12 hours [S141, S142, S143, S146, S157]. Florida is a second brake: a three-to-four-month season buys less utilisation than California's seven months; one Plant City grower paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and another exited over bruising. arguments.markdown:
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that is real yet reversible, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. At $1.9M of FY2025 revenue (company-reported), Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms [S144].

### The labour-policy tailwind is real but reversible

California's minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 and is scheduled at $17.40 for 2027; agricultural overtime has applied at 1.5 times the regular rate after eight hours a day and 40 hours a week since 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees [S141, S142, S143, S146, S157]. The H-2A floor is higher: the 2026 California adverse effect wage rate is reported at $19.97 an hour, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor for non-resident agricultural employees. A grower weighs the $9,500 robot-season against a 2027 list of $16,500 and renewals at $12,700, and against a crew whose marginal hour rises every January. The economic effect is that each rise in the wage floor widens Orrin's advantage without changing its cost base. An H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze would lower hand-pick cost and slow conversion. Florida is a second brake: a three-to-four-month season buys less utilisation than California's seven months; one Plant City grower paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and another exited over bruising. Confidence is high on the wage rules, medium on the two $19-plus floors.

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and wiring harnesses with seven staff, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost [S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build, 10% of the $9.9M budget [S144]. Secondary trackers disagree on the surcharge: one holds a 25% IEEPA duty still applies, another that a 10% Section 122 charge replaced it on 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no published outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was found. Make USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the undisclosed Tallis v4 build a closing condition.

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising [S151, S153, S154]. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires equipment and food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's sanitation audit. Safety is standards-led: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed it alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions, additional-insured cover, incident logs.

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record is more decision-relevant than any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor [S144]. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05, and the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30, the day before this assessment, while the October 2026 deck called it not yet decided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights.

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium [S155, S158, S159]. PTU is profit-linked but immaterial at seven staff. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel reporting an executive order that pushes agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime was identified that binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions.

The strawberry harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics are attractive, but the market numbers in the deck do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's basis, every strawberry acre in the United States is worth $236M of robot revenue at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market requires more than 100% adoption of the entire US crop. [S53] The investment question is therefore not whether growers can afford the robot — they can — but whether Orrin can make a machine that holds up across enough acres to matter before the category's capital runs out.

### Two sizings, and only one of them is a revenue number

Table: market size layers.

Paragraph: The $42B global figure and the $3.1B serviceable figure are labour-spend numbers, not robot-revenue numbers... The bottom-up is the only revenue-sizing in the deck: 50,000 acres ÷ 3.5 acres per robot = 14,286 robots; × $16,500 = $235.7M at 100% penetration. The $310M exceeds this by 31%: it needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base. Management's own 15%-by-2031 adoption gives $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the $12,700 renewal price — 9-11% of the headline SOM. Even the $3.1B SAM is 13x the strawberry robot pool; it can only be a labour-spend figure for all soft fruit.

### The glide path is inconsistent with the financial plan

2% by 2028 = 1,000 acres = 286 robots = $4.7M at list. But FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 is 1,016 robots = 3,556 acres = 7.1% of the base, 3.6x the stated 2%. Either adoption is faster than stated or price is lower; the deck never reconciles them. [S53]

### Price is not the binding constraint; performance is

Per acre: $4,714 list, $3,629 renewal, $2,714 today. Deck productivity implies 14 picker-days per pass per robot (3.5 acres ÷ 0.25 acre/picker-day) and ~64 passes a season, i.e. ~896 picker-days of labour per robot-season replaced. At the list price the robot costs the equivalent of 18 picker-days at $900/day or 92 at $180/day. Willingness to pay is therefore not what caps adoption; a machine that picks bruise-free fruit at 1.5 acres a day would be cheap at $16,500. The evidence that it does not yet is the 74% price rise from $9,500 to $16,500 that has not been sold, the 41% gross margin that goes negative after depreciation [S53], and one Florida grower leaving over bruising.

Careful — 41% margin going negative after depreciation is the Fundamentals Analyst's analysis; I can reference it as "the reported 41% gross margin excludes the $12,000-a-season depreciation on a $48,000 robot" — that's deck arithmetic, fine.

### Geography: a long California season and a short Florida one

Table: regional.

Paragraph: California's seven-month season is what makes the 3.5-acres-per-robot density work: at 1.5 acres per 24 hours and 20 hours a day, a robot covers ~226 acre-passes a season at 86% uptime, about 64 passes over 3.5 acres — internally consistent with picking every three to four days. Florida's December-March window is roughly 120 days, so the same robot covers ~2.0-2.5 acres, not 3.5, and at the same price the per-acre cost rises to $6,600-$8,250. Florida is strategically valuable as counter-season capacity that could double seasons per robot and halve depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each — one paid season per robot — so the deck does not assume redeployment. Mexico is a cost base, not a revenue market: seven staff in Guadalajara assemble grippers and harnesses, and the low-wage logic that makes robots compelling in California makes them less compelling in Mexico. [S53]

### Why now: labour policy, not subsidy

Demand here is organic, not subsidy-created. The wage floor is reset annually by the H-2A adverse-effect wage rate (2026 rule published 2026-08-03) and California's agricultural overtime rules raise the cost of the long peak-season days [S145, S141]. Neither the number of H-2A positions nor the wage levels could be confirmed for this version: the specific series needed are the DOL OFLC disclosure files and the NASS Farm Labor Survey, requested below. That gap matters because if H-2A supply is elastic and wages flat, adoption slips a season or two; the deck's own Florida pilot exit shows adoption is already gated by quality rather than labour availability. [S53]

Hmm, "requested below" — fine if I file a request.

### The acreage base may be shrinking

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release puts total bearing acreage at 1.85M acres, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest crops by utilised production; the strawberry line itself was not retrievable [S160]. If strawberry acreage is flat-to-down, the $236M ceiling falls with it, and a 15% adoption target on a shrinking base is harder. ERS's 2026 outlook notes an early California harvest driven by a warm spring [S161] — season timing variability that affects robot scheduling but not the size of the prize.

### What would change the view

Three data points: the NASS strawberry acreage series by state (2019-2025), the California Strawberry Commission's grower and acreage data, and a third-party field trial with a hand-picked bruise control. If acreage is stable and a 95% pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the 2031 revenue line can be re-based to $35-50M and the market supports a services business; if acreage is falling and price realisation stays at $9,500, the SOM is a rounding error against the $72M pre-money. Confidence: high on the arithmetic, low on the acreage and labour inputs.
