arguments.markdown:
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that is real yet reversible, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### The labour-policy tailwind is real but reversible

California's minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 and is scheduled at $17.40 for 2027; agricultural overtime has applied at 1.5 times the regular rate after eight hours a day and 40 hours a week since 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees [S141, S142, S143, S146, S157]. The H-2A floor is higher: the 2026 California adverse effect wage rate is reported at $19.97 an hour, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor for non-resident agricultural employees. A grower weighs the $9,500 robot-season against a 2027 list of $16,500 and renewals at $12,700, and against a crew whose marginal hour rises every January. Each rise in the wage floor widens Orrin's advantage because its cost per robot-season is fixed. An H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze would lower hand-pick cost and slow conversion. Florida is a second brake: a three-to-four-month season buys less utilisation than California's seven months; one Plant City grower paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and another exited over bruising. Confidence is high on the wage rules, medium on the two $19-plus floors.

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and wiring harnesses with seven staff, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost [S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build, 10% of the $9.9M budget [S144]. Secondary trackers disagree on the surcharge: one holds a 25% IEEPA duty still applies, another that a 10% Section 122 charge replaced it on 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no published outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was found. The implication is a closing condition: USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the undisclosed Tallis v4 build.

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising [S151, S153, S154]. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires equipment and food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's sanitation audit. Safety is standards-led: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed it alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs.

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record is more decision-relevant than any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor [S144]. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05, and the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30, the day before this assessment, while the October 2026 deck called it not yet decided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights.

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium [S155, S158, S159]. PTU is profit-linked but immaterial at seven staff. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel reporting an executive order that pushes agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime was identified that binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions.

### ESG issues that carry financial weight

| Governance and related parties | Insider cash flows; conflicts over the v4 build | Company-reported $310,000 to the COO's company, 16% of FY2025 revenue; Tallis holds five roles | Negative; require an independent director | S144 |
| Product safety | An injury at night could exceed the balance sheet | 20-hour duty cycle; 3.8% bruising; one pilot exit; no certification disclosed | Negative; price insurance and certification | S144, S151, S154 |
| Food safety | Grower audits cover the machine's surfaces | FDA 21 CFR 112 equipment and food-contact standards | Neutral to negative; cleaning validation | S153 |
| Labour practices | Technicians and Mexican staff; displacement narrative | 38 staff, 7 in Mexico; related-party night-shift contractor | Neutral; confirm licensing and payroll | S144, S155 |

### Regulatory record

| Claimed obtainable market, 2031 | $310M | Needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base | Not reachable in strawberries | S53 |
| Obtainable market implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M at list; $27.2M at renewal | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 an acre | Derived | S53 |
| Robots-as-a-Service revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported | S53 |

# Decision Framework

Use this file before drafting the executive briefing, investment thesis, recommendation, scoring, or final decision. Do not force precision when evidence does not support it.

## Contents

- Consensus / Non-Consensus View
- Scenario Analysis
- Key Assumptions
- Historical Analogs
- Capital Efficiency
- Position Sizing / Deal Sizing
- The One Question
- Three Takeaways

## Consensus / Non-Consensus View

State what the market, comparable investors, or the company's own pitch appears to assume. Then state whether the report has a differentiated view.

If there is no non-consensus insight, say the thesis is consensus and explain what that means for return expectations, valuation discipline, or margin of safety. Do not invent a variant perception for appearance.

## Scenario Analysis

Use bull/base/bear cases with explicit drivers and approximate probabilities.

- For public equities and growth companies, scenarios may use revenue, margin, multiple, cash flow, valuation, catalyst timing, or downside drawdown.
- For early-stage, biotech, hard-tech, and data-poor cases, use milestone scenarios such as product-market fit, regulatory readout, manufacturing yield, customer conversion, financing survival, or exit path.

Each scenario should include:

- Specific driver or failure mode.
- Evidence that makes it plausible.
- Financial or milestone implication.
- Investor implication.

For public equities, build scenarios from explicit financial drivers where data allows: revenue growth, segment mix, gross/operating margin, tax, share count, capex, working capital, free cash flow, net cash/debt, and valuation multiple. Include current share price context before stating upside/downside.

## Key Assumptions

Rank the 3-5 assumptions that most affect the decision. For each, state:

- Confidence.
- What would disprove it.
- Impact if wrong.
- Early warning sign.

This is often more useful than adding more facts.

## Historical Analogs

Use historical analogs only when they are close enough to teach a decision rule. A good analog matches on business model, market structure, stage, regulation, customer behavior, or capital intensity.

If no close analog exists, say so.

## Capital Efficiency

Use a capital efficiency scorecard when the company has raised material capital and data exists. Useful metrics include burn multiple, revenue per dollar raised, runway, revenue per employee, capex to next milestone, and dilution efficiency.

If data is unavailable, state which missing data would be required.

For public equities, capital efficiency should use reported financials where available: ROIC, ROE, ROA, asset turnover, incremental margins, reinvestment rate, FCF conversion, dividend/buyback yield, dilution, and M&A returns. Tie these to management capital allocation quality.

## Position Sizing / Deal Sizing

Use position sizing for public equities, liquid secondaries, or explicit portfolio-allocation requests.

For public equities, position size must reflect valuation upside/downside, balance-sheet resilience, liquidity, accounting quality, catalyst timing, volatility, evidence confidence, and whether the downside is mark-to-market volatility or permanent capital impairment.

For primary-market deals, translate this into check size, valuation discipline, downside loss, reserve strategy, and conditions for follow-on investment.

## The One Question

Before finalizing, identify the single diligence question whose truthful answer would most change the investment decision. It must be specific, answerable in principle, and decision-changing.

## Three Takeaways

End with the three things the reader should remember. These should be decision statements, not generic summaries."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,980 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet with 75 paid robot-seasons proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Every figure below is company-reported and unverified: no independent trial of this machine exists.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, which removes every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. The independent band is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry; a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success on pluckable fruit. Multiply through and at 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team reaches about its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent benchmark | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of detected ripe fruit | 74% of ripe fruit (WSU 2025); 83% of pluckable (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported in the trials reviewed | S53 unverified, S42, S56 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not reported | S53 unverified |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so the number sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over the following 24-72 hours and is the entry point for grey mould; the literature quantifies bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver along the fresh-fruit chain, but none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate, because pick success and cycle time are what get published [S50]. The sharper counter-example is in the deck: Grower E in Plant City, one of the five growers paying in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and the Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (company measurement, unverified) over a 20-hour day, which is 2.8 hours of downtime per robot; at one technician per eight robots that is 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day against an 8-10 hour shift, so either much of the downtime is unattended — a $48,000 asset standing still — or the 1:8 ratio is a best case. Over four seasons depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, or 43% of the $3,900 contribution reported per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — a 27% true margin, not the 60% projected. The advertised 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons. The deck discloses no hand-harvest cost per acre, which is what would settle whether the price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a US patent from 1986 covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — and the field has been crowded since 2020. A first-action rejection is routine, but in crowded art it points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper that would show the examiner's grounds was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, that is a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and the deck does not say whether Europe, Mexico and Australia were entered [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking performance in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is the step where the best-funded peer failed. Advanced Farm, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH minority investment, then ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. For an investor that argues for conditioning the cheque on renewal evidence at $12,700 or more and a service cost below $2,500 a robot-season, rather than paying for the patent estate.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 3 by Valuation Analyst, 7,070 characters)
The realistic exit is a sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M, which at the $72M pre-money returns Meridian 1.7x-3.3x on unaudited company figures (unverified); the outcome depends on the 2027 Calder licence test and the first full commercial season, not on an IPO, and the entry price should be set with that range in view [S53, unverified].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | Deere & Company | Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021) and GUSS in its autonomy portfolio; lacks a specialty-crop harvesting robot and the labelled strawberry dataset | 2028-2031 | Medium | S96, S92, S8 |
| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven precision-ag platform gives it autonomy software; no strawberry picker; $2.1B paid for Raven shows willingness to buy capability | 2028-2031 | Medium-low | S95 |
| Trade sale | Kubota | Series A investor in Advanced Farm Technologies, the strawberry-harvesting competitor; wants specialty-crop automation | 2029-2031 | Low-medium | S93 |
| Trade sale | AGCO or Trimble | Precision-ag software and guidance; no harvesting hardware or grower fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S12, S14 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer and $1.0M investor; the natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling in a liquidation | 2027-2029 | Low as a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer | S53 unverified |
| Secondary sale | Later-stage agtech fund or family office | Buys Meridian's stake at a discount before a trade sale; provides partial liquidity | 2028-2029 | Medium for partial liquidity | S53 unverified |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low | S53, S31 |

Deere is the most plausible buyer because it has already paid for autonomy twice and its FY2025 10-K lists GUSS among its businesses, but none of the three precedents bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network [S96, S92]. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option. Kubota is the most natural specialty-crop buyer because it already backs Advanced Farm Technologies, which AgFunder described in 2021 as the first US company to commercialize a robotic strawberry harvester; buying Orrin would give Kubota a second horse in the same race, which is a reason to bid but also a reason to wait.

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River Technology | 2017 | $305M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S96 |
| Deere / Bear Flag Robotics | 2021 | $250M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S92 |
| CNH / Raven Industries | 2021 | $2.1B enterprise value | 6.0x EV/Sales ($348.4M sales) | S95 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | not disclosed (indoor harvesting) | S91 |
| Abundant Robotics asset sale | 2021 | IP and assets sold; $12M raised in total | n/a | S91 |

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the stereo ripeness model trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost [S53, unverified]. That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, which is the single date that determines whether a buyer is acquiring an exclusive technology or a commodity one. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of real ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031, a four-to-five-year hold from the Series A.

The structural tests are as important as the buyer list. The Calder licence's assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet and carries a $1.5M minimum-cash covenant, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the 2025 noteholders convert into Series A-1 and their consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, which means the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts [S53, unverified]. A foreign buyer such as Kubota would face the same licence-consent and national-security diligence as a US buyer; the deck does not disclose whether the Calder patents or the robotics technology carry export-control or foreign-assignment restrictions, and that is a diligence item that could remove the most logical strategic buyer.

| Entry pre-money | Meridian stake for $12M | $150M exit | $250M exit | $300M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $72M (current) | 13.33% | $20.0M / 1.67x | $33.3M / 2.78x | $40.0M / 3.33x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | 17.65% | $26.5M / 2.21x | $44.1M / 3.68x | $52.9M / 4.41x | S53 unverified |

The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x over four to five years, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale returns 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.41x and 2.21x (company deck, S53; unverified). Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative and payable only if declared, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake that sits behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. Meridian should negotiate a drag-along and tag-along that make a trade sale executable without a founder veto, a right to consent to any change to the Calder licence or the Tallis manufacturing agreement, and a requirement that Kestrel be repaid or consented at closing.

The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota all have in-house autonomy programmes and can build a strawberry picker rather than buy one; the most recent harvesting-robot exit, AppHarvest's $60M purchase of Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M because commercial trials did not become a fundable revenue base [S91]. Hardware exits trade below software, ag-equipment multiples are 1.0x-4.3x sales, and the industrial sector ETF is down 6.9% over three months, 8.1 points behind the S&P 500, so a 2029-2031 window is not assured. The exit thesis survives only if the 2027 licence test is cleared, the fleet works at 360 robots, and a buyer sees the strawberry dataset as the entry to other specialty crops; on the current price that is a 1.7x-3.3x outcome, which is why the round should be repriced or tranched rather than led at $72M."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 4 by Company Analyst, 8,975 characters)
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding. All company-specific facts below are unverified company material unless marked otherwise [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against the peer set, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo about $10M, and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,913 characters)
The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 should be read as management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over the 782 seasons implied by $12.9M of RaaS is $19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The reported figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate that ends 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The projections do not use the list price: FY2027 RaaS of $4.6M divided by 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal and 23% below the $16,500 list. FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M requires 782 seasons at $16,500 or 1,016 at $12,700, 2.2-2.8 times the 2027 fleet; the deck does not say whether that needs $13.9M of unfunded robot capex or an unstated two-season-per-robot assumption. The ARR composition is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months (company-reported, unverified).** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M of year-end cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season and a Series B by mid-2028. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. These are company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield, contribution after depreciation divided by robot cost, is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the only balance-sheet facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital has to be estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. The company figures are unverified; the yield and working-capital figures are derived estimates [S53, S7].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex exhaust the round and breach the covenant by mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation: $10.8M of opex divided by 360 seasons is $30,000 per season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet. Price matters less: $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and evidence of Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. These are analyst estimates, not company guidance, based on company-reported figures [S53].

2. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at
peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.
-  Strawberries are picked by hand every three to four days through a season of up to seven months; a picker covers roughly a quarter of an acre a
day (company estimate).
-  Growers tell us their crews are smaller and older each year, while wages and worker housing keep getting more expensive (grower interviews, 2025).
-  Fruit left unpicked rots on the plant and spreads mold to the next pass, so a short crew costs more than the berries it leaves behind.
-  Harvest aids such as carts and conveyors make pickers faster, but still need a full crew.
Orrin Fieldworks: Series A investor presentation CONFIDENTIAL Slide 2 of 15

--- p.3 ---
3. Our product: the Orrin Picker
-  An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and
picks them with a soft three-finger gripper.
-  Pick rate: 94% of ripe fruit on the rows tested in our 2025 pilots (company measurement; definition on slide 4).
-  Throughput: one robot covers roughly 1.5 acres per 24 hours.
-  Two picking arms place berries straight into the grower's retail clamshells on board, so fruit is handled once.
-  Runs about 20 hours a day on swappable battery packs; one field technician supervises up to 8 robots, on site or remotely.
-  Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.
-  Current model: Orrin Picker v3, released to the field in March 2026. The v4, designed for lower cost, is planned for the 2027 season.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding. All company facts below are unverified company material unless marked [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo about $10M, and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.title: eCFR 21 CFR 112.123 — General requirements for equipment and tools used during harvest, packing and holding (Produce Safety Rule)
arguments.claims: Equipment and tools that contact covered produce during harvesting must be maintained, cleaned and sanitised so as not to contaminate produce; the duty falls on the grower operating the equipment, not on the equipment's maker. Makes the robot's gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler food-contact surfaces the customer must clean.
arguments.claims_weakened: Weakens any reading that FDA approval or certification of the machine is what matters; FDA regulates the grower's practice, so the vendor's exposure is contractual and reputational rather than a pre-market clearance.

arguments.title: ANSI Webstore — ISO 18497-1:2024, Agricultural machinery and tractors: safety of partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous machinery, Part 1 machine design principles and vocabulary (17 pp.)
arguments.claims: Scope of ISO 18497-1:2024 is design principles and vocabulary for partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous agricultural machinery; verification methods and validation principles sit in a separate part, ISO 18497-4:2024. arguments.claims_weakened: Weakens a description of Part 1 as itself the verification standard; also confirms the framework is voluntary — it creates no US certification requirement on its own.

arguments.title: The Innovation Attorney — Agriculture robotics: regulatory gaps, tort liability and IP challenges in autonomous farm technology
arguments.claims: Ground-based agricultural robots face strict product-liability exposure for worker injuries and no federal safety standard supplies a regulatory benchmark; unmanned aerial rules and FIFRA applicator certification are the regulated analogues. arguments.claims_weakened: A law-firm commentary, not a court record: it describes exposure in principle and cites no verdict or claim against a harvesting-robot maker.

arguments.claims_weakened: Does not attribute any outbreak to harvesting equipment specifically, so it establishes the category risk, not a causal link to robots.

arguments.claims: Harvest tools, equipment and containers contact crops directly; best practice is routine cleaning and sanitation of food-contact surfaces and adjacent areas. A machine with many food-contact surfaces adds cleaning labour and audit points to the grower's harvest.

arguments.markdown:
The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 should be read as management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over the 782 seasons implied by $12.9M of RaaS is $19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The reported figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate that ends 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet and 5.5% of the 50,000 US strawberry acres at one robot per 3.5 acres — but on the renewal basis the same $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. The ARR composition is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months (company-reported, unverified).** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M of year-end cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season and a Series B by mid-2028. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. These are company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield, contribution after depreciation divided by robot cost, is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the only balance-sheet facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital has to be estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. The company figures are unverified; the yield and working-capital figures are derived estimates [S53, S7].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex exhaust the round and breach the covenant by mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation: $10.8M of opex divided by 360 seasons is $30,000 per season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet. Price matters less: $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and evidence of Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. These are analyst estimates, not company guidance, based on company-reported figures [S53].

arguments.markdown:
The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 are management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet and 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres at 3.5 acres a robot — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. The ARR split is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months (company-reported, unverified).** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season and a Series B by mid-2028. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. These are company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the disclosed facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital is estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures are unverified; yields and working capital are derived estimates [S53, S7].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex exhaust the round and breach the covenant by mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation: $10.8M of opex divided by 360 seasons is $30,000 per season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet. Price matters less: $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and evidence of Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. Analyst estimates on company-reported figures, not guidance [S53].

plan.decision_question: Has Orrin proved the picking technology under conditions that generalise to commercial fields, and is the patent estate plus the safety and sanitation file strong enough to defend a $72M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on rows it chose, with no independent trial, no conformity assessment and no allowed patent claim, so at $72M pre-money an investor is buying a service organisation and a compliance file that do not yet exist rather than a defensible picking technology.
plan.why_different: Section 3 judges whether the machine physically works and can be defended - performance net of exclusions, bruising against a hand-picked control, autonomous-machinery safety and food-contact sanitation, and patent enforceability. Section 4 sizes the market and section 5 judges competitors' commercial position, so this section compares peers only on measured performance and IP, not share.
plan.mechanism: A pick rate measured over detected fruit on vendor-chosen rows inflates harvest recovery; unmeasured bruising, an unbuilt ISO 18497 verification file and food-contact surfaces the grower must clean transfer loss and liability to the customer, which caps the price the RaaS model can charge and slows the fleet ramp its unit economics need.
plan.comparison_set: Independent strawberry-harvest trials (WSU 2025, Journal of Field Robotics 2025 and 2019), the commercial status of Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm and Tortuga, and ISO 18497-1/-4 with 21 CFR 112 as the compliance baseline every peer faces equally.
plan.counter_evidence: No peer publishes a bruise rate and Advanced Farm and Tortuga failed commercially before any certification requirement bound a buyer, so the compliance gap may be immaterial to the sale; a short ISO 18497-4 verification and a clean sanitation file would convert the gap into an advantage over crowdfunded rivals.
plan.visual: Standards-and-liability table (ISO 18497-1/-4, 21 CFR 112.123, Cal/OSHA review) plus the performance metrics table with its independent benchmark column.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, clear technology lead, best-in-class, well positioned, patent-protected, world-class gripper, about/many as counts, recently, cutting-edge

rows.finding: Orrin's 94% pick rate divides by berries the vision system classified as ripe, over 212 rows it selected at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%.
rows.mechanism: A denominator of detected fruit removes every missed berry, so the metric measures gripper accuracy given detection, not harvest recovery.
rows.benchmark: WSU 2025 picked 74% of ripe fruit at 20 s/berry with 80% detection; JFR 2025 harvested 87% of detected at 83% success; JFR 2019 spanned 50-97.1%.
rows.weakens: The exclusion list omits the tunnel and slope conditions that dominate California and Florida strawberry acreage, so the sample is not the commercial field.
rows.implication: Underwrite 75-80% harvest recovery and a supplement-to-crew role; do not price a labour-replacement multiple until detection rate is reported on the same rows.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the benchmark comparison because trial configurations differ.
rows.follow_up: What is the detection rate on the same 212 rows, and what share of the 2027 target acreage is in tunnels or on slopes above 4%?

rows.finding: Bruising is 3.8% at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, the independent trials reviewed report no bruise rate, and one paying grower in Plant City left its pilot citing fruit bruising.
rows.mechanism: Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould, so damage shows up as cull and shelf-life loss at the packer, where the grower bears the cost.
rows.benchmark: No published bruise rate exists for any strawberry harvesting robot; hand-picking is the implicit control and is not benchmarked in the deck.
rows.weakens: One grower exit is a single, small-volume observation and may reflect pack-out expectations that a robotic supplement cannot meet at any bruise level.
rows.implication: Make a cold-chain bruise trial against hand-picked fruit a condition before the Series B; the current 3.8% cannot be validated or priced.
rows.confidence: medium - the exit is company-disclosed and the literature is silent rather than contradictory.
rows.follow_up: What was Grower E's pack-out before and after the robot, and does Orrin hold bruise data at 72 hours?

rows.finding: The deck discloses no ISO 18497 conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms; ISO 18497-1:2024 gives design principles and vocabulary and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods.
rows.mechanism: The standards are voluntary and no US federal rule covers a ground-based harvest robot, so the machine's safety case is built only if a buyer, insurer or state regulator demands it.
rows.benchmark: Cal/OSHA has examined ISO 18497-type frameworks against an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230; EU sales would require CE marking under that regulation.
rows.weakens: No US peer holds a published conformity assessment either, so the gap does not yet lose Orrin a sale - but the first buyer that asks will have no answer.
rows.implication: Price the absence of a safety file as an unbudgeted cost and an unbounded liability rather than as neutral; condition the cheque on an incident log and insurance terms.
rows.confidence: high that nothing is disclosed; medium that no certification exists, because non-disclosure is not proof.
rows.follow_up: Has any pilot farm's insurer, retail buyer or Cal/OSHA inspector asked for a conformity or incident file, and what did Orrin supply?

rows.finding: The gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to maintain and clean harvest equipment on the grower, not on the machine's maker.
rows.mechanism: The compliance burden lands on the customer, so a machine that is hard to clean adds sanitation labour and audit risk to the grower's harvest and depresses adoption and price.
rows.benchmark: Best practice for produce harvesting equipment is routine cleaning and sanitation of food-contact surfaces and adjacent areas; no per-machine cleaning time is published for any picker.
rows.weakens: Growers already clean harvest bins, knives and clamshells, so a cleanable robot may add less marginal labour than the surface count suggests.
rows.implication: Treat tool-free tear-down and swab-clean surfaces as a product requirement, and read the v4 cost-down for the cleanability it trades away.
rows.confidence: high on the rule; low on the size of the added labour.
rows.follow_up: How many minutes per robot per shift does cleaning take, and have any of the five growers run an ATP swab or GAP audit on the machine?

rows.finding: 32 strawberry-related foodborne outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017, and strawberries are eaten raw.
rows.mechanism: A contamination event traced to harvest equipment reaches consumers directly, so the reputational and contractual consequence for a 64-robot vendor with five customers is disproportionate to the volume of fruit handled.
rows.benchmark: No outbreak has been attributed to a harvesting robot; the record establishes category risk, not a causal link.
rows.weakens: Hand crews and bins, not machines, dominate the historical record, so a robot may reduce contamination risk by removing hand contact.
rows.implication: Sanitation design is both an insurance cost and a sales asset with retail audits; ask for swab results before scaling to 360 robots.
rows.confidence: medium - the outbreak count is peer-reviewed, the link to robots is inferential.
rows.follow_up: Do retail buyers' GAP audits treat an autonomous picker as new food-contact equipment requiring a sanitation plan?

rows.finding: US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action with a May 2026 response, core perception is licensed from two university families, and exclusivity lapses on 2027-12-31 if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service.
rows.mechanism: A narrow or absent gripper claim plus licensed perception means a funded competitor can copy the machine's function while Orrin carries royalty, minimum and reversion risk on the part that is hardest to build.
rows.benchmark: Slip-sensitive gripper art dates to a 1986 US patent; the 100-robot test sits between 64 robots today and 360 planned for 2027.
rows.weakens: First-action rejections are routinely overcome, and trade secret plus field-service know-how can protect performance without a patent.
rows.implication: Do not pay a patent-defended multiple; condition on the office-action outcome, the PCT national-phase entry and renewal evidence on the licence.
rows.confidence: high on the rejection and the licence terms; medium on the prior-art breadth.
rows.follow_up: What did the May 2026 response amend, did the PCT enter Europe, Mexico and Australia by 2026-10-30, and what are the renewal and minimum-royalty terms?

rows.finding: The 2027 plan needs unit cost to fall from $48,000 to $31,000-$33,000 and service cost to $1,750 per robot-season while price rises 74% to $16,500.
rows.mechanism: At 1:8 technician coverage, 360 robots need roughly 45 technicians against 9 field staff today, so the cost plan depends on a service ratio and a design change that are both unproven.
rows.benchmark: No contract-manufacturing quote is in the deck; the peer set (Advanced Farm, Tortuga) did not reach 300-500 unit volumes before failing.
rows.weakens: A 300-500 unit order can genuinely cut a $48,000 BOM by a third, and v4 gripper tooling is aimed at exactly that.
rows.implication: Condition the round on a competitive contract-manufacturing bid and a named hire plan for field service, not on the modelled 60% margin.
rows.confidence: medium - the arithmetic follows from the disclosed figures, the quotes do not exist.
rows.follow_up: What quotes exist from contract manufacturers for 300-500 units, and what is the technician attrition assumption behind 1:8?

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet and 75 paid robot-seasons prove the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises, an auditable safety file and an enforceable estate are what justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Every figure below is company-reported.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, removing every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement, the conclusion the WSU team draws about its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Peers, 2026-10 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | Harvest CROO: "on par with human harvesting", no rate | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57, S1 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | not disclosed | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported | not disclosed | S53 unverified, S50 |
| Uptime | 86% of scheduled hours | not reported | not disclosed | S53 unverified |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature measures bruise area at pixel level and treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet none of the strawberry-robot field papers reviewed here reports a bruise rate (S50). Grower E in Plant City, one of the five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing fruit bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, an empty incident record and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury on a night shift would be argued as strict product liability with a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163], and 32 strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017 (S164). A machine that tears down without tools and swabs clean sells into retail audits; the 35% cost cut the 2027 plan needs, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where cleanability gets traded away. One contamination or injury event traced to a machine would be existential for a vendor with five customers.

| Standard or rule | What it demands | Who carries it | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| ISO 18497-1 and -4:2024 | Design principles and verification methods for autonomous farm machinery | Voluntary; manufacturer | S166, S151 |
| 21 CFR 112.123 (FSMA) | Harvest equipment and food-contact surfaces kept clean against contamination | The grower | S163, S153 |
| EU Regulation 2023/1230 and an Australian code | Frameworks Cal/OSHA examined alongside ISO 18497-style rules for autonomous machinery | Regulators; manufacturer for CE marking | S154 |

### Uptime, supervision and a price that does not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (company measurement, unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at one technician per eight robots against an 8-10 hour shift — so either much of the downtime is unattended, a $48,000 asset standing still, or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season over four seasons, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — 27%, not the 60% projected. The 2.1-season payback omits a $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; with it, 2.5 seasons. No hand-harvest cost per acre is disclosed, which is what would settle whether price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a 1986 US patent covers a slip-sensitive robot gripper — so a routine first-action rejection in crowded art points to a narrow allowance at best, and the file wrapper was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is not disclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation is a four-to-six-year problem, and it is where the best-funded peer failed — Advanced Farm raised $25M, took a CNH investment and ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii in March 2025. Condition the cheque on licence renewal at $12,700 or more, a service cost below $2,500 and an office action that leaves a claim standing.

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 unverified, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 unverified |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry undisclosed | Platform copying | S53 unverified |
| US 19/204,876 | Gripper v4 fingers | 2026-07-08; unpublished | Cost-reduced design | S53 unverified |
| US 63/811,204 | Fleet scheduling | 2026-04-17; convert by 2027-04-17 | Service moat | S53 unverified |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented | S53 unverified |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perception and labelled data | 5 | 1.9M images, but core families are licensed and published | 2 years | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Gripper and slip sensing | 3 | Crowded art back to 1986; no allowed claim | 1 year | S130 |
| Field service at 1:8 | 6 | Seasonal crews in two states, parts network | 3-4 years | S53 unverified |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | Operations are the barrier, not patents | **24-30 months to a comparable machine** | S53, S114 |

| Product | Stage and launch | 2026E revenue | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robots-as-a-Service | Commercial, 5 growers, 2025 season | $0.71M | 41% before fleet depreciation | 360 robots in 2027 | S53 unverified |
| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 unverified |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit and the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected and pluckable fruit (JFR, 2025); harvest recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, one paying grower has left over bruising, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. [S57]
:::

The measurements that would settle this are the detection rate on the same 212 rows and a cold-chain bruise trial against a hand-picked control (S53, S56); the documents would be an ISO 18497-4 verification report and an ATP swab record from a commercial pack line (S163, S166).

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises, an auditable safety file and an enforceable estate are what justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Every figure below is company-reported.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, removing every berry the cameras never saw from the denominator. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and the rows chosen by its own field team [S56, S42]. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement, as the WSU team concludes of its own machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Peers, 2026-10 | Source |

| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | Harvest CROO: "on par with human harvesting", no rate | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57, S1 |
