{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 6 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,775 characters)
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price it covers 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost, with a 24% cushion. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season (April-October) and a three-month Florida season (December-March), at $9,500 per robot per season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. The product is sold one season at a time; payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not publicly disclosed, which matters because a collection after the harvest would put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts in this paragraph are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. At a six-season life, depreciation would be $8,000 and contribution still -$4,100. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $9,500 | $31,000 (v4 target) | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$3,850 | 8.0 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season (3.7-season payback). At $16,500 with current service cost the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 seasons at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback ($31,000 divided by $14,750) omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted 2027 renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book, not the strongest. Prices are company-reported and unverified; the recomputation is verified [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list, target service | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $12,000 | 138% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The customer counts are partially verified: the deck's grower table sums to 75, matching the stated total, but the contracts themselves are unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 and has contracted 20 for 2027, and Grower E ended its Plant City pilot in June 2026 over fruit bruising, the one customer-side data point that contradicts the 3.8% bruising claim. For 2027 Orrin shows 110 contracted robots (Marisol 40, Pajaro 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20) and 50 LOI robots from eight other pilots: 160 of the 360 planned, or 44%, with 200 uncontracted. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Those ties are disclosed and not disqualifying, but they mean the 53% concentration and the cost of field service are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many robots were idle or deployed on unpaid pilots. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot could serve Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $19,000 at the 782 seasons implied by FY2028 revenue. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025 | S54 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; commercial-viability demonstration 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. Orrin's ask is small against that record, and the economics above say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The investor implication is to wait for field data, or to structure the lead check as tranches tied to the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 unit cost at or below target; at current unit economics, more robots destroy more capital."}],"isError":false}

RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 are management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet and 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres at 3.5 acres a robot — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. The ARR split is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months (company-reported, unverified).** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the disclosed facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital is estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures are unverified; yields and working capital are derived estimates [S53, S7].

At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash, $1.5M of which the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant makes unusable: $2.2M and 5.4 months of runway at $410,000 a month, with the covenant reached around 2027-03-14. The category discloses few valuations: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C in 2025, and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014; Advanced Farm Technologies raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech, which raised a reported $47.7M, sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119]. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 4 by Valuation Analyst, 8,149 characters)
The realistic exit is a sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M, which at the $72M pre-money returns Meridian 1.7x-3.3x on unaudited company figures (unverified); the outcome depends on the 2027 Calder licence test and the first full commercial season, not on an IPO, and the category's own record — a shutdown and an asset sale among the named US strawberry-harvesting peers in 2025 — argues for setting the entry price to that range [S53, S114, S115].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | Deere & Company | Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021) and GUSS in its autonomy portfolio; lacks a specialty-crop harvesting robot and the labelled strawberry dataset | 2028-2031 | Medium | S96, S92, S8 |
| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven precision-ag platform gives it autonomy software; its 2022 stake in Advanced Farm Technologies ended with that company's 2025 closure, leaving no harvesting asset | 2028-2031 | Medium-low | S95, S117, S114 |
| Trade sale | Kubota | Backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in 2021 and saw it cease operations in July 2025; needs a specialty-crop harvesting asset | 2029-2031 | Low-medium | S93, S114 |
| Strategic | Yamaha Motor | Co-investor in Advanced Farm's 2021 Series B; outdoor-power equipment and robotics, no US harvesting platform | 2029-2031 | Low | S93 |
| Trade sale | AGCO or Trimble | Precision-ag software and guidance; no harvesting hardware or grower fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S12, S14 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling in a liquidation | 2027-2029 | Low as a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer | S53 unverified |
| Secondary sale | Later-stage agtech fund or family office | Buys Meridian's stake at a discount before a trade sale | 2028-2029 | Medium for partial liquidity | S53 unverified |
| Private equity | Paine Schwartz Partners ($5.7B AUM, $1.7B Fund VI) or similar | Needs positive EBITDA and fleet-level cash flow; the FY2028 plan still loses $6.9M | 2030-2032 | Low | S167, S53 |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low | S53, S31 |

Deere is the most plausible buyer because it has already paid for autonomy twice and its FY2025 10-K lists GUSS among its businesses, but none of the three precedents bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network [S96, S92]. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option [S95]. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which put money into Advanced Farm Technologies' $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it cease operations in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company is both a reason to buy the next asset and a reason to demand proof, and it removes the easy assumption that an OEM will pay a strategic price for a pre-scale robot company.

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River Technology | 2017 | $305M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S96 |
| Deere / Bear Flag Robotics | 2021 | $250M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S92 |
| CNH / Raven Industries | 2021 | $2.1B enterprise value | 6.0x EV/Sales ($348.4M sales) | S95 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | not disclosed (indoor harvesting) | S91 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025 | IP, assets and engineering team; value not disclosed | n/a | S115 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | 2025 | ceased operations; no sale | n/a | S114 |
| Abundant Robotics | 2021 | IP and assets sold; $12M raised in total | n/a | S91 |

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the stereo ripeness model trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost [S53, unverified]. That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, which is the single date that determines whether a buyer is acquiring an exclusive technology or a commodity one. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031, a four-to-five-year hold from the Series A; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

The structural tests are as important as the buyer list. The Calder licence's assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the 2025 noteholders convert into Series A-1 and their consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, so the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts [S53, unverified]. A foreign buyer such as Kubota would face the same licence-consent and national-security diligence as a US buyer; the deck does not disclose whether the Calder patents or the robotics technology carry export-control or foreign-assignment restrictions, and that is a diligence item that could remove the most logical strategic buyer.

| Entry pre-money | Meridian stake for $12M | $150M exit | $250M exit | $300M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $72M (current) | 13.33% | $20.0M / 1.67x | $33.3M / 2.78x | $40.0M / 3.33x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | 17.65% | $26.5M / 2.21x | $44.1M / 3.68x | $52.9M / 4.41x | S53 unverified |

The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x over four to five years, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale returns 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.41x and 2.21x (company deck, S53; unverified). Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative and payable only if declared, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake that sits behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. Meridian should negotiate a drag-along and tag-along that make a trade sale executable without a founder veto, a right to consent to any change to the Calder licence or the Tallis manufacturing agreement, and a requirement that Kestrel be repaid or consented at closing.

The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota all have in-house autonomy programmes and can build a strawberry picker rather than buy one; the US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit — Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025, Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M — while the most recent harvesting-robot purchase, AppHarvest's $60M for Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices [S115, S114, S91]. Hardware exits trade below software, ag-equipment multiples are 1.0x-4.3x sales, and the industrial sector ETF is down 6.9% over three months, 8.1 points behind the S&P 500, so a 2029-2031 window is not assured [S31]. The exit thesis survives only if the 2027 licence test is cleared, the fleet works at 360 robots, and a buyer sees the strawberry dataset as the entry to other specialty crops; on the current price that is a 1.7x-3.3x outcome, which is why the round should be repriced or tranched rather than led at $72M."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 3 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,930 characters)
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that is real yet reversible, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### The labour-policy tailwind is real but reversible

California's minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 and is scheduled at $17.40 for 2027; agricultural overtime has applied at 1.5 times the regular rate after eight hours a day and 40 hours a week since 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees [S141, S142, S143, S146, S157]. The H-2A floor is higher: the 2026 California adverse effect wage rate is reported at $19.97 an hour, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor for non-resident agricultural employees. A grower weighs the $9,500 robot-season against a 2027 list of $16,500 and renewals at $12,700, and against a crew whose marginal hour rises every January. Each rise in the wage floor widens Orrin's advantage because its cost per robot-season is fixed. An H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze would lower hand-pick cost and slow conversion. Florida is a second brake: a three-to-four-month season buys less utilisation than California's seven months; one Plant City grower paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and another exited over bruising. Confidence is high on the wage rules, medium on the two $19-plus floors.

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and wiring harnesses with seven staff, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost [S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build, 10% of the $9.9M budget [S144]. Secondary trackers disagree on the surcharge: one holds a 25% IEEPA duty still applies, another that a 10% Section 122 charge replaced it on 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no published outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was found. The implication is a closing condition: USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the undisclosed Tallis v4 build.

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising [S151, S153, S154]. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires equipment and food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's sanitation audit. Safety is standards-led: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed it alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs.

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record is more decision-relevant than any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor [S144]. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05, and the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30, the day before this assessment, while the October 2026 deck called it not yet decided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights.

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium [S155, S158, S159]. PTU is profit-linked but immaterial at seven staff. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel reporting an executive order that pushes agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime was identified that binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions.

### ESG issues that carry financial weight

| ESG issue | Why material | Evidence | Rating impact | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Governance and related parties | Insider cash flows; conflicts over the v4 build | Company-reported $310,000 to the COO's company, 16% of FY2025 revenue; Tallis holds five roles | Negative; require an independent director | S144 |
| Product safety | An injury at night could exceed the balance sheet | 20-hour duty cycle; 3.8% bruising; one pilot exit; no certification disclosed | Negative; price insurance and certification | S144, S151, S154 |
| Food safety | Grower audits cover the machine's surfaces | FDA 21 CFR 112 equipment and food-contact standards | Neutral to negative; cleaning validation | S153 |
| Labour practices | Technicians and Mexican staff; displacement narrative | 38 staff, 7 in Mexico; related-party night-shift contractor | Neutral; confirm licensing and payroll | S144, S155 |

### Regulatory record

| California DIR | Minimum wage $16.90; overtime after 8 hours/day and 40 hours/week; double time after 12 | 2026-01-01; overtime 2022/2025 | In force | S141, S142 |
| California Legislature | AB 2646, $19.75/hour floor for non-resident agricultural employees | 2026 | Enacted; operative date to confirm | S146 |
| USTR | Consultation for the 2027 USMCA review; comments due 2027-01-12 | 2026-10-02 | Open | S148, S150 |
| CBP / USTR tariff | 10% Section 301-type duty on non-USMCA Mexico-origin goods; qualifying goods 0% | 2026-07-24 | In force; rate stack contested | S152, S149 |
| Cal/OSHA Standards Board | Review of autonomous agricultural machinery standards, including ISO 18497 | Retrieved 2026-10-31 | Guidance only; no robot-specific rule found | S154 |

Now the scenario analysis. Include analogs, capital_efficiency, position_sizing optional modules.

Bear 35%, Base 45%, Bull 20%.

Outcomes:
- Bull: 360 robots deployed on time at list; $8M+ ARR exiting 2027, licence cleared, OEM partnership 2029, sale at $300-400M in 2030-31 → Meridian $40-53M, 3.3-4.4x.
- Base: ~180-250 robots at renewal; Series B at flat/down or bridge; trade sale 2029-31 at $150-250M → $20-33M, 1.7-2.8x (or 1.3-2.2x after dilution).
- Bear: build slips, covenant breach mid-2027, Kestrel secured, licence non-exclusive, asset sale → $0-12M, 0-1.0x.

Key assumptions ranked with impact.

Consensus: the pitch assumes "only autonomous open-field picker above 90%", $310M obtainable market, 41% gross margin, $3.2M ARR, $72M comparable. Our view: conditional rate, market 8.7x smaller at 100% adoption ($235.7M vs $310M — actually 1.31x smaller), negative unit economics, ARR 56% non-recurring. So the thesis is non-consensus on valuation: invest only at $48-55M or tranched.

Evidence for the difference: sections 3,4,6,7,8.

Proof event: the 2027 season's contracted hectares at list/renewal pricing plus an independent harvest-level trial.

One question: "What is the harvest-level recovery rate — marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant — and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, on blocks Orrin did not select?" Why: it decides whether the machine supplements or replaces crews, which sets the price ceiling, the service model and the exit.

Analogs: Advanced Farm ($25M Series B, CNH/Kubota, ceased 2025) cautionary; Abundant Robotics (RaaS apple, liquidated 2021) cautionary; Tortuga (sold to Oishii 2025) cautionary; Deere/Bear Flag (2021, $250M) best — small team, pre-scale autonomy sold to OEM; Blue River 2017 $305M best.

Capital efficiency: $38.5M raised including notes; $2.6M FY2026E revenue; $0.24 revenue per equity dollar; burn multiple 7.0x; fleet replacement cost $3.07M.

Position sizing: private → check size, valuation discipline, downside loss, follow-on reserve. Recommend $6M now at $48-55M pre with $6M tranche on 2027 milestones, reserve $6M follow-on; max loss $12M.

Let's write it.

assumptions.assumption: The v4 robot can be built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units (35% below the $48,000 v3 cost) by Tallis in Guadalajara
assumptions.disproof: A contract-manufacturing quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build costing more than $40,000
assumptions.early_warning: v4 design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes the BOM; gripper cost-down abandoned
assumptions.impact: -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even

assumptions.impact: -30% value; the base case becomes a bridge round at a flat or down price

assumptions.assumption: Harvest-level recovery reaches 85% or more with bruising at or below a hand-picked control
assumptions.disproof: An independent trial below 80% of fruit on the plant, or a second paying grower leaving over fruit quality
assumptions.early_warning: Further pilot exits after Grower E in Plant City; retail or grower quality audits on machine-picked fruit
assumptions.impact: -40% value; the product becomes a harvest aid, not a replacement, and the price ceiling falls

arguments.analogs: Advanced Farm Technologies (California, 2021-2025): raised a $25M Series B with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and a CNH investment, ran commercial strawberry and apple deployments with Driscoll's and California Giant, and ceased operations in July 2025 (S93, S114, S116, S117). Lesson: commercial deployments and OEM capital are not proof of a viable unit economic model in this crop. Abundant Robotics (2015-2021): raised about $12M, ran apple-harvesting trials under RaaS, and sold its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 (S91). Lesson: RaaS in fruit harvesting has a 12-month cash cycle and no margin for a missed season. Tortuga AgTech (2016-2025): raised a reported $47.7M in tabletop and greenhouse harvesting and sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii on 2025-03-24 (S115, S118). Lesson: the best available outcome for a sub-scale harvesting-robot company is an asset sale to a strategic. Deere/Bear Flag Robotics (2021, $250M) and Deere/Blue River (2017, $305M): pre-scale autonomy businesses bought by an OEM with a dealer network (S96, S92). Lesson: a $150M-$300M OEM exit for a proven autonomy stack is plausible, and it is the ceiling this case should underwrite. AppHarvest/Root AI (2021, $60M) sets the harvesting-specific clearing price far below the autonomy comparables (S91, S93).
arguments.capital_efficiency: $38.5M of equity, notes and grants raised since 2022 for $2.6M of FY2026E revenue and $0.71M of RaaS revenue: $0.24 of cumulative revenue per equity dollar, falling to $0.15 on FY2027E (S53, derived). Burn multiple of 7.0x in FY2026 ($4.9M of burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9x in FY2027, against a 3x benchmark. Fleet replacement cost of $3.07M (64 robots at $48,000) against a $90M post-money. The $18M buys one 2027 season: $9.9M of robots, $7.1M of cash operating loss and $1-2M of working capital leave $1.5-3.5M at end-2027; at the $12M minimum close there is a $1.6M shortfall before working capital. Capital efficiency is the weakest dimension: the model needs price up 74%, unit cost down 35% and service cost down 44% at the same time, while 360 robots require ~45 technicians against nine field staff (S53).

consensus.consensus: The company's pitch, and the way an ag-robotics Series A is usually framed, assumes: the only autonomous open-field strawberry picker above 90% pick accuracy; a $310M obtainable market off a $3.1B serviceable one; a 41% gross margin and a 2.1-season payback; $3.2M of ARR; and a $72M pre-money in line with what Monarch ($220M+ raised) and Carbon Robotics ($232M) have attracted.
consensus.evidence: Section 3: the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 company-chosen rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent trials report 74-87% and harvest-level recovery is ~75-80% [S53, S56, S42, S57]. Section 4: 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 caps the whole US strawberry robot-revenue pool at $235.7M, so $310M is 132% of the base [S53]. Section 6: after $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit is -$8,100 a season at the 2026 price and -$650 at the renewal price with the target cost [S53]. Section 7: 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding; 46% of FY2026E revenue is one related-party services contract that ends 2027-06-30 [S53]. Section 8: $72M pre is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted robot revenue [S53].
consensus.our_view: The labour problem is real and the machine works, but the price is not supported: the market is 8.7x smaller than the headline, the unit economics are negative at the price actually sold, and the technology moat is a conditional licence with a 2027 cliff. The thesis is non-consensus on valuation only: invest at $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M tranched with $6M released on 2027 milestones.
consensus.proof_event: The 2027 season: 360 robots in service with at least 250 contracted at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and an independent harvest-level trial above 85% with bruising no worse than a hand-picked control.

one_question.question: What is the harvest-level recovery rate — marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant — and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?
one_question.why: The 94% divides by detected ripe fruit and excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%, so it cannot tell an investor whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. If harvest-level recovery is 75-80% with 3.8% bruising, the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money all fall together; if it is above 85% with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, the same numbers become conservative and the 2027 plan is financeable. It is the one measurement that reprices every other assumption in the case.

arguments.position_sizing: Meridian's $12M at $72M pre-money buys 13.33% of a $90M post-money. Public-equity sizing rules do not apply to a pre-revenue-scale private company, so the check size is set by the downside and the follow-on reserve: the maximum loss is the full $12M, and the base case needs a further $6-10M of Series B money in 2028 to protect the stake. Recommendation: commit $6M now at a $48M-$55M pre-money, with $6M released on 2027 milestones (250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, an independent harvest-level trial above 85%, and the Calder licence confirmed exclusive), and reserve $6M for the Series B. At $50M pre-money the same $12M buys 17.65% and returns 3.68x at a $250M exit against 2.78x at $72M. A $12M cheque at $72M with no tranching and no protective provisions, with Tallis holding an observer seat and five commercial roles, is not an investable structure for a lead.

scenarios.evidence: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons already delivered; 110 contracted and 50 LOIs for 2027; $4.0M of the round committed; Tallis has quoted the v4 BOM (S53, unverified). Deere paid $250M-$305M for pre-scale autonomy businesses (S96, S92).

scenarios.driver: The build lands late or short: 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal, $2-3M of RaaS in 2027, a flat or slightly down Series B in 2028 once the 1x preference stack is visible, and an OEM trade sale at $150M-$250M in 2029-2031.

scenarios.implication: Reprice the entry to $48M-$55M or tranche; the base case is a modest venture return at $72M, not a loss.

scenarios.driver: The v4 build slips past the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, and the Calder licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31 while a second grower leaves over bruising.

2. The problem
Strawberry growers in California and Florida lose an estimated 10-15% of marketable fruit each season because they cannot hire enough pickers at
peak harvest. Harvest labor is the largest single cost line for most growers.
-  Strawberries are picked by hand every three to four days through a season of up to seven months; a picker covers roughly a quarter of an acre a

-  Growers tell us their crews are smaller and older each year, while wages and worker housing keep getting more expensive (grower interviews, 2025).

-  An autonomous, track-mounted robot that drives the furrows at night and day, finds ripe berries with stereo cameras and a ripeness model, and

-  Runs about 20 hours a day on swappable battery packs; one field technician supervises up to 8 robots, on site or remotely.
-  Sold as Robots-as-a-Service: growers pay per robot per season; we own, maintain and insure the fleet.
-  Current model: Orrin Picker v3, released to the field in March 2026. The v4, designed for lower cost, is planned for the 2027 season.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,633 characters)
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, a claim resting on company-reported, unverified acreage, price and adoption inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not a $310M one, and the binding constraint is field performance rather than grower willingness to pay.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | How it is built | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified (company estimate) | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool at 100% adoption | Unverified; framing inconsistent | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M a year (2027 list price) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 acres per robot x $16,500 | Derived from unverified company inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified; not reachable in strawberries | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M at list, $27.2M at renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 an acre | Derived from unverified company inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

The $42B and $3.1B figures are labour-spend numbers, company-reported and unverified; only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price it needs 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline number. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption, 3.6x the stated figure; the implied adoption CAGR from 2% in 2028 to 15% in 2031 is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Robot price in picker-days at $180-$900 a day | Share of the 896 picker-days replaced per robot-season | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Company price, unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Company price, unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Company price, unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent in the table follows from the deck's own productivity, which is company-reported and unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day means 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. That growers have bought only at the bottom of the price ladder, and that one Florida grower left over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Not disclosed; part of 50,000 US acres (company estimate, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month season; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded from pilots | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day season cuts acres per robot to 2.0-2.5 | Harvest CROO, Florida-based | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue modelled | Not applicable | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA 2027 joint review; tariff treatment of cross-border machinery | Not applicable | S53, S148 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | Not applicable | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1 autonomous machinery safety; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months are what make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: the same 1.5 acres per 24 hours covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, consistent with picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day window covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Florida's value is utilisation: a robot working Florida in winter and California in summer would log two seasons a year and halve depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market: the wages that make a robot compelling in California make it less compelling in Guadalajara, and the exposure is trade policy. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers [S53, S148].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways. A handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book is concentrated in two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the 2026 H-2A Adverse Effect Wage Rate rule, published on 2026-08-03, resets the wage floor annually, and California's agricultural overtime rules raise peak-season cost. But certification volumes and wage levels were not retrievable, and if guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S145, S141, S161].

### What would settle it

Three inputs would move this from estimate to evidence: NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state for 2019-2025, the California Strawberry Commission's grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection rate and bruising against a hand-picked control. If acreage is stable and the pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the 2031 line re-bases upward and supports a services business at a lower valuation than the pre-money. If acreage is falling and realised price stays near the current contract, the strawberry market is small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs, the two figures the company has had the most incentive to round up.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported and unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap is not a rounding difference; it is a different market, and it needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 6 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,775 characters)
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price it covers 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost, with a 24% cushion. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season (April-October) and a three-month Florida season (December-March), at $9,500 per robot per season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. The product is sold one season at a time; payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not publicly disclosed, which matters because a collection after the harvest would put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts in this paragraph are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. At a six-season life, depreciation would be $8,000 and contribution still -$4,100. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season (3.7-season payback). At $16,500 with current service cost the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 seasons at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback ($31,000 divided by $14,750) omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted 2027 renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book, not the strongest. Prices are company-reported and unverified; the recomputation is verified [S53].

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. ### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover. ### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,855 characters)
Orrin has the only disclosed paid fleet in open-field strawberry harvesting, but that lead is narrower than the deck's claim to be the only autonomous picker above 90%: the 94% is a conditional success rate on rows the company chose, on company-reported and unverified figures, and the category's record is one of well-funded failures and absorptions [S53]. The competitive question is whether Orrin can convert a two-season lead in paid deployments into contracted acres before Harvest CROO, an equipment maker or the hand crew closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and stage | Published performance | Price and model | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres | Fruit quality is the retail benchmark; no bruise rate published | Piece-rate or hourly wages; H-2A wage floor reset for 2026 | Near-100% of acres | Proven quality, no capex, crew flexes with volume | Wage floor and peak availability; overtime cost | S145, S141 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24 | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim; no rate published) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | A decade of NSF SBIR funding; Florida base; patents | No disclosed paid fleet, price or shipments | S1, S94, S97, S98 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple harvesting; commercial from 2019 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Exited 2025 | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments, $25M Series B, CNH investment | Ceased operations July 2025 | S93, S114, S116, S117 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Exited | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable open-field; IP and team acquired by Oishii 2025-03-24 | S115, S118 |
| Academic systems (WSU; Journal of Field Robotics) | Research prototypes | 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry; 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit | Not sold | None | Publish results and methods | Not commercial | S56, S42, S57 |
| Equipment makers (Deere, CNH) | Autonomous platforms and see-and-spray | No berry or robotic-harvest product in Deere's FY2025 10-K | Not applicable | None in berries | Capital, dealer network, acquisition record | Not in this crop today | S8, S92, S95, S96 |

The Picker competes in three arenas, and only the first is a robot market. The hand crew picks nearly every US acre and is not standing still: harvest-aid platforms make pickers faster while keeping the crew, and the H-2A wage floor is reset annually. Open-field robots are the second arena, where the table shows one long-funded competitor and one well-funded failure. Tabletop and greenhouse systems (Tortuga, Agrobot, MetoMotion, Dogtooth) serve a different production system and are not direct competitors today.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs the grower nothing when it is not working, needs no capital and already meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin has to beat that on bruising before it beats it on cost, and one Florida grower's exit over bruising shows the bar is real. Among robot vendors, Harvest CROO is the closest threat: Florida-based, 13 patents, $10M raised over 14 rounds, $1.25M of NSF SBIR Phase II funding to build a commercial strawberry harvester, and a 2025-04-24 public claim that its open-field trials match human harvesting. Its weakness is disclosure — no paid fleet, price or shipment figure — which is also Orrin's opportunity: the first vendor to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference point for growers and acquirers [S1, S94, S97, S98].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so every berry the cameras missed leaves the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and rows chosen by Orrin's field team; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a crew in year one, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team draws about its own machine — and the bruise rate has no hand-picked comparator [S53, S56, S42, S57].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: the gripper application had every claim rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families are licensed from a university and become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. What is hard to copy is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots across two states. The peers show what that costs: Monarch has raised over $220M and Carbon Robotics $232M across five rounds, while Advanced Farm's $25M Series B and Tortuga's $47.7M did not keep them independent. Orrin has raised $20.5M and is asking for $18M, 9% of Monarch's total [S54, S55, S119, S93, S115].

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025 after commercial deployments, and Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025. The exits that did happen went to equipment makers: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries in 2021. Deere's FY2025 10-K business description mentions no berry or robotic-harvesting product, so the OEM threat today is capital and acquisition appetite rather than a competing machine. That record supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and it argues for pricing the round on contracted acres rather than on a technology lead [S91, S92, S95, S96, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Orrin's position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Challenger | Hand crews and H-2A | Orrin Fieldworks: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons | Harvest CROO, Florida: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | Equipment makers and greenhouse-robot vendors moving outdoors | S53, S1, S8 |

Orrin's wedge — Robots-as-a-Service with no grower capital, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, the economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route to scale. Orrin wins if the fleet proves fruit quality at scale in 2027 and the contracted renewal robots convert at the higher price; it loses if Harvest CROO or an equipment maker demonstrates a fleet first. No private vendor discloses audited performance, price or shipments; every share statement is an absence of evidence.

::: evidence
**The "only open-field picker above 90%" claim is a measurement definition, not a moat. (S53)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin's field team selected and excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe or pluckable fruit, and the commercial record includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 claim of performance on par with human harvesting, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B and Tortuga's sale to Oishii [S53, S56, S42, S1, S114, S115].
:::

| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet in the category (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida pilot exit; gripper patent claims rejected; single product and single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,991 characters)
The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 are management accounts [S53].

| RaaS | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.38 | 0.71 | 4.6 | 12.9 | Unverified | S53 |
| Paid pilots | 0.03 | 0.12 | 0.27 | 0.34 | 0.4 | 0.3 | Unverified | S53 |
| Engineering services | 0.00 | 0.20 | 0.95 | 1.20 | 0.6 | 0.0 | Unverified | S53 |
| Grants | 0.07 | 0.08 | 0.30 | 0.35 | 0.0 | 0.0 | Unverified | S53 |

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet and 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres at 3.5 acres a robot — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. The ARR split is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months (company-reported, unverified).** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the disclosed facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital is estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures are unverified; yields and working capital are derived estimates [S53, S7].

Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex exhaust the round and breach the covenant by mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation: $10.8M of opex divided by 360 seasons is $30,000 per season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet. Price matters less: $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and evidence of Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 8 by Valuation Analyst, 8,876 characters)
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash, $1.5M of which the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant makes unusable: $2.2M and 5.4 months of runway at $410,000 a month, with the covenant reached around 2027-03-14. The category discloses few valuations: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C in 2025, and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014; Advanced Farm Technologies raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech, which raised a reported $47.7M, sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. The October 2026 deck and its 2027-2028 projections are company-provided and unverified.

On revenue the price sits at the top of any observable range: 34.6x the $90M post-money on 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR, 12.9x pre and 16.1x post on the 2027 plan, and 5.5x and 6.8x on 2028. The ARR is not recurring: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding letters of intent — 56% non-recurring or non-binding, which is why 51.4x contracted robot revenue is the honest denominator. The payback is thinner than the pitch: the 2.1-season figure assumes a $1,750 service cost and omits the $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables the deck charges against gross profit, so the same robot pays back in 2.5 seasons at the $16,500 list price and 4.4 at the $12,700 renewal with today's $3,100 service cost [S53 p.9]. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA, and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S8, S12, S14, S95]. The cap table makes it worse. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2%: the founders from 53.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7%, granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M) — 40.9% of the $90M post-money, ranking pari passu with new money — or $39.3M (43.6%) if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference. Ahead of the preferred sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt [S53, unverified]. Meridian is flat at 1.0x from a $38.4M to a $90M exit: at a $40M sale the Series A takes its $18M preference, Meridian recovers $12.0M and the common receives $1.6M after the debt. Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $272M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years), at $300M 3.33x (27.2%) and at $500M 5.56x (40.9%).

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture; so is a five-seat board with two common seats, one Seed, one Series A and one independent agreed by both.
