{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 7 by Product Analyst, 8,965 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises, an auditable safety file and an enforceable estate are what justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Orrin's figures are unverified; benchmarks are independent.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement, as the WSU team concludes of its machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower, not a paper: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163], and 32 strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017 (S164). A machine that tears down without tools and swabs clean sells into retail audits; the 35% cost cut, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where cleanability gets traded away. One contamination or injury event would be existential for a five-customer vendor.

| Standard or rule | What it demands | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ISO 18497-1 and -4:2024 | Design and verification methods for autonomous farm machinery; voluntary, on the manufacturer | S166, S151 |
| 21 CFR 112.123 (FSMA) | Harvest equipment and food-contact surfaces kept clean; on the grower | S163, S153 |
| EU Regulation 2023/1230 and an Australian code | Frameworks Cal/OSHA examined alongside ISO 18497-style rules | S154 |

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either much of the downtime is unattended, a $48,000 asset standing still, or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season over four seasons, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — 27%, not the 60% projected. No hand-harvest cost per acre is disclosed, the number that would settle whether price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a 1986 US patent — so a routine rejection in crowded art points to a narrow allowance at best; the file wrapper was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed — Advanced Farm raised $25M, took a CNH investment and ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii in March 2025. An investor should condition the cheque on licence renewal at $12,700 or more, service cost below $2,500 and an office action leaving a claim standing.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Performance | 94% of detected, 5.6 s/berry | "on par with human harvesting", no rate | not disclosed | S53 unverified, S1, S114 |
| Status at 2026-10 | 64 robots, 5 growers | operating, 13 patents | ceased 2025; IP sold 2025 | S53 unverified, S1, S114, S115 |

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 unverified, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 unverified |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry undisclosed | Platform copying | S53 unverified |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented | S53 unverified |

| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 unverified |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); harvest recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. [S57]
:::

{"url":"https://agfundernews.com/dailyrobotics-gears-up-for-commercial-launch-in-california-in-2026-with-robotic-strawberry-harvester","title":"DailyRobotics enters strawberry harvesting race with robot that can pick 2–3x faster than humans","text":"DailyRobotics' robots perform both harvesting and on-board quality grading.
Image credit: DailyRobotics

 Israeli agtech startup DailyRobotics is gearing up for commercial launch in California next April with a robotic harvester it claims can pick strawberries 2-3x faster than humans.
The Q2 harvester, which is designed for field-grown strawberries, has two robotic arms and soft grippers that gently pick the fruit and place it directly into clamshells, cofounder Adham Ghazali tells AgFunderNews.
“Our current field performance is around 30 kg/hour, and the hardware is already capable of reaching 50 kg/hour as we continue optimizing software and cycle time. One operator can manage up to eight robots, and Q2 packs strawberries directly into clamshells, fitting smoothly into existing farm workflows.”
Designed for plant beds at widths of 2.2-4.6 feet, the battery-powered ‘bot performs both harvesting and on-board quality grading, says Ghazali. “Each berry is imaged and evaluated by a perception pipeline that classifies size, surface defects, color maturity, and over-ripeness, and the manipulator then places it into the corresponding bin or clamshell. This closed-loop process ensures uniform pack quality directly in the field.”
As strawberries are often hidden underneath leaves, meanwhile, “We have a dynamic perception system that’s able to search for strawberries because the arm goes into the canopy with a camera,” he says.
Why it matters
Strawberries are a high-value but labor-intensive crop that is typically picked by hand in most parts of the world, says Ghazali, who previously led vision-based self-driving car startup Imagry. Growers struggling with labor costs and availability are looking for better options that will save time and money.
“Our focus is robotics as a service (RaaS) but we’re also open to selling the machines, so we can refine the business model. But our primary objective is to solve a problem and prove that we can reduce labor costs.
“In California, it can cost $43,000 per acre per year for picking alone, and there are thousands of acres of strawberry farms in California. And in some places up to 30% of the crop can be left to rot on the floor.”
As California strawberries are harvested for much of the year with regional hand-offs (each region has its own peak season), the ‘bots can be moved around as needed to meet regional demand, he adds.
Rise of the machines
Founded in 2023 by Adham Ghazali, Majed Jubeh, and Farah Jubran, who have expertise in robotics, AI, and large-scale engineering, DailyRobotics has not yet taken on VC money, says Ghazali. Funding to date has come from the founders, a non-dilutive grant, and angel investors.
DailyRobotics is not the only game in town when it comes to robotic strawberry harvesting, and is just one of several startups in the space including L5, Harvest CROO Robotics, Agrobot, Organifarms, Fieldwork Robotics, Dogtooth Tech and Tortuga AgTech, which is now part of Oishii.
Most are still in the trial phase, with some focusing on tabletop/greenhouse-grown fruit (Oishii, Organifarms), while others such as DailyRobotics and Harvest CROO Robotics focus on open field-grown fruit.
For picking, meanwhile, they all use slightly different approaches. Some gently grab the berries with a soft claw cutting and others grip the stems, cutting them and dropping the fruit into boxes, an approach that Ghazali says works well in greenhouses but is more challenging in open fields.
“Each berry is imaged and evaluated by a perception pipeline that classifies size, surface defects, color maturity, and over-ripeness.” Image credit: DailyRobotics
According to Ghazali, the key factors for robotic strawberry harvesting are:
👉 Speed vs cost: Humans are extremely efficient at fruit picking, says Ghazali. And if robot pickers go too slow, he says, “there’s really no business model.” But as you increase the speed, the potential for damage becomes much, much higher, he says. “We can pick 2-3x as fast as humans and it’s much more scalable with more robotic arms.”
👉 Integration with existing operations: “It’s not just about picking,” he says, it’s about real-time quality control. Effective ‘bots must be able to sort fruit as well as pick and pack it. “Once we see a strawberry, we can automatically classify it.”
👉 Bruising/damage rate: DailyRobotics is developing a new soft gripper that gently “hugs” the fruit without squeezing it, says Ghazali. “In recent field tests, the end-to-end picking process achieved a ~4% bruising rate, which falls within the expected range for skilled hand-picking under similar conditions.”
👉 Charging: According to Ghazali, the ‘bots are designed to work for a full day before needing recharging (using a regular socket and power supply), although users can also replace batteries in the field.
👉 Manufacturing/scale up: “We have a very simple design using OEM ready equipment and tools,” he says. “Our robots can be assembled in under an hour. The hardware we use is already mature and mass-produced, which makes manufacturing cost very low. The only thing that is manufactured in-house is the grippers.”
👉 Maintenance: “You have to have something that doesn’t require a lot of support,” says Ghazali. “Operators can scan a QR code on the unit to access a mobile maintenance interface that provides real-time diagnostics, subsystem health monitoring, error logs, remote control functions, and live support tools, all without requiring specialized equipment.”
What’s next?
More field trials: “We’re going to do more field trials from now until April.”
Commercialization: “We are deploying our first robots with a customer in California starting in April 2026.”

{"url":"https://futurism.com/robots-and-machines/ai-tractor-startup-founders","title":"AI-Powered Tractor Startup Burns Through a Quarter Billion Dollars, Fires All Employees in Epic Implosion","text":"Monarch Tractor

The world simply wasn’t ready for AI powered tractors.

Or perhaps it was Monarch Tractor, the much-hyped company that promised to revolutionize agriculture when it launched these electric-powered autonomous farm machines in 2023, that wasn’t prepared to deploy its own creation.

Once valued at over half a billion dollars and buoyed by over $240 million in initial funding, Monarch is now in ruins. After burning through that mountain of cash, it laid off its entire workforce late last year, warning that it may “shut down” entirely. In March, it was reported that it vacated its Livermore, California headquarters, almost certainly spelling the end.

What went wrong? There are myriad reasons at play, but chief among them is that it sounds like the AI tractors kind of sucked compared to the venture’s vast hype — a warning to AI and robotics startups everywhere that eventually reality can come crashing down like a bad harvest.

New reporting from SFGATE about the company’s undoing points to a brutal review from California winemaker Patrick O’Connor, who says he’s been testing the tractor for three years on his vineyard.

“It totally failed,” he said in a recent Instagram video that garnered over 25,000 likes. 

More worryingly, “it was actually quite dangerous,” he added. In his view, a quarter of a billion dollars had been “wasted” on developing the “failed autonomous AI robot tractor.”

In an interview with SFGATE, O’Connor drove the point home by saying he couldn’t find a single serious use for the AI tractor, and found its self-driving mode to be hazardous. “I wouldn’t let anyone else around it,” he said.

Don’t just take O’Connor’s word for it. Last September, several tractor dealerships sued Monarch for allegedly selling defective tractors and making misleading claims about their autonomy. Monarch denied the claims, but in a detail that further underscores the tumult at the company, the attorneys on at least one of the suits have stopped representing the tractor maker, SFGATE noted, citing reporting from Pleasanton Weekly.

Monarch made a heavy push to have its tractors catch on at dairy farms and vineyards. O’Connor was an early adopter, hoping that they could perform physically gruelling work like spraying pesticides on his steep plantation, adding that the machines were designed to work in the narrow lanes of vineyards.

“It was theoretically promising advancement in mechanical weed control over chemical weed control,” O’Connor told SFGATE. “But the hydraulics were finicky, the automated row follow didn’t pan out. It was hitting my vines. And it was never to a point where you could be driverless.”

Now it’s mostly a glorified mule for O’Connor, who uses it to haul around tools in its storage container and hooks power tools up to its beefy battery.

Using a custom attachment, he also uses it to split wood.

“$200 million log splitter,” O’Connor dryly enthused in the Instagram video.

More on self-driving AI: Tesla Workers Are Seizing Control of Robotaxis When They Get Stuck","truncated":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 5 by Company Analyst, 8,958 characters)
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding. All company facts below are unverified company material unless marked [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo about $10M, and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 5 by Company Analyst, 8,898 characters)
The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university, patent, employer or corporate record could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist to lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab, 2016-2021. She is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university; Orrin licenses two families, the other nine are unlicensed. Her career fits the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: no disclosed operating role outside academia, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014-2021 — 15 years running crews for berry growers. The customer list shows the conversion: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West); she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, while Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

We would not recommend leading at the proposed pre-money without those hires and a Kestrel estoppel; a smaller, tranched check at a lower price is the investable structure (company-provided, unverified).

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 7 by Product Analyst, 8,965 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises, an auditable safety file and an enforceable estate are what justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Orrin's figures are unverified; benchmarks are independent.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement, as the WSU team concludes of its machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower, not a paper: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163], and 32 strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017 (S164). A machine that tears down without tools and swabs clean sells into retail audits; the 35% cost cut, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where cleanability gets traded away. One contamination or injury event would be existential for a five-customer vendor.

| Standard or rule | What it demands | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ISO 18497-1 and -4:2024 | Design and verification methods for autonomous farm machinery; voluntary, on the manufacturer | S166, S151 |
| 21 CFR 112.123 (FSMA) | Harvest equipment and food-contact surfaces kept clean; on the grower | S163, S153 |
| EU Regulation 2023/1230 and an Australian code | Frameworks Cal/OSHA examined alongside ISO 18497-style rules | S154 |

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either much of the downtime is unattended, a $48,000 asset standing still, or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season over four seasons, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — 27%, not the 60% projected. No hand-harvest cost per acre is disclosed, the number that would settle whether price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a 1986 US patent — so a routine rejection in crowded art points to a narrow allowance at best; the file wrapper was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed — Advanced Farm raised $25M, took a CNH investment and ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii in March 2025. An investor should condition the cheque on licence renewal at $12,700 or more, service cost below $2,500 and an office action leaving a claim standing.

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); harvest recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. [S57]
:::

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 report and an ATP swab record (S163, S166)."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,633 characters)
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, a claim resting on company-reported, unverified acreage, price and adoption inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not a $310M one, and the binding constraint is field performance rather than grower willingness to pay.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | How it is built | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified (company estimate) | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool at 100% adoption | Unverified; framing inconsistent | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M a year (2027 list price) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 acres per robot x $16,500 | Derived from unverified company inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified; not reachable in strawberries | S53 |

The $42B and $3.1B figures are labour-spend numbers, company-reported and unverified; only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price it needs 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline number. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption, 3.6x the stated figure; the implied adoption CAGR from 2% in 2028 to 15% in 2031 is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Robot price in picker-days at $180-$900 a day | Share of the 896 picker-days replaced per robot-season | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Company price, unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Company price, unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Company price, unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent in the table follows from the deck's own productivity, which is company-reported and unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day means 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. That growers have bought only at the bottom of the price ladder, and that one Florida grower left over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Not disclosed; part of 50,000 US acres (company estimate, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month season; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded from pilots | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day season cuts acres per robot to 2.0-2.5 | Harvest CROO, Florida-based | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue modelled | Not applicable | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA 2027 joint review; tariff treatment of cross-border machinery | Not applicable | S53, S148 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | Not applicable | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1 autonomous machinery safety; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months are what make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: the same 1.5 acres per 24 hours covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, consistent with picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day window covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Florida's value is utilisation: a robot working Florida in winter and California in summer would log two seasons a year and halve depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market: the wages that make a robot compelling in California make it less compelling in Guadalajara, and the exposure is trade policy. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers [S53, S148].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways. A handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book is concentrated in two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the 2026 H-2A Adverse Effect Wage Rate rule, published on 2026-08-03, resets the wage floor annually, and California's agricultural overtime rules raise peak-season cost. But certification volumes and wage levels were not retrievable, and if guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S145, S141, S161].

### What would settle it

Three inputs would move this from estimate to evidence: NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state for 2019-2025, the California Strawberry Commission's grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection rate and bruising against a hand-picked control. If acreage is stable and the pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the 2031 line re-bases upward and supports a services business at a lower valuation than the pre-money. If acreage is falling and realised price stays near the current contract, the strawberry market is small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs, the two figures the company has had the most incentive to round up.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported and unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap is not a rounding difference; it is a different market, and it needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,855 characters)
Orrin has the only disclosed paid fleet in open-field strawberry harvesting, but that lead is narrower than the deck's claim to be the only autonomous picker above 90%: the 94% is a conditional success rate on rows the company chose, on company-reported and unverified figures, and the category's record is one of well-funded failures and absorptions [S53]. The competitive question is whether Orrin can convert a two-season lead in paid deployments into contracted acres before Harvest CROO, an equipment maker or the hand crew closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and stage | Published performance | Price and model | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres | Fruit quality is the retail benchmark; no bruise rate published | Piece-rate or hourly wages; H-2A wage floor reset for 2026 | Near-100% of acres | Proven quality, no capex, crew flexes with volume | Wage floor and peak availability; overtime cost | S145, S141 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24 | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim; no rate published) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | A decade of NSF SBIR funding; Florida base; patents | No disclosed paid fleet, price or shipments | S1, S94, S97, S98 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple harvesting; commercial from 2019 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Exited 2025 | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments, $25M Series B, CNH investment | Ceased operations July 2025 | S93, S114, S116, S117 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Exited | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable open-field; IP and team acquired by Oishii 2025-03-24 | S115, S118 |
| Academic systems (WSU; Journal of Field Robotics) | Research prototypes | 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry; 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit | Not sold | None | Publish results and methods | Not commercial | S56, S42, S57 |
| Equipment makers (Deere, CNH) | Autonomous platforms and see-and-spray | No berry or robotic-harvest product in Deere's FY2025 10-K | Not applicable | None in berries | Capital, dealer network, acquisition record | Not in this crop today | S8, S92, S95, S96 |

The Picker competes in three arenas, and only the first is a robot market. The hand crew picks nearly every US acre and is not standing still: harvest-aid platforms make pickers faster while keeping the crew, and the H-2A wage floor is reset annually. Open-field robots are the second arena, where the table shows one long-funded competitor and one well-funded failure. Tabletop and greenhouse systems (Tortuga, Agrobot, MetoMotion, Dogtooth) serve a different production system and are not direct competitors today.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs the grower nothing when it is not working, needs no capital and already meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin has to beat that on bruising before it beats it on cost, and one Florida grower's exit over bruising shows the bar is real. Among robot vendors, Harvest CROO is the closest threat: Florida-based, 13 patents, $10M raised over 14 rounds, $1.25M of NSF SBIR Phase II funding to build a commercial strawberry harvester, and a 2025-04-24 public claim that its open-field trials match human harvesting. Its weakness is disclosure — no paid fleet, price or shipment figure — which is also Orrin's opportunity: the first vendor to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference point for growers and acquirers [S1, S94, S97, S98].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so every berry the cameras missed leaves the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and rows chosen by Orrin's field team; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a crew in year one, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team draws about its own machine — and the bruise rate has no hand-picked comparator [S53, S56, S42, S57].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: the gripper application had every claim rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families are licensed from a university and become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. What is hard to copy is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots across two states. The peers show what that costs: Monarch has raised over $220M and Carbon Robotics $232M across five rounds, while Advanced Farm's $25M Series B and Tortuga's $47.7M did not keep them independent. Orrin has raised $20.5M and is asking for $18M, 9% of Monarch's total [S54, S55, S119, S93, S115].

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025 after commercial deployments, and Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025. The exits that did happen went to equipment makers: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries in 2021. Deere's FY2025 10-K business description mentions no berry or robotic-harvesting product, so the OEM threat today is capital and acquisition appetite rather than a competing machine. That record supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and it argues for pricing the round on contracted acres rather than on a technology lead [S91, S92, S95, S96, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Orrin's position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Challenger | Hand crews and H-2A | Orrin Fieldworks: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons | Harvest CROO, Florida: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | Equipment makers and greenhouse-robot vendors moving outdoors | S53, S1, S8 |

Orrin's wedge — Robots-as-a-Service with no grower capital, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, the economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route to scale. Orrin wins if the fleet proves fruit quality at scale in 2027 and the contracted renewal robots convert at the higher price; it loses if Harvest CROO or an equipment maker demonstrates a fleet first. No private vendor discloses audited performance, price or shipments; every share statement is an absence of evidence.

::: evidence
**The "only open-field picker above 90%" claim is a measurement definition, not a moat. (S53)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin's field team selected and excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe or pluckable fruit, and the commercial record includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 claim of performance on par with human harvesting, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B and Tortuga's sale to Oishii [S53, S56, S42, S1, S114, S115].
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet in the category (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida pilot exit; gripper patent claims rejected; single product and single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews still pick nearly all acres (company-reported, unverified); Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership through the existing manufacturing relationship | S53 |
| Threats | Harvest CROO's commercial claim and 13 patents; well-funded adjacent robotics; OEM entry; looser H-2A labour supply would slow switching | S1, S54, S55, S8, S145 |
:::"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 6 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,775 characters)
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price it covers 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost, with a 24% cushion. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season (April-October) and a three-month Florida season (December-March), at $9,500 per robot per season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. The product is sold one season at a time; payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not publicly disclosed, which matters because a collection after the harvest would put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts in this paragraph are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. At a six-season life, depreciation would be $8,000 and contribution still -$4,100. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $9,500 | $31,000 (v4 target) | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$3,850 | 8.0 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 | +$4,500 | 2.5 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season (3.7-season payback). At $16,500 with current service cost the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 seasons at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback ($31,000 divided by $14,750) omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted 2027 renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book, not the strongest. Prices are company-reported and unverified; the recomputation is verified [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list, target service | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $12,000 | 138% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The customer counts are partially verified: the deck's grower table sums to 75, matching the stated total, but the contracts themselves are unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 and has contracted 20 for 2027, and Grower E ended its Plant City pilot in June 2026 over fruit bruising, the one customer-side data point that contradicts the 3.8% bruising claim. For 2027 Orrin shows 110 contracted robots (Marisol 40, Pajaro 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20) and 50 LOI robots from eight other pilots: 160 of the 360 planned, or 44%, with 200 uncontracted. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Those ties are disclosed and not disqualifying, but they mean the 53% concentration and the cost of field service are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many robots were idle or deployed on unpaid pilots. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot could serve Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $19,000 at the 782 seasons implied by FY2028 revenue. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025 | S54 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; commercial-viability demonstration 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. Orrin's ask is small against that record, and the economics above say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The investor implication is to wait for field data, or to structure the lead check as tranches tied to the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 unit cost at or below target; at current unit economics, more robots destroy more capital."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 5 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,991 characters)
The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS revenue is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line in FY2026 is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. The history is company-reported and unverified: no audit, no public filing and a part-time head of finance are disclosed, so FY2023-FY2026 are management accounts [S53].

| $M | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RaaS | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.38 | 0.71 | 4.6 | 12.9 | Unverified | S53 |
| Paid pilots | 0.03 | 0.12 | 0.27 | 0.34 | 0.4 | 0.3 | Unverified | S53 |
| Engineering services | 0.00 | 0.20 | 0.95 | 1.20 | 0.6 | 0.0 | Unverified | S53 |
| Grants | 0.07 | 0.08 | 0.30 | 0.35 | 0.0 | 0.0 | Unverified | S53 |
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | Unverified | S53 |
| Gross profit | 0.0 | 0.3 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.9 | 8.0 | Unverified | S53 |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | Unverified | S53 |
| Operating loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | Unverified | S53 |
| RaaS gross margin | n/a | n/a | 22% | 41% | 52% | 61% | Unverified | S53 |

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. The figures are unverified; the ratios are verified arithmetic [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. The best-case recurring figure is the $1.4M of one-season contracts against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue; on those numbers the $72M pre-money is 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet and 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres at 3.5 acres a robot — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. The ARR split is verified against the deck; the contracts are unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The nine-month runway is really five months (company-reported, unverified).** $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M, or 5.4 months at $410k a month, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 California season's first collections. A Series A that slips past Q1 2027 is a default event on the secured fleet, not just a dilution event. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with a covenant in the middle. The $18M round plus $2.47M cash and $0.9M of undrawn facility gives $21.4M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M after $0.8M of depreciation, and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $1.5-3.5M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company-reported terms; the bridge is derived and unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO, goodwill and net debt cannot be calculated: the disclosed facts are $3.7M of cash and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M before the $1.5M covenant. Working capital is estimated: 360 seasons at $5,600 of direct cost is $2.0M before collection, receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days would be $0.8-1.1M, and the 300-robot order to Tallis is $9.9M paid before the season; grower payment terms and the Tallis prepayment schedule are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures are unverified; yields and working capital are derived estimates [S53, S7].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex exhaust the round and breach the covenant by mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation: $10.8M of opex divided by 360 seasons is $30,000 per season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet. Price matters less: $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and evidence of Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. Analyst estimates on company-reported figures, not guidance [S53].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 8 by Valuation Analyst, 8,876 characters)
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash, $1.5M of which the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant makes unusable: $2.2M and 5.4 months of runway at $410,000 a month, with the covenant reached around 2027-03-14. The category discloses few valuations: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C in 2025, and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014; Advanced Farm Technologies raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech, which raised a reported $47.7M, sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. The October 2026 deck and its 2027-2028 projections are company-provided and unverified.

On revenue the price sits at the top of any observable range: 34.6x the $90M post-money on 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR, 12.9x pre and 16.1x post on the 2027 plan, and 5.5x and 6.8x on 2028. The ARR is not recurring: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding letters of intent — 56% non-recurring or non-binding, which is why 51.4x contracted robot revenue is the honest denominator. The payback is thinner than the pitch: the 2.1-season figure assumes a $1,750 service cost and omits the $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables the deck charges against gross profit, so the same robot pays back in 2.5 seasons at the $16,500 list price and 4.4 at the $12,700 renewal with today's $3,100 service cost [S53 p.9]. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA, and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S8, S12, S14, S95]. On a 4.0x exit multiple the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M projected.

The cap table makes it worse. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2%: the founders from 53.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7%, granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M) — 40.9% of the $90M post-money, ranking pari passu with new money — or $39.3M (43.6%) if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference. Ahead of the preferred sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt [S53, unverified]. Meridian is flat at 1.0x from a $38.4M to a $90M exit: at a $40M sale the Series A takes its $18M preference, Meridian recovers $12.0M and the common receives $1.6M after the debt. Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $272M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years), at $300M 3.33x (27.2%) and at $500M 5.56x (40.9%).

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture; so is a five-seat board with two common seats, one Seed, one Series A and one independent agreed by both. What is missing is the protection package: Meridian would hold one of five votes, with no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package, and Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor (company deck, S53; unverified). The minimum package is a second board seat or a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilisation, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost a robot-season, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true is specific: 360 robots and $8M of ARR on a definition that no longer includes Tallis services by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence still exclusive after its 100-robot test, unit cost below $36,000, and an OEM or a revenue base of $67.5M-$84M at a 4x multiple by 2029-2031. Deere paid $305M for Blue River (2017) and $250M for Bear Flag (2021), so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy. The counter-evidence is the category's own record: Advanced Farm, which Kubota and CNH backed, ceased operations in July 2025; Tortuga sold its assets; Abundant Robotics raised $12M, ran apple trials under RaaS and sold its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 [S91, S114, S115]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on the 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment. At a $50M pre-money Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post-money, which returns 3.7x at a $250M exit and 2.9x at $200M."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,659 characters)
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services and grants supplied $1.25M of $1.9M of revenue, and both stop by mid-2027 [S53]. What the Series A must therefore prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all of them company-reported and unverified in this review — the capital, the headcount and the unit economics do not yet reconcile. The plan is not implausible: 110 robots are contracted for 2027 and 50 more are under letters of intent. It asks for four step changes at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window.

### Services and grants pay the bills; neither survives 2027

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M (company-reported, unverified) comprised $0.95M of engineering services for Tallis, $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent [S53]. On the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, which at a $72M pre-money is 51x rather than the 22x the headline figure implies. The services line was rational while the fleet was sub-scale; it becomes a valuation problem the moment the round is priced on recurring revenue.

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified) [S53]. Against $3.7M of cash on 2026-09-30 and $410,000 of monthly net burn the company has nine months of runway before the round lands, while the Kestrel facility — $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5%, secured on the fleet — requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, a covenant that binds hardest during the build. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the entire fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage. Either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the projected 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. The governance picture compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but it means neither the revenue nor the cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition rather than an intention.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established pattern in this category is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries. Deere's 2025 annual report describes autonomy, machine learning and Solutions-as-a-Service as core to a small-agriculture strategy serving high-value and small-acreage crops, which is precisely where a berry picker would fit. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, which is exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. A standalone rental fleet at 360 robots has no precedent in this review: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, and Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B [S117, S8, S114, S115]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed, not a bet on a rental business reaching escape velocity alone.
