rows.mechanism: A service model with a multi-arm harvester competes for the same grower relationship and the same harvest window; if its throughput claim holds, Orrin's 5.6 seconds a berry is an order of magnitude slower per machine.
rows.benchmark: Orrin 5.6 s/berry on 212 selected rows (company); Harvest CROO up to 8 berries/s (company). Neither is independently verified.
rows.weakens: The 'only autonomous open-field picker above 90%' positioning and any assumption that Orrin sets the service price.
rows.implication: Competitive diligence should benchmark throughput and cost per marketable berry, not pick accuracy on selected rows.

rows.finding: A 2026 peer-reviewed berry-harvesting platform reported a 72% overall harvest success rate across 50 controlled indoor trials with synthetic fruit.

one_question.question: What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?

The investment case is conditional: if the labour gap stays durable, if the machine proves harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than a hand-picked control, and if the v4 cost lands at $31,000-$33,000 so that the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce about $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM trade sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M pre-money, or 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue, Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 3.33x at $300M; at $48M-$55M the same cheque returns 2.2x-3.7x. The killer risks are the ones already visible: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant reached around 2027-03-14.

The consensus is that the labour crisis creates a large, urgent market and that Orrin leads it: the deck claims the only autonomous open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin and a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with what Monarch Tractor and Carbon Robotics raised. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision system had already classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms Orrin's field team selected, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, which puts harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, so the claimed obtainable market is 132% of the entire US acreage base. The pricing consequence is arithmetic: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 actually charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. This is a measurement disagreement rather than an information edge, and one trial can settle it [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

After the independent challenge we moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six things to go right in the same 12 months — v4 cost, a 360-robot build, 250 units at list, an independent trial above 85%, a licence test passed and an OEM or Series B — with only $4.0M of the $18M committed and 45 days to the target close. The bear is one domino with several symptoms: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. A reprice negotiation that takes three to six months consumes the runway it is meant to protect, which is why a lender standstill has to be signed with the term sheet rather than promised after it [S53, S169].

| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units; 360 robots for April 2027; 250 or more at the $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM partnership or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | S53 |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals signed at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant reached 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale in 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), and 0-1.0x is the optimistic end because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53, S169, S128 |
:::

The five assumptions below are ranked by expected damage; three carry low confidence, and the financing assumption is binary, because if it fails the equity is worth zero rather than diluted. The labour assumption is the one the market ignores: the US Department of Labor lowered the California H-2A wage in October 2025 and opened the dairy programme in June 2026, so hand-pick cost may fall rather than rise, and no scenario prices that [S169].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery reaches 85% or more, with bruising at or below a hand-picked control, on blocks Orrin did not select | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80% of ripe fruit harvested, or a second paying grower leaving over fruit quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid and the price ceiling falls | Further pilot exits after Plant City; retail or grower quality audits on machine-picked fruit | S53, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 robot can be built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis in Guadalajara | Low | A contract-manufacturing quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | v4 design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes the bill of materials | S53 |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals signed at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; the base case becomes a bridge round at a flat or down price | The 110 contracted plus 50 letters of intent unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M rather than $18M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event; the worst case is not dilution | $4.0M of the round committed at 2026-10-31; covenant reached around 2027-03-14 | S53, S128 |

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after commercial launch, sold with dealer installation and service; adoption is a decades-long replacement cycle, not a software ramp | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for the benefit of creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale about 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | About $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Cautionary | 2016-2025 | A reported $47.7M raised, then an IP and team sale to Oishii in March 2025; the best sub-scale outcome is an asset sale | S115 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M, because the price capitalises a bull case that needs six conjuncts and leaves 1.67x as the return at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, which is the recommendation: the two measurements that matter are an independent harvest-level trial and a measured v4 unit cost, and either delivered before the 2026-12-15 close moves the case. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence assignment consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent rather than covenants. At $50M pre-money Meridian buys 17.65% and earns 3.68x at a $250M exit against 2.78x at $72M. If harvest-level recovery turns out above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation [S53].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use, where the minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the 2026 California H-2A wage is reported at $19.97 an hour [S53, S141, S142, S143]. The need is real; the investment case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, the machine proves harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than a hand-picked control, and the v4 cost lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce about $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M pre-money, 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue, Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 3.33x at $300M; at $48M-$55M the same cheque returns 2.2x-3.7x. The killer risks are visible: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant reached around 2027-03-14.

The consensus is that the labour crisis creates a large, urgent market and that Orrin leads it: the deck claims the only autonomous open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision system had already classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms Orrin's field team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, which puts harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, so the claim is 132% of the entire US acreage base. The arithmetic follows: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 actually charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. This is a measurement disagreement; one trial settles it [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

After the independent challenge we moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six things to go right in the same 12 months — v4 cost, a 360-robot build, 250 units at list, an independent trial above 85%, a licence test passed and an OEM or Series B — with only $4.0M of the $18M committed and 45 days to the target close. The bear is one domino with several symptoms: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), and 0-1.0x is optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53, S169, S128 |
:::

The five assumptions below are ranked by expected damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: if it fails, the equity is worth zero, not diluted. The labour assumption is the one the market ignores: the US Department of Labor lowered the California H-2A wage in October 2025 and opened the dairy programme in June 2026, so hand-pick cost may fall rather than rise [S169].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more, with bruising at or below a hand-picked control, on blocks Orrin did not select | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80% of ripe fruit harvested, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 robot is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis in Guadalajara | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant around 2027-03-14 | S53, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor keeps rising: no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick cost advantage | Medium | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or a lower California wage floor | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S169 |

History says the technology can exit and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut is the best case: 50,000 units installed by 2024, 29 years after the first commercial unit in 1995, sold with dealer installation and after-sales service, the adoption curve for a seasonal service business, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, a 60-person pre-scale perception company, and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, so an OEM will buy a franchise-defending autonomy stack before revenue scale. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors reported in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026; Abundant Robotics raised about $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of the five funded peers here failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S176, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for the benefit of creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale about 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | About $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Cautionary | 2016-2025 | A reported $47.7M raised, then an IP and team sale to Oishii in March 2025; the best sub-scale outcome is an asset sale | S115 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M, because the price capitalises a bull case that needs six conjuncts and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: the two measurements that matter are an independent harvest-level trial and a measured v4 unit cost, and either before the 2026-12-15 close moves the case. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence assignment consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money Meridian buys 17.65% and earns 3.68x at a $250M exit against 2.78x at $72M. If harvest-level recovery turns out above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation [S53].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the 2026 California H-2A wage is reported at $19.97 an hour [S53, S141, S142, S143]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M pre-money, 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue, Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 3.33x at $300M; at $48M-$55M the same cheque returns 2.2x-3.7x. The killer risks are visible: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

The consensus is that the labour crisis creates a large, urgent market and Orrin leads it: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision system classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms Orrin's field team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, so the claim is 132% of the US acreage base. The arithmetic follows: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 actually charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. This is a measurement disagreement; one trial settles it [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

After the independent challenge we moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six things in the same 12 months — v4 cost, a 360-robot build, 250 units at list, an independent trial above 85%, a licence test passed and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days to close. The bear is one domino with several symptoms: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |
:::

The five assumptions below are ranked by expected damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: if it fails, the equity is worth zero, not diluted. The labour assumption is the one the market ignores: the US Department of Labor lowered the California H-2A wage in October 2025 and opened the dairy programme in June 2026, so hand-pick cost may fall rather than rise [S169].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, on unselected blocks | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80%, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 unverified |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor keeps rising: no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick cost advantage | Medium | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or a lower California wage floor | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S169 |

History says the technology can exit and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut is the best case: 50,000 units installed by 2024, 29 years after the first commercial unit in 1995, sold with dealer service, the adoption curve for a seasonal service, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, a 60-person pre-scale perception company, and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024, entered an assignment for creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of the five funded peers here failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S176, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M, because the price capitalises a bull case that needs six conjuncts and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest-level trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move the case. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence assignment consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money Meridian buys 17.65% and earns 3.68x at a $250M exit against 2.78x at $72M. If harvest-level recovery turns out above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Calder assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and consolidation of the fleet entity [S53, S128].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 5.4 months of usable cash. The score is not a verdict on the technology; it is a verdict on what an investor can prove today. The evidence gate for a private-company investment is not met by company material alone, and 18 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, the lender agreement and the grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027 and the 2026 H-2A wage at $19.97, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S142].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. Financial position scores 3: of $3.7M of cash, $2.2M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run harvest crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Playbook: decision_framework.md

# Decision Framework

Use this file before drafting the executive briefing, investment thesis, recommendation, scoring, or final decision. Do not force precision when evidence does not support it.

## Contents

- Consensus / Non-Consensus View
- Scenario Analysis
- Key Assumptions
- Historical Analogs
- Capital Efficiency
- Position Sizing / Deal Sizing
- The One Question
- Three Takeaways

## Consensus / Non-Consensus View

State what the market, comparable investors, or the company's own pitch appears to assume. Then state whether the report has a differentiated view.

If there is no non-consensus insight, say the thesis is consensus and explain what that means for return expectations, valuation discipline, or margin of safety. Do not invent a variant perception for appearance.

## Scenario Analysis

Use bull/base/bear cases with explicit drivers and approximate probabilities.

- For public equities and growth companies, scenarios may use revenue, margin, multiple, cash flow, valuation, catalyst timing, or downside drawdown.
- For early-stage, biotech, hard-tech, and data-poor cases, use milestone scenarios such as product-market fit, regulatory readout, manufacturing yield, customer conversion, financing survival, or exit path.

Each scenario should include:

- Specific driver or failure mode.
- Evidence that makes it plausible.
- Financial or milestone implication.
- Investor implication.

For public equities, build scenarios from explicit financial drivers where data allows: revenue growth, segment mix, gross/operating margin, tax, share count, capex, working capital, free cash flow, net cash/debt, and valuation multiple. Include current share price context before stating upside/downside.

## Key Assumptions

Rank the 3-5 assumptions that most affect the decision. For each, state:

- Confidence.
- What would disprove it.
- Impact if wrong.
- Early warning sign.

This is often more useful than adding more facts.

## Historical Analogs

Use historical analogs only when they are close enough to teach a decision rule. A good analog matches on business model, market structure, stage, regulation, customer behavior, or capital intensity.

If no close analog exists, say so.

## Capital Efficiency

Use a capital efficiency scorecard when the company has raised material capital and data exists. Useful metrics include burn multiple, revenue per dollar raised, runway, revenue per employee, capex to next milestone, and dilution efficiency.

If data is unavailable, state which missing data would be required.

For public equities, capital efficiency should use reported financials where available: ROIC, ROE, ROA, asset turnover, incremental margins, reinvestment rate, FCF conversion, dividend/buyback yield, dilution, and M&A returns. Tie these to management capital allocation quality.

## Position Sizing / Deal Sizing

Use position sizing for public equities, liquid secondaries, or explicit portfolio-allocation requests.

For public equities, position size must reflect valuation upside/downside, balance-sheet resilience, liquidity, accounting quality, catalyst timing, volatility, evidence confidence, and whether the downside is mark-to-market volatility or permanent capital impairment.

For primary-market deals, translate this into check size, valuation discipline, downside loss, reserve strategy, and conditions for follow-on investment.

## The One Question

Before finalizing, identify the single diligence question whose truthful answer would most change the investment decision. It must be specific, answerable in principle, and decision-changing.

## Three Takeaways

End with the three things the reader should remember. These should be decision statements, not generic summaries."}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the 2026 California H-2A wage is reported at $19.97 an hour [S53, S141, S142, S143]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M pre-money, 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue, Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 3.33x at $300M; at $48M-$55M the same cheque returns 2.2x-3.7x. The killer risks are visible: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

The consensus is that the labour crisis creates a large, urgent market and Orrin leads it: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision system classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms Orrin's field team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, so the claim is 132% of the US acreage base. The arithmetic follows: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 actually charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. This is a measurement disagreement; one trial settles it [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

After the independent challenge we moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six things in the same 12 months — v4 cost, a 360-robot build, 250 units at list, an independent trial above 85%, a licence test passed and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days to close. The bear is one domino with several symptoms: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |
:::

The five key assumptions below are ranked by expected damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: if it fails, the equity is worth zero, not diluted. The labour assumption is the one the market ignores: the US Department of Labor lowered the California H-2A wage in October 2025 and opened the dairy programme in June 2026, so hand-pick cost may fall rather than rise [S169].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, on unselected blocks | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80%, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 unverified |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor keeps rising: no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick cost advantage | Medium | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or a lower California wage floor | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S169 |

History says the technology can exit and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut is the best case: 50,000 units installed by 2024, 29 years after the first commercial unit in 1995, sold with dealer service, the adoption curve for a seasonal service, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017, a 60-person pre-scale perception company, and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024, entered an assignment for creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of the five funded peers here failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S176, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M, because the price capitalises a bull case that needs six conjuncts and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest-level trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move the case. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence assignment consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money Meridian buys 17.65% and earns 3.68x at a $250M exit against 2.78x at $72M. If harvest-level recovery turns out above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Calder assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and consolidation of the fleet entity [S53, S128].

Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 5.4 months of usable cash. The score is not a verdict on the technology; it is a verdict on what an investor can prove today. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 18 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, the lender agreement and the grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027 and the 2026 H-2A wage at $19.97, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S142].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. Financial position scores 3: of $3.7M of cash, $2.2M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run harvest crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. The exit record cuts both ways: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, but Root AI cleared at $60M in harvesting, and four of the five funded peers failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026, including Monarch Tractor, which raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money and sold its assets to Caterpillar 21 months later [S53, S178, S93, S176, S91].

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit | 85% or more on unselected blocks | Independent trial below 80% | -40% | High | A second grower leaves over quality | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | v4 unit cost at 300 units | $31,000-$33,000 | A quote above $36,000 | -25% to -35% | High | Design freeze slips past 2027-01 | S53 unverified |
| 3 | 2027 book | 360 robots at $12,700 or more | Fewer than 250 contracted by 2027-02 | -30% | High | 44% cover unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | Financing and covenant | $18M close by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill | A close after Q1 2027 or a $16M raise | -100% of equity | High | $4.0M of $18M committed at 2026-10-31 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | Labour policy | Wage floor keeps rising | H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze | -15% to -20% | Medium | DOL rulemaking on H-2A wages | S169 |
:::

The sensitivity analysis above ranks the five assumptions; the recommendation changes under the downside cases, and not by dilution. A market 50% smaller, at 25,000 acres, gives a $117.9M pool at list and $17.7M at 15% adoption, which kills $72M but leaves $48M-$55M defensible. Revenue 30% lower, at $3.9M instead of $5.6M, removes $0.87M of gross profit at a 52% RaaS margin and leaves end-2027 cash at $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M covenant, breached at the low end. Customer acquisition at twice the plan cannot be absorbed: 200 uncontracted robots have one selling window, four sales staff and a 5-of-14 pilot conversion record. Financing six months late adds $2.46M of burn and leaves $1.24M of cash on 2027-06-15, a secured-lender default rather than a down round. Only the bull case, at 12%, returns 3.3x-4.4x; the base case at $72M is 1.7x-2.8x and the bear is 0-1.0x at 50% [S53 unverified].

Position sizing is zero at $72M and $6M at $48M-$55M pre-money, with $6M released on 2027 milestones: an independent harvest-level trial above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and the Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test. The maximum loss is the full $12M; reserve $6M for a Series B. At $50M pre-money the same $12M buys 17.65% and returns 3.68x at a $250M exit, against 2.78x at $72M. Conditions precedent, not covenants: a Kestrel standstill or waiver signed with the term sheet, licence assignment consent, consolidation of the fleet entity and its grower contracts, and a second board seat with a veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control. Diligence next: a firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, and an insurer's view of product liability [S53, S128].

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Technology and product | 20% | 5 | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows; independent 72%-87%; no granted gripper patent; licence test on 2027-12-31 | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Market and timing | 15% | 6 | Labour cost real and rising; $235.7M pool at 100% adoption; acreage base unverified | S53 unverified, S141, S142 |
| Team and execution | 15% | 5 | Founder-market fit; CTO vacant since 2023-08-31; nine field staff against 45 needed; part-time CFO | S53 unverified |
| Business model and unit economics | 15% | 3 | -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500; $13,350 break-even; 44% of 2027 booked | S53 unverified |
| Financial position and cash | 10% | 3 | 5.4 months usable; covenant by 2027-03-14; 46% related-party revenue; 56% of ARR not recurring | S53 unverified |
| Valuation and terms | 15% | 2 | 27.7x FY2026E revenue; 51.4x contracted RaaS; $36.8M preference; no protective provisions | S53 unverified, S8, S12, S14, S95 |
| Exit path | 10% | 4 | OEM precedent of $60M-$305M; four of five peers failed or sold assets | S178, S176, S91, S115 |
| Composite | 100% | 4.1 | Weighted average of the seven dimensions | Derived from the rows above (S53, S8, S12, S14, S95) |

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 2.78x at $250M [S53 unverified].
2. The investable structure is $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M the same $12M buys 17.65% and returns 3.68x at a $250M exit [S53 unverified].
3. Harvest-level recovery decides the case: 75%-80% makes the machine a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes even $72M look cheap [S53 unverified, S56, S181].
:::

# Investor Reviewer Lens — Investment Committee Challenge

Use this lens after drafting the report and before final QA. The purpose is to simulate a skeptical investment committee partner who reads the report with fresh eyes and asks the uncomfortable questions that the analyst may have overlooked.

This is NOT the same as the red-team pass (which challenges the thesis at a strategic level). The investor reviewer focuses on **detail sharpness, completeness, and unverified claims**.

## Role

You are an experienced investment committee member with 20+ years of experience in both primary and secondary markets. You have reviewed thousands of investment memos and your specialty is finding the gaps — the competitor the analyst forgot, the founder detail that was glossed over, the market number that's cited without a source, the product comparison that's too vague to be useful.

You are skeptical but constructive. Your goal is not to kill the deal but to make the analysis bulletproof.

## Review Protocol

### Round 1: Completeness Sweep

Scan the entire report and flag anything missing or insufficient:

#### Company Overview
- [ ] Is the legal entity structure mapped with **exact ownership percentages**? If "approximately" or "estimated," flag it.
- [ ] Is the timeline specific (YYYY-MM or YYYY-MM-DD), or does it use vague language like "recently," "soon," "currently"?
- [ ] Does the cap table distinguish between share classes (ordinary, preferred A/B/C, super-voting)?
- [ ] Are liquidation preferences, anti-dilution provisions, and board composition addressed?
- [ ] Is the VIE structure (if any) explained with the names of nominee shareholders and the specific contracts?

#### Team
- [ ] For **each** founder and C-suite executive: is education specified (institution + degree + year)?
- [ ] For each: is the career chronology specific (company + role + dates + achievements), or just "worked at Google"?
- [ ] Are prior exits, patents, publications, and industry recognition listed?
- [ ] Is the "why this team for this problem" argument explicit and evidence-backed?
- [ ] Are reference check targets identified?

#### Technology & IP
- [ ] Are patents listed with **numbers, dates, jurisdictions, and legal status**?
- [ ] Is the technology explained in accessible but precise terms (not just buzzwords)?
- [ ] Is there a technology comparison table vs. competitors?
- [ ] Are third-party dependencies (APIs, cloud, hardware, licensed IP) identified?
- [ ] Is the TRL (Technology Readiness Level) assessed with evidence?

#### Products
- [ ] For **each** product: is the competitive alternative landscape mapped?
- [ ] For medical/biotech: is the current standard of care detailed with specific drugs/procedures, efficacy data, and limitations?
- [ ] For SaaS: is the customer's current workflow ("before this product") described?
- [ ] Are unit economics broken down (price, COGS, CAC, LTV, payback)?
- [ ] Are customer concentration risks quantified?

#### Market
- [ ] Is the market **bifurcated** into domestic and international (by region)?
- [ ] For each region: market size, growth rate, regulatory barriers, competitors?
- [ ] Are TAM/SAM/SOM built from bottom-up estimates, not just citing an industry report?
- [ ] Is the "why now" argument specific to this market and time?

#### Competition
- [ ] Are **ALL** material competitors listed? Challenge: "I can think of [X] — why aren't they here?"
- [ ] For each competitor: product comparison, funding, team, market share?
- [ ] Is the company's true differentiator clearly articulated vs. each major competitor?
- [ ] Are substitutes and "do nothing" (status quo) included as competitors?

#### Financials
- [ ] Are revenue/profit figures sourced and dated? If estimated, is this clearly stated?
- [ ] Are margins broken down by product line (not just blended)?
- [ ] Is burn rate, runway, and next financing need calculated?
- [ ] For public equities: are consensus estimates, guidance, and earnings surprise history included?

#### Valuation
- [ ] Are multiple valuation methods used (not just one)?
- [ ] Are comparable companies justified (not just cherry-picked to make the target look cheap)?
- [ ] Is the margin of safety explicitly calculated?

### Round 2: Claim Verification Challenge

For each **positive claim** in the report, ask:

1. **What is the exact source of this claim?** (Company pitch deck? Media article? Regulatory filing? Analyst estimate?)
2. **Has this claim been independently verified?** If only company-provided, mark as low-confidence.
3. **Is there a specific number or is it vague?** "Market-leading" → "What is the exact market share? From what year? According to whom?"
4. **Is the comparator fair?** "Better than competitors" → "Which competitors? On what dimension? Measured how?"

### Round 3: Missing Competitor Challenge

Actively think of competitors the analyst may have missed:

- **Geographic blind spot**: "You only listed US competitors. What about the Chinese company [X] doing the same thing at half the price?"
- **Adjacent entrant**: "Has [Amazon/Google/Tencent/Alibaba] shown any interest in this space? Could they enter with their existing infrastructure?"
- **Substitute**: "What if customers just use [manual process / generic tool / internal build] instead of buying this product?"
- **Open-source**: "Is there an open-source alternative that could commoditize this?"
- **Academic/lab**: "Are there research groups or university spin-outs working on the same problem?"

### Round 4: Product/Market Fit Challenge

- "What is the single hardest thing about selling this product? (Not building it — selling it.)"
- "Who is the actual budget owner? Does the buyer have authority to spend, or do they need approval from someone else?"
- "What is the typical sales cycle? Has it been validated with real customers or is it an estimate?"
- "If the product is so good, why aren't customers adopting it faster?"
- "What do the **lost deals** tell us? Which competitor did they choose and why?"

### Round 5: Number Stress-Test

For each key number in the report:

- "Where did this number come from? Is it a company projection, an industry average, or an analyst estimate?"
- "If this number is 30% worse than stated, does the investment thesis still hold?"
- "What is the range of estimates from different sources? If only one source, why?"
- "Is this number annual, quarterly, cumulative, or 'run-rate'? These are not the same thing."

## Output Format

The reviewer produces a structured challenge document at `_work/investor_review.md`:

| "[Quote]" | Media article from 2024 | Stale (>12 months old) | Search for updated data |

## Round 5: Number Stress-Test

## Overall Assessment

## Integration with Harness Loop

After the reviewer produces `_work/investor_review.md`:

1. The harness `gate` command checks that the review exists and that all "Critical" items are resolved
2. The analyst must address each item — either by adding the missing information, or by explicitly stating why it cannot be obtained
3. Unexplained "Critical" items block the gate
4. The loop re-runs the reviewer after each revision until no Critical items remain

### Reviewer Severity Levels

| Level | Gate Behavior |
|-------|--------------|
| **Critical** | Blocks gate. Must be resolved or explicitly acknowledged as unobtainable with confidence impact stated. |
| **Important** | Warning. Should be resolved but does not block gate. Unresolved items listed in report appendix as "areas for further diligence." |
| **Minor** | Informational. Does not block. |

## Reviewer Style Guide

The reviewer should be:

- **Specific, not generic.** "The competitor section is weak" → "You listed 3 competitors. I count at least 7 in this space: [A, B, C, D]. Also, what about the Chinese companies [E, F] that are doing this at 40% of the price point?"
- **Constructive, not destructive.** "This analysis is shallow" → "The unit economics section has the right structure, but needs: (1) actual CAC numbers broken down by channel, not a blended estimate; (2) LTV calculated from cohort data, not a top-down assumption; (3) payback period in months, not years."
- **Evidence-demanding, not evidence-replacing.** "You claim 80% market share. According to whom? What year? What geography? Consumer or enterprise? Units or revenue? If you can't source this, either find the data or downgrade the claim."
- **Investor-perspective, not academic.** "Interesting technology. But how does the company make money from it? What's the unit economics of one deployment? Who pays — the hospital, the insurer, or the patient? What's the reimbursement code?""}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 5 by Company Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,958 characters)
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding. All company facts below are unverified company material unless marked [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S129, S130].

The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo about $10M, and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 5 by Company Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,898 characters)
The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university, patent, employer or corporate record could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist to lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab, 2016-2021. She is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university; Orrin licenses two families, the other nine are unlicensed. Her career fits the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: no disclosed operating role outside academia, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014-2021 — 15 years running crews for berry growers. The customer list shows the conversion: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West); she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, while Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

We would not recommend leading at the proposed pre-money without those hires and a Kestrel estoppel; a smaller, tranched check at a lower price is the investable structure (company-provided, unverified).

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 7 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,965 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises, an auditable safety file and an enforceable estate are what justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Orrin's figures are unverified; benchmarks are independent.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement, as the WSU team concludes of its machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower, not a paper: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163], and 32 strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017 (S164). A machine that tears down without tools and swabs clean sells into retail audits; the 35% cost cut, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where cleanability gets traded away. One contamination or injury event would be existential for a five-customer vendor.

| Standard or rule | What it demands | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ISO 18497-1 and -4:2024 | Design and verification methods for autonomous farm machinery; voluntary, on the manufacturer | S166, S151 |
| 21 CFR 112.123 (FSMA) | Harvest equipment and food-contact surfaces kept clean; on the grower | S163, S153 |
| EU Regulation 2023/1230 and an Australian code | Frameworks Cal/OSHA examined alongside ISO 18497-style rules | S154 |

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either much of the downtime is unattended, a $48,000 asset standing still, or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season over four seasons, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — 27%, not the 60% projected. No hand-harvest cost per acre is disclosed, the number that would settle whether price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a 1986 US patent — so a routine rejection in crowded art points to a narrow allowance at best; the file wrapper was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed — Advanced Farm raised $25M, took a CNH investment and ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii in March 2025. An investor should condition the cheque on licence renewal at $12,700 or more, service cost below $2,500 and an office action leaving a claim standing.

| Status at 2026-10 | 64 robots, 5 growers | operating, 13 patents | ceased 2025; IP sold 2025 | S53 unverified, S1, S114, S115 |

| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 unverified, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 unverified |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry undisclosed | Platform copying | S53 unverified |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented | S53 unverified |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |

| Perception and labelled data | 5 | 1.9M images, but core families licensed and published | 2 years | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Gripper and slip sensing | 3 | Crowded art back to 1986; no allowed claim | 1 year | S130 |
