{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 2 by Lead Analyst, 6,311 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027 and the 2026 H-2A wage is $19.97 an hour, and an OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $2.2M of usable cash is 5.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 18 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, the pool 8.7x smaller than the headline, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 2.78x at $250M; at $48M-$55M the same $12M buys 17.65% and returns 2.2x-3.7x. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14 [S53, S8, S14].

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the 2026 California H-2A wage is $19.97 an hour [S53, S141, S142, S143]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M pre-money, 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue, Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 3.33x at $300M; a $12M cheque alone at $48M-$55M returns 2.4x-4.0x. The killer risks are visible: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision system classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms Orrin's field team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, so the claim is 132% of the US acreage base. The arithmetic follows: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 actually charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

After the independent challenge we moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts in 12 months — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 units at list, an 85% independent trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days to close. The bear is one domino with several symptoms: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. Without a minimum-cash test the failure mode is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |
:::

The five key assumptions below are ranked by expected damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: if it fails, the equity is worth zero, not diluted. The labour assumption now cuts both ways: the Department of Labor lowered the H-2A wage for many California jobs in October 2025, then the 2026-08-03 AEWR final rule set California at $19.97, just above the $19.75 AB 2646 floor. The file does not establish whether all-in hand-pick cost rose or fell year on year, so assumption 5 carries medium-low confidence, not medium, and the -15% to -20% impact stands as a downside [S169, S142].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, on unselected blocks | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80%, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 unverified |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor keeps rising: no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick cost advantage | Medium-low | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or a lower all-in hand-pick cost | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S169 |

History says the technology can exit and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after the first commercial unit in 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 after an assignment for creditors; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of five funded peers failed or sold assets in 2021-2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S176, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M, because the price capitalises a bull case that needs six conjuncts and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move the case. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence assignment consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post-money and earns 2.4x at a $150M exit and 4.0x at $250M; the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures hold only if the full $18M closes. If harvest-level recovery turns out above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm manufacturing quote at 300 units, the licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and consolidation of the fleet entity [S53, S128].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the 2026 California H-2A wage is $19.97 an hour [S53, S141, S142, S143]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M pre-money, 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue, Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M; a $12M cheque at $48M-$55M returns 2.4x-4.0x. Killer risks: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision system classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, 132% of the US acreage base. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 actually charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

After the independent challenge we moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 units at list, an 85% independent trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days left. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. Without a minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |
:::

The five assumptions are ranked by expected damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: if it fails, the equity is worth zero, not diluted. Labour now cuts both ways: the Department of Labor lowered the H-2A wage for many California jobs in October 2025, then the 2026-08-03 AEWR final rule set California at $19.97, just above the $19.75 AB 2646 floor. The file does not establish whether all-in hand-pick cost rose or fell year on year, so assumption 5 carries medium-low confidence, not medium, and the -15% to -20% impact stands as a downside [S169, S142].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, on unselected blocks | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80%, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 unverified |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor keeps rising: no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick cost advantage | Medium-low | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or a lower all-in hand-pick cost | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S169 |

History says the technology can exit and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 after an assignment for creditors; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of five funded peers failed or sold assets in 2021-2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S176, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M, because the price capitalises a six-conjunct bull case and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move the case. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence assignment consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post-money and earns 2.4x at a $150M exit and 4.0x at $250M; the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures hold only if the full $18M closes. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm 300-unit manufacturing quote, licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and fleet-entity consolidation [S53, S128].

Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 18 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, the pool 8.7x smaller than the headline, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 2.78x at $250M; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 2.4x-4.0x, while the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures need the full $18M. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

::: briefing
| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What it sells | 64 robots, 75 paid seasons and five paying growers at $9,500 a season in 2026 (company-reported, unverified); 110 robots contracted and 50 letters of intent for a 360-robot 2027 plan | S53 unverified |
| Performance | 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 selected rows with 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime (company); independent trials report 72%-87%, putting harvest-level recovery near 75%-80% | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350 | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |
:::

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. If the trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the right answer reverses and $72M is cheap [S53 unverified].

| Capital raised | $38.5M equity and notes; $0.65M grant; $2.5M equipment facility with $1.6M drawn | S53 unverified |
:::

::: one-question
What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?

The answer decides whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. At 75%-80% the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with clean bruising the same numbers become conservative and the round is financeable [S53, S56].
:::

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit [S53 unverified].
2. Reprice to $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.0x at a $250M exit, and without a minimum-cash covenant the case becomes Invest with conditions [S53 unverified].
3. The independent harvest-level trial is the gating measurement: 75%-80% makes this a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes it a crew replacement [S53 unverified, S56, S181].
:::

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 3 by Product Analyst, 8,659 characters)
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services and grants supplied $1.25M of $1.9M of revenue, and both stop by mid-2027 [S53]. What the Series A must therefore prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all of them company-reported and unverified in this review — the capital, the headcount and the unit economics do not yet reconcile. The plan is not implausible: 110 robots are contracted for 2027 and 50 more are under letters of intent. It asks for four step changes at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window.

### Services and grants pay the bills; neither survives 2027

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M (company-reported, unverified) comprised $0.95M of engineering services for Tallis, $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent [S53]. On the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, which at a $72M pre-money is 51x rather than the 22x the headline figure implies. The services line was rational while the fleet was sub-scale; it becomes a valuation problem the moment the round is priced on recurring revenue.

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified) [S53]. Against $3.7M of cash on 2026-09-30 and $410,000 of monthly net burn the company has nine months of runway before the round lands, while the Kestrel facility — $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5%, secured on the fleet — requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, a covenant that binds hardest during the build. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the entire fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage. Either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the projected 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. The governance picture compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but it means neither the revenue nor the cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition rather than an intention.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established pattern in this category is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries. Deere's 2025 annual report describes autonomy, machine learning and Solutions-as-a-Service as core to a small-agriculture strategy serving high-value and small-acreage crops, which is precisely where a berry picker would fit. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, which is exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. A standalone rental fleet at 360 robots has no precedent in this review: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, and Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B [S117, S8, S114, S115]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed, not a bet on a rental business reaching escape velocity alone.

At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M. It asks a Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not shown [S53].

The headline is not the operating price. The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M, not $72M. Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes since 2022 plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt, and enters with $3.7M of cash, $1.5M of which the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant makes unusable: $2.2M and 5.4 months of runway at $410,000 a month, with the covenant reached around 2027-03-14. The category discloses few valuations: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C in 2025, and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014; Advanced Farm Technologies raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech, which raised a reported $47.7M, sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. The October 2026 deck and its 2027-2028 projections are company-provided and unverified.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 4 by Valuation Analyst, 8,149 characters)
The realistic exit is a sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M, which at the $72M pre-money returns Meridian 1.7x-3.3x on unaudited company figures (unverified); the outcome depends on the 2027 Calder licence test and the first full commercial season, not on an IPO, and the category's own record — a shutdown and an asset sale among the named US strawberry-harvesting peers in 2025 — argues for setting the entry price to that range [S53, S114, S115].

| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven precision-ag platform gives it autonomy software; its 2022 stake in Advanced Farm Technologies ended with that company's 2025 closure, leaving no harvesting asset | 2028-2031 | Medium-low | S95, S117, S114 |

| Trade sale | AGCO or Trimble | Precision-ag software and guidance; no harvesting hardware or grower fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S12, S14 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling in a liquidation | 2027-2029 | Low as a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer | S53 unverified |
| Secondary sale | Later-stage agtech fund or family office | Buys Meridian's stake at a discount before a trade sale | 2028-2029 | Medium for partial liquidity | S53 unverified |

| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low | S53, S31 |

Deere is the most plausible buyer because it has already paid for autonomy twice and its FY2025 10-K lists GUSS among its businesses, but none of the three precedents bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network [S96, S92]. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option [S95]. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which put money into Advanced Farm Technologies' $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it cease operations in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company is both a reason to buy the next asset and a reason to demand proof, and it removes the easy assumption that an OEM will pay a strategic price for a pre-scale robot company.

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River Technology | 2017 | $305M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S96 |
| Deere / Bear Flag Robotics | 2021 | $250M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S92 |
| CNH / Raven Industries | 2021 | $2.1B enterprise value | 6.0x EV/Sales ($348.4M sales) | S95 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | not disclosed (indoor harvesting) | S91 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025 | IP, assets and engineering team; value not disclosed | n/a | S115 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | 2025 | ceased operations; no sale | n/a | S114 |
| Abundant Robotics | 2021 | IP and assets sold; $12M raised in total | n/a | S91 |

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the stereo ripeness model trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost [S53, unverified]. That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, which is the single date that determines whether a buyer is acquiring an exclusive technology or a commodity one. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031, a four-to-five-year hold from the Series A; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

The structural tests are as important as the buyer list. The Calder licence's assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the 2025 noteholders convert into Series A-1 and their consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, so the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts [S53, unverified]. A foreign buyer such as Kubota would face the same licence-consent and national-security diligence as a US buyer; the deck does not disclose whether the Calder patents or the robotics technology carry export-control or foreign-assignment restrictions, and that is a diligence item that could remove the most logical strategic buyer.

| Entry pre-money | Meridian stake for $12M | $150M exit | $250M exit | $300M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $72M (current) | 13.33% | $20.0M / 1.67x | $33.3M / 2.78x | $40.0M / 3.33x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | 17.65% | $26.5M / 2.21x | $44.1M / 3.68x | $52.9M / 4.41x | S53 unverified |

The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x over four to five years, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale returns 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.41x and 2.21x (company deck, S53; unverified). Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative and payable only if declared, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake that sits behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. Meridian should negotiate a drag-along and tag-along that make a trade sale executable without a founder veto, a right to consent to any change to the Calder licence or the Tallis manufacturing agreement, and a requirement that Kestrel be repaid or consented at closing.

The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota all have in-house autonomy programmes and can build a strawberry picker rather than buy one; the US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit — Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025, Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M — while the most recent harvesting-robot purchase, AppHarvest's $60M for Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices [S115, S114, S91]. Hardware exits trade below software, ag-equipment multiples are 1.0x-4.3x sales, and the industrial sector ETF is down 6.9% over three months, 8.1 points behind the S&P 500, so a 2029-2031 window is not assured [S31]. The exit thesis survives only if the 2027 licence test is cleared, the fleet works at 360 robots, and a buyer sees the strawberry dataset as the entry to other specialty crops; on the current price that is a 1.7x-3.3x outcome, which is why the round should be repriced or tranched rather than led at $72M."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 7 by Product Analyst, 8,965 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises, an auditable safety file and an enforceable estate are what justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Orrin's figures are unverified; benchmarks are independent.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement, as the WSU team concludes of its machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower, not a paper: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163], and 32 strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017 (S164). A machine that tears down without tools and swabs clean sells into retail audits; the 35% cost cut, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where cleanability gets traded away. One contamination or injury event would be existential for a five-customer vendor.

| Standard or rule | What it demands | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ISO 18497-1 and -4:2024 | Design and verification methods for autonomous farm machinery; voluntary, on the manufacturer | S166, S151 |
| 21 CFR 112.123 (FSMA) | Harvest equipment and food-contact surfaces kept clean; on the grower | S163, S153 |
| EU Regulation 2023/1230 and an Australian code | Frameworks Cal/OSHA examined alongside ISO 18497-style rules | S154 |

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

The Picker competes in three arenas, and only the first is a robot market. Tabletop and greenhouse systems (Tortuga, Agrobot, MetoMotion, Dogtooth) serve a different production system and are not direct competitors today.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs the grower nothing when it is not working, needs no capital and already meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin has to beat that on bruising before it beats it on cost, and one Florida grower's exit over bruising shows the bar is real. Among robot vendors, Harvest CROO is the closest threat: Florida-based, 13 patents, $10M raised over 14 rounds, $1.25M of NSF SBIR Phase II funding to build a commercial strawberry harvester, and a 2025-04-24 public claim that its open-field trials match human harvesting. ### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so every berry the cameras missed leaves the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and rows chosen by Orrin's field team; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a crew in year one, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team draws about its own machine — and the bruise rate has no hand-picked comparator [S53, S56, S42, S57].

The patents do not defend the position: the gripper application had every claim rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families are licensed from a university and become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The peers show what that costs: Monarch has raised over $220M and Carbon Robotics $232M across five rounds, while Advanced Farm's $25M Series B and Tortuga's $47.7M did not keep them independent. Orrin has raised $20.5M and is asking for $18M, 9% of Monarch's total [S54, S55, S119, S93, S115].

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025 after commercial deployments, and Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025. Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo about $10M, and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Founding Team & Key Personnel (team, revision 5 by Company Analyst, 8,898 characters)
The founding pair has real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant for 38 months, and no disclosed leader has taken a hardware fleet past 64 robots. That judgement rests on the deck: no university, patent, employer or corporate record could be retrieved, so every personal claim below is unverified company material (unverified) [S53].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, is the strongest technical credential: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010, a year at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011, then research scientist to lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab, 2016-2021. She is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university; Orrin licenses two families, the other nine are unlicensed. Her career fits the perception stack and the licence relationship, not commercial scale: no disclosed operating role outside academia, and she is both CEO and chair of a five-seat board. Key-person risk is high because the licence, the founding story and the perception roadmap all run through her (unverified) [S53].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial and operational half: a 2006 agricultural-business degree from Linden Valley College, harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014, then director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014-2021 — 15 years running crews for berry growers. The customer list shows the conversion: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027, and Pajaro Bluff took 16; together 53% of 2026 paid seasons. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales, and it creates a conflict: his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts (unverified) [S53].

The largest unexplained hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019 Calder field trials, left on 2023-08-31, keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after the round) and has no disclosed separation terms, release, IP assignment, non-compete or board role; the CTO seat has been open for 38 months. At 64 robots a VP Engineering can carry the organization; at 360, someone must own architecture, supplier qualification, reliability and the v4 design. The risk is not just hiring delay: a departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and the licence history is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor (unverified) [S53].

The hires below the founders are credible specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, has a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and 11 years at Corvane Robotics (2013-2024) moving from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005-2025 at Verdant Crop Sciences rising to regional sales director (West); she brings 20 years of agricultural selling but has four sales staff for five paying growers. Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016; part-time finance is thin for an $18M round, a secured facility with a cash covenant, a 2027 build and a 12% option pool (unverified) [S53].

On the matrix, the team scores high on technical depth and industry tenure and zero on prior exits; the gap is scaling and finance. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit, and only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin — $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots, and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, while Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge and Seabright, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder compensation and equity are not disclosed (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

We would not recommend leading at the proposed pre-money without those hires and a Kestrel estoppel; a smaller, tranched check at a lower price is the investable structure (company-provided, unverified).

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 5 by Market Analyst, 8,633 characters)
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, a claim resting on company-reported, unverified acreage, price and adoption inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not a $310M one, and the binding constraint is field performance rather than grower willingness to pay.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | How it is built | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified (company estimate) | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool at 100% adoption | Unverified; framing inconsistent | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M a year (2027 list price) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 acres per robot x $16,500 | Derived from unverified company inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified; not reachable in strawberries | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M at list, $27.2M at renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 an acre | Derived from unverified company inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

The $42B and $3.1B figures are labour-spend numbers, company-reported and unverified; only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price it needs 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline number. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption, 3.6x the stated figure; the implied adoption CAGR from 2% in 2028 to 15% in 2031 is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Robot price in picker-days at $180-$900 a day | Share of the 896 picker-days replaced per robot-season | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Company price, unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Company price, unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Company price, unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent in the table follows from the deck's own productivity, which is company-reported and unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day means 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. That growers have bought only at the bottom of the price ladder, and that one Florida grower left over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 3 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,930 characters)
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that is real yet reversible, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### The labour-policy tailwind is real but reversible

California's minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 and is scheduled at $17.40 for 2027; agricultural overtime has applied at 1.5 times the regular rate after eight hours a day and 40 hours a week since 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees [S141, S142, S143, S146, S157]. The H-2A floor is higher: the 2026 California adverse effect wage rate is reported at $19.97 an hour, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor for non-resident agricultural employees. A grower weighs the $9,500 robot-season against a 2027 list of $16,500 and renewals at $12,700, and against a crew whose marginal hour rises every January. Each rise in the wage floor widens Orrin's advantage because its cost per robot-season is fixed. An H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze would lower hand-pick cost and slow conversion. Florida is a second brake: a three-to-four-month season buys less utilisation than California's seven months; one Plant City grower paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and another exited over bruising. Confidence is high on the wage rules, medium on the two $19-plus floors.

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and wiring harnesses with seven staff, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost [S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build, 10% of the $9.9M budget [S144]. The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Company Overview (company_overview, revision 5 by Company Analyst, 8,958 characters)
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the round arithmetic is internally consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, so "legally clean" is a diligence item, not a finding. All company facts below are unverified company material unless marked [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, his employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm a $25M Series B, Harvest Croo about $10M, and Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence status and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 7 by Product Analyst, 8,965 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises, an auditable safety file and an enforceable estate are what justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Orrin's figures are unverified; benchmarks are independent.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system *classified as ripe*, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew, not a replacement, as the WSU team concludes of its machine.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick | none reported | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower, not a paper: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163], and 32 strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017 (S164). A machine that tears down without tools and swabs clean sells into retail audits; the 35% cost cut, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where cleanability gets traded away. One contamination or injury event would be existential for a five-customer vendor.

| Standard or rule | What it demands | Source |
|---|---|---|
| ISO 18497-1 and -4:2024 | Design and verification methods for autonomous farm machinery; voluntary, on the manufacturer | S166, S151 |
| 21 CFR 112.123 (FSMA) | Harvest equipment and food-contact surfaces kept clean; on the grower | S163, S153 |
| EU Regulation 2023/1230 and an Australian code | Frameworks Cal/OSHA examined alongside ISO 18497-style rules | S154 |

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either much of the downtime is unattended, a $48,000 asset standing still, or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season over four seasons, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. That contribution needs 74% more price ($16,500 in 2027), a 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and a 44% lower service cost ($1,750) to become a real margin, and even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation — 27%, not the 60% projected. No hand-harvest cost per acre is disclosed, the number that would settle whether price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented and the moat is the service organisation

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a 1986 US patent — so a routine rejection in crowded art points to a narrow allowance at best; the file wrapper was not obtained. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today and 360 planned, a binary 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed — Advanced Farm raised $25M, took a CNH investment and ceased operations in 2025; Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii in March 2025. An investor should condition the cheque on licence renewal at $12,700 or more, service cost below $2,500 and an office action leaving a claim standing.

**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); harvest recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. [S57]

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 report and an ATP swab record (S163, S166)."}],"isError":false}

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | How it is built | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

The $42B and $3.1B figures are labour-spend numbers, company-reported and unverified; only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price it needs 171%. | $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Company price, unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent in the table follows from the deck's own productivity, which is company-reported and unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day means 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. That growers have bought only at the bottom of the price ladder, and that one Florida grower left over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Not disclosed; part of 50,000 US acres (company estimate, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month season; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded from pilots | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day season cuts acres per robot to 2.0-2.5 | Harvest CROO, Florida-based | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue modelled | Not applicable | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA 2027 joint review; tariff treatment of cross-border machinery | Not applicable | S53, S148 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | Not applicable | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1 autonomous machinery safety; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months are what make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: the same 1.5 acres per 24 hours covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, consistent with picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day window covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Florida's value is utilisation: a robot working Florida in winter and California in summer would log two seasons a year and halve depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market: the wages that make a robot compelling in California make it less compelling in Guadalajara, and the exposure is trade policy. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers [S53, S148].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways. A handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book is concentrated in two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the 2026 H-2A Adverse Effect Wage Rate rule, published on 2026-08-03, resets the wage floor annually, and California's agricultural overtime rules raise peak-season cost. But certification volumes and wage levels were not retrievable, and if guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S145, S141, S161].

### What would settle it

Three inputs would move this from estimate to evidence: NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state for 2019-2025, the California Strawberry Commission's grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection rate and bruising against a hand-picked control. If acreage is stable and the pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the 2031 line re-bases upward and supports a services business at a lower valuation than the pre-money. If acreage is falling and realised price stays near the current contract, the strawberry market is small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs, the two figures the company has had the most incentive to round up.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported and unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap is not a rounding difference; it is a different market, and it needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
