{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 8,855 characters)
Orrin has the only disclosed paid fleet in open-field strawberry harvesting, but that lead is narrower than the deck's claim to be the only autonomous picker above 90%: the 94% is a conditional success rate on rows the company chose, on company-reported and unverified figures, and the category's record is one of well-funded failures and absorptions [S53]. The competitive question is whether Orrin can convert a two-season lead in paid deployments into contracted acres before Harvest CROO, an equipment maker or the hand crew closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and stage | Published performance | Price and model | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres | Fruit quality is the retail benchmark; no bruise rate published | Piece-rate or hourly wages; H-2A wage floor reset for 2026 | Near-100% of acres | Proven quality, no capex, crew flexes with volume | Wage floor and peak availability; overtime cost | S145, S141 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24 | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim; no rate published) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | A decade of NSF SBIR funding; Florida base; patents | No disclosed paid fleet, price or shipments | S1, S94, S97, S98 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple harvesting; commercial from 2019 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Exited 2025 | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments, $25M Series B, CNH investment | Ceased operations July 2025 | S93, S114, S116, S117 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Exited | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable open-field; IP and team acquired by Oishii 2025-03-24 | S115, S118 |
| Academic systems (WSU; Journal of Field Robotics) | Research prototypes | 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry; 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit | Not sold | None | Publish results and methods | Not commercial | S56, S42, S57 |
| Equipment makers (Deere, CNH) | Autonomous platforms and see-and-spray | No berry or robotic-harvest product in Deere's FY2025 10-K | Not applicable | None in berries | Capital, dealer network, acquisition record | Not in this crop today | S8, S92, S95, S96 |

The Picker competes in three arenas, and only the first is a robot market. The hand crew picks nearly every US acre and is not standing still: harvest-aid platforms make pickers faster while keeping the crew, and the H-2A wage floor is reset annually. Open-field robots are the second arena, where the table shows one long-funded competitor and one well-funded failure. Tabletop and greenhouse systems (Tortuga, Agrobot, MetoMotion, Dogtooth) serve a different production system and are not direct competitors today.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs the grower nothing when it is not working, needs no capital and already meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin has to beat that on bruising before it beats it on cost, and one Florida grower's exit over bruising shows the bar is real. Among robot vendors, Harvest CROO is the closest threat: Florida-based, 13 patents, $10M raised over 14 rounds, $1.25M of NSF SBIR Phase II funding to build a commercial strawberry harvester, and a 2025-04-24 public claim that its open-field trials match human harvesting. Its weakness is disclosure — no paid fleet, price or shipment figure — which is also Orrin's opportunity: the first vendor to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference point for growers and acquirers [S1, S94, S97, S98].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so every berry the cameras missed leaves the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and rows chosen by Orrin's field team; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a crew in year one, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team draws about its own machine — and the bruise rate has no hand-picked comparator [S53, S56, S42, S57].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: the gripper application had every claim rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families are licensed from a university and become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. What is hard to copy is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots across two states. The peers show what that costs: Monarch has raised over $220M and Carbon Robotics $232M across five rounds, while Advanced Farm's $25M Series B and Tortuga's $47.7M did not keep them independent. Orrin has raised $20.5M and is asking for $18M, 9% of Monarch's total [S54, S55, S119, S93, S115].

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025 after commercial deployments, and Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025. The exits that did happen went to equipment makers: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries in 2021. Deere's FY2025 10-K business description mentions no berry or robotic-harvesting product, so the OEM threat today is capital and acquisition appetite rather than a competing machine. That record supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and it argues for pricing the round on contracted acres rather than on a technology lead [S91, S92, S95, S96, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Orrin's position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Challenger | Hand crews and H-2A | Orrin Fieldworks: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons | Harvest CROO, Florida: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | Equipment makers and greenhouse-robot vendors moving outdoors | S53, S1, S8 |

Orrin's wedge — Robots-as-a-Service with no grower capital, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, the economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route to scale. Orrin wins if the fleet proves fruit quality at scale in 2027 and the contracted renewal robots convert at the higher price; it loses if Harvest CROO or an equipment maker demonstrates a fleet first. No private vendor discloses audited performance, price or shipments; every share statement is an absence of evidence.

::: evidence
**The "only open-field picker above 90%" claim is a measurement definition, not a moat. (S53)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin's field team selected and excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe or pluckable fruit, and the commercial record includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 claim of performance on par with human harvesting, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B and Tortuga's sale to Oishii [S53, S56, S42, S1, S114, S115].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 4 by Valuation Analyst, 8,149 characters)
The realistic exit is a sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M, which at the $72M pre-money returns Meridian 1.7x-3.3x on unaudited company figures (unverified); the outcome depends on the 2027 Calder licence test and the first full commercial season, not on an IPO, and the category's own record — a shutdown and an asset sale among the named US strawberry-harvesting peers in 2025 — argues for setting the entry price to that range [S53, S114, S115].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | Deere & Company | Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021) and GUSS in its autonomy portfolio; lacks a specialty-crop harvesting robot and the labelled strawberry dataset | 2028-2031 | Medium | S96, S92, S8 |
| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven precision-ag platform gives it autonomy software; its 2022 stake in Advanced Farm Technologies ended with that company's 2025 closure, leaving no harvesting asset | 2028-2031 | Medium-low | S95, S117, S114 |
| Trade sale | Kubota | Backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in 2021 and saw it cease operations in July 2025; needs a specialty-crop harvesting asset | 2029-2031 | Low-medium | S93, S114 |
| Strategic | Yamaha Motor | Co-investor in Advanced Farm's 2021 Series B; outdoor-power equipment and robotics, no US harvesting platform | 2029-2031 | Low | S93 |
| Trade sale | AGCO or Trimble | Precision-ag software and guidance; no harvesting hardware or grower fleet | 2029-2031 | Low | S12, S14 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling in a liquidation | 2027-2029 | Low as a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer | S53 unverified |
| Secondary sale | Later-stage agtech fund or family office | Buys Meridian's stake at a discount before a trade sale | 2028-2029 | Medium for partial liquidity | S53 unverified |
| Private equity | Paine Schwartz Partners ($5.7B AUM, $1.7B Fund VI) or similar | Needs positive EBITDA and fleet-level cash flow; the FY2028 plan still loses $6.9M | 2030-2032 | Low | S167, S53 |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low | S53, S31 |

Deere is the most plausible buyer because it has already paid for autonomy twice and its FY2025 10-K lists GUSS among its businesses, but none of the three precedents bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network [S96, S92]. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option [S95]. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which put money into Advanced Farm Technologies' $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it cease operations in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company is both a reason to buy the next asset and a reason to demand proof, and it removes the easy assumption that an OEM will pay a strategic price for a pre-scale robot company.

| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | not disclosed (indoor harvesting) | S91 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025 | IP, assets and engineering team; value not disclosed | n/a | S115 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | 2025 | ceased operations; no sale | n/a | S114 |
| Abundant Robotics | 2021 | IP and assets sold; $12M raised in total | n/a | S91 |

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the stereo ripeness model trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost [S53, unverified]. That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, which is the single date that determines whether a buyer is acquiring an exclusive technology or a commodity one. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031, a four-to-five-year hold from the Series A; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

The structural tests are as important as the buyer list. The Calder licence's assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the 2025 noteholders convert into Series A-1 and their consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, so the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts [S53, unverified]. A foreign buyer such as Kubota would face the same licence-consent and national-security diligence as a US buyer; the deck does not disclose whether the Calder patents or the robotics technology carry export-control or foreign-assignment restrictions, and that is a diligence item that could remove the most logical strategic buyer.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $72M (current) | 13.33% | $20.0M / 1.67x | $33.3M / 2.78x | $40.0M / 3.33x | S53 unverified |

The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x over four to five years, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale returns 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.41x and 2.21x (company deck, S53; unverified). Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative and payable only if declared, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake that sits behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. Meridian should negotiate a drag-along and tag-along that make a trade sale executable without a founder veto, a right to consent to any change to the Calder licence or the Tallis manufacturing agreement, and a requirement that Kestrel be repaid or consented at closing.

The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota all have in-house autonomy programmes and can build a strawberry picker rather than buy one; the US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit — Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025, Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M — while the most recent harvesting-robot purchase, AppHarvest's $60M for Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices [S115, S114, S91]. Hardware exits trade below software, ag-equipment multiples are 1.0x-4.3x sales, and the industrial sector ETF is down 6.9% over three months, 8.1 points behind the S&P 500, so a 2029-2031 window is not assured [S31]. The exit thesis survives only if the 2027 licence test is cleared, the fleet works at 360 robots, and a buyer sees the strawberry dataset as the entry to other specialty crops; on the current price that is a 1.7x-3.3x outcome, which is why the round should be repriced or tranched rather than led at $72M."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 3 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,930 characters)
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that is real yet reversible, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### The labour-policy tailwind is real but reversible

California's minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 and is scheduled at $17.40 for 2027; agricultural overtime has applied at 1.5 times the regular rate after eight hours a day and 40 hours a week since 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees [S141, S142, S143, S146, S157]. The H-2A floor is higher: the 2026 California adverse effect wage rate is reported at $19.97 an hour, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor for non-resident agricultural employees. A grower weighs the $9,500 robot-season against a 2027 list of $16,500 and renewals at $12,700, and against a crew whose marginal hour rises every January. Each rise in the wage floor widens Orrin's advantage because its cost per robot-season is fixed. An H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze would lower hand-pick cost and slow conversion. Florida is a second brake: a three-to-four-month season buys less utilisation than California's seven months; one Plant City grower paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and another exited over bruising. Confidence is high on the wage rules, medium on the two $19-plus floors.

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and wiring harnesses with seven staff, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost [S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build, 10% of the $9.9M budget [S144]. Secondary trackers disagree on the surcharge: one holds a 25% IEEPA duty still applies, another that a 10% Section 122 charge replaced it on 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no published outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was found. The implication is a closing condition: USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the undisclosed Tallis v4 build.

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising [S151, S153, S154]. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires equipment and food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's sanitation audit. Safety is standards-led: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed it alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs.

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record is more decision-relevant than any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor [S144]. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05, and the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30, the day before this assessment, while the October 2026 deck called it not yet decided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights.

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium [S155, S158, S159]. PTU is profit-linked but immaterial at seven staff. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel reporting an executive order that pushes agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime was identified that binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions.

Agrist: Series B (2025-09-17), rail-guided greenhouse, bell pepper and cucumber, 55% harvest rate in field trials (vendor-stated), Japan only, 6 announced deployments (JA co-ops), funding FaaS rental. Not strawberry, not open-field; a direct analogue only in the sense of "harvest robot with paid rentals," but a different production system and crop. Verification: vendor-stated specs, aggregator-reviewable; no audited performance.

Four Growers: greenhouse tomatoes/peppers/cucumbers, "working closely with various greenhouse growers to develop a tomato harvesting robot", two filed patents, 8 stereo cameras. So: pre-commercial development, filed (not granted) patents, no paid fleet disclosed. Funding $15.1M per Tracxn. Verification: company site says "developing"; Tracxn aggregator says $15.1M.

Carbon Robotics: laser weeding, not harvesting; 100+ growers claim; funding aggregated. Its relevance: manufacturing at scale and dealer/OEM distribution. I'd like a unit count. Let me check the startuply article? Denied earlier. I could search... I've used 5 searches. One left. Hmm, maybe not needed: I can rely on the snippet from Startuply ("now sold... 100 growers across three continents") — but I can't cite a snippet-only source? I can register the Startuply article if my search returned it. N1 allows: "a page your web search returned". The earlier denial was for web_fetch, not registration. But citing a source whose content I only have as a snippet is weak; I'd label it as trade-press and unverified. Better: register the Startuply article as independent with medium/low confidence, claims "100 growers across three continents, 30 lasers, 200,000 weeds/hour" — snippet supports it. Alternatively, skip the unit claim and describe Carbon Robotics' relevance with the funding and product record only (carbonrobotics.com: LaserWeeder, first unit March 2021, commercially sold). Hmm, the snippet from carbonrobotics.com/laserweeder says "First Autonomous LaserWeeder Unit Introduced in March of 2021 ... Used for field demos only - not for commercial sale." That is a primary-ish datum.

For the screening, the key analytical point for each:
- Agrist: nearest analogue in business model (FaaS rentals to co-ops) but rail-guided greenhouse in Japan, peppers and cucumbers; vendor-stated 55% harvest rate; Series B 2025-09-17; not a strawberry competitor and no evidence of open-field capability. Verification: company-stated performance, deployment announcements from co-ops; funding round from a tracker citing The Bridge.
- Four Growers: greenhouse tomatoes, development stage ("working closely with growers to develop"), two filed patents (company claim), $15.1M raised (Tracxn); not a competitor in open-field strawberries; but it shows the capital needed to reach a single-crop harvest product ($15M and still pre-commercial), which supports the point that $16M for Orrin is roughly one product cycle.
- Carbon Robotics: laser weeding, not harvesting; the manufacturing/distribution proof point: ~100 growers across three continents (trade press), 30 lasers, 200,000 weeds/hour; $157M through the 2024-10 Series D, aggregators disagree thereafter ($232M-$276M). Relevance to Orrin: it shows the scale of capital and distribution needed, and that non-harvest field robotics reached commercial scale before harvesting did — the picking problem (contact with fragile fruit) is where the value and the failure are.

Now for the IP discussion: Carbon Robotics has patents? Four Growers has two filed patents. Agrist presumably patents. The screen for IP: none of the three threatens Orrin's freedom to operate in soft grippers with slip sensing; they operate in different end-effectors (laser, tomato gripper, pepper rail robot). But their presence means Orrin's IP value is limited to a crowded niche.

I should also check the single Monarch record: S54 press release $133M Series C, over $220M raised to date (2025). Financials says "Monarch over $220M" — consistent. Competition says "Monarch has raised over $220M" — consistent. So I'll use S54 exactly: $133M Series C in 2025, over $220M raised to date. Fine.

Now the strategy CRITICAL: runway statement. Section 7 says $3.7M at 2026-09-30, $410k/month burn, $1.5M covenant ⇒ $2.2M usable, 5.4 months, covenant reached 2027-03-14. ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that is real yet reversible, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### The labour-policy tailwind is real but reversible

California's minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 and is scheduled at $17.40 for 2027; agricultural overtime has applied at 1.5 times the regular rate after eight hours a day and 40 hours a week since 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees [S141, S142, S143, S146, S157]. The H-2A floor is higher: the 2026 California adverse effect wage rate is reported at $19.97 an hour, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor for non-resident agricultural employees. A grower weighs the $9,500 robot-season against a 2027 list of $16,500 and renewals at $12,700, and against a crew whose marginal hour rises every January. Each rise in the wage floor widens Orrin's advantage because its cost per robot-season is fixed. An H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze would lower hand-pick cost and slow conversion. Florida is a second brake: a three-to-four-month season buys less utilisation than California's seven months; one Plant City grower paid for 11 robots in 2025-26 and another exited over bruising. Confidence is high on the wage rules, medium on the two $19-plus floors.

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and wiring harnesses with seven staff, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost [S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build, 10% of the $9.9M budget [S144]. Secondary trackers disagree on the surcharge: one holds a 25% IEEPA duty still applies, another that a 10% Section 122 charge replaced it on 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no published outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was found. The implication is a closing condition: USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the undisclosed Tallis v4 build.

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising [S151, S153, S154]. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires equipment and food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's sanitation audit. Safety is standards-led: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design and verification requirements for autonomous agricultural machinery, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed it alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs.

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record is more decision-relevant than any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor [S144]. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05, and the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30, the day before this assessment, while the October 2026 deck called it not yet decided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights.

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium [S155, S158, S159]. PTU is profit-linked but immaterial at seven staff. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel reporting an executive order that pushes agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime was identified that binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions.

, /PRNewswire/ -- Monarch Tractor, creator of the MK-V, the world's first fully electric, driver-optional smart tractor and Wingspan Ag Intelligence (WingspanAI) farm management platform, has today announced a history-making $133 million Series C, making it the largest funding raising round in agricultural robotics history.

 Monarch Tractor's MK-V all electric tractor with autonomous and data driven features. Utilized in specialty crops such as orchards, vineyards and also used for land management.

 Night time vineyard harvest with Monarch Tractor's all electric, autonomous, data driven MK-V electric tractor. With up to 14 hours run time and a swappable battery, the MK-V can operate around the clock.

 Monarch Tractor's MK-V electric tractor with implement attached and ready for work.

Monarch has quickly become a powerhouse within the agricultural space as an off-road electric vehicles (EV) and autonomous vehicles (AV) category leader. To date, the company has raised over $220 million to enable clean, efficient, and economically viable solutions as well as expanded into various agricultural markets such as vineyards, dairy, berries, orchards, and land management across 12 states and three countries. Furthermore, in just the last two years alone they have been recognized as an influential force in farming at national and international levels via accolades, including Forbes Next Billion-Dollar Startups, CNBC Disruptor 50, TIME Best Inventions, and Fast Company World's Most Innovative Companies.

The Series C funds will support the further development of Monarch's cutting-edge AI product offering, expansion of their operational footprint domestically and globally, while enabling the company's path to profitability.

Funding was co-led by global impact investor Astanor and HH-CTBC Partnership, L.P., with additional support from prominent investors, including At One Ventures, PMV and The Welvaartsfonds.
Monarch's mission with farmer success at the center
Founded on the belief that food security only exists with planet sustainability and farmer profitability, Monarch has been at the forefront of the critical transition to renewably powered and more profitable farming ecosystems, which ultimately empowers farmers worldwide.
In the United States, farm profitability has steadily declined over the past decade, with the sharpest decline in industry history occurring in 2023. Given the nascent nature of technology in agriculture, the sector is ripe with untapped growth potential across automation, digital technologies and AI efficiencies, with Monarch at the forefront of this disruption and technological advancement.
"Driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and electrification, agriculture has arrived as the next frontier for the energy transition and sustainability movement," said Praveen Penmetsa, CEO and co-founder of Monarch Tractor. "Agriculture is our planet's most important and overlooked sector, and those in the industry have faced significant challenges, including farm profitability, labor shortages, worker safety, government headwinds, data availability, and scrutiny for sustainability demands. Monarch's application of AI and introduction of a smart, electric platform will deliver robust social, economic, and environmental returns to farmers."
AI continues to revolutionize farming machinery
Tractors have been the center of all farm operations for several decades. Yet, they've been underutilized as a hub for robotics innovation and farmer payback.
In December 2022, Monarch released the world's first fully electric, driver-optional, smart tractor, the MK-V, to combat profit challenges, address sustainability demands, and revive agriculture innovation. Since then, the deployment of more than 400 MK-V's have helped; resulting in more than 850 tonnes of harmful CO2 emissions offset across 42,000 hours of tractor operations.
Monarch's WingspanAI app is equipping farmers with unprecedented access to on-farm data, integrating a farm management system, vehicle position tracking, crop image collection, and automated operations planning into one platform. The continual development of product solutions, including the introduction of new AI capabilities, will be the driving force in closing the industry's profit gap.
This funding round will support the expansion of Monarch's digital solutions and AI applications, including the development of Autodrive, Monarch's autonomous operations feature, for new global markets and crop sectors.

{"url":"https://www.tigervcfunds.com/post/the-outlier-problem-understanding-the-real-distribution-of-venture-returns","title":"The Outlier Problem: Understanding the Real Distribution of Venture Returns","text":"Notoriously, venture capital is at the mercy of “Power Law” distribution. Correlation Ventures, a firm taking a data driven approach to investing, analyzed over 21,000 funds in the US venture market from 2004 to 2013, determining the returns each generated as a multiple of the value of the fund. What they found is a sobering reality.  A majority, ~65%, failed to generate even 1x return(the value of the fund), and only 4% generated a return of 10x or more, the classic benchmark for a company “hitting it big”. Venture capital’s distribution “Power Law” continues to affect the industry today, 13 years later. Given this market reality, VC firms construct their portfolios to maximize companies in the 4% “home run” returns, while minimizing investments failing to return even 1x the fund. Firms try to accomplish this by investing in 20 to 30 companies, with a focus on balancing risk with diversification. Diversification is a key part of portfolio construction because it can minimize losses. Fund portfolios can be diversified across industry sectors, funding stage, company geographic locations, and investing timing, all protecting the fund against unique negative market forces.Investing across industry sectors enables the firm to capitalize on an industry taking off due to a new invention, while minimizing losing funds to an industry that suddenly enters an unexpected recession. Diversifying across funding stages means a VC firm doesn’t only invest in early stage start-ups, but also later funding round companies, balancing risky investments with more proven companies. Investing in varying geographic locations minimizes facing regional market issues, and increases chances of capitalizing on a global opportunity. Finally, diversification in the timing of investments, known as “initial” and “follow-on” investments, enables the VC firm to put ownership stake in a company with an \"initial\" investment, and then using 50%-70% of its remaining capital, to put in a “follow-on” investment in later funding rounds towards companies that have shown high revenue potential or in the General Partners(GPs) opinion just need more time and money. The above ways of diversifying a portfolio benefit both the fund manager and limited partners by limiting losses and maximizing success. However, there is an advantage to diversification which does not benefit limited partners, and it has played out most notably in significantly longer holding periods before GPs attempt an IPO.Diversification helps ward off “psychological ruin”. Steve Kim, a managing partner at Verdis Investment Management, states \"psychological ruin” is when a VC firm quits a fund due to poor returns. Diversification combats this by allowing fund managers to see moderate wins from some companies in the fund, providing positive reinforcement of their investing strategy and giving them confidence to not throw in the towel. As Mr. Kim states, “Power Laws take years to materialize. The critical question isn’t ‘What’s my expected value?’ It’s ‘Will I survive long enough to realize it?’” Diversification benefits skew in favor of the fund managers, because they are comfortable waiting over a decade for a company to generate 10x returns, while limited partners see few returns in that time. If a limited partners(LPs) investment does generate 10x returns on an IPO or acquisition, the reality of the returns the LP actually sees isn’t great in traditional venture capital business models. VC firms typically promise investors 2.5x returns on their investment after management fees and the VC firms share of profits. In comparison, the stock market usually generates a 1.6x return over a 5 year period. This makes a 2.5x return a good deal to the limited partner, because they get higher return in exchange for being locked in to a longer time frame, and making a riskier investment in a start-up. However, data reveals LPs rarely see the 2.5x returns promised. Cambridge Associates and the National Bureau of Economic Research(NBER) tracked VC returns from over 1,500 and over 1,300 firms respectively, from a period 1984 to 2020. The results of that study are in the chart below:As you can see, since 1984 a significant majority of the time LPs did not receive 2.5x return on their investments. Returns usually averaged much lower, with many years barely reaching 2x. It should be noted that the top 25% performing funds averaged 5.34x returns from 1984 to 2000 and 3.84x from 2001 to 2020. However, the remaining 75% of funds over this 36 year period did not reach a 2.5x return. This reveals the reality of a LPs experience in traditional venture capital, a lack of even exchange of value between the LP and VC firm.It’s clear from the data that investors need to take charge of their investing strategy, and actively avoid traditional VC firm business models. Tiger Venture Capital Management built a completely different model, one that actually aligns with investors and is meant to provide sustainable, long-term returns - independent of exits. The Department of Labor published updated Adverse Effect Wage Rates for H-2A farmworkers on August 3, 2026, and the new rates take effect the same day they hit the Federal Register. The notice, issued by the Employment and Training Administration at 91 FR 48946, also resets the national average AEWR used to size surety bonds for H-2A Labor Contractors to $15.96 per hour, down from the $17.74 in place since January 1, 2025. That is a cut of $1.78 an hour, roughly 10 percent, in one update.

The AEWR is not a suggestion. It is the floor an H-2A employer must offer in the job order, advertise during domestic recruitment, and actually pay to both H-2A workers and any U.S. workers in corresponding employment. Under 20 CFR 655.120 and 655.122(l), employers in non-range occupations must pay at least the highest of the AEWR, the applicable prevailing wage, the collective bargaining rate, the federal minimum wage, or the state minimum wage.

There are two effective dates, not one. The rates apply nationally on August 3, 2026. For employers and states covered by the court order in Kansas et al. v. U.S. Department of Labor, 749 F. Supp. 3d 1363 (S.D. Ga. 2024), the same rates instead take effect on August 17, 2026. That two week gap has become a standing feature of AEWR notices since the Southern District of Georgia enjoined the 2024 Farmworker Protection Rule in 17 plaintiff states.

DOL set new H-2A adverse effect wage rates effective August 3, 2026, with the average AEWR for surety bonds falling to $15.96 an hour.

Those 17 states are Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Virginia. Several are among the heaviest users of the H-2A program, so the later date covers a large share of certified positions.

The notice itself prints no state table. DOL directs employers to a searchable spreadsheet at flag.dol.gov/wage-data/adverse-effect-wage-rates, where rates can be looked up by state or territory and by Standard Occupational Classification code. Brian Pasternak, Administrator of the Office of Foreign Labor Certification, is listed as the contact. Marek Laco, Acting Assistant Secretary for Employment and Training, signed the three-page notice.

The numbers come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics survey, not the Department of Agriculture Farm Labor Survey that set AEWRs for decades. DOL made that switch in an interim final rule published October 2, 2025 at 90 FR 47914. This August notice is the first full annual refresh under that methodology, and it uses the OEWS release of May 15, 2026, which carries May 2025 wage estimates.

Two Skill Levels, One Housing Deduction

Job orders filed on or after August 3, 2026 use the new rates. Employers and states covered by the Kansas v. DOL order get until August 17, 2026.

The OEWS methodology splits every state into two rates instead of one. A Skill Level I AEWR applies to entry-level job opportunities where workers need no formal education or specialized training credentials. A Skill Level II AEWR applies where the employer requires qualifications typical of experienced or fully proficient workers. DOL computes Skill Level I at the equivalent of the 17th percentile of the occupational wage distribution, the same convention used for skill-based prevailing wages in other visa programs.

Most H-2A jobs still fall inside the field and livestock workers (combined) category, which aggregates five SOC codes: 45-2041, 45-2091, 45-2092, 45-2093 and 53-7064. Where OEWS reports no statewide figure at a given skill level, the national average for that level applies instead.

The notice also updates the statewide downward compensation adjustments allowed under 20 CFR 655.120(b)(3). Those deductions apply only to H-2A workers who receive housing at no cost, and they can shave another dollar or more off the hourly rate. In California the adjustment has run as much as $3.00 an hour, in Hawaii $3.18, and in Alabama $1.20.

How Far Rates Fell When DOL Switched Surveys

The August 3 update sits on top of a much larger repricing that already happened. When the OEWS methodology replaced the Farm Labor Survey in October 2025, published entry-level rates dropped by double digits in nearly every major H-2A state. The Mid-Contract Rule Employers Keep Getting Wrong

A lower AEWR does not reduce pay mid-contract. Under 20 CFR 655.120(b)(6), employers must keep paying the wage guaranteed on the existing job order.

An updated AEWR does not automatically let an employer cut pay mid-season. The regulation runs one direction only. Under 20 CFR 655.120(b)(5), if the new AEWR is higher than the rate an employer has been paying, the employer must move to the higher rate on the effective date. Under 20 CFR 655.120(b)(6), if the new AEWR comes in lower than the wage guaranteed on the job order, the employer must keep paying the guaranteed job order wage for the rest of the contract.

For a grower running a summer contract signed at the previous rate, the August reduction generally does not bite until the next job order. Employers filing new Forms ETA-790 and 790A after the effective date get the new numbers.

What a Lower Floor Means for Workers

The AEWR protects U.S. workers, not just visa holders. Because employers must pay the same rate to anyone in corresponding employment, a lower AEWR pulls down the floor for domestic farmworkers on the same crew. That is the mechanism behind the multi-billion dollar estimates on both sides of this fight.

State minimum wage law still backstops the floor in higher-wage states. A California entry-level AEWR of $16.45 sits above the state minimum, so the AEWR governs. In Alabama, Louisiana and Mississippi, which have no state minimum wage, the entry-level AEWRs of $11.25, $9.59 and $9.74 are the only meaningful floor above the $7.25 federal minimum. {"url":"https://www.agalert.com/california-ag-news/archives/june-3-2026/h-2a-rule-change-puts-spotlight-on-work-visa-program/","title":"H-2A rule change puts spotlight on work visa program","text":"By Caleb Hampton

After years of rising labor costs, some farmers have seen relief during the past several months, with those who hire foreign guestworkers benefiting from a Trump administration rule implemented last October. 

The new rule changed how the H-2A program’s minimum wage, called the Adverse Effect Wage Rate, is calculated, effectively lowering it in California from $19.97 to the state minimum wage of $16.90.

According to research by Zachariah Rutledge, assistant professor and extension specialist at Michigan State University, farmers in California could save up to $100 million this year if every employer were to reduce pay for guestworkers to the state minimum wage.

Overall farm labor costs in California are about $18 billion a year, including $655 million in wages paid to H-2A workers, according to federal data. 

Last month, Rutledge presented research showing that in the first six months after the wage rule was implemented, about 70% of H-2A employers in California adjusted pay to match the new minimum of $16.90 an hour.

He said that while some employers may opt to pay more than the minimum to retain workers or boost morale, he expects that as the year progresses, “more employers will move down to that state minimum wage” to take advantage of the new rule. 

However, that’s only if the rule survives multiple challenges it faces in California. 

In December, the United Farm Workers filed a lawsuit, claiming the new H-2A wage rule is illegal. On May 13, a federal court denied the union’s motion for a preliminary injunction, allowing the rule to remain in effect as the case plays out. 

Meanwhile, legislation written as a countermeasure passed the Assembly last month. Assembly Bill 2646, authored by Assemblymember Maggy Krell, D-Sacramento, would establish a state minimum wage of $19.75 for agricultural guestworkers. As with the H-2A program, that wage would also apply to “corresponding” local workers hired by the same employer. 

Krell said last month on the Assembly floor that the legislation, which is supported by UFW, is intended to bring financial relief to farmworkers struggling to make ends meet. 

“This is a bottom line wage that’ll help our farmworkers who bring so much to California,” she said. 

Bryan Little, senior director of policy advocacy and federal affairs lead at the California Farm Bureau, which opposes the bill, said the proposed state law is worded such that it would apply to a broader group of corresponding local workers than does the federal H-2A wage law. 

“It’s going to wind up in some areas being effectively a super minimum wage for agriculture,” Little said, adding that the expense to farmers could raise food prices. 

To become law, AB 2646 would need to pass the state Senate and be signed by the governor. 

Nationwide, the H-2A program has grown rapidly in recent years, with the number of workers more than doubling in the past decade, according to data from the U.S. Department of Labor. 

Experts project that within the next few years the number of H-2A workers in the U.S. will surpass the size of the historic Bracero program at its peak of around 450,000 workers in the late 1950s. 

Use of the H-2A program is especially high in southeastern states such as Florida, Georgia and North Carolina, while California’s use of guestworkers remains comparatively small. As of last year, H-2A workers comprised about 20% of the U.S. farm workforce but just 5% of farmworkers in California, according to federal data. 

Little said the program is nonetheless important for farmers in the state as it reduces the risk of untimely labor shortages for growers of perishable commodities.

“It provides an emergency source of labor if you don’t have enough people to do what you need to do at any given time or any given place,” he said. 

Last month, researchers at an annual farm labor conference at the University of California, Davis, said California could be a focal point of future expansion of the visa program.

The state’s labor-intensive specialty crops make it a national hub for farm work. And while California is currently home to many experienced farmworkers, research has shown that for the most part their children are not entering the field, nor are other young Americans.

Those factors mean the state is a likely “growth sector for H-2A,” said Philip Martin, professor emeritus of agricultural and resource economics at UC Davis. 

Martin said that as local farmworkers age out of the workforce, the void will likely be filled by some balance of foreign guestworkers, automation and imported produce. He said policies such as the recent change to the H-2A minimum wage could influence that balance. 

“We’ve got different factors working, and they interact with each other,” he said. “If you lower the wages for migrant H-2A workers, that’s an incentive to hire more. If you subsidize mechanization, you’re likely to get more of it.”

For now, Little said it remains unclear whether the rule change will immediately result in greater numbers of H-2A workers coming to California.  

Many farmers are struggling from years of depressed commodity prices. And despite the new H-2A rule, the program remains costly for employers, who on top of paying minimum wage must provide workers with food, housing and transportation. 

“That, obviously, is an increased cost,” Little said. “There is no reason why you would employ H-2A workers if you had any other reasonable alternative.”

rows.finding: AGRIST (Shintomi, Miyazaki, founded 2019) rents rail-guided greenhouse harvest robots for bell peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives: JA Niikappu (pepper, 2026-06-29/30), Hokuren (cucumber, 2026-07-01 to 08-31) and JA Kitasorachi (cucumber, 2026-07-02 to 10-31). Vendor-stated 55% harvest rate; Series B announced 2025-09-17; six announced deployments, all in Japan; no strawberry or open-field product.
rows.mechanism: A rental model for harvest robots can exist without solving open-field perception, because rails remove navigation, weather and canopy variability; the paid-rental model is therefore not itself a moat.
rows.benchmark: Orrin: 94% of detected ripe fruit in open field, 64 robots, five paying growers; AGRIST: 55% harvest rate, rail-guided, greenhouse.
rows.weakens: Weakens any claim that paid harvest-robot rental is novel to Orrin; weakens the idea that a rental model proves field performance. No audited fleet size or revenue, and the performance figure is vendor-stated.
rows.implication: Value the picker on the open-field problem it solves, not on the rental contract form; a co-operative rental channel is replicable and already exists in another crop system.
rows.follow_up: Has AGRIST published any strawberry or open-field trial, and does it hold patents that read on soft-fruit end-effectors?
rows.confidence: medium: deployment announcements and funding date are corroborated by co-operative notices; the 55% performance is vendor-stated.

rows.finding: Four Growers (Pittsburgh, Y Combinator-backed) says on its own site that it is 'working closely with various greenhouse growers to develop a tomato harvesting robot'; two patents are described as filed, not granted; the design uses 8 stereo cameras. Tracxn puts funding at $15.1M across 63 active competitors.
rows.mechanism: Greenhouse tomato is the easiest commercial picking case - fixed rows, no rain, uniform fruit, no bruising-sensitive soft skin - and it is still pre-commercial after $15M, which sets the capital and time required for a harder open-field crop.
rows.benchmark: Orrin has raised $20.5M and runs 64 robots; Four Growers $15.1M and no disclosed paid fleet.
rows.weakens: Weakens a reading that picking robotics is about to commoditise: a narrower task, with more capital than Orrin has spent on hardware, remains in development. Also weakens any claim that filed patents signal an enforceable position.
rows.implication: Orrin's open-field paid fleet, if verified, is ahead of a comparable team; but the capital required to get a picking product to market is of the same order as this round, not an order smaller.
rows.follow_up: Do Four Growers' two filings claim grasp or perception methods that Orrin's v4 gripper would need a licence for?
rows.confidence: medium on development stage (company's own current site); low on the $15.1M, which is an aggregator total.

rows.finding: Carbon Robotics (Seattle, founded 2018) sells the LaserWeeder, an autonomous laser weeder with 30 lasers and a claimed 200,000 weeds an hour, to roughly 100 growers across three continents. Cumulative funding is reported as $157M at the 2024-10 Series D, $232M in one 2026 tracker and $276M in another.
rows.mechanism: Field robotics has reached commercial distribution where the end-effector never touches the crop and the value is chemical replacement; distribution to 100 growers took $157M-$276M, ten to seventeen times Orrin's total raise.
rows.benchmark: Orrin total raised $20.5M, 5 growers; Carbon Robotics $157M-$276M, ~100 growers.
rows.weakens: Weakens the manufacturing argument for a $16M round: even a non-contact tool needed an order of magnitude more capital to reach 100 customers, and the grower-count and throughput are company-sourced. The three funding totals disagree, so none is reliable.
rows.implication: Distribution, not invention, is the capital sink; an OEM or dealer channel is the cheaper route to 300-500 units, and a stand-alone fleet must be priced against that alternative.
rows.follow_up: Who manufactures the LaserWeeder at volume, and on what contract terms? That is the comparable for Orrin's 300-unit BOM and ramp.
rows.confidence: medium on the product and commercial status; low on grower count and funding total, which are company or aggregator figures.

rows.finding: None of the three screened entrants builds a soft-fruit end-effector: AGRIST runs rail-guided pepper and cucumber harvesters, Four Growers files in greenhouse tomato grasping, Carbon Robotics in laser weed control. The freedom-to-operate risk to Orrin's gripper comes from crowded legacy slip-sensing art (a 1986 US patent) and the university licences, not from these peers.
rows.mechanism: The competitive set that matters for price is broader than the set that matters for patent risk; a crowded gripper art field narrows any allowance without giving a competitor a blocking position.
rows.benchmark: US 17/902,118: every claim rejected in a first office action, response filed 2026-05.
rows.weakens: Weakens the case that Orrin's patents are the barrier; also weakens the fear that a well-funded entrant will take the strawberry field in the next 12 months, since none is close in this crop.
rows.implication: Underwrite operations and contracted acres, not the estate; and do not pay for IP defensibility that the register does not support.
rows.follow_up: A freedom-to-operate search against Four Growers' two filings and the 1986 slip-sensing family before the v4 gripper is frozen.
rows.confidence: medium: the crop and product scope of each entrant is documented; the absence of soft-fruit work is an absence of evidence, not proof.

rows.finding: Orrin reports a 94% pick rate over 212 company-selected rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%, on a denominator of detected ripe berries. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU 2025), 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit (JFR 2025) and 50-97.1% (JFR 2019).
rows.mechanism: Defining the denominator as detected fruit removes missed berries from the failure count; choosing the rows removes the hard canopy and terrain, so the metric measures the arm, not the harvest.
rows.benchmark: WSU 80% detection, 74% of ripe picked; JFR 83-87% of detected; harvest recovery at 85% detection is 80%, and 75% after bruising and unripe picks.
rows.weakens: Weakens the deck's comparison with human crews and any claim that the picker replaces them in year one.
rows.implication: Price the round on supplement-to-crew economics until an independent harvest-level trial clears 85% on blocks Orrin did not choose.
rows.follow_up: What is the detection rate on the same 212 rows, and what share of those rows had slopes above 4%?
rows.confidence: high that the definition and exclusions are as stated (company documents); medium on the independent comparison, which is drawn from different cultivars and seasons.

rows.finding: The 3.8% bruise rate is measured at picking with no hand-picked control, and no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate; mechanical damage is a leading loss driver after harvest. One of five paying growers (Plant City, Florida) ended its pilot citing bruising.
rows.mechanism: Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould, so a pick-time measurement understates the loss the retailer sees; the buyer's quality bar is hand-picked fruit.
rows.benchmark: Hand-picked fruit is the retail benchmark; no published robot bruise rate exists for comparison.
rows.weakens: Weakens the credibility of the 3.8% as a quality claim: without a control it cannot be shown to meet the grower's standard, and the one revealed commercial exit points the other way.
rows.implication: A bruise trial against hand-picked fruit is a closing condition; without it the quality risk is unpriced.
rows.follow_up: What bruise rate, measured at 72 hours against hand-picked controls, did the Florida grower see before exiting?
rows.confidence: high on the absence of a benchmark; medium on how far 3.8% sits from commercial thresholds.

rows.finding: Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, CE or UKCA marking, incident log or liability-insurance terms. ISO 18497-1:2024 and -4:2024 cover design and verification of autonomous farm machinery but are voluntary; no federal US rule covers a ground-based harvest robot, so a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability. 21 CFR 112.123 puts the harvest-equipment cleaning duty on the grower.
rows.mechanism: Absent a mandatory standard, the standard of care is set after an injury by a jury; the grower bears the food-safety duty, which makes cleanability a product requirement the vendor must design for and the buyer will audit.
rows.benchmark: ISO 18497 verification is the emerging norm for autonomous farm machinery; 32 strawberry outbreaks and 933 illnesses in the US, 1997-2017.
rows.weakens: Weakens the assumption that a cheaper v4 gripper is a pure cost win: cleanability and validation are where the 35% cost cut is most likely to be taken out.
rows.implication: Require an ISO 18497-4 verification report, an ATP swab record and the insurer's terms as closing conditions; one contamination or injury event is existential for a five-customer vendor.
rows.follow_up: Has any grower's insurer or retail buyer asked for a conformity assessment or a cleaning validation record?
rows.confidence: high on the rules; not disclosed on Orrin's compliance, which is an absence in the file, not proof of absence.

plan.decision_question: Has Orrin proved the picking technology under conditions that generalise to commercial fields, and is the IP strong enough to defend a $72M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin has a working night picker and five paying growers, but the 94% is a success rate on rows it chose and detected fruit, the bruise rate has no comparator, the safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed - so the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money.
plan.why_different: Section 3 tests the machine and the estate (definitions, benchmarks, standards, patent status); market sizes the prize and competition ranks the field.
plan.mechanism: A conditional pick-rate denominator plus chosen rows converts an arm-level success rate into an apparent harvest rate; a crowded gripper art field and a licensed perception core convert R&D spend into a narrow, time-limited estate; contact with soft fruit is what separates this category from field robots that reached scale.
plan.comparison_set: Independent harvest trials (WSU 2025, JFR 2025, JFR 2019); hand-picked fruit as the quality benchmark; peers screened on the same date: Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga, AGRIST, Four Growers, Carbon Robotics.
plan.counter_evidence: Orrin's 94% could survive a detection-adjusted test if its camera recall is high; a funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; Carbon Robotics shows field robotics can reach 100 growers, so the category is not doomed; the exclusions (tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%) still leave most California acreage in play.
plan.visual: Technology comparison table with a verification-status column for each screened entrant, plus the performance metrics table and the evidence component.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, best-in-class, recently, about 5, many patents

In United Farm Workers v. United States Department of Labor,[1]  the federal district court for the Eastern District of California held that the Department of Labor’s (DOL) new methodology for calculating the H-2A Adverse Effect Wage Rate (AEWR) violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).The court found that several major components of DOL’s methodology were arbitrary and capricious and that DOL improperly bypassed the normal notice-and-comment process when adopting substantive changes to the wage system. But there is an important twist: the court did not immediately vacate the rule. Instead, the existing methodology remains temporarily operative while DOL develops a replacement.For agricultural employers, the decision creates both short-term stability and significant potential future wage exposure.Background: The H-2A Wage RequirementThe H-2A program permits agricultural employers to employ temporary foreign agricultural workers when DOL determines that doing so will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers.[2] Generally, an H-2A employer must pay the highest applicable wage among the AEWR, a prevailing wage, an agreed-upon collective bargaining wage, or the applicable federal or state minimum wage.[3] In practice, the AEWR ordinarily establishes the wage floor for H-2A workers.  For years, DOL calculated the AEWR using agricultural wage information derived from the USDA Farm Labor Survey (FLS). But USDA discontinued the FLS in August 2025. DOL responded with an Interim Final Rule (IFR), effective October 2, 2025, that substantially changed the methodology.The new methodology made four significant changes.  First, DOL substituted its Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) data for the FLS. Unlike the FLS, however, OEWS does not survey farm establishments.  Second, DOL created a two-tier wage system. Approximately 92 percent of H-2A positions were expected to fall within Skill Level I, with wages calculated at the 17th percentile. The remaining positions would generally fall within Skill Level II, calculated at the 50th percentile.  Third, DOL adopted a housing adjustment that reduced the AEWR based upon the value of employer-provided housing. Fourth, DOL adopted a “greater than 50 percent” rule for workers performing duties falling within multiple occupational classifications.New Methodology Found UnlawfulThe court held that the IFR was unlawful under the APA and remanded the matter to DOL to develop a new methodology. The court specifically concluded that the two-tier system, housing adjustment, OEWS methodology, and greater-than-50% occupational classification rule were arbitrary and capricious.  The court did not say, however, that the DOL is prohibited from changing the AEWR methodology. Rather, DOL failed to adequately explain why its methodology would satisfy the statutory requirement that H-2A employment not adversely affect U.S. workers.The decision also reflects the Supreme Court’s recent recalibration of administrative law. Under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo,[4] courts no longer defer to an agency’s reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute simply because the agency administers the statute. Courts must independently determine the meaning of the law and ensure that agencies remain within the authority Congress has delegated. The H-2A decision fits comfortably within that framework by being consistent with the post-Loper Bright administrative law environment.  DOL was free to develop a replacement methodology, but it was not free to assume that its preferred methodology was lawful merely because the agency possessed technical expertise. Jarkesy,[5] is relevant at a broader structural level. Although Jarkesy involved the Seventh Amendment and SEC administrative adjudication rather than H-2A wage regulation, the decision reflects the Supreme Court’s increasing insistence that administrative agencies remain subject to constitutional boundaries and traditional judicial safeguards. Loper Bright limits judicial deference to agency interpretations of law; Jarkesy limits agency adjudicatory power where constitutional judicial protections apply. A change in that floor can materially affect the cost of harvesting crops, caring for livestock, and performing other labor-intensive agricultural operations.Employer-Provided HousingThe court also rejected DOL’s housing adjustment.  H-2A employers generally must provide housing at no cost to H-2A workers and qualifying U.S. workers in corresponding employment.[6] Yet DOL’s methodology reduced the AEWR based upon the value of that housing.  The court reasoned that the approach effectively shifted the cost of housing from the employer to the worker through a lower wage. OEWS does not survey farm establishments in the same manner. The court also pointed out that farm labor contractors represent only part of the agricultural workforce and that contractor-employed workers generally earn less than workers employed directly by farm establishments. rows.benchmark: Target close 2026-12-15; the 2027 California season's first collections fall after the covenant date.

rows.implication: A stand-alone fleet at 360 robots must be priced against an OEM or dealer route to the same 300-500 units.
rows.mechanism: Distribution to 100 field-robotics customers took ten to seventeen times Orrin's total capital, which makes a channel partner the cheaper route to scale.

rows.benchmark: Orrin's plan: 360 robots rented to US growers, one paid season per robot.
rows.confidence: medium: deployments and funding date corroborated; performance vendor-stated.
rows.finding: AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse harvest robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives in 2026 after a Series B announced 2025-09-17, on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six announced deployments.
rows.follow_up: Does the Japanese rental model produce positive unit economics, and does AGRIST publish any fleet size?

rows.mechanism: Rail-guided greenhouse operation removes navigation and weather risk, which is why a rental harvest fleet exists there before it exists in open-field strawberries.

rows.benchmark: Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021), Raven $2.1B (2021); Advanced Farm ceased 2025 after a $25M Series B; Tortuga sold to Oishii 2025-03-24.

rows.implication: The cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed.
rows.mechanism: An equipment maker buys distribution and a validated crop workflow, not a rental fleet, so contract assignability and owned IP are what preserve the option value.
rows.weakens: Weakens the standalone-scale-up case: no peer reached independence at this capital level, and the closest comparable with a fleet claim (Harvest CROO) has disclosed no shipments.

rows.benchmark: One technician per eight robots is the company's own service ratio.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; the technician ratio is company-reported.
rows.finding: At one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the $1,750 target service cost per robot-season is $630,000 for the whole fleet.

rows.mechanism: Service labour scales with the fleet while revenue per robot is capped by the seasonal price, so the margin is a labour-productivity bet, not a hardware bet.

rows.benchmark: The company has built 64 robots in total; the plan needs 300 v4 units before April 2027.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. Orrin's figures are unverified; the benchmarks are independent.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80% of ripe fruit; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower, not a paper: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163]; 32 strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is therefore a product requirement the buyer will audit, and the 35% cost cut, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where it gets traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either much of the downtime is unattended, a $48,000 asset standing still, or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season over four seasons, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% rather than the 60% projected. No hand-harvest cost per acre is disclosed, the number that would settle whether price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented, and no entrant in this screen touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensitive gripper art is old — a 1986 US patent — so a routine rejection in crowded art points to a narrow allowance at best. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today, a binary test 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed — Advanced Farm raised $25M, took a CNH investment and ceased operations in 2025, and Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii in March 2025.

Three more entrants sharpen that read. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers and none carries a picking claim against the 94%; what they show is where capital and distribution have cleared. AGRIST, a Miyazaki robot maker founded in 2019, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for bell peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives — JA Niikappu, Hokuren and JA Kitasorachi in 2026 — on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a Series B announced on 2025-09-17 (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot on its own site as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics, the only one at scale, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company-sourced figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M in two 2026 trackers (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution either avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital than this round: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category, which is both Orrin's opportunity and its valuation risk.

| AGRIST | Rail-guided greenhouse, peppers and cucumbers | 55% harvest rate; six deployments, all Japan | Vendor-stated performance; deployments announced by co-ops | S183 |
| Four Growers | Greenhouse tomato, 8 stereo cameras | In development; two patents filed | Development stage confirmed by its own site; funding unverified | S185, S182 |
| Carbon Robotics | Laser weeding, 30 lasers | 200,000 weeds an hour; roughly 100 growers | Company-sourced count; product commercial since 2021 | S184, S186 |

| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 unverified |
