| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); harvest recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. The three screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop, and none competes in soft-fruit end-effectors. [S57]
:::

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 report and an ATP swab record (S163, S166). The cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and an office action that leaves a claim standing.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple on $2.6M of FY2026E revenue. All Orrin figures below are company-reported and unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans (58% without) at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is therefore a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where it gets traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season over four seasons, and 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% rather than the 60% projected. No hand-harvest cost per acre is disclosed, the number that would settle whether price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented, and no entrant in this screen touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a routine rejection in crowded art points to a narrow allowance at best. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today, a binary test 14 months after closing. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in Miyazaki in 2019, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a Series B announced on 2025-09-17 (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution either avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital than this round: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category, which is both Orrin's opportunity and its valuation risk.

| Company | Approach | Claim at 2026-10-31 | Verification status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin | Soft gripper, night stereo, open field | 94% of detected, 5.6 s a berry | Company-reported, unverified; conditional denominator | S53 |
| Harvest CROO | Open-field strawberry harvester | "On par with human harvesting" | Company claim; no rate, price or fleet disclosed | S1 |
| AGRIST | Rail-guided greenhouse, peppers and cucumbers | 55% harvest rate; six deployments, all Japan | Vendor-stated performance; deployments announced by co-ops | S183 |
| Four Growers | Greenhouse tomato, 8 stereo cameras | In development; two patents filed | Development stage confirmed by its own site; funding unverified | S185, S182 |
| Carbon Robotics | Laser weeding, 30 lasers | 200,000 weeds an hour; roughly 100 growers | Company-sourced count; commercial since 2021 | S184, S186 |

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 unverified, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 unverified |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry undisclosed | Platform copying | S53 unverified |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented | S53 unverified |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perception and labelled data | 5 | 1.9M images, but core families licensed and published | 2 years | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Gripper and slip sensing | 3 | Crowded art back to 1986; no allowed claim | 1 year | S130 |
| Field service at 1:8 | 6 | Seasonal crews, parts network | 3-4 years | S53 unverified |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | Operations are the barrier, not patents | **24-30 months to a comparable machine** | S53, S114 |

| Product | Stage and launch | 2026E revenue | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robots-as-a-Service | Commercial, 5 growers, 2025 season | $0.71M | 41% before fleet depreciation | 360 robots in 2027 | S53 unverified |
| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 unverified |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); harvest recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. The three screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop. [S57]
:::

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 report and an ATP swab record (S163, S166). The cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and an office action that leaves a claim standing.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead would buy preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, and the Mexican subsidiary's registry folio and the Calder licence's term are not disclosed in the deck at all. "Legally clean" is therefore a closing condition, not a finding, and every company fact below is unverified company material unless marked [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. The economics are structural: Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity, and the preference stack is paid before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility, small in dollars but senior in priority. Nor is the Mexican registry folio, deed or partner register disclosed: the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone, and a Jalisco constancia de existencia legal is what would confirm both existence and ownership (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline for Europe, Mexico and Australia fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment and change-of-control clauses, the omission that matters most to a preferred holder. Prior art in sensorised and slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so a $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the owner or head of harvest, and the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027, carrying the fleet on its balance sheet; 2027 is therefore a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo about $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence term and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

The founding pair has genuine founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, and no public record verifies a single CV line. On 2026-10-31 I checked three claims by institution and role: Calder University for the CEO's doctorate and inventor record, Marisol Ridge Farms for the COO's harvest role, and Corvane Robotics for the VP Engineering's gripper role. No university page, patent record or employer page matched, and "Calder University" returns no public web presence at all, so the credentials remain unverified company material and the confidence attaching to roles is moderate, to dates low (unverified) [S53, S128].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, holds the strongest technical credential on paper: PhD in robotics from Calder University in 2016, MS in mechanical engineering in 2012, BS in electrical engineering from Ridgemont State in 2010; controls engineer at Tallis Agricultural Machinery in 2010-2011; research scientist, then lead of perception, at Calder's Field Robotics Lab from 2016 until the company's incorporation on 2021-09-14, when she became CEO. Her dated inventor record runs through the 2019-05 first strawberry trials, a granted US patent from docket CU-2017-031 in 2020 and a second from CU-2019-114 in 2022, both licensed to Orrin on 2022-01-20; she is a named inventor on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university, of which Orrin licenses two families. The deck does not enumerate the eleven application numbers — only the two dockets — and no USPTO record could be retrieved, so inventorship, title and the scope of the nine unlicensed filings remain open [S53, S128].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial half: BS in agricultural business, Linden Valley College, 2006; harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014; director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014 to 2021-09 — about 15 years running berry harvest crews. The customer list dates the relationship: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, ran 18 robots in 2025, 24 in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027; Pajaro Bluff took 16 in 2026 and 30 for 2027. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales: 53% of 2026 paid seasons sit with two growers tied to him, and his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date for moving robots and supervising night shifts [S53].

The largest hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019-05 Calder field trials and the 2021-09-14 incorporation, separated on 2023-08-31 — 38 months before this round — keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after), and has no disclosed separation agreement, release, non-compete, board role or consulting term. Whether his invention assignments to the company were executed is not disclosed; no USPTO assignment record could be retrieved, and he is not named on the deck's five company applications. A departed co-founder who knows the perception stack and licence history is simultaneously a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor; the seat has stayed open through the v3 release in 2026-03 and the v4 filing of 2026-07-08 [S53, S128].

Below the founders the hires are competent specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, holds a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and spent 2013 to 2024-02 at Corvane Robotics, rising from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005 to 2025-06 at Verdant Crop Sciences, rising to regional sales director (West). Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016. Month-level start dates for pre-2021 roles are not disclosed; end dates are bounded only by the next dated event, and the company has not produced payroll or reference confirmation [S53].

The matrix reads the same way: technical depth and industry tenure are high, prior exits zero, and scaling and finance thin. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit; only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin, $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff — about 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots — and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06, while Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role and inventorship, Vashti's scope at Marisol Ridge, Hollander's Corvane management record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; compensation and non-founder equity are not disclosed. We would not recommend leading at the proposed pre-money without a permanent CTO, a full-time CFO and a Kestrel estoppel; a smaller, tranched check at a lower price is the investable structure (company-provided, unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. All Orrin figures below are company-reported and unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot citing bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no federal US rule covering a ground-based harvest robot, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut, led by a cheaper v4 gripper, is where it gets traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% rather than the 60% projected. No hand-harvest cost per acre is disclosed, the number that would settle whether price can rise [S53].

### The IP is rented, and no entrant in this screen touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a routine rejection in crowded art points to a narrow allowance at best. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today. The platform PCT's national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a Series B announced on 2025-09-17 (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution either avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital than this round: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

| Company | Approach | Claim at 2026-10-31 | Verification status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin | Soft gripper, night stereo, open field | 94% of detected, 5.6 s a berry | Company-reported, unverified; conditional denominator | S53 |
| Harvest CROO | Open-field strawberry harvester | "On par with human harvesting" | Company claim; no rate, price or fleet disclosed | S1 |
| AGRIST | Rail-guided greenhouse, peppers and cucumbers | 55% harvest rate; six deployments, all Japan | Vendor-stated; deployments announced by co-ops | S183 |
| Four Growers | Greenhouse tomato, 8 stereo cameras | In development; two patents filed | Development stage confirmed by its own site | S185, S182 |
| Carbon Robotics | Laser weeding, 30 lasers | 200,000 weeds an hour; roughly 100 growers | Company-sourced count; commercial since 2021 | S184, S186 |

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 unverified, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 unverified |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry undisclosed | Platform copying | S53 unverified |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented | S53 unverified |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perception and labelled data | 5 | 1.9M images, but core families licensed and published | 2 years | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Gripper and slip sensing | 3 | Crowded art back to 1986; no allowed claim | 1 year | S130 |
| Field service at 1:8 | 6 | Seasonal crews, parts network | 3-4 years | S53 unverified |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | Operations are the barrier, not patents | **24-30 months to a comparable machine** | S53, S114 |

| Product | Stage and launch | 2026E revenue | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robots-as-a-Service | Commercial, 5 growers, 2025 season | $0.71M | 41% before fleet depreciation | 360 robots in 2027 | S53 unverified |
| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 unverified |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. The three screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop. [S57]
:::

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 report and an ATP swab record (S163, S166). Condition the cheque on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and an office action that leaves a claim standing.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin figures are company-reported and unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising, and Florida growers carry part of the 2027 plan.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower rather than on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it gets traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — with 64 today. The platform PCT's national phase fell due on 2026-10-30 and entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution either avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital than this round: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

| Company | Approach | Claim at 2026-10-31 | Verification status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin | Soft gripper, night stereo, open field | 94% of detected, 5.6 s a berry | Company-reported; conditional denominator | S53 |
| Harvest CROO | Open-field strawberry harvester | "On par with human harvesting" | Company claim; no rate or fleet | S1 |
| AGRIST | Rail-guided greenhouse, peppers and cucumbers | 55% harvest rate; six deployments, all Japan | Vendor-stated; co-op announcements | S183 |
| Four Growers | Greenhouse tomato, 8 stereo cameras | In development; two patents filed | Development stage per its own site | S185, S182 |
| Carbon Robotics | Laser weeding, 30 lasers | 200,000 weeds an hour; roughly 100 growers | Company-sourced; commercial since 2021 | S184, S186 |

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 unverified, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 unverified |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry undisclosed | Platform copying | S53 unverified |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented | S53 unverified |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perception and labelled data | 5 | 1.9M images; core families licensed | 2 years | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Gripper and slip sensing | 3 | Crowded art; no allowed claim | 1 year | S130 |
| Field service at 1:8 | 6 | Seasonal crews, parts network | 3-4 years | S53 unverified |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | Operations are the barrier, not patents | **24-30 months to a comparable machine** | S53, S114 |

| Product | Stage and launch | 2026E revenue | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robots-as-a-Service | Commercial, 5 growers, 2025 season | $0.71M | 41% before fleet depreciation | 360 robots in 2027 | S53 unverified |
| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 unverified |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. The screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop. [S57]
:::

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 report and an ATP swab record (S163, S166); the cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and a surviving claim.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin's figures are unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry, and a modular system in the *Journal of Field Robotics* harvested 87% of detected fruit at 83% success. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31, with 64 today. The platform PCT's national phase fell due on 2026-10-30; entry into Europe, Mexico and Australia is undisclosed [S53, S114]. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. The screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop. [S57]

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 report and an ATP swab record (S163, S166); the cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and a surviving claim.

arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M, not as a price for the business that exists [S53].

The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M. Orrin has raised $20.5M of equity and notes since 2022, and $38.5M including this round, plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt; it has $3.7M of cash, $1.5M of which the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant makes unusable: $2.2M and 5.4 months of runway at $410,000 a month, with the covenant reached around 2027-03-14. Peer disclosure is thin: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014; Advanced Farm Technologies raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S54, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119, S189]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. The Jalisco assembly subsidiary, Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. (formed 2024-07-19), has no registry extract, and the Calder licence's term is not stated (unverified).

On revenue the price sits at the top of any observable range: 34.6x the $90M post-money on 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR (unverified), 12.9x pre and 16.1x post on the 2027 plan, and 6.8x on 2028. The ARR is not recurring: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding letters of intent — 56% non-recurring or non-binding, which is why 51.4x contracted robot revenue is the honest denominator. The payback is thinner than the pitch: the 2.1-season figure assumes a $1,750 service cost and omits the $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables charged against gross profit, so the same robot pays back in 2.5 seasons at the $16,500 list price and 4.4 at the $12,700 renewal. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA, and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95]. On a 4.0x exit multiple the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M projected.

The cap table makes it worse. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2%: the founders from 53.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7%, granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M) — 40.9% of the $90M post-money, ranking pari passu with new money — or $39.3M (43.6%) if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference. Ahead of the preferred sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt (unverified). Meridian is flat at 1.0x from a $38.4M to a $90M exit: at a $40M sale the Series A takes its $18M preference, Meridian recovers $12.0M and the common receives $1.6M after the debt [S53]. Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $272M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years), at $300M 3.33x (27.2%) and at $500M 5.56x (40.9%).

| Exit value, 2029-2031 | Meridian at 13.33%, no dilution | MOIC | After 20% Series B dilution (10.67%) | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $150M | $20.0M | 1.67x | $16.0M | 1.33x | S53 unverified |
| $250M | $33.3M | 2.78x | $26.7M | 2.22x | S53 unverified |
| $300M | $40.0M | 3.33x | $32.0M | 2.67x | S53 unverified |
| $500M | $66.7M | 5.56x | $53.3M | 4.44x | S53 unverified |

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture; so is a five-seat board with two common seats, one Seed, one Series A and one independent agreed by both. What is missing is the protection package: Meridian would hold one of five votes, with no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package, and Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor (unverified) [S53]. The minimum package is a second board seat or a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilisation, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true is specific: 360 robots and $8M of ARR on a definition that no longer includes Tallis services by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence still exclusive after its 100-robot test, unit cost below $36,000, and $67.5M-$84M of revenue at a 4x multiple by 2029-2031 (company plan, unverified). Deere paid $305M for Blue River (2017) and $250M for Bear Flag (2021), so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy. The counter-evidence is the category's own record: Advanced Farm, which Kubota and CNH backed, ceased operations in July 2025; Tortuga sold its assets; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and sold its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 [S91, S114, S115, S53]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on the 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment. The repriced case depends on round size: at a $50M pre-money with all $18M subscribed, Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post and returns 2.2x at a $150M exit and 3.7x at $250M; if Meridian's $12M is the only money, the same pre-money buys 19.35% of a $62M post and returns 2.4x at $150M and 4.0x at $250M, but leaves the 2027 plan $6M short.

Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead buys preferred in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is not an exotic structure but an unverified one. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved, and the Mexican registry folio and Calder licence term are not disclosed. "Legally clean" is a closing condition, not a finding; company facts below are unverified unless marked [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican two-partner assembly company runs Guadalajara. Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity and the preference stack before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility. Nor is the registry folio, deed or partner register disclosed: the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone, and a Jalisco constancia would confirm existence and ownership (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin for a deep-tech round. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment and change-of-control clauses. Prior art in slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. Two terms are not clean: the 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference it reaches $39.3M, so the $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the harvest owner, the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027; 2027 is a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. The related-party map is crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo about $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more operating proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders secure collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence term and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin's figures are unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Compared with Harvest CROO, which discloses no rate, price or fleet, Orrin's 64 robots are the category's only disclosed paid deployment. Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 report and an ATP swab record (S163, S166). For an investor, the cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and a surviving claim.

ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The Farm Labor Survey AEWR of $19.97 an hour governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, with a theoretical saving of up to $100M a year on $655M of H-2A wages within an $18B state farm-labour bill. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, which was the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology arbitrary and capricious and procedurally defective in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. For non-H-2A growers the 2026 minimum rose 2.4%, from $16.50 to $16.90; for H-2A crews the wage fell about 15%. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost per hour for both seasons could be obtained; housing and transport of $25-30 per worker-day mean the all-in rate probably fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, from $16.23 to $12.47, with the later 2026-08-17 effective date. Confidence is high on the rates, medium on the all-in direction. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. The company-reported, unverified related-party record is more decision-relevant than any environmental metric. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

arguments.markdown:
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The Farm Labor Survey AEWR of $19.97 an hour governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, against a theoretical $100M saving on $655M of H-2A wages. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, which was the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology arbitrary and capricious and procedurally defective in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. For non-H-2A growers the 2026 minimum rose 2.4%, from $16.50 to $16.90; for H-2A crews the wage fell about 15%. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost per hour for both seasons could be obtained; housing and transport of $25-30 per worker-day mean the all-in rate probably fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, from $16.23 to $12.47, under the later 2026-08-17 date. Confidence is high on the rates, medium on the all-in direction. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and wiring harnesses with seven staff, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build. Secondary trackers disagree on the surcharge: one holds a 25% IEEPA duty still applies, another that a 10% Section 122 charge replaced it on 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no published outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was found. The implication is a closing condition: USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the undisclosed Tallis v4 build. [S144, S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires equipment and food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's sanitation audit. Safety is standards-led: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous agricultural machinery but certifies nothing, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed the family alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs. [S144, S151, S153, S154, S166]

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record is more decision-relevant than any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05, and the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 while the October 2026 deck called it not yet decided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel reporting an executive order that pushes agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime was identified that binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions. [S144, S155, S158, S159]

arguments.markdown:
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services and grants supplied $1.25M of $1.9M of revenue, and both stop by mid-2027 [S53]. What the Series A must therefore prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all of them company-reported and unverified in this review — the $16M the round actually assembles buys one season and 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a path to a Series B. The plan is not implausible: 110 robots are contracted for 2027 and 50 more are under LOIs. It asks for four step changes at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window.

### Services and grants pay the bills; neither survives 2027

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M (company-reported, unverified) comprised $0.95M of engineering services for Tallis, $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent [S53]. On the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, which at a $72M pre-money is 51x rather than the 22x the headline figure implies. The services line was rational at sub-scale; it becomes a valuation problem once the round is priced on recurring revenue.

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified) [S53]. The $3.7M of cash on 2026-09-30 is 9.0 gross months to zero cash at $410,000 of monthly net burn; the Kestrel facility, $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5% and secured on the fleet, also requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times. At 2026-10-31 the balance is $3.29M and usable cash above that covenant is $1.79M, 4.4 months, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14 — before the 2027 California season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the fleet, not only a dilution. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the entire fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage. Either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the projected 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. Governance compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. The established pattern in this category is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. A standalone rental fleet at 360 robots has no precedent in this review: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, and Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B. The one field-robotics company at commercial distribution, Carbon Robotics, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D — ten times Orrin's capital [S117, S8, S114, S115, S184].
