arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead buys preferred in an IP holding company whose operating value is pledged and whose core licence is performance-contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is not exotic but unverified. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved. "Legally clean" is a closing condition, not a finding; company facts below are unverified unless marked [S53].

The asset map matters more than the org chart. Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican assembly company runs Guadalajara. Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity and the preference stack before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. The economic consequence is that the cash-generating fleet sits one level below the shares being sold, so a buyer must take or refinance the Kestrel claim, and the licence's 100-robot test therefore decides whether the parent's exclusivity survives to that exit. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility. Nor is the registry folio, deed or partner register disclosed: the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone, and a Jalisco constancia would confirm existence and ownership (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected in a first office action and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment clauses. Prior art in slip-sensing grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the SAFEs carry a preference it reaches $39.3M, so the $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the harvest owner, the budget owner the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027; 2027 is a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. Related parties are crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier board visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo about $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders take collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence term and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.markdown:
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, against a theoretical $100M saving on $655M of H-2A wages. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful on APA grounds in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. Non-H-2A growers saw a 2.4% rise, $16.50 to $16.90; H-2A crews saw about a 15% cut. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost for both seasons was obtainable; $25-30 per worker-day of housing and transport means the all-in rate fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, from $16.23 to $12.47, under the later 2026-08-17 date. Confidence is high on the rates, medium on the all-in direction. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's seven-staff Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and harnesses, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build. Trackers disagree on the surcharge: a 25% IEEPA duty or a 10% Section 122 charge from 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was published. Make USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the Tallis v4 build a closing condition. [S144, S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's audit. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous machinery but certifies nothing, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed the family alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs. [S144, S151, S153, S154, S166]

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record matters more than any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05; the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 while the October 2026 deck called it undecided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel citing an executive order pushing agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions. [S144, S155, S158, S159]

arguments.markdown:
The realistic exit is a trade sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M conditional on a sale, but the probability-weighted value across all outcomes is $116.8M, which returns Meridian 1.4x at the $72M pre-money, 1.8x at a $50M pre-money with the full $18M round and 1.9x if its $12M is the only money; all 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were M&A and none was an IPO, so the question is which OEM buys, when, and what the preference stack leaves [S187, S188].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood and independent basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | Deere & Company | Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021) and GUSS Automation (2025); no harvesting robot | 2028-2031 | Medium — three autonomy acquisitions in eight years | S96, S92, S8, S187 |
| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven gives it autonomy software; its 2022 Advanced Farm stake ended in that company's 2025 closure | 2028-2031 | Low-medium — one platform deal, no harvesting acquisition | S95, S117, S114 |
| Trade sale | Kubota | Backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in 2021; needs a specialty-crop harvesting asset | 2029-2031 | Low — no disclosed acquisition in the category | S93, S114 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling in a liquidation | 2027-2029 | Not a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer (company relationship, unverified) | S53 unverified |
| Private equity | Paine Schwartz Partners or similar | Needs positive EBITDA and fleet-level cash flow; the FY2028 plan still loses $6.9M | 2030-2032 | Low — no agtech robotics buyout disclosed | S167, S53 unverified |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low — 0 of 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were IPOs | S187, S53 unverified |

Deere is the most plausible buyer because it has already paid for autonomy three times — Blue River ($305M, 2017), Bear Flag ($250M, 2021) and GUSS Automation (2025) — but none of the three bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which put money into Advanced Farm Technologies' $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it cease operations in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S96, S92, S8, S95, S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company is both a reason to buy the next asset and a reason to demand proof that an OEM will pay a strategic price for a pre-scale robot company.

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River Technology | 2017 | $305M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S96 |
| Deere / Bear Flag Robotics | 2021 | $250M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S92 |
| CNH / Raven Industries | 2021 | $2.1B enterprise value | 6.0x EV/Sales ($348.4M sales) | S95 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | not disclosed | S91 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025 | IP and team; value not disclosed | n/a | S115 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | 2025 | ceased operations | n/a | S114 |
| Abundant Robotics | 2021 | IP and assets sold; $12M raised | n/a | S91 |

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the stereo ripeness model trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost (unverified). That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, the date that determines whether a buyer acquires an exclusive technology or a commodity one [S53]. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

| Outcome, 2028-2032 | Probability | Basis for the weight | Company value | Meridian at $72M pre (13.33%) | Meridian at $50M pre, $12M only (19.35%) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liquidation or asset sale | 30% | 3 of 5 named US strawberry-harvesting peers closed or sold assets 2021-2025; 65% of VC investments return under 1x | $10M | $4.1M / 0.34x | $3.3M / 0.27x | S91, S114, S115, S188 |
| Stalled, sold at the preference | 25% | $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack; 65% below-1x base rate | $75M | $12.0M / 1.00x | $14.5M / 1.21x | S53 unverified, S188 |
| Modest OEM trade sale | 25% | Deere precedents at $250M-$305M, discounted for pre-scale | $150M | $20.0M / 1.67x | $29.0M / 2.42x | S92, S96 |
| Good OEM trade sale | 15% | Same precedents at full value | $250M | $33.3M / 2.78x | $48.4M / 4.03x | S92, S96 |
| Bidding war or platform sale | 5% | Requires 360 robots and a cleared licence | $400M | $53.3M / 4.44x | $77.4M / 6.45x | S53 unverified |
| Probability-weighted | 100% | | $116.8M | $16.9M / 1.41x | $23.0M / 1.92x | S53, S188, S91, S114, S115 |

On those weights the expected exit is $116.8M; Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.41x at the current price and 1.92x at a $50M pre-money if its $12M is the whole round. The weights put 55% of outcomes at or below 1.0x, which is more generous than the 65% base rate for venture investments, because Orrin already has five paying growers; applying the base rate gives a lower expected value, not a higher one [S188, S53]. The modal successful outcome remains a $150M-$250M OEM sale, but a 30% failure tail at $10M — the category's own record — pulls the probability-weighted value below that range, and the preference stack caps the low-exit recovery.

The structural tests are as important as the buyer list. The Calder licence's term, assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the noteholders' Series A-1 consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, so the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts (unverified) [S53]. A foreign buyer such as Kubota also faces undisclosed licence-consent and export-control diligence, which could remove the most logical buyer.

| Entry pre-money | Round | Meridian stake for $12M | $150M exit | $250M exit | $300M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $72M (current) | $18M | 13.33% | $20.0M / 1.67x | $33.3M / 2.78x | $40.0M / 3.33x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | $18M | 17.65% | $26.5M / 2.21x | $44.1M / 3.68x | $52.9M / 4.41x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | $12M only | 19.35% | $29.0M / 2.42x | $48.4M / 4.03x | $58.1M / 4.84x | S53 unverified |

The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.41x and 2.21x on the full round, or 4.84x and 2.42x if Meridian's $12M is the only money. Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake that sits behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota all have in-house autonomy programmes and can build a strawberry picker rather than buy one; the US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit — Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025, Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M — while the most recent harvesting-robot purchase, AppHarvest's $60M for Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices. Hardware exits trade below software, ag-equipment multiples are 1.0x-4.3x sales, and the industrial sector ETF is down 6.9% over three months, 8.1 points behind the S&P 500, so a 2029-2031 window is not assured [S53, S115, S114, S91, S31]. Meridian should negotiate a drag-along and tag-along that make a trade sale executable without a founder veto, a right to consent to any change to the Calder licence or the Tallis manufacturing agreement, and a requirement that Kestrel be repaid or consented at closing.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead buys preferred in an IP holdco whose operating value is pledged and whose licence is contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is unverified. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved. "Legally clean" is a closing condition, not a finding; company facts below are unverified unless marked [S53].

Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican assembly company runs Guadalajara. Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity and the preference stack before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. The economic consequence is that the cash-generating fleet sits one level below the shares sold, so a buyer must take or refinance the Kestrel claim, and the licence's 100-robot test decides whether the parent's exclusivity survives to that exit. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility. Nor is the registry folio, deed or partner register disclosed: the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone, and a Jalisco constancia would confirm existence and ownership (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment clauses. Prior art in slip grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the SAFEs carry a preference it reaches $39.3M, so the $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the harvest owner, the budget the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027; 2027 is a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. Related parties are crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof real but narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders take collateral, related-party terms can be at market, and the maths is right. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence term and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck; the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.markdown:
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, against a theoretical $100M saving on $655M of H-2A wages. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. Non-H-2A growers saw a 2.4% rise, $16.50 to $16.90; H-2A crews saw about a 15% cut. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost for both seasons was obtainable; $25-30 per worker-day of housing and transport means the all-in rate fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, from $16.23 to $12.47. Confidence: high on rates, medium on all-in. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's seven-staff Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and harnesses, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build. Trackers disagree on the surcharge: a 25% IEEPA duty or a 10% Section 122 charge from 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was published. Make USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the Tallis v4 build a closing condition. [S144, S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's audit. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous machinery but certifies nothing, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed the family alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs. [S144, S151, S153, S154, S166]

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record outweighs any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05; the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 while the October 2026 deck called it undecided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel citing an executive order pushing agencies to take title and domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions. [S144, S155, S158, S159]

### ESG issues that carry financial weight

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 6 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,775 characters)
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price it covers 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost, with a 24% cushion. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season (April-October) and a three-month Florida season (December-March), at $9,500 per robot per season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. The product is sold one season at a time; payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not publicly disclosed, which matters because a collection after the harvest would put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts in this paragraph are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. At a six-season life, depreciation would be $8,000 and contribution still -$4,100. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $9,500 | $31,000 (v4 target) | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$3,850 | 8.0 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 | +$4,500 | 2.5 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season (3.7-season payback). At $16,500 with current service cost the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 seasons at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback ($31,000 divided by $14,750) omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line entirely; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted 2027 renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book, not the strongest. Prices are company-reported and unverified; the recomputation is verified [S53].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list, target service | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $12,000 | 138% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and related parties carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The customer counts are partially verified: the deck's grower table sums to 75, matching the stated total, but the contracts themselves are unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 and has contracted 20 for 2027, and Grower E ended its Plant City pilot in June 2026 over fruit bruising, the one customer-side data point that contradicts the 3.8% bruising claim. For 2027 Orrin shows 110 contracted robots (Marisol 40, Pajaro 30, Grower B 20, Grower C 20) and 50 LOI robots from eight other pilots: 160 of the 360 planned, or 44%, with 200 uncontracted. That requires 3.3 times the contracted base in one selling cycle, from four sales staff, after converting only five of 14 pilots to paid. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Those ties are disclosed and not disqualifying, but they mean the 53% concentration and the cost of field service are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many robots were idle or deployed on unpaid pilots. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot could serve Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $19,000 at the 782 seasons implied by FY2028 revenue. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger, not smaller, and the plan does not reach that crossover. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025 | S54 |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 3 by Red Team Analyst, 8,864 characters)
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and a discount to $48M-$55M does not pay for that clock. Company-reported and unverified figures put $2.2M of usable cash — $3.7M less the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — at 5.4 months of burn, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of the $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. Bull at 20% needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots built, 250 sold at list, 85% harvest recovery and the licence test cleared. The bear is one domino with several symptoms, not four risks to multiply: the round slipping or underclosing carries a 55% probability on that commitment book, which puts the bear at 50%, not 35%. Bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50% is what the evidence supports. It changes the answer because the $36.8M preference (40.9% of the $90M post-money) sits behind $1.6M of secured debt: at a $40M sale Meridian takes 1.0x, so the base case returns capital, not a multiple [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms the field team chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising and 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the one failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and every price in the plan assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR would be 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M covenant: breached at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted, 4 sales staff, one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second cycle the 2027 season does not allow | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15, below the covenant from 2027-03-14: default, not dilution | S53, unverified; derived |

A reprice that takes three to six months is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet, not only a lower price.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on that fleet sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence or change-of-control term disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would be buying different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating, it removes the barrier for a competitor and an acquirer, so the impact lands on exit value rather than the business, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner still: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M of FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers and harnesses, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also the largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision — inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics — and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified, but the 41% margin and the 53% concentration are not arm's-length evidence [S53].

### Two policy winds have turned

The labour mechanism assumes a rising floor, and the floor moved the other way: the US Department of Labor lowered the H-2A wage for many California jobs in October 2025 and made dairy farms eligible in June 2026. Cheaper, elastic hand labour slows a purchase made once a year, before planting. The tariff is nearer and quantifiable: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin products from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin goods exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against a $36,000 milestone ceiling — and $825 a season of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475. The USMCA joint review falls in July 2027, inside the 2027 season [S169, S174, S148].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics reported a first California customer deployment from April 2026 at 30 kilograms an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, so being the only open-field picker above 90% is already out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating its Livermore headquarters in March 2026; Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% between Q2 and Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is being underwritten in a market that has just repriced [S170, S168, S171].

### What to settle before signing

Four requests carry most of the weight: the Kestrel agreement with its minimum-cash definition, cross-default and waiver price; the Calder licence with assignment, change-of-control and "commercial service" definitions and the sub-licence; a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement with tooling ownership and a second source; and an independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and the tariff, medium on the covenant terms and harvest recovery, low on the 2027 build and the exit price; the Kestrel text and the Calder licence decide whether the bear case returns capital or nothing."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, 8,970 characters)
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services and grants supplied $1.25M of $1.9M of revenue, and both stop by mid-2027 [S53]. What the Series A must therefore prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all of them company-reported and unverified in this review — the $16M the round actually assembles buys one season and 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a path to a Series B. The plan is not implausible: 110 robots are contracted for 2027 and 50 more are under LOIs. It asks for four step changes at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window.

### Services and grants pay the bills; neither survives 2027

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M (company-reported, unverified) comprised $0.95M of engineering services for Tallis, $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent [S53]. On the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, which at a $72M pre-money is 51x rather than the 22x the headline figure implies. The services line was rational at sub-scale; it becomes a valuation problem once the round is priced on recurring revenue.

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified) [S53]. The $3.7M of cash on 2026-09-30 is 9.0 gross months to zero cash at $410,000 of monthly net burn; the Kestrel facility, $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5% and secured on the fleet, also requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times. At 2026-10-31 the balance is $3.29M and usable cash above that covenant is $1.79M, 4.4 months, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14 — before the 2027 California season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the fleet, not only a dilution. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the entire fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage. Either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the projected 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. Governance compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but neither revenue nor cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established pattern in this category is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries. Deere's 2025 annual report names autonomy and Solutions-as-a-Service as core to a high-value, small-acreage strategy, which is precisely where a berry picker would fit. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, which is exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. A standalone rental fleet at 360 robots has no precedent in this review: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, and Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B. The one field-robotics company at commercial distribution, Carbon Robotics, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D — ten times Orrin's capital [S117, S8, S114, S115, S184]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed, not a bet on a rental business reaching escape velocity alone.

arguments.markdown:
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, against a theoretical $100M saving on $655M of H-2A wages. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. Non-H-2A growers saw a 2.4% rise, $16.50 to $16.90; H-2A crews saw about a 15% cut. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost for both seasons was obtainable; $25-30 per worker-day of housing and transport means the all-in rate fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, $16.23 to $12.47. Confidence: high on rates, medium on all-in. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's seven-staff Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and harnesses, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build. Trackers disagree: a 25% IEEPA duty or a 10% Section 122 charge from 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was published. Make USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the Tallis v4 build a closing condition. [S144, S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's audit. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous machinery but certifies nothing, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed the family alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs. [S144, S151, S153, S154, S166]

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record outweighs any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05; the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 while the October 2026 deck called it undecided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel citing an executive order pushing agencies to take title and domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions. [S144, S155, S158, S159]

### ESG issues that carry financial weight

| ESG issue | Why material | Evidence | Rating impact | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Governance and related parties | Insider cash flows; conflicts over the v4 build | Company-reported $310,000 to the COO's company, 16% of FY2025 revenue; Tallis holds five roles | Negative; require an independent director | S144 |
| Product safety | An injury at night could exceed the balance sheet | 20-hour duty cycle; 3.8% bruising; one pilot exit; no certification disclosed | Negative; price insurance and certification | S144, S151, S154 |
| Food safety | Grower audits cover the machine's surfaces | FDA 21 CFR 112 equipment and food-contact standards | Neutral to negative; cleaning validation | S153 |

### Regulatory record

|---|---|---|---|---|
| DOL OFLC | AEWR notice 91 FR 48946: California Skill I $16.45, Skill II $18.71; $16.90 state minimum binds | 2026-08-03 | In force; national bond average $15.96 | S191 |
| DOL / E.D. Cal. | Interim final rule 90 FR 47914 cut California from $19.97 to $16.90; UFW v. DOL held it unlawful and remanded | 2025-10-02; 2026-08-26 | Rates temporarily in place; backpay possible | S190, S193, S194 |
| California DIR | Minimum wage $16.90; overtime after 8 hours/day and 40/week; double time after 12 | 2026-01-01; overtime 2022/2025 | In force | S141, S142 |
| California Legislature | AB 2646, $19.75/hour floor for approved agricultural and corresponding employees | Signed 2026; operative 2027-01-01 | Enacted; COLA-indexed | S195 |
| USTR | Consultation for the 2027 USMCA review; comments due 2027-01-12 | 2026-10-02 | Open | S148, S150 |
| CBP / USTR tariff | 10% Section 301-type duty on non-USMCA Mexico-origin goods; qualifying goods 0% | 2026-07-24 | In force; rate stack contested | S149, S152 |
| Cal/OSHA Standards Board | Review of autonomous agricultural machinery standards, including ISO 18497 | Retrieved 2026-10-31 | Guidance only; no robot-specific rule found | S154 |
| FDA | Produce Safety Rule, 21 CFR 112, equipment and food-contact sanitation | In force | Binds growers, not Orrin directly | S153 |

### Policy impact matrix

| Factor | Exposure | Probability | Impact on company | Mitigant | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California wage floor and overtime | California revenue; hand-pick cost | High, in force | Positive demand: $16.90 rising to $17.40 | 2027 list $16,500 | S141, S142, S157 |
| H-2A AEWR 2026 cut and AB 2646 rebound | California labour cost | In force; rebound 2027-01-01 | Negative near term: $19.97→$16.90 in 2026; positive 2027: $19.75 | Underwrite the 2027 rebound | S190, S191, S195 |
| UFW v. DOL remand and backpay | H-2A cost and the 2026 rate | Medium | Could restore $19.97 or raise rates; backpay | Monitor the replacement rule and any appeal | S190, S194 |
| USMCA origin failure | Guadalajara assembly | Low to medium | Negative: $3,300 per robot, $0.99M on 300 | USMCA certification; US dual assembly | S144, S152, S156 |
| USMCA 2027 review | Mexican assembly and pricing | Medium | Rules could tighten | Diversify assembly; comment by 2027-01-12 | S148, S150 |
| Cal/OSHA and ISO 18497 | Product design and certification | Medium | Cost and delay; weaker liability defence | Design to ISO 18497-1:2024 | S151, S154, S166 |

arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M, not as a price for the business that exists [S53].

The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M. Orrin has raised $20.5M of equity and notes since 2022, and $38.5M including this round, plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt; it has $3.7M of cash, $1.5M of which the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant makes unusable: $2.2M and 5.4 months of runway at $410,000 a month, with the covenant reached around 2027-03-14. Peer disclosure is thin: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014; Advanced Farm Technologies raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S54, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119, S189]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. No Mexican registry extract could be retrieved for the Jalisco assembly subsidiary, Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. (formed 2024-07-19), and the Calder licence's term is not disclosed (unverified).

| 2025-06-16 | Equipment facility (debt) | $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 11.5% | n/a | Kestrel Equipment Finance | fleet build | S53 unverified |

On revenue the price sits at the top of any observable range: 34.6x the $90M post-money on 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR (unverified), 12.9x pre and 16.1x post on the 2027 plan, and 6.8x on 2028. The ARR is not recurring: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding letters of intent — 56% non-recurring or non-binding, which is why 51.4x contracted robot revenue is the honest denominator. The payback is thinner than the pitch: the 2.1-season figure assumes a $1,750 service cost and omits the $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables charged against gross profit, so the same robot pays back in 2.5 seasons at the $16,500 list price and 4.4 at the $12,700 renewal. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA, and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95]. On a 4.0x exit multiple the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M projected.

The cap table makes it worse. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2%: the founders from 53.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7%, granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M) — 40.9% of the $90M post-money, ranking pari passu with new money — or $39.3M (43.6%) if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference. Ahead of the preferred sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt (unverified). Meridian is flat at 1.0x from a $38.4M to a $90M exit: at a $40M sale the Series A takes its $18M preference, Meridian recovers $12.0M and the common receives $1.6M after the debt [S53]. Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $272M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years), at $300M 3.33x (27.2%) and at $500M 5.56x (40.9%).

| $150M | $20.0M | 1.67x | $16.0M | 1.33x | S53 unverified |

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture; so is a five-seat board with two common seats, one Seed, one Series A and one independent agreed by both. What is missing is the protection package: Meridian would hold one of five votes, with no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package, and Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor (unverified) [S53]. The minimum package is a second board seat or a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilisation, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true is specific: 360 robots and $8M of ARR on a definition that no longer includes Tallis services by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence still exclusive after its 100-robot test, unit cost below $36,000, and $67.5M-$84M of revenue at a 4x multiple by 2029-2031 (company plan, unverified). Deere paid $305M for Blue River (2017) and $250M for Bear Flag (2021), so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy. The counter-evidence is the category's own record: Advanced Farm, which Kubota and CNH backed, ceased operations in July 2025; Tortuga sold its assets; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and sold its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 [S91, S114, S115, S53]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on the 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment. The repriced case depends on round size: at a $50M pre-money with all $18M subscribed, Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post and returns 2.2x at a $150M exit and 3.7x at $250M; if Meridian's $12M is the only money, the same pre-money buys 19.35% of a $62M post and returns 2.4x at $150M and 4.0x at $250M, but leaves the 2027 plan $6M short.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead buys preferred in an IP holdco whose value is pledged and whose licence is contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is unverified. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved. "Legally clean" is a closing condition, not a finding; company facts below are unverified unless marked [S53].

Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican assembly company runs Guadalajara. Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity and the preference stack before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. The economic consequence is that the cash-generating fleet sits below the shares sold, so a buyer must take or refinance the Kestrel claim before it reaches the parent's exclusivity. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility. Nor is the registry folio, deed or partner register disclosed: the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone, and a Jalisco constancia would confirm existence and ownership (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment. Prior art in slip grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the SAFEs carry a preference it reaches $39.3M, so the $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the harvest owner, the budget the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027; 2027 is a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. Related parties are crowded: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital position is modest and its proof narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders take collateral, related-party terms can be at market. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence term and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck. Strategically the lead buys the parent's licence and team, not the fleet; economically it buys a claim behind $18.8M of seed and note money and a $1.6M secured lender, so the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead buys preferred in an IP holdco whose value is pledged and whose licence is contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is unverified. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved. "Legally clean" is a closing condition, not a finding; company facts below are unverified unless marked [S53].

Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican assembly company runs Guadalajara. Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity and the preference stack before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. Economically, the cash-generating fleet sits below the shares sold, so a buyer must take or refinance the Kestrel claim before it reaches the parent's exclusivity. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility. Nor is the registry folio, deed or partner register disclosed: the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone, and a Jalisco constancia would confirm existence and ownership (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment. Prior art in slip grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the SAFEs carry a preference it reaches $39.3M, so the $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the harvest owner, the budget the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027; 2027 is a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. Related parties crowd the file: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital is modest and its proof narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders take collateral, related-party terms can be market. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence term and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck. Strategically the lead buys the parent's licence and team, not the fleet; economically it buys a claim behind $18.8M of seed and note money and a $1.6M secured lender, so the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].
