{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 3 by Red Team Analyst, 8,864 characters)
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and a discount to $48M-$55M does not pay for that clock. Company-reported and unverified figures put $2.2M of usable cash — $3.7M less the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — at 5.4 months of burn, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of the $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. Bull at 20% needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots built, 250 sold at list, 85% harvest recovery and the licence test cleared. The bear is one domino with several symptoms, not four risks to multiply: the round slipping or underclosing carries a 55% probability on that commitment book, which puts the bear at 50%, not 35%. Bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50% is what the evidence supports. It changes the answer because the $36.8M preference (40.9% of the $90M post-money) sits behind $1.6M of secured debt: at a $40M sale Meridian takes 1.0x, so the base case returns capital, not a multiple [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms the field team chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising and 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the one failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and every price in the plan assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR would be 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M covenant: breached at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted, 4 sales staff, one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second cycle the 2027 season does not allow | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15, below the covenant from 2027-03-14: default, not dilution | S53, unverified; derived |

A reprice that takes three to six months is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet, not only a lower price.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on that fleet sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence or change-of-control term disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would be buying different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating, it removes the barrier for a competitor and an acquirer, so the impact lands on exit value rather than the business, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner still: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M of FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers and harnesses, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also the largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision — inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics — and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified, but the 41% margin and the 53% concentration are not arm's-length evidence [S53].

### Two policy winds have turned

The labour mechanism assumes a rising floor, and the floor moved the other way: the US Department of Labor lowered the H-2A wage for many California jobs in October 2025 and made dairy farms eligible in June 2026. Cheaper, elastic hand labour slows a purchase made once a year, before planting. The tariff is nearer and quantifiable: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin products from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin goods exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against a $36,000 milestone ceiling — and $825 a season of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475. The USMCA joint review falls in July 2027, inside the 2027 season [S169, S174, S148].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics reported a first California customer deployment from April 2026 at 30 kilograms an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, so being the only open-field picker above 90% is already out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating its Livermore headquarters in March 2026; Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% between Q2 and Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is being underwritten in a market that has just repriced [S170, S168, S171].

### What to settle before signing

Four requests carry most of the weight: the Kestrel agreement with its minimum-cash definition, cross-default and waiver price; the Calder licence with assignment, change-of-control and "commercial service" definitions and the sub-licence; a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement with tooling ownership and a second source; and an independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. arguments.markdown:
Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead buys preferred in an IP holdco whose value is pledged and whose licence is contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is unverified. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved. "Legally clean" is a closing condition, not a finding; company facts below are unverified unless marked [S53].

Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican assembly company runs Guadalajara. Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity and the preference stack before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. Economically, the cash-generating fleet sits below the shares sold, so a buyer must take or refinance the Kestrel claim before it reaches the parent's exclusivity. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility. Nor is the registry folio, deed or partner register disclosed: the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone, and a Jalisco constancia would confirm existence and ownership (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment. Prior art in slip grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if SAFEs carry a preference it reaches $39.3M, so the $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the harvest owner, the budget the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027; 2027 is a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. Related parties crowd the file: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital is modest and its proof narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders take collateral, related-party terms can be market. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence term and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck. Strategically the lead buys the parent's licence and team, not the fleet; economically it buys a claim behind $18.8M of seed and note money and $1.6M secured lender, so the decision is "invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents" (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

The founders have genuine founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, and no public record verifies a single CV line. On 2026-10-31 I checked three claims by institution and role: Calder University (CEO doctorate and inventorship), Marisol Ridge Farms (COO role) and Corvane Robotics (VP Engineering role). No university page, patent record or employer page matched, and Calder University has no public web presence, so the credentials are unverified company material, with low confidence on dates (unverified) [S53, S128].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, has the strongest technical credential on paper: PhD in robotics, Calder University, 2016; MS mechanical engineering, 2012; BS electrical engineering, Ridgemont State, 2010; controls engineer at Tallis Agricultural Machinery 2010-2011; research scientist then lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab 2016 until the company's incorporation on 2021-09-14. Her inventor record is dated by the 2019-05 trials, a 2020 grant from docket CU-2017-031 and a 2022 grant from CU-2019-114, both licensed to Orrin on 2022-01-20; she is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university, of which Orrin licenses two families. The deck does not enumerate the eleven application numbers, only the two dockets, and no USPTO record could be retrieved, so title and the scope of the nine unlicensed filings remain open [S53, S128].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial half: BS in agricultural business, Linden Valley College, 2006; harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014; director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014 to 2021-09 — about 15 years running berry harvest crews. The relationship is dated: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, ran 18 robots in 2025, 24 in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027; Pajaro Bluff took 16 in 2026 and 30 for 2027. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales: 53% of 2026 paid seasons sit with two growers tied to him, and his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025-2026 for moving robots and night supervision [S53].

The largest hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019-05 Calder trials and the 2021-09-14 incorporation, separated on 2023-08-31 — 38 months before this round — keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after), and has no disclosed separation agreement, release, non-compete, board role or consulting term. Whether his invention assignments to the company were executed is not disclosed; no USPTO assignment record could be retrieved, and he is not named on the deck's five company applications. A departed co-founder who knows the perception stack is a reference, a potential claimant and a possible competitor; the seat has stayed open through the v3 release in 2026-03 and the v4 filing of 2026-07-08 [S53, S128].

Below the founders the hires are competent specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, holds a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and spent 2013 to 2024-02 at Corvane Robotics, rising from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005 to 2025-06 at Verdant Crop Sciences, rising to regional sales director (West). Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016. Month-level start dates for pre-2021 roles are not disclosed; end dates are bounded by the next dated event [S53].

The matrix reads the same way: technical depth and industry tenure are high, prior exits zero, and scaling and finance thin. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit; only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin, $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff — about 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots — and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06 and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role, Vashti's Marisol scope, Hollander's Corvane record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder pay and equity are not disclosed. arguments.markdown:
The founders have real founder-market fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, and no public record verifies a single CV line. On 2026-10-31 I checked three claims by institution and role: Calder University (CEO doctorate and inventorship), Marisol Ridge Farms (COO role) and Corvane Robotics (VP Engineering role). No university, patent or employer page matched, and Calder University has no public web presence, so the credentials are unverified company material, low confidence on dates (unverified) [S53, S128].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, has the strongest technical credential on paper: PhD in robotics, Calder University, 2016; MS mechanical engineering, 2012; BS electrical engineering, Ridgemont State, 2010; controls engineer at Tallis Agricultural Machinery 2010-2011; research scientist then lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab 2016 until the company's incorporation on 2021-09-14. Her inventor record is dated by the 2019-05 trials, a 2020 grant from docket CU-2017-031 and a 2022 grant from CU-2019-114, both licensed to Orrin on 2022-01-20; she is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university, of which Orrin licenses two families. The deck does not enumerate the eleven application numbers, only the two dockets, and no USPTO record could be retrieved, so title and the scope of the nine unlicensed filings remain open [S53, S128].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial half: BS in agricultural business, Linden Valley College, 2006; harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014; director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014 to 2021-09 — 15 years running berry harvest crews. The relationship is dated: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, ran 18 robots in 2025, 24 in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027; Pajaro Bluff took 16 in 2026 and 30 for 2027. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales: 53% of 2026 paid seasons sit with two growers tied to him, and his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025-2026 for moving robots and night supervision [S53].

The largest hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019-05 Calder trials and the 2021-09-14 incorporation, separated on 2023-08-31 — 38 months before this round — keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after), and has no disclosed separation agreement, release, non-compete, board role or consulting term. Whether his invention assignments to the company were executed is not disclosed; no USPTO assignment record could be retrieved, and he is not named on the deck's five company applications. A departed co-founder who knows the perception stack is a reference, a potential claimant and competitor; the seat has stayed open through the v3 release in 2026-03 and the v4 filing of 2026-07-08 [S53, S128].

Below the founders the hires are competent specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, holds a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and spent 2013 to 2024-02 at Corvane Robotics, rising from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005 to 2025-06 at Verdant Crop Sciences, rising to regional sales director (West). Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016. Month-level start dates for pre-2021 roles are not disclosed; end dates are bounded by the next dated event [S53].

The matrix reads the same way: technical depth and industry tenure are high, prior exits zero, and scaling and finance thin. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit; only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin, $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff — about 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots — and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06 and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role, Vashti's Marisol scope, Hollander's Corvane record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder pay and equity are not disclosed. We would not lead at the proposed pre-money without a permanent CTO, a full-time CFO and a Kestrel estoppel; a smaller, tranched check at a lower price is investable (company-provided, unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 9 by Product Analyst, 8,890 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin's figures are unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Compared with Harvest CROO, which discloses no rate, price or fleet, Orrin's 64 robots are the category's only disclosed paid deployment. Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M. Orrin has raised $20.5M of equity and notes since 2022, and $38.5M including this round, plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt; it has $3.7M of cash, $1.5M of which the Kestrel minimum-cash covenant makes unusable: $2.2M and 5.4 months of runway at $410,000 a month, with the covenant reached around 2027-03-14. What is missing is the protection package: Meridian would hold one of five votes, with no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package, and Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor (unverified) [S53]. arguments.markdown:
The founders have real fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, and no public record verifies a single CV line. On 2026-10-31 I checked three claims by institution and role: Calder University (CEO doctorate and inventorship), Marisol Ridge Farms (COO role) and Corvane Robotics (VP Engineering role). No university, patent or employer page matched, and Calder University has no public web presence, so the credentials are unverified company material, low confidence on dates (unverified) [S53, S128].

Dr. Imani Castellano, CEO and board chair, has the strongest paper credential: PhD in robotics, Calder University, 2016; MS mechanical engineering, 2012; BS electrical engineering, Ridgemont State, 2010; controls engineer at Tallis Agricultural Machinery 2010-2011; research scientist then lead of perception at Calder's Field Robotics Lab 2016 until the company's incorporation on 2021-09-14. Her inventor record is dated by the 2019-05 trials, a 2020 grant from docket CU-2017-031 and a 2022 grant from CU-2019-114, both licensed to Orrin on 2022-01-20; she is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university, of which Orrin licenses two families. The deck does not enumerate the eleven application numbers, only the two dockets, and no USPTO record could be retrieved, so title and the scope of the nine unlicensed filings remain open [S53, S128].

Teodor Vashti, COO and director, supplies the commercial half: BS in agricultural business, Linden Valley College, 2006; harvest supervisor to field operations manager at Seabright Produce Partners, 2006-2014; director of harvest operations at Marisol Ridge Farms, 2014 to 2021-09 — 15 years running berry harvest crews. The relationship is dated: Marisol Ridge, his former employer, ran 18 robots in 2025, 24 in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027; Pajaro Bluff took 16 in 2026 and 30 for 2027. That is relationship-led traction, not repeatable third-party sales: 53% of 2026 paid seasons sit with two growers tied to him, and his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025-2026 for moving robots and night supervision (unverified) [S53].

The largest hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019-05 Calder trials and the 2021-09-14 incorporation, separated on 2023-08-31 — 38 months before this round — keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after), and has no disclosed separation agreement, release, non-compete, board role or consulting term. Whether his invention assignments to the company were executed is not disclosed; no USPTO assignment record could be retrieved, and he is not named on the deck's five company applications. A departed co-founder who knows the stack is a reference, a potential claimant and competitor; the seat has stayed open through the v3 release in 2026-03 and the v4 filing of 2026-07-08 [S53, S128].

Below the founders the hires are specialists, not a scale bench. Dr. Mei Hollander, VP Engineering since 2024-02, holds a 2013 mechanical-engineering PhD from Brightwater State and spent 2013 to 2024-02 at Corvane Robotics, rising from manipulation engineer to gripper engineering manager — the most relevant CV, but no CTO title, no disclosed equity and no manufacturing-scale record. Dolores Achterberg, VP Sales and Customer Success since 2025-06, spent 2005 to 2025-06 at Verdant Crop Sciences, rising to regional sales director (West). Arturo Benedetti, CPA, part-time head of finance since 2024-09, has a 1998 accounting degree from Linden Valley College and has been a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016. Month-level start dates for pre-2021 roles are not disclosed; end dates are bounded by the next dated event (unverified) [S53].

The matrix reads the same way: technical depth and industry tenure are high, prior exits zero, and scaling and finance thin. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit; only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin, $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff — about 45 technician-equivalents at one technician per eight robots — and no hiring plan is shown. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06 and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role, Vashti's Marisol scope, Hollander's Corvane record, Achterberg's sales numbers, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder pay and equity are not disclosed. We would not lead at this pre-money without a permanent CTO, a full-time CFO and a Kestrel estoppel; for an investor, a smaller, tranched check at a lower price is investable (company-provided, unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, against a theoretical $100M saving on $655M of H-2A wages. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. Non-H-2A growers saw a 2.4% rise, $16.50 to $16.90; H-2A crews saw about a 15% cut. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost for both seasons was obtainable; $25-30 per worker-day of housing and transport means the all-in rate fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, $16.23 to $12.47. Confidence: high on rates, medium on all-in. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's seven-staff Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and harnesses, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build. Trackers disagree: a 25% IEEPA duty or a 10% Section 122 charge from 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was published. Make USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the Tallis v4 build a closing condition. [S144, S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's audit. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous machinery but certifies nothing, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed the family alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs. [S144, S151, S153, S154, S166]

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record outweighs any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05; the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 while the October 2026 deck called it undecided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel citing an executive order pushing agencies to take title and domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions. [S144, S155, S158, S159]

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 3 by Lead Analyst, 6,733 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the 2026 H-2A wage is $19.97 an hour, set on 2026-08-03 after an October 2025 cut for many California jobs. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 18 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, the pool 8.7x smaller than the headline, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 2.78x at $250M; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 2.4x-4.0x, while the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures need the full $18M. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

::: briefing
| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What it sells | 64 robots, 75 paid seasons and five paying growers at $9,500 a season in 2026 (company-reported, unverified); 110 robots contracted and 50 letters of intent for a 360-robot 2027 plan | S53 unverified |
| Performance | 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 selected rows with 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime (company); independent trials report 72%-87%, putting harvest-level recovery near 75%-80% | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350 | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |
:::

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. If the trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the right answer reverses and $72M is cheap [S53 unverified].

::: efficiency
| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| FY2026E revenue | $2.6M, 46% Tallis engineering services and 13% grants | S53 unverified |
| 2026 RaaS revenue | $0.71M | S53 unverified |
| Gross margin | 41% as reported; -85% after fleet depreciation | S53 unverified |
| Contribution per robot-season | -$8,100 at $9,500; -$650 at $12,700 with $31,000 cost | S53 unverified |
| Net burn and runway | $410,000 a month; 4.4 usable months to covenant at 2026-10-31 | S53 unverified |
| Pre-money / FY2026E revenue | $72M / 27.7x | S53 unverified |
| Burn multiple | 7.0x FY2026; 5.9x FY2027 | S53 unverified |
| Capital raised | $38.5M equity and notes; $0.65M grant; $2.5M equipment facility with $1.6M drawn | S53 unverified |
:::

::: one-question
What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?

The answer decides whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. At 75%-80% the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with clean bruising the same numbers become conservative and the round is financeable [S53, S56].
:::

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit [S53 unverified].
2. Reprice to $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.0x at a $250M exit, and without a minimum-cash covenant the case becomes Invest with conditions [S53 unverified].
3. The independent harvest-level trial is the gating measurement: 75%-80% makes this a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes it a crew replacement [S53 unverified, S56, S181].
:::

Diligence next: the independent trial, the firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, insurer terms for product liability, and the corporate records that confirm entity and IP ownership. Until those arrive, the deck's operating and financial claims are unverified company material [S53, S128]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 5 by Lead Analyst, 8,519 characters)
Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score is not a verdict on the technology; it is a verdict on what an investor can prove today. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 18 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, the lender agreement and the grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027 and the 2026 H-2A wage at $19.97, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S142].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions. The covenant itself rests on the deck: no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. If no minimum-cash test exists, the 2027 failure is a 25%-40% down round rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls to about 35%, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95, S128].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run harvest crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. The exit record cuts both ways: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, but Root AI cleared at $60M in harvesting, and four of the five funded peers failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026, including Monarch Tractor, which raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money and sold its assets to Caterpillar 21 months later [S53, S178, S93, S176, S91].

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit | 85% or more on unselected blocks | Independent trial below 80% | -40% | High | A second grower leaves over quality | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | v4 unit cost at 300 units | $31,000-$33,000 | A quote above $36,000 | -25% to -35% | High | Design freeze slips past 2027-01 | S53 unverified |
| 3 | 2027 book | 360 robots at $12,700 or more | Fewer than 250 contracted by 2027-02 | -30% | High | 44% cover unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | Financing and covenant | $18M close by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill; if no minimum-cash test exists, bear 50% to ~35% and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions | A close after Q1 2027 or a $16M raise | -100% of equity | High | $4.0M of $18M committed at 2026-10-31 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | Labour policy | Wage floor keeps rising | H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze | -15% to -20% | Medium | DOL rulemaking on H-2A wages | S169 |
:::

rows.benchmark: Base case 50% bear weight in the risk assessment; $72M pre-money Series A.

rows.confidence: High on the split (deck arithmetic); low on contract enforceability.

rows.implication: Underwrite on contracted robot-seasons at list or renewal price, not on the $3.2M; a price above $50M needs the services line replaced by robot revenue.
rows.mechanism: The headline blends a one-season rental book, a related-party services contract and non-binding letters, so it overstates revenue that recurs without re-selling.
rows.weakens: The $1.4M contracts are themselves unverified and are one-season, so even the 51x base may not recur.

rows.benchmark: Deck's 2% 2028 adoption assumption; 3.5 acres per robot; 50,000 US strawberry acres.
rows.confidence: Medium; arithmetic high, inputs unverified.

rows.implication: Treat the 2028 plan as a capacity requirement, not a forecast; the round does not fund the fleet it implies.

rows.benchmark: Five paying growers in 2026; four contracted for 2027; 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 those four rented in 2026.
rows.confidence: High on the counts; low on causation.

rows.implication: Diligence the reason for the cut and the renewal terms before pricing; a second Grower B would remove 20 of the 110 contracted robots.
rows.mechanism: The 2027 contracted book is an expansion bet on four relationships, one of which just cut its fleet; retention, not new logos, carries the plan.
rows.weakens: The deck does not disclose why Grower B cut, so the cut could reflect acreage or planting rather than performance.

rows.benchmark: 3x LTV:CAC venture benchmark; $12,600 of four-season contribution per robot at the $16,500 list.
rows.confidence: Low-to-medium; an estimate with stated assumptions, not a disclosed figure.
rows.finding: CAC is not reported; an estimated $0.9-1.2M of sales cost (five sales staff at $180,000-240,000 fully loaded) over three new paying growers in 2026 is $300,000-400,000 a grower, $8,000-11,000 per contracted 2027 robot or $24,000-32,000 per robot added in 2026; LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal.

rows.benchmark: Deere FY2024: 17.5% operating margin and 22.8% ROIC on a mature equipment book.

rows.finding: Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the $9,500 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead.

rows.mechanism: Depreciation is a real cash-equivalent cost of the fleet; excluding it from gross margin turns a -85% contract at the 2026 price into a reported 41% margin.
rows.weakens: The four-season life and $31,000 target cost are company assumptions; a six-season life raises the renewal yield toward zero, not to Deere's level.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M pre-money, 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue, Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M; a $12M cheque at $48M-$55M returns 2.4x-4.0x. Killer risks: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision system classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, 132% of the US acreage base. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

After the independent challenge we moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 at list, an 85% independent trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days left. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. Without a minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |
:::

The five assumptions are ranked by damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: failure means zero equity, not dilution. Labour now cuts both ways: the H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 on 2026-01-01 under the October 2025 interim rule, the 2026-08-03 notice set skill tiers at $16.45-$18.71, a federal court held that method unlawful on 2026-08-26 with backpay possible, and AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01. The file does not establish the all-in hand-pick cost year on year, so assumption 5 carries medium-low confidence, not medium, and the -15% to -20% impact stands as a downside [S190, S192, S195].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, on unselected blocks | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80%, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 unverified |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor rebounds: AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01, and no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick advantage | Medium-low | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S190, S195 |
History says the technology exits and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 after an assignment for creditors; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of five funded peers failed or sold assets in 2021-2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S176, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M, because the price capitalises a six-conjunct bull case and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move the case. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post-money and earns 2.4x at a $150M exit and 4.0x at $250M; the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures hold only if the full $18M closes. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm 300-unit quote, licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and fleet-entity consolidation [S53, S128].

rows.follow_up: Reconcile the $3,100 service line to the 9 field staff and the 1:8 technician ratio; at 360 robots the line implies 45 technicians.
rows.implication: The renewal price is 5% below break-even; a 2027 book at $12,700 cannot fund the fleet, and the plan's 52% RaaS margin assumes a service cost the organisation cannot yet deliver.
rows.mechanism: Service intensity is set by robots per technician and the harvest calendar; the price only clears cost if service cost falls $1,350 a season, which is a 44% reduction in the largest direct-cost line.
rows.weakens: If remote supervision reaches 1:25, the target service cost could be reached; the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet show it.

rows.benchmark: Five paying growers in 2026; four contracted for 2027; 110 contracted robots versus 64 rented by those four in 2026 (+72%).
rows.confidence: High on the counts; low on the reasons, which the deck does not disclose.
rows.finding: 53% of 2026 paid seasons sit with Marisol Ridge (24) and Pajaro Bluff (16). Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots (-36%) with no reason disclosed and is contracted for 20 in 2027; Grower E exited in 2026-06 over bruising, Grower D has no 2027 contract, 6 of 8 other pilots have no LOI and 9 of 14 pilot farms never paid.
rows.follow_up: Ask Grower B and Grower D for the reason for the cut and their 2027 intentions; obtain the 110 executed contracts and 50 LOIs.
rows.implication: The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four relationships, one of which just cut its fleet; a second Grower B would remove 20 of 110 contracted robots.
rows.mechanism: With five paying growers, each relationship is 20% of the book; retention and expansion, not new logos, carry the plan, and a single non-renewal is material.
rows.weakens: The Grower B cut could reflect acreage or planting rather than performance; the deck does not say.

rows.benchmark: 3x LTV:CAC venture benchmark; $12,600 of four-season contribution per robot at the $16,500 list.
rows.confidence: Low-to-medium; an estimate with stated assumptions, not a disclosed figure.
rows.finding: CAC is not reported. Five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new paying growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted 2027 robot and $24,000-32,000 per robot added in 2026; LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal.
rows.follow_up: Request sales and marketing spend by year, pilot cost per farm and the sales-qualified opportunity count.
rows.implication: CAC payback at list is 2.5-3.5 seasons on top of 2.8 seasons of hardware payback, beyond the four-season life; at renewal it never pays back.
rows.mechanism: Pilots and a once-a-year buying window front-load selling cost before a four-season asset earns contribution, so acquisition cost has to be recovered within the same four seasons as the robot.
rows.weakens: Sales and marketing spend is not a reported line; the estimate rests on headcount and an assumed fully loaded cost.

rows.benchmark: Deere FY2024 17.5% operating margin and 22.8% ROIC; United Rentals fleet rental at scale.
rows.confidence: Medium; the fleet-rental comparison is directionally right but Orrin is pre-scale.
rows.finding: Overhead is $92,000 per paid robot-season in FY2026, $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $14,700-19,000 in FY2028; gross profit per season is $3,900 at the 2026 price and $3,150 at list with target cost.
rows.follow_up: Show the operating-expense build at 360 robots, including the 45 technicians implied by a 1:8 ratio.
rows.implication: Until opex per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger; the plan never reaches that crossover.
rows.mechanism: Operating leverage only works if revenue per season grows faster than the fixed field and engineering base; the plan grows the fleet 4.8x while opex grows 1.6x, which is the right direction but not enough.
rows.weakens: FY2028 is a projection; the 2027 opex line could be cut, but the field organisation needed for 360 robots is not in the deck.

rows.benchmark: Private ag-robotics: Monarch over $220M raised (S54), Carbon $157M at the 2024-10 Series D (S55), Advanced Farm ceased operations 2025 (S93, S114), Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds (S94), Abundant Robotics shut down 2021 (S91).
rows.confidence: Medium; funding and shutdown facts are sourced, but the peer set is small and private.
rows.finding: The category has absorbed several hundred million dollars without a scaled commercial strawberry winner; two entrants shut down and one, Monarch, wound down in 2026 after raising over $220M.
rows.follow_up: Compare Orrin's capital intensity with Harvest CROO and Carbon on robots in service, not dollars raised.
rows.implication: A $72M pre-money for a 64-robot fleet with $1.4M of contracted robot revenue is a pre-commercial price; the peer base rate supports a milestone-based entry, not a full-cycle bet.
rows.mechanism: Hardware fleets need capex, service density and a seasonal selling window; capital raised does not shorten the field-validation clock, so well-funded entrants still fail on unit economics.
rows.weakens: Survivorship cuts both ways: Carbon and Monarch raised at large multiples, so a strategic buyer may still pay for the technology.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M — 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue — Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M; at $48M-$55M, 2.4x-4.0x. Killer risks: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, 132% of the US acreage base. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

The independent challenge moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 at list, an 85% trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days left. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses April 2027, the fleet stays below 100, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is registered. Without a minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |
:::

The five assumptions are ranked by damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: failure means zero equity, not dilution. Labour now cuts both ways: the H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 on 2026-01-01, the 2026-08-03 notice set skill tiers at $16.45-$18.71, a federal court held that method unlawful on 2026-08-26 with backpay possible, and AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01. The file does not establish the all-in hand-pick cost year on year, so assumption 5 carries medium-low confidence and the -15% to -20% impact stands [S190, S192, S195].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, on unselected blocks | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80%, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 unverified |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor rebounds: AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01, and no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick advantage | Medium-low | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S190, S195 |
History says the technology exits and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 after an assignment for creditors; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of five funded peers failed or sold assets in 2021-2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S176, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M: the price capitalises a six-conjunct bull case and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move it. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post-money and earns 2.4x at a $150M exit and 4.0x at $250M; the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures hold only if the full $18M closes. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm 300-unit quote, licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and fleet-entity consolidation [S53, S128].
