Market draft:

The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, a claim resting on company-reported, unverified acreage, price and adoption inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not a $310M one, and the binding constraint is field performance rather than grower willingness to pay.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

[table]

The $42B and $3.1B figures are labour-spend numbers, company-reported and unverified; only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price it needs 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline number. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption, 3.6x the stated figure; the implied adoption CAGR from 2% in 2028 to 15% in 2031 is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

[price table]

The picker-day equivalent in the table follows from the deck's own productivity, which is company-reported and unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day means 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. That growers have bought only at the bottom of the price ladder, and that one Florida grower left over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

[regional table]

California's seven months are what make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: the same 1.5 acres per 24 hours covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, consistent with picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window — a company assumption, unverified, with no public instrument setting it — covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Florida's value is utilisation: a robot working Florida in winter and California in summer would log two seasons a year and halve depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market: the wages that make a robot compelling in California make it less compelling in Guadalajara. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Caterpillar bought Monarch Tractor's assets in April 2026 after a January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors [S53, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways. | SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M a year (2027 list price) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 acres per robot x $16,500 | Derived from unverified company inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified; not reachable in strawberries | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M at list, $27.2M at renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 an acre | Derived from unverified company inputs | S53 |

The $42B and $3.1B figures are labour-spend numbers, company-reported and unverified; only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M. |---|---|---|---|---|---|

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M — 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue — Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M; at $48M-$55M, 2.4x-4.0x. Killer risks: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, 132% of the US acreage base. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

The independent challenge moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 at list, an 85% trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days left. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses April 2027, the fleet stays below 100, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is registered. Without a minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |

History says the technology exits and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M: the price capitalises a six-conjunct bull case and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move it. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post-money and earns 2.4x at a $150M exit and 4.0x at $250M; the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures hold only if the full $18M closes. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm 300-unit quote, licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and fleet-entity consolidation [S53, S128].

arguments.markdown:
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, company-reported and unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's productivity, company-reported and unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the price ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | n/a | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1:2024; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Caterpillar bought Monarch Tractor's assets in April 2026 after a January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors [S53, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor is contested

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01 [S141, S142]. The federal H-2A adverse effect wage rate for California non-range occupations was republished on 2026-08-03 at a reported $19.97 an hour [S145]. The floor is contested: a district court ruled against the department's late-2025 AEWR changes on 2026-08-28, and a federal court invalidated the new methodology in September 2026, with one estimate putting the 2026 national H-2A wage reduction at $100M [S190, S194, S192]. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12 [S150, S148]. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; a holding floor widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified [S160]. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the H-2A floor has been lowered and relitigated, not simply raised, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers [S169, S190]. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Three inputs would move this from estimate to evidence: NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state for 2019-2025, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. If acreage is stable and the pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the 2031 line re-bases upward and supports a services business below the pre-money. If acreage is falling and realised price stays near $9,500, the strawberry market is small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53; unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported and unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap is not a rounding difference; it is a different market, and it needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 19 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, the pool 8.7x smaller than the headline, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 2.78x at $250M; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 2.4x-4.0x, while the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures need the full $18M. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

::: briefing
| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What it sells | 64 robots, 75 paid seasons and five paying growers at $9,500 a season in 2026 (company-reported, unverified); 110 robots contracted and 50 letters of intent for a 360-robot 2027 plan | S53 unverified |
| Performance | 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 selected rows with 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime (company); independent trials report 72%-87%, putting harvest-level recovery near 75%-80% | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350 | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |
:::

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. If the trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the right answer reverses and $72M is cheap [S53 unverified].

At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M balance is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, reaching 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of the $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. Bull at 20% needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots built, 250 sold at list, 85% harvest recovery and the licence test cleared. The bear is one domino with several symptoms: the round slipping carries 55% probability on that commitment book. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No loan agreement or UCC-1 filing is in the register, so the covenant rests on the deck alone, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms the field team chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit and 83-87% of detected fruit, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising and 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and every price in the plan assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M against the $1.5M minimum: breached at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second cycle | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15, below the minimum from 2027-03-14: default | S53, unverified; derived |

A reprice that takes three to six months is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet, not only a lower price.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on that fleet sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or intercompany IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would be buying different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating, it removes the barrier for a competitor and an acquirer, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M of FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers and harnesses, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also the largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length evidence [S53].

### The wage floor fell in 2026 and rebounds in 2027

The dated record is a step down, then a statutory rebound. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 cut the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left the rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01 (+16.9%). So 2026 faces cheaper hand labour, 2027 a floor back near the 2025 level, and the backpay tail is a grower cost shock that favours automation: the risk is a one-season delay in a purchase made once a year, before planting, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer and quantifiable: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin products from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin goods exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against a $36,000 milestone ceiling — and $825 a season of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics reported a first California customer deployment from April 2026 at 30 kilograms an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, so being the only open-field picker above 90% is already out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating its Livermore headquarters in March 2026; Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% between Q2 and Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is being underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S168, S171].

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | A second pilot exit; grower quality audit | Independent trial above 85% with a bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips into the minimum-cash test | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed unchanged through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver and standstill; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| No minimum-cash test: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 produced | Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M; $6M now, $6M on milestones | S53, unverified |
| Licence in the issuer, fleet and debt in the subsidiary | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence, parent guarantee, Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Second tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis withdraws as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply, tooling ownership, second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including the Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA origin opinion | S174 |
| H-2A floor falls 15.4% in 2026, rebounds in 2027 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not a wage floor | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata right at the Series A | S171, S168 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests carry most of the weight: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 with the minimum-cash definition, cross-default and waiver price; the Calder licence with assignment, change-of-control and "commercial service" definitions and the sub-licence; a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement with tooling ownership and a second source; and an independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and the tariff, medium on the covenant terms and harvest recovery, low on the 2027 build and the exit price; the Kestrel text and the Calder licence decide whether the bear case returns capital or nothing.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score is not a verdict on the technology; it is a verdict on what an investor can prove today. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 19 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, the lender agreement and the grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and the H-2A floor cut from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 in 2027, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions. The covenant itself rests on the deck: no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. If no minimum-cash test exists, the 2027 failure is a 25%-40% down round rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls to about 35%, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95, S128].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run harvest crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. The exit record cuts both ways: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, but Root AI cleared at $60M in harvesting, and four of the five funded peers failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026, including Monarch Tractor, which raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money and sold its assets to Caterpillar 21 months later [S53, S178, S93, S176, S91].

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit | 85% or more on unselected blocks | Independent trial below 80% | -40% | High | A second grower leaves over quality | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | v4 unit cost at 300 units | $31,000-$33,000 | A quote above $36,000 | -25% to -35% | High | Design freeze slips past 2027-01 | S53 unverified |
| 3 | 2027 book | 360 robots at $12,700 or more | Fewer than 250 contracted by 2027-02 | -30% | High | 44% cover unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | Financing and covenant | $18M close by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill; if no minimum-cash test exists, bear 50% to ~35% and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions | A close after Q1 2027 or a $16M raise | -100% of equity | High | $4.0M of $18M committed at 2026-10-31 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | Labour policy | AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01; no H-2A expansion | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling | -15% to -20% | Medium | DOL rulemaking on H-2A wages | S190, S195 |
:::

The sensitivity analysis above ranks the five assumptions; the recommendation changes under the downside cases, and not by dilution. A market 50% smaller, at 25,000 acres, gives a $117.9M pool at list and $17.7M at 15% adoption, which kills $72M but leaves $48M-$55M defensible. Revenue 30% lower, at $3.9M instead of $5.6M, removes $0.87M of gross profit at a 52% RaaS margin and leaves end-2027 cash at $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M covenant, breached at the low end. Customer acquisition at twice the plan cannot be absorbed: 200 uncontracted robots have one selling window, four sales staff and a 5-of-14 pilot conversion record. Financing six months late adds $2.46M of burn and leaves $1.24M of cash on 2027-06-15, a secured-lender default rather than a down round. Only the bull case, at 12%, returns 3.3x-4.4x; the base case at $72M is 1.7x-2.8x, and the bear is 0-1.0x at 50% with the covenant, 35% without it [S53 unverified].

Position sizing is zero at $72M and $6M at $48M-$55M pre-money, with $6M released on 2027 milestones: an independent harvest-level trial above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and the Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test. The maximum loss is the full $12M; reserve $6M for a Series B. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.03x at a $250M exit, against 2.78x at $72M; the 17.65% and 3.68x figures need the full $18M to close. Conditions precedent, not covenants: a Kestrel standstill or waiver signed with the term sheet, licence assignment consent, consolidation of the fleet entity and its grower contracts, and a second board seat with a veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control. Diligence next: a firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, and an insurer's view of product liability [S53, S128].

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Technology and product | 20% | 5 | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows; independent 72%-87%; no granted gripper patent; licence test on 2027-12-31 | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Market and timing | 15% | 6 | Labour cost real; 2026 H-2A cut, 2027 statutory rebound; $235.7M pool at 100% adoption; acreage unverified | S53 unverified, S141, S190 |
| Team and execution | 15% | 5 | Founder-market fit; CTO vacant since 2023-08-31; nine field staff against 45 needed; part-time CFO | S53 unverified |
| Business model and unit economics | 15% | 3 | -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500; $13,350 break-even; 44% of 2027 booked | S53 unverified |
| Financial position and cash | 10% | 3 | 4.4 months usable at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14; 46% related-party revenue; 56% of ARR not recurring | S53 unverified |
| Valuation and terms | 15% | 2 | 27.7x FY2026E revenue; 51.4x contracted RaaS; $36.8M preference; no protective provisions | S53 unverified, S8, S12, S14, S95 |
| Exit path | 10% | 4 | OEM precedent of $60M-$305M; four of five peers failed or sold assets | S178, S176, S91, S115 |
| Composite | 100% | 4.1 | Weighted average of the seven dimensions | Derived from the rows above (S53, S8, S12, S14, S95) |

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 2.78x at $250M [S53 unverified].
2. The investable structure is $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.03x at a $250M exit, while 17.65% and 3.68x need the full $18M [S53 unverified].
3. Harvest-level recovery decides the case: 75%-80% makes the machine a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes even $72M look cheap [S53 unverified, S56, S181].
:::

Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. arguments.markdown:
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's productivity, unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the price ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | n/a | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1:2024; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Caterpillar bought Monarch Tractor's assets in April 2026 after a January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors [S53, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor is contested

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The federal H-2A adverse effect wage rate for California non-range occupations was republished on 2026-08-03 at a reported $19.97 an hour. The floor is contested: a district court ruled against the department's late-2025 AEWR changes on 2026-08-28, and a federal court invalidated the new methodology in September 2026, with one estimate putting the 2026 national H-2A wage reduction at $100M. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S145, S190, S194, S192, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; a holding floor widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the H-2A floor has been lowered and relitigated, not simply raised, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Three inputs would move this from estimate to evidence: NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. If acreage is stable and the pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the 2031 line re-bases upward and supports a services business below the pre-money. If acreage is falling and realised price stays near $9,500, the strawberry market is small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53; unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported and unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap is not a rounding difference; it is a different market, and it needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
:::

Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin's figures are unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

arguments.markdown:
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's productivity, unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the price ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | n/a | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1:2024; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Caterpillar bought Monarch Tractor's assets in April 2026 after a January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors [S53, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor is contested

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The federal H-2A adverse effect wage rate for California non-range occupations was republished on 2026-08-03 at a reported $19.97 an hour. The floor is contested: a district court ruled against the department's late-2025 AEWR changes on 2026-08-28, and a federal court invalidated the new methodology in September 2026, with one estimate putting the 2026 national H-2A wage reduction at $100M. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S145, S190, S194, S192, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; a holding floor widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the H-2A floor has been lowered and relitigated, not simply raised, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

The inputs that would move this from estimate to evidence are NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. If acreage is stable and the pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the out-year line re-bases upward and supports a services business below the pre-money. If acreage is falling and realised price stays near the current contract, the strawberry market is small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53; unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported and unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap is not a rounding difference; it is a different market, and it needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M balance is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, reaching 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of the $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 sold at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 55% probability on that commitment book. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No loan agreement or UCC-1 filing is in the register, so the covenant rests on the deck alone, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit and 83-87% of detected fruit, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising and 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15, below the minimum from 2027-03-14: default | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet, not a lower price.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on that fleet sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would be buying different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating, it removes the barrier for a competitor, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M of FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also the largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length evidence [S53].

### The wage floor fell in 2026 and rebounds in 2027

The dated record: a step down, then a statutory rebound. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 cut the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left the rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01 (+16.9%). So 2026 faces cheaper hand labour and 2027 a floor back near the 2025 level; the risk is a one-season delay in a purchase made once a year, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 milestone ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics reported a first California customer deployment from April 2026 at 30 kilograms an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, so the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in March 2026; Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% between Q2 and Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is being underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S168, S171].

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | A second pilot exit; grower quality audit | Independent trial above 85% with a bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips into the minimum-cash test | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver and standstill; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| No minimum-cash test: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 produced | Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M; $6M now, $6M later | S53, unverified |
| Entity split: IP in issuer, fleet and debt in subsidiary | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence, parent guarantee, Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Second tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis exits as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply, tooling ownership, second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including the Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA origin opinion | S174 |
| H-2A floor falls 15.4% in 2026, rebounds in 2027 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not a wage floor | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata right at the Series A | S171, S168 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter most: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 with the minimum-cash definition, cross-default and waiver price; the Calder licence with assignment, change-of-control and sub-licence terms; a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement with tooling ownership and a second source; and an independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and the tariff, medium on the covenant terms and harvest recovery, low on the 2027 build and the exit price; the Kestrel text and the Calder licence decide whether the bear case returns capital or nothing.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. The operating facts are company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. Prices are company-reported and unverified; the recomputation is verified [S53].

The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. ### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; the deck does not say how many were idle or on unpaid pilots. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year, so the three growers added in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted 2027 robot; at the $16,500 list a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x, below 3x, and negative at renewal. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; commercial-viability demonstration 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. Orrin's ask is small against that record, and the economics above say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The investor implication is to wait for field data, or to structure the lead check as tranches tied to the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 unit cost at or below target; at current unit economics, more robots destroy more capital.

Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. ### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.
