| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles for autonomous farm machinery and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods (S166); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Compared with Harvest CROO, which discloses no rate, price or fleet, Orrin's 64 robots are the category's only disclosed paid deployment. Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

arguments.markdown:
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's productivity, unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the price ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Caterpillar bought Monarch Tractor's assets in April 2026 after a January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors [S53, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor is contested

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The federal H-2A adverse effect wage rate for California non-range occupations was republished on 2026-08-03 at a reported $19.97 an hour. The floor is contested: a district court ruled against the department's late-2025 AEWR changes on 2026-08-28, and a federal court invalidated the new methodology in September 2026, with one estimate putting the 2026 national H-2A wage reduction at $100M. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S145, S190, S194, S192, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; a holding floor widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the H-2A floor has been lowered and relitigated, not simply raised, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Inputs that would move this from estimate to evidence are NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. If acreage is stable and the pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the out-year line re-bases up and supports a services business below the pre-money. If acreage is falling and realised price stays near the current contract, the strawberry market is small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53, unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported, unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap is not a rounding difference; it is a different market, and it needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M balance is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, reaching 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of the $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 sold at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 55% probability on that commitment book. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No loan agreement or UCC-1 filing is in the register, so the covenant rests on the deck alone, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit and 83-87% of detected fruit, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising and 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15, below the minimum from 2027-03-14: default | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on that fleet sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would be buying different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating, it removes the barrier for a competitor, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M of FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also the largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length evidence [S53].

### The wage floor fell in 2026 and rebounds in 2027

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 cut the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left the rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01 (+16.9%). So 2026 faces cheaper hand labour and 2027 a floor back near the 2025 level; the risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 milestone ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics reported a first California customer deployment from April 2026 at 30 kilograms an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, so the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in March 2026; Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% between Q2 and Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is being underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S168, S171].

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | A second pilot exit; grower quality audit | Independent trial above 85% with a bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips into the minimum-cash test | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver and standstill; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| No minimum-cash test: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 produced | Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M; $6M now, $6M later | S53, unverified |
| Entity split: IP in issuer, fleet and debt in subsidiary | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence, parent guarantee, Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Second tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis exits as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply, tooling ownership, second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including the Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA origin opinion | S174 |
| H-2A floor falls 15.4% in 2026, rebounds in 2027 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not a wage floor | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata right at the Series A | S171, S168 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter most: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 with the minimum-cash definition, cross-default and waiver price; the Calder licence with assignment, change-of-control and sub-licence terms; a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement with tooling ownership and a second source; and an independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and the tariff, medium on the covenant terms and harvest recovery, low on the 2027 build and the exit price; the Kestrel text and the Calder licence decide whether the bear case returns capital or nothing.

Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; idle robots and unpaid pilots are not disclosed. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year, so the three growers added in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted 2027 robot; at the $16,500 list a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x, below 3x, and negative at renewal. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 | +$4,500 | 2.5 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; verified recomputation [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The counts are partially verified: the grower table sums to 75, but the contracts are unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026, down 36%, and has contracted 20 for 2027; the deck gives no reason. The cut matters because it came in the second paid season, from a reference customer, while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].

| Deal | Status | Date | Reason | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grower E, Plant City FL | Pilot ended; no 2027 robots | 2026-06 | Fruit bruising; unverified | S53 p.6, p.13 |
| Grower D, Plant City FL | 11 paid robots in 2025-26; no 2027 contract, "in discussion" | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| Grower B, Santa Maria CA | Cut from 22 to 14 robots (-36%) | 2026 season | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 6 of 8 other pilot farms | 2025 and 2026 pilots; no LOI or 2027 order | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 9 of 14 pilot farms | Never a paid season | 2024-2026 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; idle robots and unpaid pilots are not disclosed. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025; wound down | S54, S168 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; demo 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The economics above say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" is a statement about what competitors have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California commercial deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO has claimed human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The competitive question is whether Orrin converts a two-season paid-deployment lead into contracted acres before DailyRobotics, Harvest CROO or an equipment maker closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product, stage and status at 2026-10-31 | Published performance | Price and model | Share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Piece-rate or hourly; California AEWR reported at $19.97/hour | Near-100% of acres | Proven quality, no capex, flexes with volume | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24 (company claim) | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Decade of NSF SBIR funding; Florida base; patents | No disclosed paid fleet, price or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers, onboard grading; announced 2025-11 for a first California deployment from April 2026; not confirmed deployed at 2026-10-31 | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | RaaS primary; sale possible; price not disclosed | No confirmed fleet | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment, price or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial from 2019; ceased operations July 2025 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Exited | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B; CNH investment | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; IP, assets and team acquired by Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Exited | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic systems (WSU; Journal of Field Robotics) | Research prototypes | 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry; 83-87% of detected fruit | Not sold | None | Publish methods and results | Not commercial | S56, S42, S57 |
| Equipment makers (Deere, CNH, Caterpillar) | Autonomous platforms and see-and-spray; no berry product in Deere's FY2025 10-K | n/a | n/a | None in berries | Capital, dealer network, acquisition record | Not in this crop today | S8, S95, S196 |

The Picker competes in three arenas, and only the first is a robot market. The hand crew picks nearly every US acre and is not standing still: harvest-aid platforms make pickers faster while keeping the crew, and the H-2A floor is contested rather than rising [S169]. Open-field robots are the second arena, where the table shows one long-funded claimant, one announced entrant and one well-funded failure. Tabletop and greenhouse systems (Tortuga, Agrobot, MetoMotion, Dogtooth) serve a different production system and are not direct competitors today.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs the grower nothing when it is not working, needs no capital and already meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin has to beat that on bruising before it beats it on cost, and one Florida grower's exit over bruising shows the bar is real. Among robot vendors, Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: Florida-based, 13 patents, $10M raised over 14 rounds, $1.25M of NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 public claim that its open-field trials match human harvesting. Its weakness is disclosure — no paid fleet, price or shipment figure — which is also Orrin's opportunity: the first vendor to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference point for growers and acquirers [S1, S179].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so every berry the cameras missed leaves the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and rows chosen by Orrin's field team; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit. At 85% detection Orrin's harvest recovery is 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell. DailyRobotics' 30 kg/hour and roughly 4% bruise rate are its own claims, not a benchmark. That is a supplement to a crew in year one, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team draws about its own machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

| Entrant | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Funding | Why not direct today | Threat path | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AGRIST (Japan) | Rail-guided greenhouse robot for peppers and cucumbers; Series B 2025-09-17; six deployments, all Japan | Not disclosed | Vendor-stated 55% harvest rate; no strawberry or open-field product | Rail-guided harvest could move to tabletop berries | S183 |
| Four Growers (US) | Greenhouse tomato harvesting robot in development; two filed patents | $15.1M raised | Development stage; no strawberry | Greenhouse tomato transfers to tabletop strawberry | S185, S182 |
| Carbon Robotics (US) | Laser weeder; about 100 growers | $157M at the 2024-10 Series D; $232M-$276M by 2026 trackers | Never touches the crop | Dealer base and capital could fund a harvest arm or an acquisition | S184, S186, S55 |

None builds a soft-fruit end-effector or carries a picking claim against the 94%, so none is a direct competitor today. The threat is capital and distribution: Carbon Robotics' installed base and $232M-$276M of funding, and AGRIST's co-operative channel in Japan, are the assets a strawberry arm would need. Orrin's $20.5M raised is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's, which is why the entrant screen matters more than the current product list [S183, S185, S186, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: the gripper application had every claim rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families are licensed from a university and become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. What is hard to copy is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots across two states. The peers show what that costs: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M at that point and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026; Carbon Robotics has $157M at its 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026 trackers [S54, S189, S168, S196, S55, S186].

| Replication route | What it supplies | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | Motion planning, grasp control, labelled berry perception | 6-9 months | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |
| Contract manufacturer | Build capacity and tooling | 3-6 months | Demand and service network | S53 |
| Team hired from a failed peer | Hands-on strawberry experience | 6-12 months | Installed base and grower references | S114, S115 |

The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 manipulation stack and the published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but they supply none of the seasonal service organisation that takes four to six years to build [S181, S42, S56].

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025 after commercial deployments, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch Tractor's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits that did happen went to equipment makers: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI, a fraction of the row-crop prices. Deere's FY2025 10-K mentions no berry or robotic-harvesting product, so the OEM threat today is capital and acquisition appetite rather than a competing machine. That record supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and it argues for pricing the round on contracted acres rather than a technology lead [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Orrin's position | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Challenger | Hand crews and H-2A | Orrin: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS with no grower capital, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. Scale, not invention, decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route to scale. Orrin wins if the fleet proves fruit quality at scale in 2027 and contracted renewal robots convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them. No private vendor discloses audited performance, price or shipments; every share statement is an absence of evidence.

(S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin's field team selected and excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe or pluckable fruit. The commercial record includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 claim of performance on par with human harvesting, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 California deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery [S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; verified recomputation [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The counts are partially verified: the grower table sums to 75, but the contracts are unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026, down 36%, and has contracted 20 for 2027; the deck gives no reason. The cut matters because it came in the second paid season, from a reference customer, while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].

| Deal | Status | Date | Reason | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grower E, Plant City FL | Pilot ended; no 2027 robots | 2026-06 | Fruit bruising; unverified | S53 p.6, p.13 |
| Grower D, Plant City FL | 11 paid robots in 2025-26; no 2027 contract, "in discussion" | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| Grower B, Santa Maria CA | Cut from 22 to 14 robots (-36%) | 2026 season | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 6 of 8 other pilot farms | 2025 and 2026 pilots; no LOI or 2027 order | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 9 of 14 pilot farms | Never a paid season | 2024-2026 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; idle robots and unpaid pilots are not disclosed. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025; wound down | S54, S168 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; demo 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The economics above say why: the current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target. Source: S53.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M balance is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, reaching 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of the $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 sold at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 55% probability on that commitment book. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No loan agreement or UCC-1 filing is disclosed, so the covenant rests on the deck alone, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit and 83-87% of detected fruit, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising and 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15, below the minimum from 2027-03-14: default | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on that fleet sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would be buying different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating, it removes the barrier for a competitor, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M of FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also the largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length evidence [S53].

### The wage floor fell in 2026 and rebounds in 2027

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 cut the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left the rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01 (+16.9%). So 2026 faces cheaper hand labour and 2027 a floor back near the 2025 level; the risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 milestone ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics reported a first California customer deployment from April 2026 at 30 kilograms an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, so the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in March 2026; Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% between Q2 and Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is being underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S168, S171].

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | A second pilot exit; grower quality audit | Independent trial above 85% with a bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips into the minimum-cash test | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver and standstill; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| No minimum-cash test: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 disclosed | Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M; $6M now, $6M later | S53, unverified |
| Entity split: IP in issuer, fleet and debt in subsidiary | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence, parent guarantee, Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Second tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis exits as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply, tooling ownership, second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including the Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA origin opinion | S174 |
| H-2A floor falls 15.4% in 2026, rebounds in 2027 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not a wage floor | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata right at the Series A | S171, S168 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter most: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 with the minimum-cash definition, cross-default and waiver price; the Calder licence with assignment, change-of-control and sub-licence terms; a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement with tooling ownership and a second source; and an independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and the tariff, medium on the covenant terms and harvest recovery, low on the 2027 build and the exit price; the Kestrel text and the Calder licence decide whether the bear case returns capital or nothing.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO has claimed human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin converts a two-season paid-deployment lead into contracted acres before DailyRobotics, Harvest CROO or an equipment maker closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Model and share | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Piece-rate or hourly; California AEWR reported at $19.97/hour; near-100% share | Proven quality, no capex, flexes with volume | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24 | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | Not disclosed; no disclosed fleet | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31 | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | RaaS; price not disclosed; no confirmed fleet | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed; exited | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed; exited | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic systems (WSU; Journal of Field Robotics) | Research prototypes | 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry; 83-87% of detected fruit | Not sold | Published methods | Not commercial | S56, S42, S57 |
| Equipment makers (Deere, CNH, Caterpillar) | Autonomous platforms and see-and-spray; no berry product in Deere's FY2025 10-K | n/a | None in berries | Capital, dealer network, acquisition record | Not in this crop today | S8, S95, S196 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market, and only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default on US acreage and is not standing still: harvest aids make pickers faster while keeping the crew, and the H-2A floor is contested rather than rising. Open-field robots are the second arena, with one long-funded claimant, one announced entrant and one well-funded failure. Tabletop and greenhouse systems (Tortuga, Agrobot, MetoMotion, Dogtooth) serve a different production system and are not direct competitors today.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs the grower nothing when it is not working, needs no capital and already meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before it beats it on cost, and one Florida grower's exit over bruising shows the bar is real. Among robot vendors, Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: Florida-based, 13 patents, $10M raised over 14 rounds, $1.25M of NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim that its open-field trials match human harvesting. Its weakness is disclosure — no paid fleet, price or shipments — which is also Orrin's opportunity: the first vendor to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference for growers and acquirers [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so every missed berry leaves the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and rows chosen by Orrin's field team; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell. DailyRobotics' 30 kg/hour and roughly 4% bruise rate are its own claims, not a benchmark. That is a supplement to a crew in year one, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team draws about its own machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST, a Miyazaki company, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six deployments, all in Japan. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026 trackers. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector or carries a picking claim against the 94%, so the threat is capital and distribution: Carbon's installed base and AGRIST's co-operative channel are the assets a strawberry arm would need. Orrin's $20.5M raised is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: the gripper application had every claim rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families are licensed from a university and become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 manipulation stack and the published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the seasonal service organisation that takes four to six years to build. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M at that point and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026; Carbon has $157M at its 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026 trackers [S54, S189, S168, S196, S55, S186, S181, S42, S56].

| Team hired from a failed peer | 6-12 | Installed base and grower references | S114, S115 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. arguments.markdown:
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin's figures are unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, CE or UKCA marking, incident log or insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous farm machinery (S166), and ISO 18497-4:2024, published 2024-07-31, the verification and validation methods (S199); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Compared with Harvest CROO, which discloses no rate, price or fleet, Orrin's 64 robots are the category's only disclosed paid deployment. Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

| Company | Approach | Claim at 2026-10-31 | Verification status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin | Soft gripper, night stereo, open field | 94% of detected, 5.6 s a berry | Company-reported; conditional denominator | S53 |
| Harvest CROO | Open-field strawberry harvester | "On par with human harvesting" | Company claim; no rate or fleet | S1 |
| AGRIST | Rail-guided greenhouse, peppers and cucumbers | 55% harvest rate; six deployments, all Japan | Vendor-stated; co-op announcements | S183 |
| Four Growers | Greenhouse tomato, 8 stereo cameras | In development; two patents filed | Development stage per its own site | S185, S182 |
| Carbon Robotics | Laser weeding, 30 lasers | 200,000 weeds an hour; roughly 100 growers | Company-sourced; commercial since 2021 | S184, S186 |

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |

| Gripper and slip sensing | 3 | Crowded art; no allowed claim | 1 year | S130 |

| **Composite** | **4/10** | Operations are the barrier, not patents | **24-30 months to a comparable machine** | S53, S114 |

| Robots-as-a-Service | Commercial, 5 growers, 2025 season | $0.71M | 41% before fleet depreciation | 360 robots in 2027 | S53 unverified |
| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 unverified |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. The screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop. [S57]
:::

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 verification report and an ATP swab record (S163, S199). For an investor, the cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and a surviving claim.
