{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 6 by Lead Analyst, 8,685 characters)
Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score is not a verdict on the technology; it is a verdict on what an investor can prove today. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 19 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, the lender agreement and the grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and the H-2A floor cut from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 in 2027, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions. The covenant itself rests on the deck: no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. If no minimum-cash test exists, the 2027 failure is a 25%-40% down round rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls to about 35%, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95, S128].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run harvest crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. The exit record cuts both ways: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, but Root AI cleared at $60M in harvesting, and four of the five funded peers failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026, including Monarch Tractor, which raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money and sold its assets to Caterpillar 21 months later [S53, S178, S93, S176, S91].

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit | 85% or more on unselected blocks | Independent trial below 80% | -40% | High | A second grower leaves over quality | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | v4 unit cost at 300 units | $31,000-$33,000 | A quote above $36,000 | -25% to -35% | High | Design freeze slips past 2027-01 | S53 unverified |
| 3 | 2027 book | 360 robots at $12,700 or more | Fewer than 250 contracted by 2027-02 | -30% | High | 44% cover unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | Financing and covenant | $18M close by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill; if no minimum-cash test exists, bear 50% to ~35% and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions | A close after Q1 2027 or a $16M raise | -100% of equity | High | $4.0M of $18M committed at 2026-10-31 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | Labour policy | AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01; no H-2A expansion | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling | -15% to -20% | Medium | DOL rulemaking on H-2A wages | S190, S195 |
:::

The sensitivity analysis above ranks the five assumptions; the recommendation changes under the downside cases, and not by dilution. A market 50% smaller, at 25,000 acres, gives a $117.9M pool at list and $17.7M at 15% adoption, which kills $72M but leaves $48M-$55M defensible. Revenue 30% lower, at $3.9M instead of $5.6M, removes $0.87M of gross profit at a 52% RaaS margin and leaves end-2027 cash at $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M covenant, breached at the low end. Customer acquisition at twice the plan cannot be absorbed: 200 uncontracted robots have one selling window, four sales staff and a 5-of-14 pilot conversion record. Financing six months late adds $2.46M of burn and leaves $1.24M of cash on 2027-06-15, a secured-lender default rather than a down round. Only the bull case, at 12%, returns 3.3x-4.4x; the base case at $72M is 1.7x-2.8x, and the bear is 0-1.0x at 50% with the covenant, 35% without it [S53 unverified].

Position sizing is zero at $72M and $6M at $48M-$55M pre-money, with $6M released on 2027 milestones: an independent harvest-level trial above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and the Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test. The maximum loss is the full $12M; reserve $6M for a Series B. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.03x at a $250M exit, against 2.78x at $72M; the 17.65% and 3.68x figures need the full $18M to close. Conditions precedent, not covenants: a Kestrel standstill or waiver signed with the term sheet, licence assignment consent, consolidation of the fleet entity and its grower contracts, and a second board seat with a veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control. Diligence next: a firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, and an insurer's view of product liability [S53, S128].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so every missed berry leaves the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and rows chosen by Orrin's field team; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell. That is a supplement to a crew in year one, not a replacement — the conclusion the WSU team draws about its own machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST, a Miyazaki company, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six deployments, all in Japan. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and describes its greenhouse tomato robot as in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026 trackers. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector or carries a picking claim against the 94%, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M raised is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. What is hard to copy is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots across two states. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 manipulation stack and the published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years to build. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M at that point and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |
| Team hired from a failed peer | 6-12 | Installed base and grower references | S114, S115 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to equipment makers: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI, a fraction of the row-crop prices. Deere's FY2025 10-K mentions no berry or robotic-harvesting product, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite rather than a competing machine. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Orrin | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS with no grower capital, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. Scale decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if the fleet proves fruit quality at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them. No private vendor discloses audited performance, price or shipments.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin's field team selected and excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe or pluckable fruit. The commercial record includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 claim of performance on par with human harvesting, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 California deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery [S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197].

Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. ### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, CE or UKCA marking, incident log or insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous farm machinery (S166), and ISO 18497-4:2024, published 2024-07-31, the verification and validation methods (S199); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. No audit or public filing exists and the head of finance is part-time, so FY2023-FY2026 are unverified management accounts [S53].

| $M | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Source |

| RaaS | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.38 | 0.71 | 4.6 | 12.9 | S53 (unverified) |
| Paid pilots | 0.03 | 0.12 | 0.27 | 0.34 | 0.4 | 0.3 | S53 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 0.00 | 0.20 | 0.95 | 1.20 | 0.6 | 0.0 | S53 (unverified) |
| Grants | 0.07 | 0.08 | 0.30 | 0.35 | 0.0 | 0.0 | S53 (unverified) |

| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S53 (unverified) |
| Operating loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S53 (unverified) |

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue, the $1.4M of one-season contracts makes the $72M pre-money 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet and 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres at 3.5 acres a robot — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after one month of $410k burn and about $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. The deck's 9 months is gross from 2026-09-30, before the covenant. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register: the minimum-cash test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and a $48-55M structure becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Until the agreement is produced, the covenant date is the planning case. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with the covenant in the middle. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO and goodwill cannot be calculated; the facts are $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M ($1.69M at 2026-10-31) before the $1.5M minimum. The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. No audit or public filing exists and the head of finance is part-time, so FY2023-FY2026 are unverified management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit per season at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue, the $1.4M of one-season contracts makes the $72M pre-money 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet and 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres at 3.5 acres a robot — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after one month of $410k burn and about $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. The deck's 9 months is gross from 2026-09-30, before the covenant. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register: the minimum-cash test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and a $48-55M structure becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Until the agreement is produced, the covenant date is the planning case. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with the covenant in the middle. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin converts a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival or an equipment maker closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03; near-100% share | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes with volume | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and Journal of Field Robotics prototypes; Deere, CNH and Caterpillar sell no berry robot | 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry; 83-87% of detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisition record | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95, S196 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market, and only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids make pickers faster without replacing them, and tabletop systems (Tortuga, Agrobot, MetoMotion, Dogtooth) serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and already meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M raised over 14 rounds, $1.25M of NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first vendor to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%, on rows Orrin chose; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its own machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026 trackers. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. What is hard to copy is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 manipulation stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |
| Team hired from a failed peer | 6-12 | Installed base and grower references | S114, S115 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to equipment makers: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K mentions no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Orrin | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS with no grower capital, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. Scale decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose and excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe or pluckable fruit. The record includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 California deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery [S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197].
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews still pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's human-parity claim and 13 patents; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's purchase of Monarch's assets; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |
:::

consensus.consensus: The pitch, and the way an ag-robotics Series A is usually framed, assumes the only autonomous open-field strawberry picker above 90% accuracy, a $310M obtainable market off a $3.1B serviceable one, a 41% gross margin and a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with large peer rounds such as Monarch's.
consensus.our_view: The labour problem is real and the machine sells seasons, but the price is not supported: the observable market is 8.7x smaller than the headline, unit contribution is negative at the price actually sold, and the technology moat is a conditional licence with a 2027 cliff. The thesis is non-consensus on valuation and on harvest-level performance, not on the existence of the problem. We would not lead at $72M; the investable structure is $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M tranched on 2027 milestones and a Kestrel standstill.
consensus.evidence: Section 3: 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 company-chosen rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent trials report 72%-87% and harvest-level recovery is about 75%-80% [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181]. Section 4: 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 caps the whole US strawberry robot-revenue pool at $235.7M, so $310M is 132% of the base [S53]. Section 6: after $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit is -$8,100 a season at the 2026 price and -$650 at the renewal with the target cost [S53]. Section 7: 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding; 46% of FY2026E revenue is one related-party services contract ending 2027-06-30 [S53]. Section 8: $72M pre is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted robot revenue [S53].
consensus.proof_event: An independent harvest-level trial above 85% with bruising no worse than a hand-picked control, 250 robots contracted for 2027 at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and a Kestrel standstill signed before the money is wired.

one_question.question: What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?
one_question.why: The 94% divides by detected ripe fruit and excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%, so it cannot tell an investor whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. At 75%-80% recovery with 3.8% bruising the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the same numbers become conservative and the 2027 plan is financeable. It is the one measurement that reprices every other assumption in the case.

arguments.position_sizing: Zero at $72M pre-money; $6M at $48M-$55M with $6M released on 2027 milestones (independent harvest trial above 85% with clean bruising, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, measured v4 cost at or below $33,000, Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test). Maximum loss $12M; $6M reserved for a Series B. At $50M pre-money a $12M-only cheque buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.0x at a $250M exit; 17.65% and 3.68x need the full $18M.
arguments.capital_efficiency: FY2026E revenue $2.6M against $38.5M of equity and notes raised, $0.24 of revenue per equity dollar (0.15 on FY2027E); burn multiple 7.0x FY2026 and 5.9x FY2027; $18M buys 300 robots at $33,000 but leaves $1.5-3.5M at end-2027.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin converts a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival or an equipment maker closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03; near-100% share | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes with volume | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74% of ripe at 20 s/berry; 83-87% of detected | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids make pickers faster without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and already meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M of NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first vendor to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its own machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at the 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response filed in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |
| Team hired from a failed peer | 6-12 | Installed base and grower references | S114, S115 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to equipment makers: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Orrin | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS with no grower capital, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. Scale decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose and excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe or pluckable fruit. The record includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 California deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery [S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197].
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews still pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's human-parity claim and 13 patents; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's purchase of Monarch's assets; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |
:::

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue, the $1.4M of one-season contracts makes the $72M pre-money 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet, 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after $410k of burn and $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. The deck's 9 months is gross from 2026-09-30, before the covenant. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register: the minimum-cash test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and a $48-55M structure becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Until produced, the covenant date is the planning case. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with the covenant in the middle. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO and goodwill cannot be calculated; the facts are $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M ($1.69M at 2026-10-31) before the $1.5M minimum. Working capital is estimated: $2.0M of direct cost, $0.8-1.1M of receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days, and $9.9M paid to Tallis before the season; grower and Tallis payment terms are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 4 by Regulatory Analyst, 8,983 characters)
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, against a theoretical $100M saving on $655M of H-2A wages. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. Non-H-2A growers saw a 2.4% rise, $16.50 to $16.90; H-2A crews saw about a 15% cut. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost for both seasons was obtainable; $25-30 per worker-day of housing and transport means the all-in rate fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, $16.23 to $12.47. Confidence: high on rates, medium on all-in. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's seven-staff Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and harnesses, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build. Trackers disagree: a 25% IEEPA duty or a 10% Section 122 charge from 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was published. Make USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the Tallis v4 build a closing condition. [S144, S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's audit. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous machinery but certifies nothing, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed the family alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs. [S144, S151, S153, S154, S166]

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record outweighs any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05; the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 while the October 2026 deck called it undecided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel citing an executive order pushing agencies to take title and domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions. [S144, S155, S158, S159]

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin converts a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival or an equipment maker closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its own machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at the 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. Scale decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 6 by Lead Analyst, 8,994 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 so the $12,700 renewal clears the $13,350 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M — 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue — Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M; at $48M-$55M, 2.4x-4.0x. Killer risks: negative contribution per robot-season, a licence that lapses on 2027-12-31 below 100 robots, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, 132% of the US acreage base. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

The independent challenge moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 at list, an 85% trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days left. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses April 2027, the fleet stays below 100, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is registered. Without a minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |
:::

The five assumptions are ranked by damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: failure means zero equity, not dilution. Labour now cuts both ways: the H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 on 2026-01-01, the 2026-08-03 notice set skill tiers at $16.45-$18.71, a federal court held that method unlawful on 2026-08-26 with backpay possible, and AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01. The file does not establish the all-in hand-pick cost year on year, so assumption 5 carries medium-low confidence and the -15% to -20% impact stands [S190, S192, S195].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, on unselected blocks | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80%, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 unverified |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027, a $16M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor rebounds: AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01, and no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick advantage | Medium-low | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S190, S195 |

History says the technology exits and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 after an assignment for creditors; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of five funded peers failed or sold assets in 2021-2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S176, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2024-2026 | $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money, then an assignment for creditors and a Caterpillar asset sale 21 months later | S176 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
:::

The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M: the price capitalises a six-conjunct bull case and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move it. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post-money and earns 2.4x at a $150M exit and 4.0x at $250M; the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures hold only if the full $18M closes. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm 300-unit quote, licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and fleet-entity consolidation [S53, S128]."}],"isError":false}

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's quality bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its own machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at the 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Orrin | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |

| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. Scale decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.
