(S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery [S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197].

arguments.markdown:
The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. No audit or public filing exists; the head of finance is part-time, so FY2023-FY2026 are unverified management accounts [S53].

| $M | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RaaS | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.38 | 0.71 | 4.6 | 12.9 | S53 (unverified) |
| Paid pilots | 0.03 | 0.12 | 0.27 | 0.34 | 0.4 | 0.3 | S53 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 0.00 | 0.20 | 0.95 | 1.20 | 0.6 | 0.0 | S53 (unverified) |
| Grants | 0.07 | 0.08 | 0.30 | 0.35 | 0.0 | 0.0 | S53 (unverified) |
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S53 (unverified) |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S53 (unverified) |
| Operating loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S53 (unverified) |

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue, the $1.4M of one-season contracts makes the $72M pre-money 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet, 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after $410k of burn and $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. The deck's 9 months is gross from 2026-09-30, before the covenant. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register: the minimum-cash test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and a $48-55M structure becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Until produced, the covenant date is the planning case. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with the covenant in the middle. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO and goodwill cannot be calculated; the facts are $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M ($1.69M at 2026-10-31) before the $1.5M minimum. Working capital is estimated: $2.0M of direct cost, $0.8-1.1M of receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days, and $9.9M paid to Tallis before the season; grower and Tallis payment terms are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures unverified; yields and working capital are derived estimates [S53, S7].

| Opex per paid robot-season | n/d | $155k | $92k | $30k | Price $9,500-16,500 | Derived; unverified | S53 |

| DSO / DIO / DPO | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | n/a | Not publicly disclosed | S53 |
| Peer capital raised | n/d | n/d | n/d | n/d | Monarch over $220M; Carbon $232M; 2 shutdowns | Independent | S54, S55, S91, S119 |

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex take usable cash below $1.5M in mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. The variable that moves the outcome most is utilisation: $10.8M of opex divided by 360 seasons is $30,000 per season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet; $1,000 on 360 robots is only $0.36M. Retention is second: Grower B cut its fleet 36% in 2026 for reasons not given, Grower D has no 2027 contract, Grower E exited over bruising, and four of five 2026 payers signed for 2027 (section 6). The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. Analyst estimates on unverified company figures [S53].

|---|---|---|---|---|
| RaaS gross margin 41% | $3,900 on $9,500 | Contradicted as economic margin | Excludes $12,000 fleet depreciation; fully loaded -$8,100 (-85%) | S53 p.9 |
| ARR $3.2M | 1.4 + 1.2 + 0.6 | Contradicted as ARR | 56% non-recurring or non-binding; contracted robot revenue $1.4M | S53 p.10 |
| 360 robots; $8M ARR 2027 | 110 contracted + 50 LOI | Contradicted by plan arithmetic | 44% covered; $12,778 a robot; $8M cannot include Tallis after June 2027 | S53 pp.10, 15 |
| 9-month runway | $3.7M / $410k | Contradicted as stated | 9.0 gross months from 2026-09-30; 4.4 usable from 2026-10-31 to 2027-03-14 | S53 p.10 |
| Robot cost $48,000; target $31,000 | v3 / v4 | Unverified | No purchase orders; Tallis BOM quote August 2026 | S53 pp.9, 15 |

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival closes the gap.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at the 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry harvest, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. The strategic reading is that scale, not invention, decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's 2025-04 human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership (company-reported, unverified) | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's human-parity claim and 13 patents; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's Monarch asset purchase; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 | +$4,500 | 2.5 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; verified recomputation [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. Counts partially verified; contracts unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026, down 36%, and has contracted 20 for 2027; the deck gives no reason, and acreage, price or performance would each imply a different 2027. The cut matters because it came in the second paid season, from a reference customer, while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].

| Deal | Status | Date | Reason | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grower E, Plant City FL | Pilot ended; no 2027 robots | 2026-06 | Fruit bruising; unverified | S53 p.6, p.13 |
| Grower D, Plant City FL | 11 paid robots in 2025-26; no 2027 contract, "in discussion" | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| Grower B, Santa Maria CA | Cut from 22 to 14 robots (-36%) | 2026 season | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 6 of 8 other pilot farms | 2025 and 2026 pilots; no LOI or 2027 order | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 9 of 14 pilot farms | Never a paid season | 2024-2026 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot; idle robots and unpaid pilots are not disclosed. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025; wound down | S54, S168 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; demo 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target. Source: S53, S54, S55, S91, S93, S94.

Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at the 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. The strategic reading: scale, not invention, decides the winner: whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference, which makes an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership (company-reported, unverified) | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's 13 patents and claim; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's Monarch purchase; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 | +$4,500 | 2.5 | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |
| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Unverified inputs; derived | S53 |

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; verified recomputation [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Unverified price; derived | S53 |

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. Counts partially verified; contracts unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026, down 36%, and has contracted 20 for 2027; the deck gives no reason, and acreage, price or performance would each imply a different 2027. The cut matters because it came in the second paid season, from a reference customer, while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].

| Deal | Status | Date | Reason | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grower E, Plant City FL | Pilot ended; no 2027 robots | 2026-06 | Fruit bruising; unverified | S53 p.6, p.13 |
| Grower D, Plant City FL | 11 paid robots in 2025-26; no 2027 contract, "in discussion" | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| Grower B, Santa Maria CA | Cut from 22 to 14 robots (-36%) | 2026 season | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 6 of 8 other pilot farms | 2025 and 2026 pilots; no LOI or 2027 order | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 9 of 14 pilot farms | Never a paid season | 2024-2026 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C; over $220M in total | Private, 2025; wound down | S54, S168 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; demo 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target. Source: S53, S54, S55, S91, S93, S94.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at the 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, the economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres and service density first sets the price reference; making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership (company-reported, unverified) | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's 13 patents and claim; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's Monarch purchase; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at the 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres first sets the price reference; making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership (company-reported, unverified) | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's 13 patents and claim; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's Monarch purchase; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |
:::

| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15, below the minimum from 2027-03-14: default | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on that fleet sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would be buying different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating, it removes the barrier for a competitor, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M of FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also the largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length evidence [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left the rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. So 2026 faces a floor 15.4% below 2025 and 2027 a floor 1.1% below it; the risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 milestone ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics reported a first California deployment from 2026-04 at 30 kilograms an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, so the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in March 2026; Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% between Q2 and Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is being underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S168, S171].

| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | A second pilot exit; grower quality audit | Independent trial above 85% with a bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips past 2027-03-14 with covenant binding | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver and standstill; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| Covenant absent: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% of outcomes | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 disclosed | Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M; $6M now, $6M later | S53, unverified |
| Entity split: IP in issuer, fleet and debt in subsidiary | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence, parent guarantee, Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Second tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis exits as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply, tooling ownership, second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including the Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA origin opinion | S174 |
| 2026 AEWR 15.4% below 2025; 2027 AB 2646 at $19.75 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not a wage floor | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata right at the Series A | S171, S168 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter most: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 with the minimum-cash definition, cross-default and waiver price; the Calder licence with assignment, change-of-control and sub-licence terms; a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement with tooling ownership and a second source; and an independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and the tariff, medium on the covenant terms and harvest recovery, low on the 2027 build and the exit price; the Kestrel text and the Calder licence decide whether the bear case returns capital or nothing.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 8 by Market Analyst, 8,992 characters)
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up is a revenue sizing, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. The $3.1B serviceable figure is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend, and the deck does not say which acres fill the difference. The adoption path is equally unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's productivity, unverified: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day California season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the price ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | n/a | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1:2024; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Caterpillar bought Monarch Tractor's assets in April 2026 after a January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors [S53, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor is contested

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The federal H-2A adverse effect wage rate for California non-range occupations was republished on 2026-08-03 at a reported $19.97 an hour. The floor is contested: a district court ruled against the department's late-2025 AEWR changes on 2026-08-28, and a federal court invalidated the new methodology in September 2026, with one estimate putting the 2026 national H-2A wage reduction at $100M. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S145, S190, S194, S192, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; a holding floor widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the H-2A floor has been lowered and relitigated, not simply raised, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Inputs that would move this from estimate to evidence are NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. If acreage is stable and the pick rate holds without the row exclusions, the out-year line re-bases up and supports a services business below the pre-money. If acreage is falling and realised price stays near the current contract, the strawberry market is small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53, unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported, unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap is not a rounding difference; it is a different market, and it needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
