{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 6 by Market Analyst, 8,983 characters)
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers, after $157M at the 2024-10 Series D and $232M-$276M by 2026. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, over $220M then and over $240M by its collapse, was valued above $500M, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres first sets the price reference; making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership (company-reported, unverified) | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's 13 patents and claim; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's Monarch purchase; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financial Analysis (financials, revision 8 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,994 characters)

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 6 by Valuation Analyst, 8,951 characters)
The realistic exit is a trade sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M conditional on a sale, but the probability-weighted value across all outcomes is $116.8M, which returns Meridian 1.4x at the $72M pre-money, 1.8x at a $50M pre-money with the full $18M round and 1.9x if its $12M is the only money; all 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were M&A and none was an IPO, so the question is which OEM buys, when, and what the preference stack leaves [S187, S188].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood and independent basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | Deere & Company | Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021) and GUSS Automation (2025); no harvesting robot | 2028-2031 | Medium — three autonomy acquisitions in eight years | S96, S92, S8, S187 |
| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven gives it autonomy software; its 2022 Advanced Farm stake ended in that company's 2025 closure | 2028-2031 | Low-medium — one platform deal, no harvesting acquisition | S95, S117, S114 |
| Trade sale | Kubota | Backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in 2021; needs a specialty-crop harvesting asset | 2029-2031 | Low — no disclosed acquisition in the category | S93, S114 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling in a liquidation | 2027-2029 | Not a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer (company relationship, unverified) | S53 unverified |
| Private equity | Paine Schwartz Partners or similar | Needs positive EBITDA and fleet-level cash flow; the FY2028 plan still loses $6.9M | 2030-2032 | Low — no agtech robotics buyout disclosed | S167, S53 unverified |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low — 0 of 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were IPOs | S187, S53 unverified |

Deere is the most plausible buyer because it has already paid for autonomy three times — Blue River ($305M, 2017), Bear Flag ($250M, 2021) and GUSS Automation (2025) — but none of the three bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which put money into Advanced Farm Technologies' $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it cease operations in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S96, S92, S8, S95, S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company is both a reason to buy the next asset and a reason to demand proof that an OEM will pay a strategic price for a pre-scale robot company.

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River Technology | 2017 | $305M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S96 |
| Deere / Bear Flag Robotics | 2021 | $250M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S92 |
| CNH / Raven Industries | 2021 | $2.1B enterprise value | 6.0x EV/Sales ($348.4M sales) | S95 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | not disclosed | S91 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025 | IP and team; value not disclosed | n/a | S115 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | 2025 | ceased operations | n/a | S114 |
| Abundant Robotics | 2021 | IP and assets sold; $12M raised | n/a | S91 |

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the stereo ripeness model trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost (unverified). That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, the date that determines whether a buyer acquires an exclusive technology or a commodity one [S53]. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

| Outcome, 2028-2032 | Probability | Basis for the weight | Company value | Meridian at $72M pre (13.33%) | Meridian at $50M pre, $12M only (19.35%) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liquidation or asset sale | 30% | 3 of 5 named US strawberry-harvesting peers closed or sold assets 2021-2025; 65% of VC investments return under 1x | $10M | $4.1M / 0.34x | $3.3M / 0.27x | S91, S114, S115, S188 |
| Stalled, sold at the preference | 25% | $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack; 65% below-1x base rate | $75M | $12.0M / 1.00x | $14.5M / 1.21x | S53 unverified, S188 |
| Modest OEM trade sale | 25% | Deere precedents at $250M-$305M, discounted for pre-scale | $150M | $20.0M / 1.67x | $29.0M / 2.42x | S92, S96 |
| Good OEM trade sale | 15% | Same precedents at full value | $250M | $33.3M / 2.78x | $48.4M / 4.03x | S92, S96 |
| Bidding war or platform sale | 5% | Requires 360 robots and a cleared licence | $400M | $53.3M / 4.44x | $77.4M / 6.45x | S53 unverified |
| Probability-weighted | 100% | | $116.8M | $16.9M / 1.41x | $23.0M / 1.92x | S53, S188, S91, S114, S115 |

On those weights the expected exit is $116.8M; Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.41x at the current price and 1.92x at a $50M pre-money if its $12M is the whole round. The weights put 55% of outcomes at or below 1.0x, which is more generous than the 65% base rate for venture investments, because Orrin already has five paying growers; applying the base rate gives a lower expected value, not a higher one [S188, S53]. The modal successful outcome remains a $150M-$250M OEM sale, but a 30% failure tail at $10M — the category's own record — pulls the probability-weighted value below that range, and the preference stack caps the low-exit recovery.

The structural tests are as important as the buyer list. The Calder licence's term, assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the noteholders' Series A-1 consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, so the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts (unverified) [S53]. A foreign buyer such as Kubota also faces undisclosed licence-consent and export-control diligence, which could remove the most logical buyer.

| Entry pre-money | Round | Meridian stake for $12M | $150M exit | $250M exit | $300M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $72M (current) | $18M | 13.33% | $20.0M / 1.67x | $33.3M / 2.78x | $40.0M / 3.33x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | $18M | 17.65% | $26.5M / 2.21x | $44.1M / 3.68x | $52.9M / 4.41x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | $12M only | 19.35% | $29.0M / 2.42x | $48.4M / 4.03x | $58.1M / 4.84x | S53 unverified |

The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.41x and 2.21x on the full round, or 4.84x and 2.42x if Meridian's $12M is the only money. Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake that sits behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota all have in-house autonomy programmes and can build a strawberry picker rather than buy one; the US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit — Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025, Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M — while the most recent harvesting-robot purchase, AppHarvest's $60M for Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices. Hardware exits trade below software, ag-equipment multiples are 1.0x-4.3x sales, and the industrial sector ETF is down 6.9% over three months, 8.1 points behind the S&P 500, so a 2029-2031 window is not assured [S53, S115, S114, S91, S31]. Meridian should negotiate a drag-along and tag-along that make a trade sale executable without a founder veto, a right to consent to any change to the Calder licence or the Tallis manufacturing agreement, and a requirement that Kestrel be repaid or consented at closing."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 10 by Product Analyst, 8,944 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin's figures are unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, CE or UKCA marking, incident log or insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous farm machinery (S166), and ISO 18497-4:2024, published 2024-07-31, the verification and validation methods (S199); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Compared with Harvest CROO, which discloses no rate, price or fleet, Orrin's 64 robots are the category's only disclosed paid deployment. Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. The screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop. [S57]
:::

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 verification report and an ATP swab record (S163, S199). For an investor, the cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and a surviving claim."}],"isError":false}

arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M balance is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 sold at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No loan agreement or UCC-1 is publicly disclosed, so the covenant rests on the deck alone, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%; it is a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit and 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would buy different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a competitor's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected with a response filed in 2026-05, and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also the largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. So 2026 faces a floor 15.4% below 2025, 2027 one 1.1% below it; the risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics reported a first California deployment from 2026-04 at 30 kg an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, so the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in 2026-03; Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S168, S171].

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | A second pilot exit; grower quality audit | Independent trial above 85% with a bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips past 2027-03-14 with covenant binding | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver and standstill; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| Covenant absent: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% of outcomes | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 disclosed | Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M; $6M now, $6M later | S53, unverified |
| Entity split: IP in issuer, fleet and debt in subsidiary | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence, parent guarantee, Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Second tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis exits as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply, tooling ownership, second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including the Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA origin opinion | S174 |
| 2026 AEWR 15.4% below 2025; 2027 AB 2646 at $19.75 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not a wage floor | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata right at the Series A | S171, S168 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 with the minimum-cash definition, cross-default and waiver price; the Calder licence with assignment, change-of-control and sub-licence terms; a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement with tooling ownership and a second source; and an independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and tariff, medium on the covenant terms and harvest recovery, low on the 2027 build and the exit price; the Kestrel text and the Calder licence decide whether the bear case returns capital or nothing.

The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No loan agreement or UCC-1 is publicly disclosed, so the covenant rests on the deck alone, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%; it is a company measurement, unverified. plan.decision_question: Is $72M pre-money defensible against comparable rounds and precedent transactions, and what must be true for a Series A investor to earn a venture return?
plan.thesis_sentence: $72M pre-money is not defensible: it is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS, and at a $12M cheque the probability-weighted return is about 1.4x, so Meridian should reprice to $48M-$55M or tranche $6M against the 2027 milestones.
plan.why_different: This section prices the round itself: the per-share price, the dilution, the preference stack, the dated liquidity position and the return at each exit value. The product, market and financial sections test whether the plan can be delivered; this one tests what the investor pays for it.
plan.mechanism: The $72M pre-money bundles a note-conversion discount and a pool top-up, so part of the price is a transfer to existing holders; the $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack then absorbs the first exit proceeds, leaving Meridian flat until roughly $38.4M and wholly dependent on entry price for its multiple. The minimum-cash covenant turns the dated cash balance into a closing deadline.
plan.comparison_set: Announced agricultural robotics rounds (Monarch Tractor, Carbon Robotics, Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga); listed ag-equipment and precision-ag multiples (Deere, CNH, AGCO, Trimble) at a 2.7x median EV/Sales; precedent M&A (Blue River $305M, Bear Flag $250M, CNH/Raven 6.0x sales).
plan.counter_evidence: The category's failure record (Advanced Farm shutdown 2025-07, Tortuga asset sale 2025-03, Abundant liquidation 2021), hardware multiples below software, 65% of venture investments returning under 1x, and the preference overhang that makes a $40M sale return only capital.
plan.visual: The repriced return table showing the $12M-only versus full $18M cases, the dated cash-to-covenant line, and the funding-round table with sources.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, about/many/experienced, any mention of the report's process, bots, tools or internal records.

arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M, not as a price for the business that exists [S53].

The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M. Orrin has raised $20.5M of equity and notes since 2022 and $38.5M including this round, plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt. Cash is $3.7M at 2026-09-30 and $3.29M at 2026-10-31 on $410,000 a month of burn: $1.79M usable above the $1.5M Kestrel minimum-cash covenant, 4.4 usable months to 2027-03-14, or 9.0 gross months to zero from 2026-09-30. A 2026-12-15 close funds ahead of the covenant; a slip into Q2 2027 does not. Peer disclosure is thin: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014; Advanced Farm Technologies raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S54, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119, S189]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. No Mexican registry extract could be retrieved for Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. (Jalisco, formed 2024-07-19), and the Calder licence term is not disclosed (unverified).

| Date | Round | Amount | Valuation | Investors | Use of funds | Source (company deck, unverified) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022-04 | Pre-seed SAFEs | $2.5M | not disclosed | Furrowline Angels (lead) | not disclosed | S53 unverified |
| 2023-03-08 | Series Seed | $11.0M | not disclosed | Granary Ventures (lead); pre-seed SAFEs converted | not disclosed | S53 unverified |
| 2024-09 to 2026 | USDA SBIR Phase II grant | $0.65M | n/a | USDA | R&D | S53 unverified |
| 2025-02-10 | Convertible notes | $7.0M ($7.77M with interest at conversion) | 80% of the Series A price, $3.7716 a share | Granary $3.5M; Tallis $2.5M; others $1.0M | bridge to Series A | S53 unverified |
| 2025-06-16 | Equipment facility (debt) | $2.5M, $1.6M drawn at 11.5% | n/a | Kestrel Equipment Finance | fleet build | S53 unverified |
| 2026-12-15 (target) | Series A | $18.0M | $72M pre / $90M post | Granary $3.0M; Tallis $1.0M; Meridian proposed $12.0M; $2.0M open | 300 robots 55%, R&D 25%, sales and field operations 20% | S53 unverified |

On revenue the price sits at the top of any observable range: 34.6x the $90M post-money on 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR (unverified), 12.9x pre and 16.1x post on the 2027 plan, and 6.8x on 2028. The ARR is not recurring: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding letters of intent — 56% non-recurring or non-binding, which is why 51.4x contracted robot revenue is the honest denominator. The payback is thinner than the pitch: the 2.1-season figure assumes a $1,750 service cost and omits the $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables charged against gross profit, so the same robot pays back in 2.5 seasons at the $16,500 list price and 4.4 at the $12,700 renewal. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA, and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95]. On a 4.0x exit multiple the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post-money, 70% above the $13.2M projected.

The cap table makes it worse. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2%: the founders from 53.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7%, granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), Series A-1 ($7.77M) and Series Seed ($11.0M) — 40.9% of the $90M post-money, ranking pari passu with new money — or $39.3M (43.6%) if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into the Seed preference. Ahead of the preferred sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt (unverified). Meridian is flat at 1.0x from a $38.4M to a $90M exit: at a $40M sale the Series A takes its $18M preference, Meridian recovers $12.0M and the common receives $1.6M after the debt [S53]. Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, 13.33% of the $90M post-money. A 3x on that stake requires $36M of exit proceeds: $272M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after a 20% Series B dilution in 2028. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years), at $300M 3.33x (27.2%) and at $500M 5.56x (40.9%).

| Exit value, 2029-2031 | Meridian at 13.33%, no dilution | MOIC | After 20% Series B dilution (10.67%) | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $150M | $20.0M | 1.67x | $16.0M | 1.33x | S53 unverified |
| $250M | $33.3M | 2.78x | $26.7M | 2.22x | S53 unverified |
| $300M | $40.0M | 3.33x | $32.0M | 2.67x | S53 unverified |
| $500M | $66.7M | 5.56x | $53.3M | 4.44x | S53 unverified |

The terms are conventional where disclosed and incomplete where it matters. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard Series A architecture; so is a five-seat board with two common seats, one Seed, one Series A and one independent agreed by both. What is missing is the protection package: Meridian would hold one of five votes, with no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package, and Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor (unverified) [S53]. The minimum package is a second board seat or a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilisation, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true is specific: 360 robots and $8M of ARR on a definition that no longer includes Tallis services by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence still exclusive after its 100-robot test, unit cost below $36,000, and $67.5M-$84M of revenue at a 4x multiple by 2029-2031 (company plan, unverified). Deere paid $305M for Blue River (2017) and $250M for Bear Flag (2021), so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy. The counter-evidence is the category's own record: Advanced Farm, which Kubota and CNH backed, ceased operations in July 2025; Tortuga sold its assets; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and sold its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 [S91, S114, S115, S53]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on the 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment. The repriced case depends on round size: at a $50M pre-money with all $18M subscribed, Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of $68M and returns 2.2x at $150M and 3.7x at $250M; as the only money it buys 19.35% of $62M, returns 2.4x and 4.0x, and leaves the 2027 plan $6M short.

rows.finding: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California commercial deployment from April 2026 at about 30 kg/hour, with RaaS as the primary model; as of 2026-10-31 no unit count, price, contracted acreage or confirmed deployment was found.
rows.mechanism: An announced launch is a credible threat to the 'only picker above 90%' claim but not evidence of a competing fleet.
rows.benchmark: Orrin: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons, 5.6 s per berry, 94% of detected fruit (company-reported, unverified).
rows.weakens: The April 2026 date passed without public confirmation, so the launch may have slipped.
rows.implication: The disclosure moat is closing; underwrite on contracted acres, not on a claim of uniqueness.
rows.confidence: medium on announcement; low on deployment
rows.follow_up: How many DailyRobotics units are in commercial service in California at 2026-10-31?

rows.finding: Harvest CROO Robotics claimed on 2025-04-24 that its open-field harvester is commercially viable and on par with human harvesting, but discloses no rate, price, fleet or shipments.
rows.mechanism: A performance claim without a fleet leaves the paid-deployment lead with Orrin, but it also means the closest competitor's true position is unknown.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons are the only disclosed paid fleet in the category.
rows.weakens: The claim is company-reported and unverified.
rows.implication: Harvest CROO is the most dangerous named rival on patents and tenure, not on disclosed commercial traction.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Has Harvest CROO sold or leased any harvester, and at what price?

rows.finding: The category's base rate is failure or absorption: Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, Tortuga AgTech sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, Abundant Robotics sold its IP in 2021, and Monarch Tractor entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 with assets bought by Caterpillar in April 2026.
rows.mechanism: Hardware-heavy ag robotics consumes capital faster than seasonal revenue can repay it; OEMs buy assets after the equity is gone.
rows.benchmark: Deere paid $305M for Blue River (2017) and $250M for Bear Flag (2021); AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI (2021).
rows.weakens: Survivorship is possible: the failures were in adjacent crops or business models, and Orrin has paid seasons.
rows.implication: A trade sale is the realistic exit; the round should be priced on contracted acres, not technology leadership.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What did Caterpillar and Oishii pay for the failed assets?

rows.finding: Screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today: AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a 2025-09-17 Series B at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate; Four Growers has $15.1M raised and a greenhouse tomato robot still in development; Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder to about 100 growers after a $70M Series D in 2024-10, $157M cumulative at that date, with 2026 trackers disagreeing on the total at $232M (S119) and $276M (S186).
rows.mechanism: Each has distribution or capital that could fund a strawberry arm, but none has a contact-based open-field picking claim.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's $20.5M raised is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's.
rows.weakens: The trackers' figures disagree by $44M and no filing settles the total; the entrants' capital and dealer access could compress Orrin's window faster than their product roadmaps suggest.
rows.implication: The near-term threat is an OEM or platform entrant buying the capability, not these products pivoting organically.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Which of these has filed a strawberry-harvesting patent or hired a berry team?

rows.finding: An open-source ROS 2 manipulation stack, the published berry-perception literature and a general-purpose berry-harvesting platform remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but none supplies field service or grower contracts.
rows.mechanism: Perception and arm control are commoditising; the durable barrier is the seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots.
rows.benchmark: Composite replication estimate of 24 months for a comparable machine; four to six years for a 300-robot service organisation.
rows.weakens: A well-funded entrant can now buy most of the software stack, so the lead is operational and time-limited.
rows.implication: Technology is not the moat; contracted acres and service density are.
rows.confidence: medium; estimate
rows.follow_up: What did the general-purpose platform achieve on strawberry in field trials?

plan.counter_evidence: H-2A wage relief and litigation lower the hand-labour floor; strawberry acreage may be shrinking; one Florida grower exited over bruising.
plan.decision_question: Is the strawberry harvest-labour problem large and urgent enough to support the company's claimed $3.1B serviceable and $310M obtainable market by 2031, and does the bottom-up robot math hold?
plan.mechanism: Robot revenue equals acres divided by acres per robot times price per robot-season; adoption is gated by harvest quality and season length, not by willingness to pay.
plan.prohibited: 'huge market', 'strong tailwind', 'frictionless adoption', 'recently', 'about', 'many growers'
plan.thesis_sentence: The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: 100% of US strawberry acres is worth $235.7M of robot revenue at the 2027 list price, so the $310M obtainable market is 31% larger than the entire crop, and the policy dates that support urgency are contested rather than permanent.

plan.why_different: Sizes the opportunity and tests the deck's arithmetic against USDA, wage and trade records; the other sections test the machine, the price and the exit.

rows.benchmark: 100% adoption vs 15% adoption ($35.4M at list; $27.2M at renewal) vs FY2028 revenue-implied 7.1% adoption.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; low on inputs
rows.finding: 50,000 US strawberry acres ÷ 3.5 acres per robot × $16,500 = $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market that needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base.
rows.follow_up: Will the company disclose realised price and acres per robot by farm for 2025-2026?
rows.implication: Price the round on a $27-35M revenue pool by 2031, not a $310M one; the headline is a top-down hope.
rows.mechanism: Robot revenue is acres divided by acres per robot times price; the claimed SOM exceeds the whole crop at the company's own density and price.
rows.weakens: All inputs are company-reported and unverified; if price per robot-season rises or the robot covers more acres, the ceiling moves.

rows.benchmark: H-2A AEWR for California reported at $19.97/hour in the 2026-08-03 notice.
rows.confidence: high
rows.finding: California AB 1066 (2016) phased agricultural overtime to 1.5x after 8 hours a day and 40 hours a week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees; the 2026 minimum wage is $16.90 an hour.
rows.follow_up: What share of California strawberry acreage is farmed by employers with 26 or more employees?
rows.implication: Supports adoption in California, weaker in Florida and for small growers.
rows.mechanism: A rising statutory wage floor raises the hand-crew cost the robot displaces, but only for growers above the employee threshold.
rows.weakens: Overtime is a cost on hours, not a shortage; growers can restructure crews and schedules.

rows.benchmark: Giannini estimates H-2A changes could reduce H-2A wages by $100M in 2026.
rows.confidence: medium; litigation pending
rows.finding: The H-2A wage floor is contested: the 2026 AEWR notice took effect 2026-08-03 at a reported $19.97/hour for California, but a district court ruled against the late-2025 AEWR changes on 2026-08-28 and a federal court invalidated the new methodology in September 2026.
rows.follow_up: What is the final 2027 AEWR for California strawberry counties after the litigation?
rows.implication: Labour urgency is real but reversible; do not underwrite a permanent wage tailwind.
rows.mechanism: If the wage floor falls or certification expands, hand labour gets cheaper and the annual purchase decision slips.
rows.weakens: The deck's labour-gap story assumes scarcity that policy is actively offsetting.

rows.benchmark: California's April-October seven-month season covers 3.5 acres per robot.
rows.confidence: low
rows.finding: Florida's season is a 120-day December-March window assumed by the deck, which cuts acres per robot to 2.0-2.5 versus 3.5 in California and raises the effective price per acre to $6,600-$8,250.
rows.follow_up: Will the company disclose Florida contracted acres and season length by grower?
rows.implication: Florida is counter-season capacity, not a stand-alone market; redeployment would halve depreciation per season.
rows.mechanism: Utilisation, not acres, drives payback: a short season spreads fixed robot cost over fewer acre-passes.
rows.weakens: No public instrument sets the season length; it is a company assumption and unverified.

rows.benchmark: A 10% strawberry acreage decline cuts the ceiling by $23.6M.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.finding: USDA NASS reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 noncitrus crops in 2025, down 2% year on year; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base remains unverified.
rows.follow_up: What is NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state for 2019-2025?
rows.implication: The acreage trend is a course correction risk, not a tailwind.
rows.mechanism: A shrinking acreage base reduces the full-adoption ceiling and makes the adoption path steeper.
rows.weakens: The 2% figure is across 21 crops, not strawberries; it cannot stand in for the strawberry trend.

rows.benchmark: Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B.
rows.confidence: high on dates; medium on funding total
rows.finding: Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 and had raised over $220M; it entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026.
rows.follow_up: What did Caterpillar pay for Monarch's assets?
rows.implication: Supports an OEM trade sale at a modest multiple, not an independent scale-up.
rows.mechanism: Even the best-funded ag-robot platform could not hold independence; the exit market is OEM asset purchases.
rows.weakens: A single failure does not set the base rate for every category, but it removes the 'best-funded wins' argument.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M balance is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No loan agreement or UCC-1 is publicly disclosed, so the covenant rests on the deck alone, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery the unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would buy different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a competitor's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also its largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment from 2026-04 at 30 kg an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, both unconfirmed; the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in 2026-03; Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S168, S171].

arguments.markdown:
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up sizes revenue, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. At $3.1B it is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend; the deck does not say which acres fill the gap. The adoption path is unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's unverified productivity: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each for one paid season, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Monarch Tractor, a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor is contested

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The federal H-2A adverse effect wage rate for California non-range occupations was republished on 2026-08-03 at a reported $19.97 an hour. The floor is contested: a district court ruled against the department's late-2025 AEWR changes on 2026-08-28, and a federal court invalidated the new methodology in September 2026, with one estimate of a $100M national H-2A wage reduction in 2026. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S145, S190, S194, S192, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; a holding floor widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the H-2A floor has been lowered and relitigated, not simply raised, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Inputs that would move this from estimate to evidence are NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. Stable acreage and a pick rate that holds without the row exclusions re-base the out-year line up; falling acreage with realised price near the current contract leaves the strawberry market small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53, unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported, unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported and unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a two-season paid lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour market, a harvest-aid market and a tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers; it raised a $70M Series D in 2024-10, $157M cumulative at that date, and two 2026 trackers put the total at $232M and $276M. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S119, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a response in May 2026, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised to date, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell, and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres first sets the price reference; making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys one of them.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

::: quad
| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership (company-reported, unverified) | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's 13 patents and claim; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's Monarch purchase; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |
