The realistic exit is a trade sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M conditional on a sale, but the probability-weighted value across all outcomes is $116.8M, which returns Meridian 1.4x at the $72M pre-money, 1.8x at a $50M pre-money with the full $18M round and 1.9x if its $12M is the only money; all 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were M&A and none was an IPO, so the question is which OEM buys, when, and what the preference stack leaves [S187, S188].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood and independent basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | Deere & Company | Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021) and GUSS Automation (2025); no harvesting robot | 2028-2031 | Medium — three autonomy acquisitions in eight years | S96, S92, S8, S187 |
| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven gives it autonomy software; its 2022 Advanced Farm stake ended in that company's 2025 closure | 2028-2031 | Low-medium — one platform deal, no harvesting acquisition | S95, S117, S114 |
| Trade sale | Kubota | Backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in 2021; needs a specialty-crop harvesting asset | 2029-2031 | Low — no disclosed acquisition in the category | S93, S114 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling in a liquidation | 2027-2029 | Not a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer (company relationship, unverified) | S53 unverified |
| Private equity | Paine Schwartz Partners or similar | Needs positive EBITDA and fleet-level cash flow; the FY2028 plan still loses $6.9M | 2030-2032 | Low — no agtech robotics buyout disclosed | S167, S53 unverified |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low — 0 of 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were IPOs | S187, S53 unverified |

Deere is the most plausible buyer because it has already paid for autonomy three times — Blue River ($305M, 2017), Bear Flag ($250M, 2021) and GUSS Automation (2025) — but none of the three bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which put money into Advanced Farm Technologies' $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it cease operations in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S96, S92, S8, S95, S93, S117, S114]. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 4 by Lead Analyst, 6,792 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 19 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, the pool 8.7x smaller than the headline, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 2.78x at $250M; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 2.4x-4.0x, while the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures need the full $18M. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |
:::

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. If the trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the right answer reverses and $72M is cheap [S53 unverified].

::: one-question
What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?

The answer decides whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. At 75%-80% the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with clean bruising the same numbers become conservative and the round is financeable [S53, S56].
:::

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit [S53 unverified].

3. The independent harvest-level trial is the gating measurement: 75%-80% makes this a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes it a crew replacement [S53 unverified, S56, S181].

Until those arrive, the deck's operating and financial claims are unverified company material [S53, S128]."}],"isError":false}

Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score is not a verdict on the technology; it is a verdict on what an investor can prove today. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 19 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, the lender agreement and the grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and the H-2A floor cut from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 in 2027, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions. The covenant itself rests on the deck: no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. If no minimum-cash test exists, the 2027 failure is a 25%-40% down round rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls to about 35%, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95, S128].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run harvest crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. The exit record cuts both ways: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, but Root AI cleared at $60M in harvesting, and four of the five funded peers failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026, including Monarch Tractor, which raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money and sold its assets to Caterpillar 21 months later [S53, S178, S93, S176, S91].

The sensitivity analysis above ranks the five assumptions; the recommendation changes under the downside cases, and not by dilution. arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported, unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a paid two-season lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour, harvest-aid and tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is on 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers; it raised a $70M Series D in 2024-10, $157M cumulative at that date, and 2026 trackers put the total at $232M and $276M. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S119, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a May 2026 response, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised to date, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres first sets the price reference, making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys either.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

| Quadrant | Points | Source |

| Strengths | Only disclosed paid fleet (company-reported, unverified), 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons; night picking and pack-on-board; RaaS removes grower capex; five paying growers | S53 |
| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership (company-reported, unverified) | S53 |
| Threats | DailyRobotics' announced California launch; Harvest CROO's 13 patents and claim; Carbon Robotics' capital; Caterpillar's Monarch purchase; looser H-2A supply | S1, S170, S186, S196, S169 |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 8 by Red Team Analyst, 9,000 characters)
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M balance is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No loan agreement or UCC-1 is publicly disclosed, so the covenant rests on the deck alone, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery the unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would buy different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a competitor's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also its largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment from 2026-04 at 30 kg an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, both unconfirmed; the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in 2026-03; Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score is not a verdict on the technology; it is a verdict on what an investor can prove today. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 19 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, the lender agreement and the grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and the H-2A floor cut from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 in 2027, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions. The covenant itself rests on the deck: no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. If no minimum-cash test exists, the 2027 failure is a 25%-40% down round rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls to about 35%, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95, S128].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. ::: takeaways

Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 12 by Fundamentals Analyst, 8,957 characters)
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; verified recomputation [S53].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M balance is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is publicly disclosed, so the covenant rests on deck p.10, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery the unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would buy different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a competitor's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also its largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment from 2026-04 at 30 kg an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, both unconfirmed; the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in 2026-03; Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S168, S171].

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | Second pilot exit; grower audit | Independent trial above 85%, bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips past 2027-03-14 with covenant binding | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| Covenant absent: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% of outcomes | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 disclosed | Invest with conditions; $6M now, $6M later | S53, unverified |
| Entity split: IP in issuer, fleet and debt in subsidiary | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence; parent guarantee; Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis exits as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply; tooling ownership; second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including the Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA opinion | S174 |
| 2026 AEWR 15.4% below 2025; 2027 AB 2646 at $19.75 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not wages | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata at the Series A | S171, S168 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, waiver price); the Calder licence (assignment, change of control, sub-licence); a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement (tooling ownership, second source); and an independent harvest trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and tariff, medium on the covenant and harvest recovery, low on the 2027 build and exit; the Kestrel text and Calder licence decide whether the bear returns capital or nothing.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 9 by Red Team Analyst, 8,995 characters)
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, failure is a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions rather than Wait for milestone. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is disclosed; the covenant rests on deck p.10, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery the unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would buy different companies, so the bear case's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a competitor's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also its largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed and the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a permanent reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment from 2026-04 at 30 kg an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, both unconfirmed; the only open-field picker above 90% claim is out of date. Monarch Tractor raised over $240M and was valued above $500M before laying off its workforce and vacating Livermore in 2026-03; Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S168, S171].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 with service at $1,750 so the $12,700 renewal clears a $12,000 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M — 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS — Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M, 3.33x at $300M and 1.41x on the probability-weighted $116.8M exit; at $48M-$55M, 2.4x-4.0x. Killer risks: negative contribution, a licence that lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption, 132% of the US acreage base. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 at list, an 85% trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with only $4.0M of $18M committed. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses April 2027, the fleet stays below 100, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 20 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, a $35.4M pool at the claimed 15% share rather than $310M, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 2.78x at $250M and 1.41x on the probability-weighted $116.8M; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 2.4x-4.0x, while the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures need the full $18M. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

::: briefing
| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What it sells | 64 robots, 75 paid seasons and five paying growers at $9,500 a season in 2026 (company-reported, unverified); 110 robots contracted and 50 letters of intent for a 360-robot 2027 plan | S53 unverified |
| Performance | 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 selected rows with 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime (company); independent trials report 72%-87%, putting harvest-level recovery near 75%-80% | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350; a grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |
:::

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. If the trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the right answer reverses and $72M is cheap [S53 unverified].

What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?

The answer decides whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. At 75%-80% the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with clean bruising the same numbers become conservative and the round is financeable [S53, S56].
:::

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit [S53 unverified].
2. Reprice to $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.0x at a $250M exit, and without a minimum-cash covenant the case becomes Invest with conditions [S53 unverified].
3. The independent harvest-level trial is the gating measurement: 75%-80% makes this a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes it a crew replacement [S53 unverified, S56, S181].
:::

Diligence next: the independent trial, the firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, insurer terms for product liability, and the corporate records that confirm entity and IP ownership. Until those arrive, the deck's operating and financial claims are unverified company material [S53, S128].

Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead buys preferred in an IP holdco whose value is pledged and whose licence is contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is unverified. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved. "Legally clean" is a closing condition, not a finding; company facts below are unverified unless marked [S53].

Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican assembly company runs Guadalajara. Kestrel is paid before the parent's equity and the preference stack before common, so the lead buys a residual claim on a residual claim. Economically, the cash-generating fleet sits below the shares sold, so a buyer must take or refinance the Kestrel claim before it reaches the parent's exclusivity. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; if the lien reaches receivables and contracts too, the Series A is junior to a $2.5M facility. Nor is the registry folio, deed or partner register disclosed: the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone, and a Jalisco constancia would confirm existence and ownership (unverified) [S53].

The IP estate is thin. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment. Prior art in slip grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money, which at $4.7145 gives $72.0M; adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if SAFEs carry a preference it reaches $39.3M, so the $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer is a strawberry grower, the buyer the harvest owner, the budget the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027; 2027 is a manufacturing and field-service problem as much as a demand problem. Related parties crowd the file: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; and Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one independent, vacant; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five, and Tallis's observer seat gives a supplier visibility (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital is modest and its proof narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised roughly $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field-operations staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders take collateral, related-party terms can be market. arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is disclosed; the covenant rests on deck p.10, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery the unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would buy different companies, so the bear's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a competitor's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also its largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed, the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not the superseded $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment for 2026-04 at 30 kg an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, both unconfirmed at 2026-10-31. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 on over $220M raised, was assigned for the benefit of creditors in 2026-01 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in 2026-04; the category kills entrants with more capital than Orrin. Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S54, S196, S171].

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harvest recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | Second pilot exit; grower audit | Independent trial above 85%, bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips past 2027-03-14, covenant binding | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| Covenant absent: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% of outcomes | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 disclosed | Invest with conditions; $6M now, $6M later | S53, unverified |
| Entity split: IP in issuer, fleet and debt in subsidiary | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence; parent guarantee; Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis exits as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply; tooling ownership; second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including the Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA opinion | S174 |
| 2026 AEWR 15.4% below 2025; 2027 AB 2646 at $19.75 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not wages | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata at the Series A | S171, S168 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, waiver price); the Calder licence (assignment, change of control, sub-licence); a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement (tooling ownership, second source); and an independent harvest trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and tariff, medium on the covenant and harvest, low on the 2027 build and exit; the Kestrel text and Calder licence decide whether the bear returns capital or nothing.

consensus.consensus: The pitch, and the way an ag-robotics Series A is usually framed, assumes the only autonomous open-field strawberry picker above 90% accuracy, a $310M obtainable market off a $3.1B serviceable one, a 41% gross margin and a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with large peer rounds such as Monarch's.
consensus.evidence: Section 3: 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 company-chosen rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent trials report 72%-87% and harvest-level recovery is about 75%-80% [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181]. Section 4: 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 caps the whole US strawberry robot-revenue pool at $235.7M, so $310M is 132% of the base; the 15%-by-2031 pool is $35.4M at list [S53]. Section 6: after $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit is -$8,100 a season at the 2026 price and -$650 at the renewal with the target cost [S53]. Section 7: 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding; 46% of FY2026E revenue is one related-party services contract ending 2027-06-30 [S53]. Section 8: $72M pre is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted robot revenue, and section 12's probability-weighted exit value is $116.8M, 1.41x at the current price [S53].
consensus.our_view: The labour problem is real and the machine sells seasons, but the price is not supported: the observable market is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M headline, unit contribution is negative at the price actually sold, and the technology moat is a conditional licence with a 2027 cliff. The thesis is non-consensus on valuation and on harvest-level performance, not on the existence of the problem. We would not lead at $72M; the investable structure is $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M tranched on 2027 milestones and a Kestrel standstill.
consensus.proof_event: An independent harvest-level trial above 85% with bruising no worse than a hand-picked control, 250 robots contracted for 2027 at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and a Kestrel standstill signed before the money is wired.

one_question.question: What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?
one_question.why: The 94% divides by detected ripe fruit and excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%, so it cannot tell an investor whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. At 75%-80% recovery with 3.8% bruising the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the same numbers become conservative and the 2027 plan is financeable. It is the one measurement that reprices every other assumption in the case.

scenarios.driver: The v4 robot hits $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units, 360 robots are delivered for the April 2027 season, at least 250 sell at the $16,500 list, an independent trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the Calder licence clears its 100-robot test on 2027-12-31.
scenarios.evidence: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons already delivered; 110 contracted and 50 LOIs for 2027; Tallis has quoted the v4 BOM (S53, unverified). Deere paid $250M-$305M for pre-scale autonomy businesses (S178, S92, S96).
scenarios.implication: This is the case the $72M price already assumes; only a tranche that captures it at a lower entry makes it an investment.
scenarios.outcome: $8M+ of ARR exiting 2027, an OEM partnership or Series B in 2028, and a trade sale at $300M-$400M in 2030-2031; Meridian returns 3.3x-4.4x before further dilution ($40M-$53M on $12M).

scenarios.driver: The build lands late or short: 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal, $2-3M of RaaS in 2027, a flat or down Series B in 2028 once the $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack is visible, and an OEM trade sale at $150M-$250M in 2029-2031.
scenarios.evidence: 2027 is 44% covered (110 contracted plus 50 LOIs of 360); renewal is below the $13,350 break-even at current service cost; the $18M funds one season and leaves $1.5-3.5M at end-2027 (S53, derived). Agtech deal count fell about 20% in 2025 (S180), and the category base rate is failure or absorption (S91, S114, S115, S176).
scenarios.implication: Reprice the entry or tranche; at $72M the base case is a thin venture return, not a loss.
scenarios.outcome: $150M-$250M sale in 2029-2031; Meridian returns 1.7x-2.8x at $72M, or 1.3x-2.2x after a 20% Series B dilution. At $50M pre-money a $12M-only cheque (19.35% of a $62M post) returns 2.4x-4.0x; 2.2x-3.7x holds only if the full $18M closes.

scenarios.driver: One domino takes several symptoms: the round slips past Q1 2027, the v4 build misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, the Calder licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31, a second grower leaves over bruising, and cheaper hand labour after the 2025-10 H-2A wage cut slows conversion.

scenarios.implication: Do not lead without a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet, a licence assignment consent and a covenant waiver as closing conditions.
scenarios.outcome: A secured-lender event or a distressed asset sale in 2027-2028; the entity split may prevent the licence and fleet from being sold together, so Meridian recovers $0-$12M (0-1.0x). If the facility has no minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round rather than a secured-lender event: bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, base rises to 53%, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions.

arguments.capital_efficiency: FY2026E revenue $2.6M against $38.5M of equity and notes raised, $0.24 of revenue per equity dollar (0.15 on FY2027E); burn multiple 7.0x FY2026 and 5.9x FY2027; $18M buys 300 robots at $33,000 but leaves $1.5-3.5M at end-2027.
arguments.position_sizing: Zero at $72M pre-money; $6M at $48M-$55M with $6M released on 2027 milestones (independent harvest trial above 85% with clean bruising, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, measured v4 cost at or below $33,000, Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test). Maximum loss $12M; $6M reserved for a Series B. At $50M pre-money a $12M-only cheque buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.0x at a $250M exit; 17.65% and 3.68x need the full $18M.

| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $1.24M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would buy different companies, so the bear's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a competitor's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also its largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed, the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not the superseded $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment for 2026-04 at 30 kg an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, both unconfirmed at 2026-10-31. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 on over $220M raised, was assigned for the benefit of creditors in 2026-01 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in 2026-04; the category kills entrants with more capital than Orrin. Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S54, S196, S171].

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, waiver price); the Calder licence (assignment, change of control, sub-licence); a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement (tooling ownership, second source); and an independent harvest trial on unselected blocks with a hand-picked bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and tariff, medium on the covenant and harvest, low on the 2027 build and exit; the Kestrel text and Calder licence decide whether the bear returns capital or nothing.
