{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competitive Landscape (competition, revision 7 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,956 characters)
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported, unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a paid two-season lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A rate republished 2026-08-03 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor contested; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour, harvest-aid and tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds, $1.25M NSF SBIR Phase II funding, and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is on 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development, with two patents filed. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers; it raised a $70M Series D in 2024-10, $157M cumulative at that date, and 2026 trackers put the total at $232M and $276M. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S119, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a May 2026 response, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised to date, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres first sets the price reference, making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys either.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

| Weaknesses | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows (company-reported, unverified); 3.8% bruising and one Florida exit; gripper claims rejected; single crop; two growers are 53% of paid seasons | S53 |
| Opportunities | Hand crews pick most acres; Florida is counter-season capacity; expansion beyond strawberries; equipment-maker partnership (company-reported, unverified) | S53 |

The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS is 75 seasons at $9,500 and is the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest line is a related-party engineering contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS revenue, the $1.4M of one-season contracts makes the $72M pre-money 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use the list price: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet, 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after $410k of burn and $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. The deck's 9 months is gross from 2026-09-30, before the covenant. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register: the minimum-cash test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and a $48-55M structure becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Until produced, the covenant date is the planning case. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with the covenant in the middle. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital: the minimum close cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: the round slipping carries 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is disclosed; the covenant rests on deck p.10, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery the unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger: the remedy needs a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. A buyer of the technology and a buyer of the fleet would buy different companies, so the bear's 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than the thesis treats it: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a competitor's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier who is also its largest customer and a creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics, and Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer until 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons. The ties are disclosed, the amounts unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not the superseded $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment for 2026-04 at 30 kg an hour and a ~4% bruise rate it calls within hand-picked range, both unconfirmed at 2026-10-31. Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter. The five assumptions are ranked by damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: failure means zero equity, not dilution. History says the technology exits and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28, raised over $220M, assigned its assets for creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. The decision tree has three branches. Pass at $72M: the price capitalises a six-conjunct bull case and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move it. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and earns 2.4x at a $150M exit, 4.0x at $250M and 1.92x weighted on $116.8M; the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures hold only if the full $18M closes. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm 300-unit quote, licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and fleet-entity consolidation [S53, S128]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 9 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,983 characters)
Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score is a verdict on what an investor can prove today, not on the technology. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 20 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, lender agreement and grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and the H-2A floor cut from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 in 2027, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. A grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, $8,000-$11,000 per contracted robot, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions. The covenant itself rests on the deck: no loan agreement or UCC filing is in the register. If no minimum-cash test exists, the 2027 failure is a 25%-40% down round rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls to about 35%, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95, S128].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run harvest crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. The exit record cuts both ways: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, but Root AI cleared at $60M in harvesting, and four of the five funded peers failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026, including Monarch Tractor, which announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026; weighted across five outcomes the company is worth $116.8M, 1.41x at $72M [S53, S178, S93, S54, S189, S196, S91].

The sensitivity analysis above ranks the five assumptions; the recommendation changes under the downside cases, not by dilution. A market 50% smaller, at 25,000 acres, gives a $117.9M pool at list and $17.7M at 15% adoption, which kills $72M but leaves $48M-$55M defensible. Revenue 30% lower, at $3.9M instead of $5.6M, removes $0.87M of gross profit at a 52% RaaS margin and leaves end-2027 cash at $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M covenant, breached at the low end. Customer acquisition at twice the plan cannot be absorbed: 200 uncontracted robots have one selling window, four sales staff and a 5-of-14 pilot conversion record. Financing six months late adds $2.46M of burn and leaves $1.24M of cash on 2027-06-15, a secured-lender default rather than a down round. Only the bull case, at 12%, returns 3.3x-4.4x; the base case at $72M is 1.7x-2.8x, and the bear is 0-1.0x at 50% with the covenant, 35% without it [S53 unverified].

Position sizing is zero at $72M and $6M at $48M-$55M pre-money, with $6M released on 2027 milestones: an independent harvest-level trial above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and the Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test. The maximum loss is the full $12M; reserve $6M for a Series B. At $50M pre-money a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.03x at a $250M exit, against 2.78x at $72M; the 17.65% and 3.68x figures need the full $18M to close. Conditions precedent, not covenants: a Kestrel standstill or waiver signed with the term sheet, licence assignment consent, consolidation of the fleet entity and its grower contracts, and a second board seat with a veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control. Diligence next: a firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, and an insurer's view of product liability [S53, S128].

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 1.41x on the probability-weighted $116.8M and 2.78x at $250M [S53 unverified].
2. The investable structure is $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.03x at a $250M exit, while 17.65% and 3.68x need the full $18M [S53 unverified].
3. Harvest-level recovery decides the case: 75%-80% makes the machine a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes even $72M look cheap [S53 unverified, S56, S181].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 6 by Valuation Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,951 characters)
The realistic exit is a trade sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M conditional on a sale, but the probability-weighted value across all outcomes is $116.8M, which returns Meridian 1.4x at the $72M pre-money, 1.8x at a $50M pre-money with the full $18M round and 1.9x if its $12M is the only money; all 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were M&A and none was an IPO, so the question is which OEM buys, when, and what the preference stack leaves [S187, S188].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood and independent basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | Deere & Company | Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021) and GUSS Automation (2025); no harvesting robot | 2028-2031 | Medium — three autonomy acquisitions in eight years | S96, S92, S8, S187 |
| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven gives it autonomy software; its 2022 Advanced Farm stake ended in that company's 2025 closure | 2028-2031 | Low-medium — one platform deal, no harvesting acquisition | S95, S117, S114 |
| Trade sale | Kubota | Backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in 2021; needs a specialty-crop harvesting asset | 2029-2031 | Low — no disclosed acquisition in the category | S93, S114 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling in a liquidation | 2027-2029 | Not a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer (company relationship, unverified) | S53 unverified |
| Private equity | Paine Schwartz Partners or similar | Needs positive EBITDA and fleet-level cash flow; the FY2028 plan still loses $6.9M | 2030-2032 | Low — no agtech robotics buyout disclosed | S167, S53 unverified |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low — 0 of 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were IPOs | S187, S53 unverified |

Deere is the most plausible buyer because it has already paid for autonomy three times — Blue River ($305M, 2017), Bear Flag ($250M, 2021) and GUSS Automation (2025) — but none of the three bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which put money into Advanced Farm Technologies' $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it cease operations in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S96, S92, S8, S95, S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company is both a reason to buy the next asset and a reason to demand proof that an OEM will pay a strategic price for a pre-scale robot company.

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River Technology | 2017 | $305M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S96 |
| Deere / Bear Flag Robotics | 2021 | $250M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S92 |
| CNH / Raven Industries | 2021 | $2.1B enterprise value | 6.0x EV/Sales ($348.4M sales) | S95 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | not disclosed | S91 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025 | IP and team; value not disclosed | n/a | S115 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | 2025 | ceased operations | n/a | S114 |
| Abundant Robotics | 2021 | IP and assets sold; $12M raised | n/a | S91 |

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the stereo ripeness model trained on 1.9 million labelled berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost (unverified). That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, the date that determines whether a buyer acquires an exclusive technology or a commodity one [S53]. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

| Outcome, 2028-2032 | Probability | Basis for the weight | Company value | Meridian at $72M pre (13.33%) | Meridian at $50M pre, $12M only (19.35%) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liquidation or asset sale | 30% | 3 of 5 named US strawberry-harvesting peers closed or sold assets 2021-2025; 65% of VC investments return under 1x | $10M | $4.1M / 0.34x | $3.3M / 0.27x | S91, S114, S115, S188 |
| Stalled, sold at the preference | 25% | $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack; 65% below-1x base rate | $75M | $12.0M / 1.00x | $14.5M / 1.21x | S53 unverified, S188 |
| Modest OEM trade sale | 25% | Deere precedents at $250M-$305M, discounted for pre-scale | $150M | $20.0M / 1.67x | $29.0M / 2.42x | S92, S96 |

| Probability-weighted | 100% | | $116.8M | $16.9M / 1.41x | $23.0M / 1.92x | S53, S188, S91, S114, S115 |

On those weights the expected exit is $116.8M; Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.41x at the current price and 1.92x at a $50M pre-money if its $12M is the whole round. The weights put 55% of outcomes at or below 1.0x, which is more generous than the 65% base rate for venture investments, because Orrin already has five paying growers; applying the base rate gives a lower expected value, not a higher one [S188, S53]. The structural tests are as important as the buyer list. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 9 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,856 characters)
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up sizes revenue, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. At $3.1B it is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend; the deck does not say which acres fill the gap. The adoption path is unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's unverified productivity: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | n/a | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1:2024; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each for one paid season, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Monarch Tractor, a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor is contested

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The federal H-2A adverse effect wage rate for California non-range occupations was republished on 2026-08-03 at a reported $19.97 an hour. The floor is contested: a district court ruled against the department's late-2025 AEWR changes on 2026-08-28, and a federal court invalidated the new methodology in September 2026, with one estimate of a $100M national H-2A wage reduction in 2026. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S145, S190, S194, S192, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; a holding floor widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the H-2A floor has been lowered and relitigated, not simply raised, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Inputs that would move this from estimate to evidence are NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. Stable acreage and a pick rate that holds without the row exclusions re-base the out-year line up; falling acreage with realised price near the current contract leaves the strawberry market small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 12 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,957 characters)
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and remote supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charge it to the contract and contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. The inputs are company-reported and unverified; the arithmetic is verified against the deck's line items [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (a gross margin of -85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

### Only list price, target cost and lower service cost together make a season profitable

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; verified recomputation [S53].

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. Counts partially verified; contracts unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026, down 36%, and has contracted 20 for 2027; the deck gives no reason, and acreage, price or performance would each imply a different 2027. The cut matters because it came in the second paid season, from a reference customer, while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI that decides the model is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. These are derived from company-reported figures and are unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate says this is a milestone, not a finished model

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target. Source: S53, S54, S55, S91, S93, S94."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## ESG Assessment (esg, revision 4 by Regulatory Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,983 characters)
ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, against a theoretical $100M saving on $655M of H-2A wages. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. Non-H-2A growers saw a 2.4% rise, $16.50 to $16.90; H-2A crews saw about a 15% cut. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost for both seasons was obtainable; $25-30 per worker-day of housing and transport means the all-in rate fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, $16.23 to $12.47. Confidence: high on rates, medium on all-in. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's seven-staff Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and harnesses, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build. Trackers disagree: a 25% IEEPA duty or a 10% Section 122 charge from 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was published. Make USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the Tallis v4 build a closing condition. [S144, S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's audit. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous machinery but certifies nothing, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed the family alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs. [S144, S151, S153, S154, S166]

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record outweighs any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05; the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 while the October 2026 deck called it undecided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel citing an executive order pushing agencies to take title and domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 6 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 6,961 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 20 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

::: verdict

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, a $35.4M pool at the claimed 15% share rather than $310M, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 2.78x at $250M and 1.41x on the probability-weighted $116.8M; at $50M a $12M cheque alone buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 2.4x-4.0x, or 1.92x on the weighted value, while the 17.65% and 2.2x-3.7x figures need the full $18M. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 4 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,970 characters)
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services and grants supplied $1.25M of $1.9M of revenue, and both stop by mid-2027 [S53]. What the Series A must therefore prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all of them company-reported and unverified in this review — the $16M the round actually assembles buys one season and 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a path to a Series B. The plan is not implausible: 110 robots are contracted for 2027 and 50 more are under LOIs. It asks for four step changes at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window.

### Services and grants pay the bills; neither survives 2027

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M (company-reported, unverified) comprised $0.95M of engineering services for Tallis, $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent [S53]. On the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, which at a $72M pre-money is 51x rather than the 22x the headline figure implies. The services line was rational at sub-scale; it becomes a valuation problem once the round is priced on recurring revenue.

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified) [S53]. The $3.7M of cash on 2026-09-30 is 9.0 gross months to zero cash at $410,000 of monthly net burn; the Kestrel facility, $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5% and secured on the fleet, also requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times. At 2026-10-31 the balance is $3.29M and usable cash above that covenant is $1.79M, 4.4 months, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14 — before the 2027 California season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the fleet, not only a dilution. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the entire fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage. Either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the projected 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. Governance compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but neither revenue nor cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established pattern in this category is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries. Deere's 2025 annual report names autonomy and Solutions-as-a-Service as core to a high-value, small-acreage strategy, which is precisely where a berry picker would fit. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, which is exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. A standalone rental fleet at 360 robots has no precedent in this review: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, and Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B. The one field-robotics company at commercial distribution, Carbon Robotics, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D — ten times Orrin's capital [S117, S8, S114, S115, S184]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed, not a bet on a rental business reaching escape velocity alone.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Technology & Product (technology_product, revision 10 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,944 characters)
Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin's figures are unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, CE or UKCA marking, incident log or insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous farm machinery (S166), and ISO 18497-4:2024, published 2024-07-31, the verification and validation methods (S199); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Compared with Harvest CROO, which discloses no rate, price or fleet, Orrin's 64 robots are the category's only disclosed paid deployment. Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

| Company | Approach | Claim at 2026-10-31 | Verification status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Orrin | Soft gripper, night stereo, open field | 94% of detected, 5.6 s a berry | Company-reported; conditional denominator | S53 |
| Harvest CROO | Open-field strawberry harvester | "On par with human harvesting" | Company claim; no rate or fleet | S1 |
| AGRIST | Rail-guided greenhouse, peppers and cucumbers | 55% harvest rate; six deployments, all Japan | Vendor-stated; co-op announcements | S183 |
| Four Growers | Greenhouse tomato, 8 stereo cameras | In development; two patents filed | Development stage per its own site | S185, S182 |
| Carbon Robotics | Laser weeding, 30 lasers | 200,000 weeds an hour; roughly 100 growers | Company-sourced; commercial since 2021 | S184, S186 |

| Patent or application | Subject | Filed and status at 2026-10-31 | Relevance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US 17/902,118 | Soft gripper, slip sensing | 2022-09-02; all claims rejected, response 2026-05 | End-effector barrier, unenforceable | S53 unverified, S130 |
| US 18/655,430 | Night stereo detection | 2024-05-06; awaiting examination | Night operation | S53 unverified |
| PCT/US2025/027761 | Furrow-following platform | 2025-04-29; national phase due 2026-10-30, entry undisclosed | Platform copying | S53 unverified |
| Two university families | Ripeness model (2020), stem localisation (2022) | Licensed 2022-01-20; non-exclusive below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 | Core perception rented | S53 unverified |

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Perception and labelled data | 5 | 1.9M images; core families licensed | 2 years | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Gripper and slip sensing | 3 | Crowded art; no allowed claim | 1 year | S130 |
| Field service at 1:8 | 6 | Seasonal crews, parts network | 3-4 years | S53 unverified |
| **Composite** | **4/10** | Operations are the barrier, not patents | **24-30 months to a comparable machine** | S53, S114 |

| Product | Stage and launch | 2026E revenue | Margin | Next milestone | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Robots-as-a-Service | Commercial, 5 growers, 2025 season | $0.71M | 41% before fleet depreciation | 360 robots in 2027 | S53 unverified |
| Engineering services | Contract to 2027-06-30 | $1.20M | not disclosed | Replace by FY2028 | S53 unverified |
| Paid pilots and grants | Pilot; grant to FY2026 | $0.69M | not disclosed | Convert 8 pilot farms | S53 unverified |

::: evidence
**Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on company-chosen rows, its safety and sanitation file is not disclosed, and no gripper claim is allowed: the technology does not defend the $72M pre-money. (S53, S56)**

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. The screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop. [S57]
:::

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 verification report and an ATP swab record (S163, S199). For an investor, the cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and a surviving claim."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Funding History & Valuation (funding_valuation, revision 12 by Valuation Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,883 characters)
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M, not as a price for the business that exists [S53].

The $18M Series A at $72M pre-money implies a $90M post-money, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share, with new Series A stock at 20.0%, the 2025 notes at 10.8% and an unallocated pool at 12.0% — on top of 8.2% of granted options, a 20.2% total overhang. The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value at the round price; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M. Orrin has raised $20.5M of equity and notes since 2022 and $38.5M including this round, plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt. Cash is $3.7M at 2026-09-30 and $3.29M at 2026-10-31 on $410,000 a month of burn: $1.79M usable above the $1.5M Kestrel minimum-cash covenant, 4.4 usable months to 2027-03-14, or 9.0 gross months to zero from 2026-09-30. A 2026-12-15 close funds ahead of the covenant; a slip into Q2 2027 does not. Peer disclosure is thin: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M across five rounds, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28, and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014; Advanced Farm Technologies raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha Motor and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S54, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119, S189]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. No Mexican registry extract could be retrieved for Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. (Jalisco, formed 2024-07-19), and the Calder licence term is not disclosed (unverified).

On revenue the price sits at the top of any observable range: 34.6x the $90M post-money on 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR (unverified), 12.9x pre and 16.1x post on the 2027 plan, and 6.8x on 2028. The ARR is not recurring: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering-services contract that ends on 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding letters of intent — 56% non-recurring or non-binding, which is why 51.4x contracted robot revenue is the honest denominator. The payback is thinner than the pitch: the 2.1-season figure assumes a $1,750 service cost and omits the $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables charged against gross profit, so the same robot pays back in 2.5 seasons at the $16,500 list price and 4.4 at the $12,700 renewal. Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 on 2026-01-01 ($17.40 scheduled for 2027), overtime starts after eight hours a day, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap stays durable, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 with service at $1,750 so the $12,700 renewal clears a $12,000 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M — 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS — Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M, 3.33x at $300M and 1.41x on the probability-weighted $116.8M exit; at $48M-$55M, 2.4x-4.0x and 1.92x weighted. Killer risks: negative contribution, a licence that lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms its team selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83%-87% of detected fruit, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption; the $310M claim is 132% of that pool. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

The challenge moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 at list, an 85% trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with only $4.0M of $18M committed. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses April 2027, the fleet stays below 100, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is registered. Without a minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A three-to-six-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; a lender standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic because the entity split may block a clean sale | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |

The five assumptions are ranked by damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: failure means zero equity, not dilution. Labour now cuts both ways: the H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 on 2026-01-01, the 2026-08-03 notice set skill tiers at $16.45-$18.71, a federal court held that method unlawful on 2026-08-26 with backpay possible, and AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01. History says the technology exits and the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28, raised over $220M, assigned its assets for creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of five funded peers failed or sold assets in 2021-2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S54, S189, S196, S91, S114, S115].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met.
