arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is disclosed; the covenant rests on deck p.10, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $0.83M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

A three-to-six-month reprice is itself the bear trigger.

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. Technology and fleet buyers would buy different companies, so 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than it looks: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a rival's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier that is also its largest customer and creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics. The reference grower, Marisol Ridge (the COO's employer until 2021; 24 of 75 paid seasons), cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) in its second paid season while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons; an acreage or price cut leaves the renewal story intact, a performance or bruising cut strengthens the bear, and with its 2026 record requested and not disclosed, the 12/38/50 weights stand (12/53/35 without the minimum-cash test) until it arrives. The ties are disclosed but unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not the superseded $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment for 2026-04; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 on over $220M raised, was assigned for the benefit of creditors in 2026-01 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in 2026-04; the category kills entrants with more capital than Orrin. Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below a year earlier. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S54, S196, S171].

Four requests matter: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, waiver price); the Calder licence (assignment, change of control, sub-licence); a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement; and an independent harvest trial on unselected blocks with a bruise control. arguments.markdown:
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up sizes revenue, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. At $3.1B it is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend; the deck does not say which acres fill the gap. The adoption path is unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's unverified productivity: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | n/a | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1:2024; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each for one paid season, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Monarch Tractor, a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor fell in 2026

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The H-2A adverse effect wage rate was $19.97 through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule of 2025-10-02 (90 FR 47914) cut the operative California floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71; the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful on 2026-08-26, leaving the rates in place with backpay possible; and AB 2646 restores a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; the 2027 statutory rebound widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the floor fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Inputs that would move this from estimate to evidence are NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. Stable acreage and a pick rate that holds without the row exclusions re-base the out-year line up; falling acreage with realised price near the current contract leaves the strawberry market small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53, unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported, unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)
:::

rows.finding: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California commercial deployment from April 2026 at about 30 kg/hour, with RaaS as the primary model; as of 2026-10-31 no unit count, price, contracted acreage or confirmed deployment was found.
rows.mechanism: An announced launch is a credible threat to the 'only picker above 90%' claim but not evidence of a competing fleet.
rows.benchmark: Orrin: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons, 5.6 s per berry, 94% of detected fruit (company-reported, unverified).
rows.weakens: The April 2026 date passed without public confirmation, so the launch may have slipped.
rows.implication: The disclosure moat is closing; underwrite on contracted acres, not on a claim of uniqueness.
rows.confidence: medium on announcement; low on deployment
rows.follow_up: How many DailyRobotics units are in commercial service in California at 2026-10-31?

rows.finding: Harvest CROO Robotics claimed on 2025-04-24 that its open-field harvester is commercially viable and on par with human harvesting, but discloses no rate, price, fleet or shipments.
rows.mechanism: A performance claim without a fleet leaves the paid-deployment lead with Orrin, but it also means the closest competitor's true position is unknown.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons are the only disclosed paid fleet in the category.
rows.weakens: The claim is company-reported and unverified.
rows.implication: Harvest CROO is the most dangerous named rival on patents and tenure, not on disclosed commercial traction.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Has Harvest CROO sold or leased any harvester, and at what price?

rows.finding: The category's base rate is failure or absorption: Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B, Tortuga AgTech sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, Abundant Robotics sold its IP in 2021, and Monarch Tractor entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 with assets bought by Caterpillar in April 2026.
rows.mechanism: Hardware-heavy ag robotics consumes capital faster than seasonal revenue can repay it; OEMs buy assets after the equity is gone.
rows.benchmark: Deere paid $305M for Blue River (2017) and $250M for Bear Flag (2021); AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI (2021).
rows.weakens: Survivorship is possible: the failures were in adjacent crops or business models, and Orrin has paid seasons.
rows.implication: A trade sale is the realistic exit; the round should be priced on contracted acres, not technology leadership.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What did Caterpillar and Oishii pay for the failed assets?

rows.finding: Screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries today: AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a 2025-09-17 Series B at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate; Four Growers has $15.1M raised and a greenhouse tomato robot still in development; Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder to about 100 growers after a $70M Series D in 2024-10, $157M cumulative at that date, with $232M-$276M across two 2026 trackers and the $44M gap unresolved, unverified.
rows.mechanism: Each has distribution or capital that could fund a strawberry arm, but none has a contact-based open-field picking claim.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's $20.5M raised is 9% of Monarch's total and under a tenth of Carbon's.
rows.weakens: The trackers disagree by $44M and no filing settles the total; the entrants' capital and dealer access could compress Orrin's window faster than their product roadmaps suggest.
rows.implication: The near-term threat is an OEM or platform entrant buying the capability, not these products pivoting organically.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Which of these has filed a strawberry-harvesting patent or hired a berry team?

rows.finding: An open-source ROS 2 manipulation stack, the published berry-perception literature and a general-purpose berry-harvesting platform remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but none supplies field service or grower contracts.
rows.mechanism: Perception and arm control are commoditising; the durable barrier is the seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots.
rows.benchmark: Composite replication estimate of 24 months for a comparable machine; four to six years for a 300-robot service organisation.
rows.weakens: A well-funded entrant can now buy most of the software stack, so the lead is operational and time-limited.
rows.implication: Technology is not the moat; contracted acres and service density are.
rows.confidence: medium; estimate
rows.follow_up: What did the general-purpose platform achieve on strawberry in field trials?

plan.decision_question: Who else is going after open-field strawberry harvesting, and is Orrin's claimed 'only autonomous picker above 90%' and 'only disclosed paid fleet' a defensible lead or a disclosure artefact?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin has the only disclosed paid fleet in open-field strawberry harvesting, but that is company-reported and unverified and the field is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026, Harvest CROO claims human parity, and the category's base rate is failure or absorption.
plan.why_different: Maps competitors per product with stage, funding and published performance, and tests the uniqueness claim; the technology section tests the machine, and the risk section tests the financing clock.
plan.mechanism: Advantage equals contracted acres times service density times verified fruit quality; disclosure gaps are not moats, and OEMs buy assets after equity failures.
plan.comparison_set: Per-product rival table; failed peers (Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Traptic, Abundant, Monarch); acquisition precedents; open-source replication.
plan.counter_evidence: DailyRobotics, AGRIST, Four Growers and Carbon Robotics could enter; hand crews retain near-100% share; the 2026 H-2A cut slows switching.
plan.visual: Competitor table, entrant screen, moat table, positioning table and SWOT quad.
plan.prohibited: 'only player', 'no competition', 'fierce competition', 'high barriers to entry', 'well positioned', 'recently'

arguments.markdown:
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services for Tallis ($0.95M), USDA SBIR grants ($0.30M), RaaS ($0.38M) and paid pilots ($0.27M) made up $1.9M, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots, and both non-robot lines stop by mid-2027. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent; on the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, 51x rather than the 22x the headline implies. The services line was rational at sub-scale; it is a valuation problem once the round is priced on recurring revenue. What the Series A must prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all company-reported and unverified in this review — the $16M the round actually assembles buys one season and 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a path to a Series B. The plan asks the company to build, service, reprice and cost-reduce at once, and all four land in the same four-month build window [S53].

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified). Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is 9.0 gross months to zero at $410,000 of monthly net burn; the Kestrel facility, $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5% and secured on the fleet, requires $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so usable cash is $1.79M at 2026-10-31, 4.4 months, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections: a close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the fleet, not only a dilution. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage; either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption [S53].

### Price the round, not the plan

The $16M the company can assemble is the case to underwrite, not the $18M plan. At a $50M pre-money with all $18M subscribed, Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post and returns 2.21x at a $150M exit and 3.68x at $250M; with the $16M — $12M from Meridian, $3.0M Granary and $1.0M Tallis — it buys 18.18% of $66M, returns 2.27x and 3.79x, and about 1.77x on the $116.8M probability-weighted exit value; as the only money it buys 19.35% of $62M, returns 2.42x and 4.03x, and leaves the 2027 plan $6M short [S53, S188]. The 2027 milestones later in this section assume the full $18M: $9.9M of robot capex plus a $7.1M operating loss cannot be carried on $12M, so a $12M-only close moves the 300-robot build and the 360-robot season into 2028 and pushes the Series B back with them, while the $16M close funds the season with no reserve.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. Governance compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but neither revenue nor cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established route is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017; Deere's 2025 annual report makes autonomy central to its small-acreage strategy, where a berry picker fits. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. No standalone rental fleet at this scale has precedent here: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B, and the one field-robotics company at commercial distribution, Carbon Robotics, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D [S117, S8, S114, S115, S184]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with contracts assignable and IP owned rather than licensed.

### What must be true twelve months from closing

Five signposts, all company-reported and unverified until they appear in telemetry, decide whether a Series B is financeable. A 20-unit v4 pilot build before February 2027, with unit cost measured rather than quoted. At least 200 robots working by May 2027 rather than 360 announced. Renewals signed at $12,700 or more instead of the $9,500 of 2026. Uptime above 92% and a technician ratio near 1:20 shown in telemetry rather than in a slide. An independent harvest-level trial above 85% on blocks the company did not choose. The Calder 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 should be cleared by a wide margin under any credible plan, making it an early-warning indicator rather than a live risk. Confidence in the arithmetic is high because every input is in the deck; confidence in the demand read-through is medium, because the 110 contracted robots sit with four growers, two related to the team, and the Florida season has already lost one customer [S53].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported, unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a paid two-season lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A floor $16.45-$18.71 (2026-08-03), $19.75 by statute from 2027-01-01 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor fell in 2026; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour, harvest-aid and tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is on 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers; it raised a $70M Series D in 2024-10, $157M cumulative at that date, and $232M-$276M across two 2026 trackers with the $44M gap unresolved, unverified. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S119, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a May 2026 response, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised to date, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

| Product | Leader | Position | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Open-field strawberry, California and Florida | Hand crews and H-2A | Challenger: Orrin, 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons (company-reported, unverified) | Harvest CROO: commercial claim, no disclosed fleet | DailyRobotics: announced April 2026 California launch; equipment makers | S53, S1, S170, S196 |

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres first sets the price reference, making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys either.

::: evidence
**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. (S53, S170; unverified)**

The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74-87% of ripe fruit. It includes Harvest CROO's human-parity claim, DailyRobotics' 2025-11 announcement of an April 2026 deployment with no confirmed units, Advanced Farm's shutdown after a $25M Series B, Tortuga's sale to Oishii and Traptic's 2022 sale to Bowery (S53, S56, S42, S1, S170, S114, S115, S197).
:::

arguments.markdown:
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: a slipped round or a reprice, at 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is disclosed; the covenant rests on deck p.10, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $0.83M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. Technology and fleet buyers would buy different companies, so 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than it looks: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a rival's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier that is also its largest customer and creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics. The reference grower, Marisol Ridge (the COO's employer until 2021; 24 of 75 paid seasons), cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) in its second paid season while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons; an acreage or price cut leaves the renewal story intact, a performance or bruising cut strengthens the bear, and with its 2026 record requested and not disclosed, the 12/38/50 weights stand (12/53/35 without the minimum-cash test) until it arrives. The ties are disclosed but unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not the superseded $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment for 2026-04; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 on over $220M raised, was assigned for the benefit of creditors in 2026-01 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in 2026-04; the category kills entrants with more capital than Orrin. Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below a year earlier. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S54, S196, S171].

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recovery 75-80%: a harvest aid | 55-65% | -40% to -60% EV | critical | 2026-11 to 2027-10 | Second pilot exit; grower audit | Independent trial above 85%, bruise control | S53, unverified; S56 |
| Round slips past 2027-03-14 | 50-60% | -100% of equity | critical | 2027-03-14 | $4.0M committed through 2026-11 | Kestrel waiver; close by 2027-01 | S53, unverified |
| Covenant absent: 2027 bridge at a down round | 35% of outcomes | -25% to -40% dilution | high | 2027-01 to 2027-06 | No loan agreement or UCC-1 disclosed | Invest with conditions; $6M now, $6M later | S53, unverified |
| Entity split: IP vs fleet | 65% that recovery falls short | -20% to -40% of recovery | high | exit or insolvency | No intercompany IP licence; no parent guarantee | Intercompany licence; parent guarantee; Calder consent | S53, unverified |
| Licence becomes non-exclusive | 25% | -20% exit value | high | 2027-12-31 | Fleet below 150 robots by 2027-06 | Tranche on 100 robots in service by 2027-09 | S53, unverified |
| Tallis exits as customer or manufacturer | 25-35% | -35% to -50% EV | high | 2027-06-30 | BOM re-quote; tooling delay; its $1.0M unfunded | Fixed-price supply; tooling ownership; second source | S53, unverified |
| v4 cost overrun including Section 301 duty | 50% | -25% to -35% EV | high | 2027-01 design freeze | Quote above $36,000; first 20 units above $40,000 | Fixed-price supply; USMCA opinion | S174 |
| 2026 AEWR 15.4% below 2025; AB 2646 $19.75 in 2027 | 65% | -10% to -20% EV | medium | 2026-2027 | UFW v. DOL remedy; backpay; 2027 AEWR | Price on fruit quality and hours, not wages | S190, S191, S193, S195 |
| Series B repriced or unavailable | 55% | -15% to -25% through dilution | high | 2028 | Q4 2026 farm-robotics funding | Reserve and pro-rata at the Series A | S171, S196 |
:::

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, waiver price); the Calder licence (assignment, change of control, sub-licence); a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement; and an independent harvest trial on unselected blocks with a bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and tariff, medium on the covenant and harvest, low on the 2027 build and exit; the Kestrel text and Calder licence decide whether the bear returns capital or nothing.

arguments.markdown:
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services for Tallis ($0.95M), USDA SBIR grants ($0.30M), RaaS ($0.38M) and paid pilots ($0.27M) made up $1.9M, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots, and both non-robot lines stop by mid-2027. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent; on the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, 51x rather than the 22x the headline implies. The services line was rational at sub-scale; it is a valuation problem once the round is priced on recurring revenue. What the Series A must prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all company-reported and unverified in this review — the $16M the round actually assembles buys one season and 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a path to a Series B. The plan asks the company to build, service, reprice and cost-reduce at once, all four in the same four-month build window [S53].

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified). Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is 9.0 gross months to zero at $410,000 of monthly net burn; the Kestrel facility, $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5% and secured on the fleet, requires $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so usable cash is $1.79M at 2026-10-31, 4.4 months, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections: a close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the fleet, not only a dilution. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage; either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption [S53].

### Price the round, not the plan

The $16M the company can assemble is the case to underwrite, not the $18M plan. At a $50M pre-money with all $18M subscribed, Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post and returns 2.21x at a $150M exit and 3.68x at $250M; with the $16M — $12M from Meridian, $3.0M Granary and $1.0M Tallis — it buys 18.18% of $66M, returns 2.27x and 3.79x, and about 1.77x on the $116.8M probability-weighted exit value; as the only money it buys 19.35% of $62M, returns 2.42x and 4.03x, and leaves the 2027 plan $6M short [S53, S188]. The 2027 milestones below assume the full $18M: $9.9M of robot capex plus a $7.1M operating loss cannot be carried on $12M, so a $12M-only close moves the 300-robot build and the 360-robot season into 2028 and pushes the Series B back with them, while the $16M close funds the season with no reserve.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. Governance compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but neither revenue nor cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established route is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017; Deere's 2025 annual report makes autonomy central to its small-acreage strategy, where a berry picker fits. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. No standalone rental fleet at this scale has precedent: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B, and the one field-robotics company at commercial distribution, Carbon Robotics, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D [S117, S8, S114, S115, S184]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with contracts assignable and IP owned, not licensed.

| Calder University | Exclusive licence for agricultural harvesting, 2.5% royalty, $40,000 minimum | 2022-01-20 | Conditional to 2027-12-31 | S53 unverified |
| Vashti Harvest Services LLC | Robot transport and night-shift supervision, $310,000 paid | Board-approved | Active; related party | S53 unverified |
| USDA SBIR Phase II | $650,000 grant over 2024-2026 | 2024-09 | Ends with FY2026 | S53 unverified |

### What must be true twelve months from closing

Five signposts, all company-reported and unverified until they appear in telemetry, decide whether a Series B is financeable. A 20-unit v4 pilot build before February 2027, with unit cost measured rather than quoted. At least 200 robots working by May 2027 rather than 360 announced. Renewals signed at $12,700 or more instead of the $9,500 of 2026. Uptime above 92% and a technician ratio near 1:20 shown in telemetry rather than in a slide. An independent harvest-level trial above 85% on blocks the company did not choose. The Calder 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 should be cleared by a wide margin under any credible plan, making it an early-warning indicator, not a live risk. Confidence in the arithmetic is high because every input is in the deck; confidence in the demand read-through is medium, because the 110 contracted robots sit with four growers, two related to the team, and the Florida season has already lost one customer [S53].

arguments.markdown:
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services for Tallis ($0.95M), USDA SBIR grants ($0.30M), RaaS ($0.38M) and paid pilots ($0.27M) made up $1.9M, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots, and both non-robot lines stop by mid-2027. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent; on the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, 51x at the $72M pre-money rather than the 22x the headline implies. The services line was rational at sub-scale; it is a valuation problem once the round is priced on recurring revenue. What the Series A must prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all company-reported and unverified in this review — the $16M the round actually assembles buys one season and 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a path to a Series B. The plan asks the company to build, service, reprice and cost-reduce at once, all four in one four-month build window [S53].

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified). Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is 9.0 gross months to zero at $410,000 of monthly net burn; the Kestrel facility, $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5% and secured on the fleet, requires $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so usable cash is $1.79M at 2026-10-31, 4.4 months, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections: a close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the fleet, not only a dilution. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage; either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption [S53].

### Price the round, not the plan

The $16M the company can assemble is the case to underwrite, not the $18M plan. At a $50M pre-money with all $18M subscribed, Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post and returns 2.21x at a $150M exit and 3.68x at $250M; with the $16M — $12M from Meridian, $3.0M Granary and $1.0M Tallis — it buys 18.18% of $66M, returns 2.27x and 3.79x, and about 1.77x on the $116.8M probability-weighted exit value; as the only money it buys 19.35% of $62M, returns 2.42x and 4.03x, and leaves the 2027 plan $6M short [S53, S188]. The 2027 milestones below assume the full $18M: $9.9M of robot capex plus a $7.1M operating loss cannot be carried on $12M, so a $12M-only close moves the 300-robot build and the 360-robot season into 2028 and pushes the Series B back with them, while the $16M close funds the season with no reserve.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. Governance compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but neither revenue nor cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established route is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017; Deere's 2025 annual report makes autonomy central to its small-acreage strategy, where a berry picker fits. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. No standalone rental fleet at this scale has precedent: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B, and the one field-robotics company at commercial distribution, Carbon Robotics, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D [S117, S8, S114, S115, S184]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with contracts assignable and IP owned, not licensed.

### What must be true twelve months from closing

Five signposts, all company-reported and unverified until they appear in telemetry, decide whether a Series B is financeable. A 20-unit v4 pilot build before February 2027, with unit cost measured rather than quoted. At least 200 robots working by May 2027 rather than 360 announced. Renewals signed at $12,700 or more instead of the $9,500 of 2026. Uptime above 92% and a technician ratio near 1:20 shown in telemetry rather than in a slide. An independent harvest-level trial above 85% on blocks the company did not choose. The Calder 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 should be cleared by a wide margin under any credible plan, making it an early-warning indicator, not a live risk. Confidence in the arithmetic is high because every input is in the deck; confidence in the demand read-through is medium, because the 110 contracted robots sit with four growers, two related to the team, and the Florida season has already lost one customer [S53].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, 7,159 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 20 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, a $35.4M pool at the claimed 15% share rather than $310M, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 2.78x at $250M and 1.30x on the $116.8M weighted value. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350; a grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. plan.decision_question: Is $72M pre-money defensible against comparable rounds and precedent transactions, and what must be true for a Series A investor to earn a venture return?
plan.thesis_sentence: $72M pre-money is not defensible: it is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS, while the $16M round that assembles at a $50M pre-money returns Meridian 1.77x on the $116.8M weighted value, so Meridian should reprice to $48M-$55M or tranche $6M against the 2027 milestones.
plan.why_different: This section prices the round itself: the per-share price, the dilution, the preference stack, the dated liquidity position and the return at each exit value. The product, market and financial sections test whether the plan can be delivered; this one tests what the investor pays for it.
plan.mechanism: The $72M pre-money bundles a note-conversion discount and a pool top-up, so part of the price is a transfer to existing holders; the $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack then absorbs the first exit proceeds, leaving Meridian flat until roughly $38.4M and wholly dependent on entry price for its multiple. The $16M assembled round is the case that exists: $12M Meridian plus $4.0M of committed co-investors, with the $18M plan still $2.0M short.
plan.comparison_set: Announced agricultural robotics rounds (Monarch Tractor, Carbon Robotics, Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga); listed ag-equipment and precision-ag multiples (Deere, CNH, AGCO, Trimble) at a 2.7x median EV/Sales; precedent M&A (Blue River $305M, Bear Flag $250M, CNH/Raven 6.0x sales).
plan.counter_evidence: The category's failure record (Advanced Farm shutdown 2025-07, Tortuga asset sale 2025-03, Abundant liquidation 2021), hardware multiples below software, 65% of venture investments returning under 1x, and the preference overhang that makes a $40M sale return only capital.
plan.visual: The repriced return table with the $16M assembled round as the base case alongside the $18M full-round and $12M-only cases, the funding-round table and the dated cash-to-covenant line.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, about/many/experienced, any mention of the report's process, bots, tools or internal records.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score reflects what can be proved today, not the technology. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 20 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, lender agreement and grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and the H-2A floor cut from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 in 2027, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. A grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, $8,000-$11,000 per contracted robot, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions. The covenant rests on the deck alone; without that test the 2027 failure is a 25%-40% down round, the bear weight falls to about 35%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95, S128].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. The exit record cuts both ways: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, but Root AI cleared at $60M in harvesting, and four of the five funded peers failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026, including Monarch Tractor ($133M Series C announced 2025-02-28; assets sold to Caterpillar in April 2026); weighted across five outcomes the company is worth $116.8M, 1.30x at $72M (1.39x as the weighted average of scenario multiples) [S53, S178, S93, S54, S189, S196, S91].

::: sensitivity
| Rank | Assumption | Base | What would disprove it | Impact on value | Impact level | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit | 85% or more on unselected blocks | Independent trial below 80% | -40% | High | A second grower leaves over quality | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | v4 unit cost at 300 units | $31,000-$33,000 | A quote above $36,000 | -25% to -35% | High | Design freeze slips past 2027-01 | S53 unverified |
| 3 | 2027 book | 360 robots at $12,700 or more | Fewer than 250 contracted by 2027-02 | -30% | High | 44% cover unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | Financing and covenant | Close by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill; if no minimum-cash test exists, bear 50% to ~35% and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions | A close after Q1 2027 or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of equity | High | $4.0M of $18M committed at 2026-10-31 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | Labour policy | AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01; no H-2A expansion | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling | -15% to -20% | Medium | DOL rulemaking on H-2A wages | S190, S195 |
:::

The five assumptions are ranked above; the recommendation changes under the downside cases, not by dilution. A market 50% smaller, at 25,000 acres, gives a $117.9M pool at list and $17.7M at 15% adoption, which kills $72M but leaves $48M-$55M defensible. Revenue 30% lower, at $3.9M instead of $5.6M, removes $0.87M of gross profit at a 52% RaaS margin and leaves end-2027 cash at $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M covenant, breached at the low end. Customer acquisition at twice the plan cannot be absorbed: 200 uncontracted robots have one selling window, four sales staff and a 5-of-14 pilot conversion record. Financing six months late adds $2.46M of burn and leaves $0.83M of cash on 2027-06-15, a secured-lender default rather than a down round. Only the bull case, at 12%, returns 3.3x-4.4x; the base case at $72M is 1.7x-2.8x, and the bear is 0-1.0x at 50% with the covenant, 35% without it [S53 unverified].

Position sizing is zero at $72M and $6M at $48M-$55M pre-money, with $6M released on 2027 milestones: an independent trial above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and the Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test. The maximum loss is the full $12M; reserve $6M for a Series B. At $50M the assembled $16M round buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M and 3.79x at $250M (1.77x weighted on $116.8M), against 2.78x at $72M; the full $18M gives 17.65% and 3.68x, a $12M-only close 19.35% and 4.03x. Conditions precedent, not covenants: a Kestrel standstill or waiver signed with the term sheet, licence assignment consent, consolidation of the fleet entity and its grower contracts, and a second board seat with a veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control. Diligence next: a firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, and an insurer's view of product liability [S53, S128].

| Dimension | Weight | Score (1-10) | Rationale | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Technology and product | 20% | 5 | 94% conditional on detected fruit and chosen rows; independent 72%-87%; no granted gripper patent; licence test on 2027-12-31 | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Market and timing | 15% | 6 | Labour cost real; 2026 H-2A cut, 2027 statutory rebound; $235.7M pool at 100% adoption; acreage unverified | S53 unverified, S141, S190 |
| Team and execution | 15% | 5 | Founder-market fit; CTO vacant since 2023-08-31; nine field staff against 45 needed; part-time CFO | S53 unverified |
| Business model and unit economics | 15% | 3 | -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500; $13,350 break-even; CAC $300,000-$400,000 a grower; 44% of 2027 booked | S53 unverified |
| Financial position and cash | 10% | 3 | 4.4 months usable at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14; 46% related-party revenue; 56% of ARR not recurring | S53 unverified |
| Valuation and terms | 15% | 2 | 27.7x FY2026E revenue; 51.4x contracted RaaS; $36.8M preference; no protective provisions | S53 unverified, S8, S12, S14, S95 |
| Exit path | 10% | 4 | OEM precedent of $60M-$305M; probability-weighted value $116.8M, 1.30x; four of five peers failed or sold assets | S178, S176, S91, S115 |
| Composite | 100% | 4.1 | Weighted average of the seven dimensions | Derived from the rows above (S53, S8, S12, S14, S95) |

::: takeaways
1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 1.30x on the $116.8M weighted value and 2.78x at $250M [S53 unverified].
2. The investable structure is $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M the assembled $16M round buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 3.79x at a $250M exit, while the full $18M gives 17.65% and a $12M-only close 19.35% [S53 unverified].
3. Harvest-level recovery decides the case: 75%-80% makes the machine a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes even $72M look cheap [S53 unverified, S56, S181].
:::

Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charged to the contract, contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%); payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. ### Only list price at target cost clears a season

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; recomputed [S53].

Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charged to the contract, contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%); payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. Company-reported inputs; arithmetic verified against the deck [S53].

### Only list price at target cost clears a season

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; recomputed [S53].

[table]

The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M.
