None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. No Mexican registry extract confirms Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. On revenue the price sits at the top of any observable range: 34.6x the $90M post on 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 22.5x the $3.2M company-defined ARR (unverified), 12.9x pre and 16.1x post on the 2027 plan, 6.8x on 2028. The ARR is not recurring: $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M from the Tallis engineering contract ending 2027-06-30 and $0.6M of non-binding letters of intent — 56% non-recurring or non-binding, which is why 51.4x contracted robot revenue is the honest denominator. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA, and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95]. Existing holders fall from 100% to 69.2%: founders from 53.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7%, granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%. The 1x non-participating stack is $36.8M across Series A ($18.0M), A-1 ($7.77M) and Seed ($11.0M) — 40.9% of the $90M post, pari passu with new money — or $39.3M (43.6%) if the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs converted into Seed. Ahead of the preferred sits $1.6M of Kestrel equipment debt (unverified). Meridian is flat at 1.0x from a $38.4M to a $90M exit: at a $40M sale the Series A takes its $18M preference, Meridian recovers $12.0M and the common gets $1.6M after debt [S53]. At the current price Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 shares, 13.33% of the $90M post. A 3x needs $36M of proceeds: $272M of company value with no further dilution, or $337.5M after 20% of Series B dilution in 2028. At $150M the return is 1.67x (10.8% a year over five years), at $300M 3.33x (27.2%) and at $500M 5.56x (40.9%).

| Exit value, 2029-2031 | Meridian at 13.33%, no dilution | MOIC | After 20% Series B dilution (10.67%) | MOIC | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $150M | $20.0M | 1.67x | $16.0M | 1.33x | S53 unverified |
| $250M | $33.3M | 2.78x | $26.7M | 2.22x | S53 unverified |
| $300M | $40.0M | 3.33x | $32.0M | 2.67x | S53 unverified |

The terms are conventional but incomplete. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard; so is a five-seat board with two common seats, one Seed, one Series A and one independent agreed by both. Missing is the protection package: Meridian would hold one of five votes, with no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package, and Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor (unverified) [S53]. The minimum package is a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilisation, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true is specific: 360 robots and $8M of ARR excluding Tallis services by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence still exclusive after its 100-robot test, unit cost below $36,000, and $67.5M-$84M of revenue at a 4x multiple by 2029-2031 (company plan, unverified). Deere paid $305M for Blue River (2017) and $250M for Bear Flag (2021), so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy. The counter-evidence is the category's own record: Advanced Farm, backed by Kubota and CNH, ceased operations in July 2025; Tortuga sold its assets; Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 [S91, S114, S115, S53]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charged to the contract, contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%); payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. Company-reported inputs; arithmetic verified against the deck [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 | +$4,500 | 2.5 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Derived; unverified | S53 |

### Only list price at target cost clears a season

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; recomputed [S53].

| Offer | Price per robot-season | Acres per robot | Price per acre-season | Fully loaded break-even price | Cover of break-even | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Derived; unverified | S53 |

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. Counts partially verified; contracts unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) then contracted 20 for 2027 (+43%); its 2026 season record (acres, yield, bruising, uptime, price) is not disclosed and has been requested. An acreage or price cut leaves the renewal story intact; a performance or bruising cut from a reference grower contradicts it, and the 2027 increase to 20 favours acreage. The cut came in its second paid season while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].

| Deal | Status | Date | Reason | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grower E, Plant City FL | Pilot ended; no 2027 robots | 2026-06 | Fruit bruising; unverified | S53 p.6, p.13 |
| Grower D, Plant City FL | 11 paid robots in 2025-26; no 2027 contract, "in discussion" | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| Grower B, Santa Maria CA | Cut from 22 to 14 robots (-36%) | 2026 season | Not disclosed; season record requested | S53 p.6 |
| 6 of 8 other pilot farms | 2025 and 2026 pilots; no LOI or 2027 order | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 9 of 14 pilot farms | Never a paid season | 2024-2026 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |

### The KPI is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. Derived; unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate: a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C announced 2025-02-28; over $220M raised; January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors; April 2026 Caterpillar asset purchase | Wound down; assets sold | S54, S196 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; demo 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target. Source: S53, S54, S196, S55, S91, S93, S94.

| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling | 2027-2029 | Not a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer (company relationship, unverified) | S53 unverified |

| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low — 0 of 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were IPOs | S187, S53 unverified |

Deere is the most plausible buyer: it has paid for autonomy three times — Blue River ($305M, 2017), Bear Flag ($250M, 2021) and GUSS Automation (2025) — but none of the three bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it close in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S96, S92, S8, S95, S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company cuts both ways: it makes the next asset strategic and the buyer tougher on price.

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the ripeness model trained on 1.9 million berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost (unverified). A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

On those weights the expected company value is $116.8M; at 13.33% that is $15.6M, 1.30x, while the weighted average of the scenario multiples is 1.39x because the preference lifts the low-exit recoveries. The weights put 55% of outcomes at or below 1.0x, which is more generous than the 65% base rate for venture investments, because Orrin already has five paying growers; applying the base rate gives a lower expected value, not a higher one [S188, S53]. The modal successful outcome remains a $150M-$250M OEM sale, but a 30% failure tail at $10M — the category's own record — pulls the probability-weighted value below that range, and the preference stack caps the low-exit recovery.

Structure can block the buyer list. The Calder licence's term, assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the noteholders' Series A-1 consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, so the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts (unverified) [S53]. The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.55x and 2.27x on the $16M that assembles, 4.41x and 2.21x on the full $18M, or 4.84x and 2.42x if Meridian's $12M is the only money. Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota can build a picker in-house; the US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit — Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025, Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M — while the most recent harvesting-robot purchase, AppHarvest's $60M for Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices. arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charged to the contract, contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%); payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. Company-reported inputs; arithmetic verified against the deck [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

| Price per unit (robot-season) | Unit cost | Depreciation per season (4-season straight line) | Direct cost per unit | Contribution per unit | Cash payback (seasons) | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 | +$4,500 | 2.5 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 | $48,000 | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$1,100 | never | Derived; unverified | S53 |

### Only list price at target cost clears a season

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; recomputed [S53].

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026 contract | $9,500 | 3.5 | $2,714 | $17,600 | 54% | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| 2027 renewal | $12,700 | 3.5 | $3,629 | $13,350 | 95% | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| 2027 list | $16,500 | 3.5 | $4,714 | $13,350 | 124% | Derived; unverified | S53 |

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. Counts partially verified; contracts unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) then contracted 20 for 2027 (+43%); its 2026 season record (acres, yield, bruising, uptime, price) is not disclosed and has been requested. An acreage or price cut leaves the renewal story intact; a performance or bruising cut from a reference grower contradicts it, and the 2027 increase to 20 favours acreage. The cut came in its second paid season while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].

| Deal | Status | Date | Reason | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grower E, Plant City FL | Pilot ended; no 2027 robots | 2026-06 | Fruit bruising; unverified | S53 p.6, p.13 |
| Grower D, Plant City FL | 11 paid robots in 2025-26; no 2027 contract, "in discussion" | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| Grower B, Santa Maria CA | Cut from 22 to 14 robots (-36%) | 2026 season | Not disclosed; season record requested; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 6 of 8 other pilot farms | 2025 and 2026 pilots; no LOI or 2027 order | 2026-10 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |
| 9 of 14 pilot farms | Never a paid season | 2024-2026 | Not disclosed; unverified | S53 p.6 |

### The KPI is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. Derived; unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate: a milestone, not a finished model

| Peer | Capital raised | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C announced 2025-02-28; over $220M raised; January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors; April 2026 Caterpillar asset purchase | Wound down; assets sold | S54, S196 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | $25M Series B | Ceased operations 2025 | S93, S114 |
| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; demo 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target. Source: S53, S54, S196, S55, S91, S93, S94.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charged to the contract, contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. Company-reported inputs; arithmetic verified against the deck [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

### Only list price at target cost clears a season

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; recomputed [S53].

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS is 75 seasons at $9,500, the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest is a related-party engineering contract ending 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. No audit exists and finance is part-time; FY2023-FY2026 are unverified management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit at either price. FY2028 still loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS, $1.4M of one-season contracts makes $72M 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use list: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet, 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified.

::: info danger
**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after $410k of burn and $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register; the test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and $48-55M becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Until produced, the covenant date is the planning case. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with the covenant in the middle. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. Without the round, the dated $3.29M at 2026-10-31 less $2.46M of burn leaves $0.83M, and the $1.5M covenant is reached on 2027-03-14 first. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital; it cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 a season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO and goodwill cannot be calculated; the facts are $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M ($1.69M at 2026-10-31) before the $1.5M minimum. Working capital is estimated: $2.0M of direct cost, $0.8-1.1M of receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days, and $9.9M paid to Tallis before the season; grower and Tallis payment terms are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures unverified; yields and working capital derived [S53, S7].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex take usable cash below $1.5M in mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. Utilisation moves the outcome most: $10.8M of opex over 360 seasons is $30,000 a season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet; $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. Retention is second: Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%), and its season record (acres, yield, bruising, uptime, price) is not disclosed and has been requested; an acreage or price cause leaves renewal intact, a performance cause contradicts it, and its 20 contracted 2027 robots (+43%) favour acreage. Grower D has no 2027 contract, Grower E exited over bruising, and four of five 2026 payers signed for 2027 (section 6). The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. Analyst estimates on unverified company figures [S53].

arguments.markdown:
At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M, not as a price for the business that exists. At $50M pre the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M and $1.0M from the two co-investors) buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at a $150M exit, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x on the $116.8M weighted value; the full $18M buys 17.65% at 2.21x-3.68x and a $12M-only round 19.35% at 2.42x-4.03x [S53].

The $18M round at $72M pre implies a $90M post, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share: new Series A 20.0%, the 2025 notes 10.8%, the unallocated pool 12.0%, granted options 8.2% — a 20.2% total overhang. At the deck's $72M pre, Granary's $3.0M and Tallis's $1.0M are new cash on the same terms and $4.7145 price as Meridian's $12M; the $7.77M of notes convert separately into Series A-1 (company deck, unverified). The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M. Orrin has raised $20.5M of equity and notes to 2026-10-31 and $38.5M including the proposed $18M round, plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt. Cash is $3.7M at 2026-09-30 and $3.29M at 2026-10-31 at $410,000 monthly burn: $1.79M usable above the $1.5M Kestrel minimum-cash covenant, 4.4 usable months to 2027-03-14, or 9.0 gross months to zero from 2026-09-30. Peer disclosure is thin: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28 and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds; Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S54, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119, S189]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. No Mexican registry extract confirms Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. (Jalisco, formed 2024-07-19); the Calder licence term is not disclosed (unverified).

On revenue the price sits at the top of any observable range: 34.6x the $90M post on 2026E revenue of $2.6M, 22.5x the $3.2M company-defined ARR (unverified), 12.9x pre and 16.1x post on the 2027 plan, 6.8x on 2028. Payback is thinner than the pitch: the 2.1-season figure assumes a $1,750 service cost and omits the $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables in gross profit, so a robot pays back in 2.5 seasons at the $16,500 list price and 4.4 at the $12,700 renewal. Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales and 15.6x EV/EBITDA, and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven Industries' $348.4M of revenue in 2021 [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95]. On a 4.0x exit multiple the 2028 plan would need $22.5M of revenue to justify the $90M post, 70% above the $13.2M projected.

arguments.markdown:
The company's growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS is 75 seasons at $9,500, the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest is a related-party engineering contract ending 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. No audit exists and finance is part-time; FY2023-FY2026 are unverified management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but composition flatters it. Removing the $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit at either price. FY2028 loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS, $1.4M of one-season contracts makes $72M 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use list: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet, 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified.

::: info danger
**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after $410k of burn and $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register; the test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and $48-55M becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Until produced, the covenant date is the planning case. Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan is a bridge with the covenant in the middle. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. Without the round, the dated $3.29M at 2026-10-31 less $2.46M of burn leaves $0.83M, and the $1.5M covenant is reached on 2027-03-14 first. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital; it cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 a season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO and goodwill cannot be calculated; the facts are $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M ($1.69M at 2026-10-31) before the $1.5M minimum. Working capital is estimated: $2.0M of direct cost, $0.8-1.1M of receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days, and $9.9M paid to Tallis before the season; grower and Tallis payment terms are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures unverified; yields and working capital derived [S53, S7].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex take usable cash below $1.5M in mid-2027. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, 7,159 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 20 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, a $35.4M pool at the claimed 15% share rather than $310M, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 2.78x at $250M and 1.30x on the $116.8M weighted value. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. arguments.markdown:
Growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS is 75 seasons at $9,500, the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest is a related-party engineering contract ending 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. No audit exists and finance is part-time; FY2023-FY2026 are unverified management accounts [S53].

| $M | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | FY2028P | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RaaS | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.38 | 0.71 | 4.6 | 12.9 | S53 (unverified) |
| Paid pilots | 0.03 | 0.12 | 0.27 | 0.34 | 0.4 | 0.3 | S53 (unverified) |
| Engineering services | 0.00 | 0.20 | 0.95 | 1.20 | 0.6 | 0.0 | S53 (unverified) |
| Grants | 0.07 | 0.08 | 0.30 | 0.35 | 0.0 | 0.0 | S53 (unverified) |
| Revenue | 0.1 | 0.4 | 1.9 | 2.6 | 5.6 | 13.2 | S53 (unverified) |
| Operating expenses | 2.6 | 4.3 | 6.2 | 6.9 | 10.8 | 14.9 | S53 (unverified) |
| Operating loss | (2.6) | (4.0) | (5.2) | (5.4) | (7.9) | (6.9) | S53 (unverified) |

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but mix flatters it. Removing $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit at either price. FY2028 loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS, $1.4M of one-season contracts makes $72M 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use list: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet, 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified [S53].

::: info danger
**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after $410k of burn and $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register; the test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and $48-55M becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Source: S53.
:::

The cash plan bridges the covenant. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. Without the round, the dated $3.29M at 2026-10-31 less $2.46M of burn leaves $0.83M, and the $1.5M covenant is reached on 2027-03-14 first. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital; it cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 a season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO and goodwill cannot be calculated; the facts are $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M ($1.69M at 2026-10-31) before the $1.5M minimum. Working capital is estimated: $2.0M of direct cost, $0.8-1.1M of receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days, and $9.9M paid to Tallis before the season; grower and Tallis payment terms are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures unverified; yields and working capital derived. Monarch raised $133M in its 2025 Series C and collapsed in 2026 [S53, S7, S54, S196].

| Metric | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E | FY2027P | Benchmark | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opex per paid robot-season | n/d | $155k | $92k | $30k | Price $9,500-16,500 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| Burn multiple | n/d | n/d | 7.0x | 5.9x | Above 3x is capital-inefficient | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| Fleet cash yield | n/d | n/d | (16.9%) | (2.1%) renewal; +10.2% list | Deere ROIC 22.8% | Derived | S53, S7 |
| Net cash (debt) | n/d | n/d | $2.1M | n/d | $1.5M minimum | Unverified; dated 2026-09-30 | S53 |
| DSO / DIO / DPO | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | not disclosed | n/a | Not publicly disclosed | S53 |

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex take usable cash below $1.5M in mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. Utilisation moves the outcome most: $10.8M of opex over 360 seasons is $30,000 a season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet; $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. Retention is second: Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%), and its season record (acres, yield, bruising, uptime, price) is not disclosed and has been requested; an acreage or price cause leaves renewal intact, a performance cause contradicts it, and its 20 contracted 2027 robots (+43%) favour acreage. Grower D has no 2027 contract, Grower E exited over bruising, and four of five 2026 payers signed for 2027 (section 6). The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. Analyst estimates on unverified company figures [S53].

| RaaS gross margin 41% | $3,900 on $9,500 | Contradicted as economic margin | Excludes $12,000 fleet depreciation; fully loaded -$8,100 (-85%) | S53 p.9 |
| ARR $3.2M | 1.4 + 1.2 + 0.6 | Contradicted as ARR | 56% non-recurring or non-binding; contracted robot revenue $1.4M | S53 p.10 |
| 360 robots; $8M ARR 2027 | 110 contracted + 50 LOI | Contradicted by plan arithmetic | 44% covered; $12,778 a robot; $8M cannot include Tallis after June 2027 | S53 pp.10, 15 |
| 9-month runway | $3.7M / $410k | Contradicted as stated | 9.0 gross months from 2026-09-30; 4.4 usable from 2026-10-31 to 2027-03-14 | S53 p.10 |
| Robot cost $48,000; target $31,000 | v3 / v4 | Unverified | No purchase orders; Tallis BOM quote August 2026 | S53 pp.9, 15 |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 11 by Lead Analyst, 8,992 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 on 2026-01-01, overtime starts after eight hours, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap holds, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 with service at $1,750 so the $12,700 renewal clears a $12,000 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M — 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS — Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. Killer risks: negative contribution, a licence lapsing below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms it selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83%-87% of detected fruit, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption; the $310M claim is 132% of that pool. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

The challenge moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The score reflects what can be proved today, not the technology. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 20 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, lender agreement and grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and the H-2A floor cut from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 in 2027, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. A grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, $8,000-$11,000 per contracted robot, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. # Decision Framework

Use this file before drafting the executive briefing, investment thesis, recommendation, scoring, or final decision. Do not force precision when evidence does not support it.

## Contents

- Consensus / Non-Consensus View
- Scenario Analysis
- Key Assumptions
- Historical Analogs
- Capital Efficiency
- Position Sizing / Deal Sizing
- The One Question
- Three Takeaways

## Consensus / Non-Consensus View

State what the market, comparable investors, or the company's own pitch appears to assume. Then state whether the report has a differentiated view.

If there is no non-consensus insight, say the thesis is consensus and explain what that means for return expectations, valuation discipline, or margin of safety. Do not invent a variant perception for appearance.

## Scenario Analysis

Use bull/base/bear cases with explicit drivers and approximate probabilities.

- For public equities and growth companies, scenarios may use revenue, margin, multiple, cash flow, valuation, catalyst timing, or downside drawdown.
- For early-stage, biotech, hard-tech, and data-poor cases, use milestone scenarios such as product-market fit, regulatory readout, manufacturing yield, customer conversion, financing survival, or exit path.

Each scenario should include:

- Specific driver or failure mode.
- Evidence that makes it plausible.
- Financial or milestone implication.
- Investor implication.

For public equities, build scenarios from explicit financial drivers where data allows: revenue growth, segment mix, gross/operating margin, tax, share count, capex, working capital, free cash flow, net cash/debt, and valuation multiple. Include current share price context before stating upside/downside.

## Key Assumptions

Rank the 3-5 assumptions that most affect the decision. For each, state:

- Confidence.
- What would disprove it.
- Impact if wrong.
- Early warning sign.

This is often more useful than adding more facts.

## Historical Analogs

Use historical analogs only when they are close enough to teach a decision rule. A good analog matches on business model, market structure, stage, regulation, customer behavior, or capital intensity.

If no close analog exists, say so.

## Capital Efficiency

Use a capital efficiency scorecard when the company has raised material capital and data exists. Useful metrics include burn multiple, revenue per dollar raised, runway, revenue per employee, capex to next milestone, and dilution efficiency.

If data is unavailable, state which missing data would be required.

A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. A grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, $8,000-$11,000 per contracted robot, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Market & Industry Analysis (market, revision 10 by Market Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,909 characters)
The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| Layer | Figure (year) | Build | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAM: global harvest-labour spend | $42B (2026) | Company top-down; labour spend, not robot revenue | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM: claimed US soft-fruit service | $3.1B (2026) | 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool | Unverified | S53 |
| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| Revenue, 2026 estimate | $0.71M (2026) | 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 | Company-reported, unverified | S53 |

Only the bottom-up sizes revenue, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. At $3.1B it is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend; the deck does not say which acres fill the gap. The adoption path is unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's unverified productivity: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | n/a | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1:2024; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each for one paid season, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Monarch Tractor, a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor fell in 2026

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The H-2A adverse effect wage rate was $19.97 through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule of 2025-10-02 (90 FR 47914) cut the operative California floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71; the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful on 2026-08-26, leaving the rates in place with backpay possible; and AB 2646 restores a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; the 2027 statutory rebound widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the floor fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Inputs that would move this from estimate to evidence are NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. Stable acreage and a pick rate that holds without the row exclusions re-base the out-year line up; falling acreage with realised price near the current contract leaves the strawberry market small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

::: evidence
**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53, unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported, unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business Model (business_model, revision 15 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,966 characters)
Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charged to the contract, contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. Company-reported inputs; arithmetic verified against the deck [S53].

::: evidence
**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].
:::

### Only list price at target cost clears a season

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; recomputed [S53].

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. Counts partially verified; contracts unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) then contracted 20 for 2027 (+43%); its 2026 season record (acres, yield, bruising, uptime, price) is not disclosed and has been requested. An acreage or price cut leaves the renewal story intact; a performance or bruising cut from a reference grower contradicts it, and the 2027 increase to 20 favours acreage. The cut came in its second paid season while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].
