### The KPI is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. Derived; unverified [S53].

### The peer base rate: a milestone, not a finished model

| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 7,159 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 20 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, a $35.4M pool at the claimed 15% share rather than $310M, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 2.78x at $250M and 1.30x on the $116.8M weighted value. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

::: briefing

| What it sells | 64 robots, 75 paid seasons and five paying growers at $9,500 a season in 2026 (company-reported, unverified); 110 robots contracted and 50 letters of intent for a 360-robot 2027 plan | S53 unverified |
| Performance | 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 selected rows with 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime (company); independent trials report 72%-87%, putting harvest-level recovery near 75%-80% | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350; a grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |
:::

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. If the trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the right answer reverses and $72M is cheap [S53 unverified].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Investment Potential & Thesis (thesis, revision 11 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,992 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 on 2026-01-01, overtime starts after eight hours, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap holds, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 with service at $1,750 so the $12,700 renewal clears a $12,000 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M — 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS — Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. Killer risks: negative contribution, a licence lapsing below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms it selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83%-87% of detected fruit, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption; the $310M claim is 132% of that pool. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

The challenge moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 at list, an 85% trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses April 2027, the fleet stays below 100, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is registered. Without a minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A 3-6-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; the standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

::: scenarios
| Scenario | Probability | Drivers | Outcome | Signposts | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | v4 at $31,000-$33,000; 360 robots for April 2027; 250+ at $16,500 list; independent trial above 85%; Calder test passed | $8M+ ARR exiting 2027; OEM or Series B in 2028; $300M-$400M sale in 2030-2031; Meridian 3.3x-4.4x | 20-unit v4 build under $33,000 by 2027-01; 250 contracted by 2027-02 | S53 unverified |
| Base | 38% | 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal; $2M-$3M of RaaS in 2027; flat or down Series B in 2028 | $150M-$250M OEM sale in 2029-2031; Meridian 1.7x-2.8x, or 1.3x-2.2x after 20% dilution | Renewals at or below $12,700; 2027 book stays at 44% cover | S53 unverified |
| Bear | 50% | Close after Q1 2027; covenant at 2027-03-14; v4 misses April 2027; fleet below 100; licence lapses; second grower exits; cheaper hand labour | Secured-lender event or distressed sale 2027-2028; Meridian $0-$12M (0-1.0x), optimistic given the entity split | $4.0M of $18M committed; close slips past 2027-03-31; DOL H-2A rulemaking | S53 unverified, S169, S128 |
:::

The five assumptions are ranked by damage; three carry low confidence, and financing is binary: failure means zero equity, not dilution. Labour now cuts both ways: the 2026-08-03 notice set H-2A skill tiers at $16.45-$18.71, a federal court held that method unlawful on 2026-08-26 with backpay possible, and AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01. The file does not establish all-in hand-pick cost year on year, so assumption 5 is medium-low confidence [S190, S192, S195].

| Rank | Assumption | Confidence | What would disprove it | Impact if wrong | Early warning | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harvest-level recovery of 85% or more with bruising at or below hand-picked fruit, on unselected blocks | Medium-low | Independent trial below 80%, or a second grower leaving over quality | -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid | Further pilot exits; grower quality audits | S53 unverified, S56 |
| 2 | The v4 is built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units by Tallis | Low | A quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build above $40,000 | -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even | Design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes | S53 unverified |
| 3 | The 2027 book clears at $12,700 or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160 | Low | Renewals at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02 | -30% value; a bridge round at a flat or down price | 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027 | S53 unverified |
| 4 | The round closes by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, reaching a Series B without breaching the $1.5M covenant | Low | A close after Q1 2027 or a burn above $410,000 a month | -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event | $4.0M committed at 2026-10-31; covenant by 2027-03-14 | S53 unverified, S128 |
| 5 | The wage floor rebounds: AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01, and no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick advantage | Medium-low | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling | -15% to -20% value; adoption slows | DOL rulemaking; surveys showing crews available | S190, S195 |

The technology exits; the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28, raised over $220M, assigned its assets for creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of five funded peers failed or sold assets in 2021-2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S54, S189, S196, S91, S114, S115].

::: analogs
| Analog | Kind | Period | Lesson | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lely Astronaut | Best | 1992-2024 | 50,000 units 29 years after launch, sold with dealer service; a decades-long replacement cycle | S177 |
| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2025-2026 | $133M Series C announced 2025-02-28; over $220M raised; creditors' assignment 2026-01, Caterpillar sale 2026-04 | S54, S189, S196 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |
:::

Three branches. Pass at $72M: the price capitalises a six-conjunct bull case and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move it. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M the assembled $16M round buys 18.18% of the $66M post and earns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x on the $116.8M weighted value; the $18M and $12M-only cases give 2.21x-3.68x and 2.42x-4.03x. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm 300-unit quote, licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and fleet-entity consolidation [S53, S128]."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Exit Strategy Analysis (exit, revision 7 by Valuation Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,784 characters)
The realistic exit is a trade sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M; on the $116.8M probability-weighted value the $16M round that assembles at a $50M pre-money returns Meridian 1.77x (18.18% of the $66M post), against 1.30x on the same value at the current $72M pre-money; all 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were M&A and none was an IPO, so the question is which OEM buys, when, and what the preference stack leaves [S187, S188].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood and independent basis | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Trade sale | Deere & Company | Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021) and GUSS Automation (2025); no harvesting robot | 2028-2031 | Medium — three autonomy acquisitions in eight years | S96, S92, S8, S187 |
| Trade sale | CNH Industrial | Raven gives it autonomy software; its 2022 Advanced Farm stake ended in that company's 2025 closure | 2028-2031 | Low-medium — one platform deal, no harvesting acquisition | S95, S117, S114 |
| Trade sale | Kubota | Backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in 2021; needs a specialty-crop harvesting asset | 2029-2031 | Low — no disclosed acquisition in the category | S93, S114 |
| Asset sale | Tallis Agricultural Machinery | Contract manufacturer, $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M customer and $1.0M investor; natural buyer of the fleet and v4 tooling | 2027-2029 | Not a venture exit; high as a liquidation buyer (company relationship, unverified) | S53 unverified |
| Private equity | Paine Schwartz Partners or similar | Needs positive EBITDA and fleet-level cash flow; the FY2028 plan still loses $6.9M | 2030-2032 | Low — no agtech robotics buyout disclosed | S167, S53 unverified |
| IPO | Nasdaq or NYSE | $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M net loss fail any listing scale test | 2031 or later | Very low — 0 of 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were IPOs | S187, S53 unverified |

Deere is the most plausible buyer: it has paid for autonomy three times — Blue River ($305M, 2017), Bear Flag ($250M, 2021) and GUSS Automation (2025) — but none of the three bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it close in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S96, S92, S8, S95, S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company cuts both ways: it makes the next asset strategic and the buyer tougher on price.

| Transaction | Year | Value | Multiple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Deere / Blue River Technology | 2017 | $305M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S96 |
| Deere / Bear Flag Robotics | 2021 | $250M | not disclosed (pre-scale) | S92 |
| CNH / Raven Industries | 2021 | $2.1B enterprise value | 6.0x EV/Sales ($348.4M sales) | S95 |
| AppHarvest / Root AI | 2021 | $60M | not disclosed | S91 |
| Oishii / Tortuga AgTech | 2025 | IP and team; value not disclosed | n/a | S115 |
| Advanced Farm Technologies | 2025 | ceased operations | n/a | S114 |
| Abundant Robotics | 2021 | IP and assets sold; $12M raised | n/a | S91 |

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the ripeness model trained on 1.9 million berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost (unverified). That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, the date that determines whether a buyer acquires an exclusive technology or a commodity one [S53]. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

| Outcome, 2028-2032 | Probability | Basis for the weight | Equity value | Meridian at $72M pre (13.33%) | Meridian at $50M pre, $12M only (19.35%) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liquidation or asset sale | 30% | 3 of 5 named US strawberry-harvesting peers closed or sold assets 2021-2025; 65% of VC investments return under 1x | $10M | $3.3M / 0.27x | $3.3M / 0.27x | S91, S114, S115, S188 |
| Stalled, sold at the preference | 25% | $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack; 65% below-1x base rate | $75M | $12.0M / 1.00x | $14.5M / 1.21x | S53 unverified, S188 |
| Modest OEM trade sale | 25% | Deere precedents at $250M-$305M, discounted for pre-scale | $150M | $20.0M / 1.67x | $29.0M / 2.42x | S92, S96 |
| Good OEM trade sale | 15% | Same precedents at full value | $250M | $33.3M / 2.78x | $48.4M / 4.03x | S92, S96 |
| Bidding war or platform sale | 5% | Requires 360 robots and a cleared licence | $400M | $53.3M / 4.44x | $77.4M / 6.45x | S53 unverified |
| Probability-weighted | 100% | | $116.8M | $16.6M / 1.39x | $23.0M / 1.92x | S53, S188, S91, S114, S115 |

On those weights the expected company value is $116.8M; at 13.33% that is $15.6M, 1.30x, while the weighted average of the scenario multiples is 1.39x because the preference lifts the low-exit recoveries. The weights put 55% of outcomes at or below 1.0x, which is more generous than the 65% base rate for venture investments, because Orrin already has five paying growers; applying the base rate gives a lower expected value, not a higher one [S188, S53]. The modal successful outcome remains a $150M-$250M OEM sale, but a 30% failure tail at $10M — the category's own record — pulls the probability-weighted value below that range, and the preference stack caps the low-exit recovery.

Structure can block the buyer list. The Calder licence's term, assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the noteholders' Series A-1 consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, so the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts (unverified) [S53]. A foreign buyer such as Kubota also faces undisclosed licence-consent and export-control diligence, which could remove the most logical buyer.

| Entry pre-money | Round | Meridian stake for $12M | $150M exit | $250M exit | $300M exit | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $72M (current) | $18M | 13.33% | $20.0M / 1.67x | $33.3M / 2.78x | $40.0M / 3.33x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | $16M assembled | 18.18% | $27.3M / 2.27x | $45.5M / 3.79x | $54.5M / 4.55x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | $12M only | 19.35% | $29.0M / 2.42x | $48.4M / 4.03x | $58.1M / 4.84x | S53 unverified |

The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.55x and 2.27x on the $16M that assembles, 4.41x and 2.21x on the full $18M, or 4.84x and 2.42x if Meridian's $12M is the only money. Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota can build a picker in-house; the US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit — Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025, Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M — while the most recent harvesting-robot purchase, AppHarvest's $60M for Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices. Hardware exits trade below software, ag-equipment multiples are 1.0x-4.3x sales, and the industrial sector ETF is down 6.9% over three months, 8.1 points behind the S&P 500, so a 2029-2031 window is not assured [S53, S115, S114, S91, S31]. Meridian should negotiate a drag-along and tag-along that make a trade sale executable without a founder veto, a right to consent to any change to the Calder licence or the Tallis manufacturing agreement, and a requirement that Kestrel be repaid or consented at closing."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation (scoring, revision 12 by Lead Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,994 characters)
Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score reflects what can be proved today, not the technology. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 20 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, lender agreement and grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported, unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a paid two-season lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A floor $16.45-$18.71 (2026-08-03), $19.75 by statute from 2027-01-01 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor fell in 2026; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour, harvest-aid and tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is on 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers; it raised a $70M Series D in 2024-10, $157M cumulative at that date, and $232M-$276M across two 2026 trackers with the $44M gap unresolved, unverified. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S119, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a May 2026 response, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised to date, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

### Positioning

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres first sets the price reference, making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys either.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Risk Assessment (risk, revision 13 by Red Team Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,980 characters)
Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: a slipped round or a reprice, at 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is disclosed; the covenant rests on deck p.10, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

::: info danger
**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.
:::

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |

| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |
| CAC doubled | 5 of 14 pilots converted; four sales staff; one window a year | 200 uncontracted robots need a second season | S53, unverified |
| Financing six months late | $2.46M of extra burn | Cash $0.83M on 2027-06-15; default if the test exists, dilution if not | S53, unverified; derived |

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. Technology and fleet buyers would buy different companies, so 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than it looks: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a rival's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier that is also its largest customer and creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics. The reference grower, Marisol Ridge (the COO's employer until 2021; 24 of 75 paid seasons), cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) in its second paid season while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons; an acreage or price cut leaves the renewal story intact, a performance or bruising cut strengthens the bear, and with its 2026 record requested and not disclosed, the 12/38/50 weights stand (12/53/35 without the minimum-cash test) until it arrives. The ties are disclosed but unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not the superseded $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment for 2026-04; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 on over $220M raised, was assigned for the benefit of creditors in 2026-01 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in 2026-04; the category kills entrants with more capital than Orrin. Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below a year earlier. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S54, S196, S171].

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, waiver price); the Calder licence (assignment, change of control, sub-licence); a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement; and an independent harvest trial on unselected blocks with a bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and tariff, medium on the covenant and harvest, low on the 2027 build and exit; the Kestrel text and Calder licence decide whether the bear returns capital or nothing."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Development Strategy (strategy, revision 6 by Product Analyst, changed since the previous version, 8,990 characters)
The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services for Tallis ($0.95M), USDA SBIR grants ($0.30M), RaaS ($0.38M) and paid pilots ($0.27M) made up $1.9M, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots, and both non-robot lines stop by mid-2027. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent; on the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, 51x at the $72M pre-money rather than the 22x the headline implies. The services line was rational at sub-scale; it is a valuation problem once the round is priced on recurring revenue. What the Series A must prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all company-reported and unverified in this review — the $16M the round actually assembles buys one season and 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a path to a Series B. The plan asks the company to build, service, reprice and cost-reduce at once, all four in one four-month build window [S53].

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified). Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is 9.0 gross months to zero at $410,000 of monthly net burn; the Kestrel facility, $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5% and secured on the fleet, requires $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so usable cash is $1.79M at 2026-10-31, 4.4 months, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections: a close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the fleet, not only a dilution. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage; either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption [S53].

### Price the round, not the plan

The $16M the company can assemble is the case to underwrite, not the $18M plan. At a $50M pre-money with all $18M subscribed, Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post and returns 2.21x at a $150M exit and 3.68x at $250M; with the $16M — $12M from Meridian, $3.0M Granary and $1.0M Tallis — it buys 18.18% of $66M, returns 2.27x and 3.79x, and about 1.77x on the $116.8M probability-weighted exit value; as the only money it buys 19.35% of $62M, returns 2.42x and 4.03x, and leaves the 2027 plan $6M short [S53, S188]. The 2027 milestones below assume the full $18M: $9.9M of robot capex plus a $7.1M operating loss cannot be carried on $12M, so a $12M-only close moves the 300-robot build and the 360-robot season into 2028 and pushes the Series B back with them, while the $16M close funds the season with no reserve.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. Governance compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but neither revenue nor cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established route is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017; Deere's 2025 annual report makes autonomy central to its small-acreage strategy, where a berry picker fits. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. No standalone rental fleet at this scale has precedent: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B, and the one field-robotics company at commercial distribution, Carbon Robotics, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D [S117, S8, S114, S115, S184]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with contracts assignable and IP owned, not licensed.

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Executive Briefing (executive_summary, revision 7 by Lead Analyst, 7,159 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 20 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

::: verdict
| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |
:::

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, a $35.4M pool at the claimed 15% share rather than $310M, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 2.78x at $250M and 1.30x on the $116.8M weighted value. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What it sells | 64 robots, 75 paid seasons and five paying growers at $9,500 a season in 2026 (company-reported, unverified); 110 robots contracted and 50 letters of intent for a 360-robot 2027 plan | S53 unverified |
| Performance | 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 selected rows with 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime (company); independent trials report 72%-87%, putting harvest-level recovery near 75%-80% | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350; a grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. ## Rating: Wait for milestone — composite 4.1 / 10 (confidence: medium)

**Action:** do not lead at $72M pre-money. Indicate $48M–$55M pre, with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest-level trial. Horizon: 6–12 months.

## Thesis

The labour problem is real and Orrin has a working machine: five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons and the California hand-pick wage floor fell to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 — but the company's 94% pick rate is a share of *detected* ripe fruit on rows Orrin selected, and independent trials imply 75%–80% harvest-level recovery. At $72M pre-money (27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue) the price already pays for the bull case; at $48M–$55M with tranching the same evidence pays for an option on a proven autonomy stack that an OEM would likely buy.

It is not a Pass because the gating measurement is close and measurable: an independent trial, a firm v4 cost quote and a lender standstill could all arrive before the target close.

## Main risks

1. **Harvest-level recovery (most damaging).** 94% is conditional on detected fruit and selected rows; if detection is near 100% on unselected blocks the reprice is an expensive pass, if it is near 90% the robot is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.
2. **Unit economics at the price actually charged.** 41% gross margin becomes −$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the $9,500 price once $12,000 of fleet depreciation is charged; the plan needs +74% price, −35% cost and −44% service cost simultaneously.
3. **Cash clock.** $3.29M gross at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable above the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months to the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 season's first collections; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed.
4. **IP and licence cliff.** Zero granted company patents, all gripper claims rejected, the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30, and the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 (64 robots today).
5. **Entity/asset mismatch.** IP sits in the issuer, but the fleet, grower contracts and $1.6M of secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC with no disclosed parent guarantee; in a sale the Series A may sit behind the lender.
6. **Concentration and market size.** 53% of 2026 paid seasons with two growers; Tallis is customer, contract manufacturer, noteholder and board observer (46% of FY2026E revenue); the claimed $310M obtainable market requires 132% of the observable $235.7M US robot pool.

## The one question

**What is the harvest-level recovery rate — marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant — and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?** At 75%–80% the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with clean bruising the same numbers become conservative and the round is financeable.

## Three takeaways

1. **Do not lead at $72M pre-money:** 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case; Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 1.30x on the $116.8M probability-weighted value.
2. **Reprice to $48M–$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones:** at $50M the assembled $16M round ($12M Meridian, $3.0M and $1.0M from the two co-investors) buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M and 3.79x at $250M; if the facility turns out to have no minimum-cash test, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35% and this becomes Invest with conditions.
3. **The independent harvest-level trial is the gating measurement:** 75%–80% makes this a harvest aid, above 85% with clean bruising makes it a crew replacement.

## What we need from you (21 open data requests)

- **Corporate and IP records** — Delaware certificate/good standing for Orrin Fieldworks, Inc.; California SOS bizfile and UCC-1 filings for Orrin Fleet Services LLC; the Jalisco registry extract for the Mexican subsidiary; USPTO file wrapper and assignments for the five applications and the two university families; court dockets (California superior courts, Delaware Chancery, PACER). *Why:* every entity, ownership and credential claim in the deck is currently unverified, and a lien on receivables would change what the preferred reaches.
- **Kestrel equipment facility agreement, UCC-1 and the September 2026 bank statement.** *Why:* the minimum-cash definition, cross-default, cure and waiver price decide whether the 2027 failure mode is a secured-lender event or dilution.
- **Calder University licence (assignment, change-of-control, termination) and the 2025 note purchase agreement.** *Why:* the exit depends on whether the licence survives a sale and who must consent.
- **Grower contracts (110 robots), the 50 LOIs, the Tallis engineering-services agreement and firm v4 BOM quote, the Vashti contract and payment terms.** *Why:* these verify the $1.4M contracted revenue and the $31,000–$33,000 unit cost, and the related-party terms.
- **Grower B's 2026 season record** (acres, yield, bruising, uptime, price). It cut from 22 robots to 14 (−36%) in its second paid season; an acreage or price cause leaves the renewal story intact, a performance cause strengthens the bear.
- **DOL OFLC H-2A data and the 2026 AEWR table; a USMCA/CBP origin ruling for HTS 8433; insurance certificates and Cal/OSHA logs; PitchBook/Caplight post-money valuations for the seven private comps.** *Why:* the first settles the wage floor direction, the second a potential 10% duty (~$3,300 a robot), the third the product-liability exposure, the fourth whether $72M is at, above or below the private market.

## Areas for further diligence

The independent harvest trial on unselected blocks; a firm Tallis quote at 300 units; a condition precedent moving grower contracts and IP into the issuer with a parent guarantee; the vacant CTO seat (38 months) and the thin bench behind two founders; insurer terms and exclusions for autonomous night operation; renewal pricing power at $12,700; and the related-party roles that let one counterparty sit across customer, supplier, noteholder and board observer.

sources.title: Orrin Fieldworks Series A investor presentation (confidential)
sources.claims: Series A terms: $18M at $72M pre-money, ~$4.7145/share, 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A/A-1/Seed, broad-based weighted average, 8% non-cumulative dividends, 5-seat board; cap table pre/post (19,090,116 FD post); 2025 notes ~$7.77M convert at 80% into 2,061,303 A-1 shares; pool rises to 12% post; revenue FY2025 $1.9M, FY2026E $2.6M, FY2027P $5.6M, FY2028P $13.2M; RaaS $9,500/robot-season, 41% gross margin ex-depreciation; unit cost $48,000 v3, target $31,000 v4; 75 paid robot-seasons 2026; ARR $3.2M company definition; cash $3.7M, burn $410k/month; Kestrel $2.5M facility; Tallis related-party roles; Calder licence 100-robot test at 2027-12-31; exit milestones.
sources.claims_weakened: Unaudited company projections and company-defined ARR (includes $1.2M Tallis engineering services ending 2027-06-30 and $0.6M letters of intent); 2027/2028 forecasts are plan, not evidence.

sources.title: Monarch Tractor press release: $133M Series C, over $220M raised to date
sources.claims: Monarch Tractor raised $133M Series C co-led by Astanor and HH-CTBC Partnership, with At One Ventures, PMV, Welvaartsfonds; over $220M raised to date; 400+ MK-V tractors deployed; 42,000 hours of operation; largest agricultural robotics round.
sources.claims_weakened: Company press release: no valuation or revenue disclosed, so no revenue multiple can be derived.

sources.title: AgFunderNews: Carbon Robotics raises $70M Series D, total funding $157M
sources.claims: Carbon Robotics $70M Series D led by BOND with NVentures, Anthos, Fuse, Ignition, Revolution, Sozo, Voyager; total funding $157M; farm robotics/mechanisation funding fell 21.1% in H1 2024 vs H1 2023; LaserWeeder deployed US, Canada, UK, Europe, Australia.
sources.claims_weakened: Shows the category's largest rounds still need large capital and the sector capital crunch; no valuation disclosed.

sources.title: Researchers design robot that can pick hidden strawberries (Washington State University, 2025-09-04)
sources.claims: Washington State University-led open-field strawberry harvester (He et al., Computers and Electronics in Agriculture, July 2025): average detection rate 80%, hidden-fruit classification 93%, picked 58% of ripe fruit without leaf-blowing fans and 74% with fans, at about 20 seconds per berry. Team is explicit that robots will supplement rather than replace hand crews.
sources.claims_weakened: Directly contradicts a 94% pick rate at 5.6 seconds per berry as representative of open-field conditions; shows that leaf occlusion, not ripeness detection, sets the ceiling, and that per-berry cycle time in independent work is 3-4x slower.

sources.title: An autonomous strawberry-harvesting robot: design, development, integration and field evaluation, Journal of Field Robotics (Xiong, Peng, Grimstad, From)
sources.claims: Peer-reviewed field evaluation of an autonomous strawberry-harvesting robot: first-attempt picking success ranged from 50% to 97.1% depending on how much the fruit was occluded by leaves; the authors emphasise that success is highly situation-dependent. Provides the independent range against which a single 94% aggregate should be judged.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens a single-number pick rate as a generalisable performance claim; shows occlusion is the dominant driver of failure.

The Robot Report: Abundant Robotics shuts down fruit harvesting business
sources.claims: Abundant Robotics (Hayward, CA; founded 2016; apple-picking robot; vacuum manipulation and vision IP) shut down and put its IP and assets up for sale on 2021-06-29 after failing to raise another round; it had raised $12M total, including a $10M Series A in May 2017; it planned a RaaS model with a claimed $100M+ pipeline and cash-flow positive target in Q2 2024.
sources.claims_weakened: Strongest counter-evidence to the RaaS harvesting thesis: a well-regarded robot with commercial trials and a claimed pipeline could not raise a follow-on or reach scale; liquidation is a realistic base-rate outcome.

sources.title: John Deere press release: to acquire Bear Flag Robotics for $250M
sources.claims: Deere & Company signed a definitive agreement on 2021-08-05 to acquire Bear Flag Robotics, a developer of self-driving retrofit technology for tractors founded in 2017, for $250M; acquisition builds Deere's autonomous tractor strategy.
sources.claims_weakened: Deere paid $250M for a pre-scale autonomy software/hardware company: strategic option value, not a revenue multiple; shows OEM appetite but also that the target was row-crop tractors, not specialty-crop harvesting.

sources.title: AgFunderNews: Advanced Farm Technologies closes $25M Series B
sources.claims: Advanced Farm Technologies closed a $25M Series B (announced 2021-09-21) led by Catapult Ventures, with existing Series A investors Kubota, Yamaha Motor and Impact Ventures; TX Robotic Strawberry Harvester works alongside hand crews; valuation not disclosed.
sources.claims_weakened: Peak-2021 agtech round with two strategic OEMs; no valuation or revenue disclosed, so no multiple can be derived; the fact that a 2018-founded strawberry robot leader raised only $25M in its Series B caps the plausible Series A size for Orrin.

sources.title: Tracxn company profile: Harvest Croo Robotics, $10M raised over 14 rounds
sources.claims: Harvest CROO Robotics (Tampa, founded 2013, strawberry harvesting-as-a-service) has raised a total of $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 and remains at seed stage with 4 institutional investors.
sources.claims_weakened: Aggregator data, not a filing; but shows the leading dedicated strawberry-harvesting startup raised less in 12 years than Orrin's proposed Series A, evidence that the category has not supported large private valuations.

sources.title: CNH Industrial press release: acquisition of Raven Industries for $2.1B EV
sources.claims: CNH Industrial agreed on 2021-06-21 to acquire Raven Industries for $58/share, a 33.6% premium to the 4-week VWAP, at a $2.1B enterprise value; Raven's consolidated net sales were $348.4M for the twelve months to 2021-01-31, implying about 6.0x EV/Sales; $400M of run-rate revenue synergies and $150M incremental EBITDA expected by 2025.
sources.claims_weakened: The $2.1B headline is a precision-agriculture software/hardware platform with $348M revenue at ~6x sales, not a pre-scale harvesting robot; it sets the high end of strategic multiples, not the base case for Orrin.

sources.title: AgFunderNews: John Deere acquires Blue River Technology for $305M
sources.claims: Deere acquired Blue River Technology for $305M, announced 2017-09-06; Sunnyvale, California see-and-spray computer-vision robotics startup; brought full-stack AI to agriculture.
sources.claims_weakened: $305M for a company with negligible revenue at the time: an option-value benchmark, not evidence that a $72M pre-money for $2.6M revenue is conservative.

sources.title: Robotic fruit-picker maker Advanced Farm ceases operations, Sacramento Business Journal (2025-07-08)
sources.claims: Advanced Farm Technologies Inc. (Davis, CA), which began commercial robotic strawberry harvesting in the US in 2019 and had named commercial growers, quietly ceased operations in 2025 (reported 2025-07-08). Establishes that the leading US open-field strawberry robot, backed by a $25M Series B and an OEM minority investment, failed commercially before reaching scale.
sources.claims_weakened: Undercuts any inference that technical capability and named growers imply commercial durability in this category; sets the base rate for failure high even for well-funded teams.

sources.title: Oishii acquires Tortuga AgTech's IP, assets and engineering team (AgFunderNews, 2025-03-24)
sources.claims: Oishii announced on 2025-03-24 the acquisition of Tortuga AgTech's key IP, assets and members of its engineering team, including AI models, robotics software and custom hardware. Shows the second exit route for a strawberry-harvesting robotics company was an asset sale to an indoor-farming buyer rather than a fleet-scale commercial business.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens the case that a standalone RaaS fleet business is the natural end state; suggests strategic value concentrates in IP and team rather than installed fleet.

sources.title: Advanced Farm Technologies closes $25M Series B to expand robot picking of strawberries and apples
sources.claims: Advanced Farm Technologies closed a $25M Series B (reported by Global AgInvesting) to expand robotic picking of strawberries and apples, after starting commercial robotic strawberry harvesting in the US in 2019 with its T-6 platform for soil-planted beds. Establishes the capital scale at which a direct peer failed.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens the idea that an $18M Series A is enough for a capital-intensive fleet business when a $25M-backed peer still ran out of money.

sources.title: CNH expands high-tech harvesting stake with investment in Advanced Farm Technologies (CNH press release)
sources.claims: CNH Industrial made a minority investment in Advanced Farm Technologies and agreed to partner across R&D and commercialisation of robotic harvesting of apples, strawberries and other fruits - the archetypal OEM-plus-startup route for a harvesting-robotics company.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens the claim that an independent RaaS fleet is the only viable commercial model; shows OEM partnership as the established pattern, while noting that CNH's investment did not prevent Advanced Farm's closure.

sources.title: Private Market View: Tortuga AgTech funding rounds, $47.7M total raised (summary only)

sources.claims_weakened: Paywalled/blocked aggregator page; total only, no dates, investors, valuation or revenue; treat as indicative and not as a valuation anchor.
