sources.title: Court Docket — California minimum wage for farm workers: rates, overtime and breaks
sources.claims: California farm workers are entitled to the $16.90 state minimum wage from 2026-01-01 and H-2A workers have a higher floor of $19.97 per hour (2026 California AEWR); overtime after 8 hours/day and 40 hours/week.
sources.claims_weakened: Secondary summary rather than the DOL wage table; the $19.97 AEWR figure could not be read from a primary DOL table in this run, so it is medium confidence.

sources.title: Orrin Fieldworks Series A investor presentation (client deck, 15 pp.)
sources.claims: Company structure (Delaware parent; California fleet LLC; Jalisco subsidiary with 7 staff), 38 employees, RaaS price $9,500/robot-season (2027 list $16,500), $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II 2024-2026, related-party payments of $310,000 to Vashti Harvest Services and Tallis roles (noteholder, $1.2M/yr customer, v4 manufacturer, board observer, $1.0M round commitment), patent status, 94% pick rate and 3.8% bruising in 2025 pilots, Grower E exited over bruising.
sources.claims_weakened: All performance and unit-economics data are company measurements without audit or independent field trial; the deck omits any regulatory, safety-certification, insurance or compliance record, so it cannot support a claim that Orrin is compliant.

sources.title: Federal Register 2026-15673 — H-2A Adverse Effect Wage Rates, non-range occupations
sources.claims: DOL Employment and Training Administration issued a notice on 2026-08-03 announcing updated Adverse Effect Wage Rates for H-2A workers in non-range agricultural occupations (91 FR 48946), the category covering strawberry harvest work.
sources.claims_weakened: The rate table itself could not be opened (federalregister.gov blocked to this research), so the 2026 California rate is not verified from the primary notice.

sources.title: FELS — H-2A worker minimum wage, AB 2646 (Krell, 2026)
sources.claims: California AB 2646 (Krell), passed and signed in 2026, sets a $19.75/hour minimum wage for certain non-California-resident agricultural employees and California residents working alongside them, raising the state floor above the $16.90 general minimum for H-2A-type crews.
sources.claims_weakened: Snippet-level reading only; the operative date and coverage tests need the chaptered bill text, so the $19.75 figure is medium confidence.

sources.title: US Department of Labor — H-2A Adverse Effect Wage Rates (FLAG wage data)
sources.claims: H-2A employers must offer, advertise and pay at least the Adverse Effect Wage Rate (AEWR), the minimum hourly wage for H-2A workers and workers in corresponding employment, when it is the highest applicable wage.
sources.claims_weakened: The page did not expose the 2026 California rate in the search result, so the AEWR mechanism is verified but the dollar value rests on secondary reporting.

sources.title: USTR — USTR Seeks Public Comment on the 2027 Joint Review of USMCA
sources.claims: USTR announced on 2026-10-02 a public consultation ahead of the 2027 USMCA joint review, with comments and hearing requests due 2027-01-12; the annual review cycle continues after the 1 July 2026 review.
sources.claims_weakened: USTR gives no outcome for the July 2026 review or any change to tariff treatment in this release, so the review's effect on Orrin's Mexican assembly is unresolved.

sources.title: Cello Square — 2026 USMCA and US-Mexico tariffs and logistics impact
sources.claims: Reports that the 25% IEEPA-based tariff on Mexican goods was terminated on 2026-02-20 by the US Supreme Court and replaced from 2026-02-24 by a temporary 10% global tariff under Trade Act Section 122, with USMCA-compliant goods exempt.
sources.claims_weakened: Logistics-company commentary, not a primary proclamation; conflicts with sources saying a 25% IEEPA surtax still applies to non-USMCA Mexican goods.

sources.title: Federal Register 2025-18010 — USTR request for comments, USMCA joint review 1 July 2026
sources.claims: USTR gave notice on 2025-09-17 of public consultation ahead of the USMCA joint review on 1 July 2026, confirming the scheduled review date and Congress-directed process.
sources.claims_weakened: Does not establish what the parties decided at the July 2026 review.

sources.title: ISO 18497-1:2024 — Safety of agricultural machinery with autonomous functions
sources.claims: ISO 18497-1:2024 sets safety requirements, means of verification and information for use for agricultural machinery and tractors with partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous functions, the international design standard relevant to the Orrin Picker.
sources.claims_weakened: A voluntary international standard; it does not by itself create US legal liability, and Orrin's compliance with it is not disclosed.

sources.title: US Tariff Rates — US tariff rates on Mexico 2026, USMCA compliance and IEEPA surtax
sources.claims: As of 2026, Mexico-origin goods split by USMCA compliance: qualifying goods enter at 0% MFN, non-qualifying goods carry a 25% IEEPA-derived surtax, and from 2026-07-24 a Section 301 action adds 10% on most Mexico-origin products.
sources.claims_weakened: Commercial tariff-tracking site, not an official customs notice; its account conflicts with another source that says the Supreme Court terminated the 25% IEEPA tariff on 2026-02-20 and replaced it with a 10% Section 122 surcharge, so the exact 2026 rate stack is uncertain.

sources.title: FDA — FSMA Final Rule on Produce Safety (21 CFR Part 112)
sources.claims: The FDA Produce Safety Rule (21 CFR 112) sets science-based minimum standards for growing, harvesting, packing and holding produce, including requirements for equipment, tools, buildings and sanitation, and inspection of food-contact and non-food-contact surfaces of equipment.
sources.claims_weakened: The rule binds the grower, not the equipment maker; Orrin's exposure is contractual and reputational through grower audits and sanitation instructions, not direct FDA registration.

sources.title: Cal/OSHA Standards Board — Overview of safety standards and practices for autonomous agricultural machinery
sources.claims: Cal/OSHA Standards Board published an overview of safety standards and practices for autonomous agricultural machinery, mapping ISO 18497, an Australian code of practice and EU Regulation 2023/1230, indicating the regulator is studying a framework for autonomous field machinery rather than leaving it unaddressed.
sources.claims_weakened: A presentation, not a rule; no California-specific mandatory standard for autonomous harvesters was identified, so the exposure is prospective and certification-based.

sources.title: NAPS — Mexico payroll, benefits and PTU explained
sources.claims: Mexican employers must provide IMSS healthcare and social-security contributions, INFONAVIT housing-fund contributions, aguinaldo (Christmas bonus) and 10% PTU profit sharing, on top of payroll; dismissal without cause costs at least three months' salary plus seniority premium.
sources.claims_weakened: Advisory-firm summary rather than the Ley Federal del Trabajo text; the subsidiary's 7 staff make absolute cost small, but the obligations are mandatory and PTU is a profit-linked liability.

sources.title: Peacock Tariff Consulting — USMCA rules of origin for machinery
sources.claims: USMCA rules of origin for machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally require regional value content of 60% under the transaction-value method or 50% under the net-cost method, with tariff-shift rules for some categories; origin must be documented to claim 0% duty.
sources.claims_weakened: Consultancy summary; the product-specific rule for heading 8433 harvesting machinery was not read from the USMCA text, so Orrin's qualification for its robots is unverified.

sources.title: WageTable — California minimum wage 2026 and 2027 schedule
sources.claims: California minimum wage rises from $16.90/hour on 2026-01-01 to $17.40/hour on 2027-01-01, a scheduled increase.
sources.claims_weakened: Secondary wage tracker; the 2027 figure is not confirmed against a DIR publication, so treat as indicative.

sources.title: 35 U.S.C. §204 — Preference for United States industry
sources.claims: 35 U.S.C. §204 bars a contractor from granting exclusive rights to use or sell a federally funded subject invention in the US unless products embodying it will be manufactured substantially in the US, subject to an agency waiver where reasonable but unsuccessful efforts were made to license US manufacturers.
sources.claims_weakened: Waiver is available, and the clause binds only inventions made under the federal award; whether the Orrin Picker embodies a USDA-funded invention is not disclosed.

sources.title: Akin Gump — Federally funded R&D: new executive order pushes agencies to take title and require domestic manufacturing
sources.claims: A US executive order pushes federal agencies to take title to subject inventions and to require domestic manufacturing of federally funded technology, increasing the enforcement risk around Bayh-Dole's US-manufacturing preference.
sources.claims_weakened: Law-firm alert without visible date in the search result; the order's applicability to existing USDA SBIR awards is unverified.

sources.title: USDA NASS, Noncitrus Fruits and Nuts 2025 Summary (ncit0526.pdf), released 2026-05-01
sources.claims: US noncitrus utilized production 15.8 million tons in 2025, down 1% from 2024; bearing acreage 1.85 million acres, down 2%; strawberries among the three largest noncitrus crops by utilized production alongside grapes and apples.
sources.claims_weakened: Provides no strawberry-specific acreage in the retrievable text; the deck's ~50,000 US strawberry acres could not be confirmed from this release in this run. Aggregate noncitrus bearing acreage is shrinking 2% a year.

sources.title: USDA Economic Research Service, Fruit and Tree Nuts Market Outlook (2026)
sources.claims: Warmer-than-average spring 2026 accelerated crop development across California fruit regions and brought an earlier-than-usual strawberry harvest; 2026 California stone-fruit forecasts are mixed.
sources.claims_weakened: Gives no strawberry acreage, price or harvest-labour figures; supports season-timing variability rather than market size.

sources.title: Food Protection Trends (2023-03) — Fresh produce harvesting equipment: a review of cleaning and sanitizing practices
sources.claims: Harvest tools, equipment and containers contact crops directly; best practice is routine cleaning and sanitation of food-contact surfaces and adjacent areas. A machine with many food-contact surfaces adds cleaning labour and audit points to the grower's harvest.
sources.claims_weakened: A review of practice, not a measurement of cleaning time per machine or per acre, so it does not size the labour the robot adds.

sources.title: eCFR 21 CFR 112.123 — General requirements for equipment and tools used during harvest, packing and holding (Produce Safety Rule)
sources.claims: Equipment and tools that contact covered produce during harvesting must be maintained, cleaned and sanitised so as not to contaminate produce; the duty falls on the grower operating the equipment, not on the equipment's maker. Makes the robot's gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler food-contact surfaces the customer must clean.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens any reading that FDA approval or certification of the machine is what matters; FDA regulates the grower's practice, so the vendor's exposure is contractual and reputational rather than a pre-market clearance.

sources.title: Food Protection Trends (2023-03) — Assessing physical attributes associated with implementation of risk management practices; strawberry outbreak record 1997-2017
sources.claims: 32 strawberry-related foodborne outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017, with STEC, Salmonella, Cyclospora, norovirus and hepatitis A implicated; strawberries are eaten raw, so harvest-stage contamination reaches the consumer.
sources.claims_weakened: Does not attribute any outbreak to harvesting equipment specifically, so it establishes the category risk, not a causal link to robots.

sources.title: The Innovation Attorney — Agriculture robotics: regulatory gaps, tort liability and IP challenges in autonomous farm technology
sources.claims: Ground-based agricultural robots face strict product-liability exposure for worker injuries and no federal safety standard supplies a regulatory benchmark; unmanned aerial rules and FIFRA applicator certification are the regulated analogues. Implies a jury sets the standard of care where no certification exists.
sources.claims_weakened: A law-firm commentary, not a court record: it describes exposure in principle and cites no verdict or claim against a harvesting-robot maker.

sources.title: ANSI Webstore — ISO 18497-1:2024, Agricultural machinery and tractors: safety of partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous machinery, Part 1 machine design principles and vocabulary (17 pp.)
sources.claims: Scope of ISO 18497-1:2024 is design principles and vocabulary for partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous agricultural machinery; verification methods and validation principles sit in a separate part, ISO 18497-4:2024. Confirms there is an international design/verification framework a buyer or insurer could require.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens a description of Part 1 as itself the verification standard; also confirms the framework is voluntary — it creates no US certification requirement on its own.

sources.title: Paine Schwartz Partners closes $1.7B food and agribusiness Fund VI (2023-09-26)
sources.claims: Paine Schwartz Partners is a food and agribusiness private equity firm with $5.7B of assets under management; it closed a $1.7B Fund VI on 2023-09-26 and invests in productivity/sustainability and health/wellness businesses, including Costa Group, Monterey Mushrooms and AgroFresh Solutions. Supports naming it as the largest dedicated agribusiness PE buyer in an exit-route map.
sources.claims_weakened: Its portfolio and stated themes are cash-generating food and agribusiness businesses, not pre-profit robotics; a Series A-stage harvesting-robot company is not a fit until it has positive EBITDA, which weakens a private-equity exit route in 2028-2031.

sources.title: AI-powered tractor startup burns through a quarter billion dollars, fires all employees (Futurism, on Monarch Tractor)
sources.claims: Monarch Tractor, once valued above $500M with over $240M raised, laid off its entire workforce, warned it may shut down, vacated its Livermore, California headquarters in March, and faced dealership lawsuits in September alleging defective tractors and misleading autonomy claims; a California winegrower testing it for three years said it failed and was dangerous.
sources.claims_weakened: The use of Monarch as a live, well-funded comparable supporting a high ag-robotics valuation; the assumption that scale of capital protects an ag-robot vendor.

sources.title: The Changing H-2A Program (Giannini Foundation ARE Update Vol. 29 No. 6)
sources.claims: In October 2025 the US Department of Labor lowered the H-2A wage for many California jobs, and in June 2026 dairy farms were made eligible for H-2A workers; California could become the largest employer of H-2A guest workers.
sources.claims_weakened: The thesis that a rising wage floor and shrinking labour supply make robot conversion urgent in California; a lower AEWR and wider H-2A eligibility reduce hand-pick cost and slow the switch.

sources.title: DailyRobotics enters strawberry harvesting race with robot that can pick 2-3x faster than humans (AgFunderNews)
sources.claims: An Israeli open-field strawberry harvester (Q2, two arms, soft grippers, packs into clamshells) reported ~30 kg/hour, ~4% end-to-end bruising in field tests, one operator per eight robots, and a first customer deployment in California starting April 2026; the article names Harvest CROO, L5, Agrobot, Fieldwork Robotics and Dogtooth as other entrants and says most remain in trials.
sources.claims_weakened: The claim that a single vendor is the only autonomous open-field picker; the 3.8% bruise rate as a differentiator, since a competitor quotes ~4% as close to skilled hand-picking; the idea that one operator per eight robots is unusual.

sources.title: Farm robotics in the weeds as funding declines 36% from Q2 to Q3 (AgFunderNews)
sources.claims: Venture funding for agrifood robotics and mechanization fell 36% from $168M in Q2 to $108M in Q3, a 57% year-on-year decline against Q3 2024, on preliminary AgFunder data.
sources.claims_weakened: The assumption that a 2028 Series B will be available on planned terms; the comparison to Monarch and Carbon Robotics as evidence of abundant category capital.

sources.title: Bruise Damage Susceptibility of Blueberry and Strawberry (Springer, 2024)
sources.claims: A Springer chapter on bruise-damage susceptibility in blueberry and strawberry reports that a study by Brown et al. (1996) found severe bruises in 78% of mechanically harvested blueberries against 23% of hand-harvested fruit; bruising reduces commercial potential and raises susceptibility to microbial damage. It supplies the mechanical-versus-hand bruising base rate that the picking literature otherwise lacks.
sources.claims_weakened: Any claim that a 3.8% bruise rate at pick time is close to hand-picking; the absence of a hand-picked control makes the machine's number uncomparable.

sources.title: Quality Assurance for Strawberries: A Case Study (UC ANR Postharvest Technology Center)
sources.claims: A University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources postharvest case study puts strawberry losses at wholesale and retail at 9-11% (28-41% including consumer level) and attributes the major cause to grey mould associated with bruising and soft or leaky berries, with a worked example on 100,000 trays a month at $6.50 a tray.
sources.claims_weakened: The idea that a 3.8% bruise rate is immaterial: bruising converts into grey mould and the retail loss line is where the grower and the shipper, not the robot vendor, bear the cost.

sources.title: Trade Alert Oct 2026: CBP MPF, Section 301, USMCA (Eilan Trade Advisory)
sources.claims: A trade-compliance advisory posts an October 2026 alert on US-Mexico trade covering a 10% Section 301 tariff on most Mexico-origin products effective 2026-07-24, a USMCA-origin exemption, Section 232 measures and new CBP merchandise-processing-fee limits. Cross-border assembly therefore faces duty on non-USMCA-qualifying content rather than a blanket zero rate.
sources.claims_weakened: The assumption that Guadalajara assembly carries no tariff cost and that the v4 unit-cost target of $31,000-$33,000 is reachable on landed-cost terms.

sources.title: Carbon Robotics funding and valuation (CB Insights company financials)
sources.claims: CB Insights records Carbon Robotics as having raised $213.65M across nine rounds, the latest a $20.85M Series D-II on 2025-10-22, with a December 2023 valuation of $119M-$169M. Other trackers report totals from $128M to $232M and a $548M 2025-10 valuation, so the private valuation is not reliably triangulated.
sources.claims_weakened: Any claim that a peer's disclosed or reported valuation justifies Orrin's $72M pre-money: peer valuations are undisclosed or disputed across trackers.

sources.title: Monarch Tractor funding, valuation and wind-down (Clay company dossier)
sources.claims: Monarch Tractor raised about $217M in total, including a $133M Series C in July 2024 at a reported $518M post-money valuation with CNH Industrial among earlier investors; it ceased operations, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors reported in a January 2026 court filing, auctioned tractors in early 2026, and Caterpillar bought its assets including technology in April 2026 for an undisclosed price.
sources.claims_weakened: The idea that a large round and a strategic OEM investor de-risk an ag-robotics company: a $518M post-money company reached an asset sale about 21 months later.

sources.title: Northern Ireland farmer installs Lely's 50,000th milking robot (The Fence Post)
sources.claims: Lely installed its 50,000th Astronaut robotic milking unit in 2024; the first prototype ran in 1992 and the first commercial unit sold in 1995; 100 robots were in use by 1997; units operate in 50 countries and milk about 3 million cows a day. Adoption took roughly 29 years from commercial launch and runs through a dealer service network.
sources.claims_weakened: Any assumption that agricultural robotics adoption is fast: the most successful farm robot took three decades to reach 50,000 units, and it sells with installation and after-sales service.

sources.title: Deere is acquiring Blue River Technology for $305 million (CNBC)
sources.claims: Deere & Company agreed on 2017-09-06 to acquire Blue River Technology, a Sunnyvale, California precision-agriculture robotics company, for $305 million; its 60-person team was to remain in Sunnyvale.
sources.claims_weakened: The idea that $300M OEM exits require revenue scale: Blue River was bought pre-scale on the strength of its perception and spraying technology.

sources.title: Harvest CROO Robotics — technology and service model (company site)
sources.claims: Harvest CROO's B8 harvester carries 16 independently working picking robots on a self-propelled chassis spanning six beds, uses AI vision to classify each berry and offers harvesting as a service rather than equipment for sale; it claims picking rates of up to 8 berries per second in company material.
sources.claims_weakened: The claim that Orrin is the only autonomous open-field strawberry picker: a Florida competitor is marketing a 16-arm service harvester in the same crop and season.

sources.title: AgTech 2025 review: VC funding drops as robotics and AI draw investment (IndexBox, citing PitchBook)
sources.claims: PitchBook data show agtech venture funding of $4.799 billion across 735 deals through 2025-12-23, down from $5.099 billion across 913 deals in 2024, the lowest level in several years, with capital concentrating in robotics and AI.
sources.claims_weakened: The assumption that a 2026 Series A in ag robotics faces an easy financing market: deal count fell 20% year on year.

sources.title: Development of a general-purpose AI-powered robotic platform for berry harvesting (Agriculture, MDPI 16(7):769)
sources.claims: A 2026 peer-reviewed berry-harvesting platform reported a 72% overall harvesting success rate across 50 controlled indoor trials using synthetic strawberries.
sources.claims_weakened: Claims of 90%+ picking reliability under commercial open-field conditions: even controlled indoor trials report 72%.

sources.title: Tracxn company profile: Four Growers, $15.1M raised, 63 active competitors
sources.claims: Four Growers has raised $15.1M from Y Combinator and Bassett Capital Group, and has 63 active competitors including 26 funded and 3 exited; its listed competitors include Advanced Farm Technologies and Harvest CROO Robotics.
sources.claims_weakened: Aggregator figures are not audited; the total may omit or double-count rounds. It sets an order of magnitude, not an exact capital figure.

sources.title: AGRIST Inc. dossier: rail-guided greenhouse harvest robots, bell pepper and cucumber, Series B 2025-09-17
sources.claims: AGRIST is a Japanese robot maker founded 2019 in Shintomi, Miyazaki; rail-guided greenhouse harvest robots for bell peppers and cucumbers; 55% harvest rate in field trials, vendor-stated; Series B announced 2025-09-17; rentals to JA co-ops in Hokkaido in 2026 (JA Niikappu pepper 2026-06-29/30, Hokuren cucumber 2026-07-01 to 08-31, JA Kitasorachi cucumber 2026-07-02 to 10-31); six announced deployments, all Japan; no strawberry or open-field product.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens the idea that paid rental robots in specialty crops are unique to Orrin: a Japanese vendor rents harvest robots to agricultural co-operatives, but on rails, in greenhouses, for peppers and cucumbers, with vendor-stated performance and no audited fleet numbers.

sources.title: Startuply.vc: 100 growers across three continents — Carbon Robotics LaserWeeder
sources.claims: Carbon Robotics' LaserWeeder is a 20-foot-wide autonomous machine with 30 high-powered lasers that kills up to 200,000 weeds an hour at night; the company has sold to 100 growers across three continents.
sources.claims_weakened: Trade-press summary of company claims: the 100-grower figure and throughput are company-sourced and not independently audited. It is a weeding machine, not a harvester, so it says nothing about soft-fruit picking.

sources.title: Four Growers company site: greenhouse tomato harvesting robot in development, two filed patents
sources.claims: Four Growers builds robotic harvesting and plant analytics for greenhouse growers of tomatoes, peppers and cucumbers; its own site says it is "working closely with various greenhouse growers to develop a tomato harvesting robot"; the design uses 8 stereo cameras and two filed patents protect the technology; no paid fleet, unit price or shipment figure is disclosed.
sources.claims_weakened: Weakens any claim that greenhouse picking is close to commercial: a well-funded, Y Combinator-backed team describes its tomato robot as in development in its own current material, and describes patents as filed rather than granted.

sources.title: Tracxn company profile: Carbon Robotics, $276M raised, Series D
sources.claims: Carbon Robotics is a Seattle Series D company founded in 2018 by Paul Mikesell, selling AI-powered laser weeding; Tracxn puts cumulative funding at $276M with 12 active competitors, against $232M in another tracker and $157M reported at the 2024-10 Series D.
sources.claims_weakened: Shows that aggregator funding totals for private ag-robotics companies disagree by tens of millions; any single cumulative figure for Carbon Robotics is unverified.

sources.title: Q3 2025 AgTech Venture Capital Investment and Exit Round Up (CropLife/Global AgTech Initiative)
sources.claims: 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025, all through M&A (0 IPOs); John Deere acquired GUSS Automation in Q3 2025; Growcer bought Freight Farms for $2.6M; CropX bought Acclym; PitchBook counted 811 venture-backed exits globally that quarter; median AgTech round $3.8M.
sources.claims_weakened: Any assumption that an AgTech IPO window exists for a sub-$50M-revenue company in 2026-2028; the idea that strategic acquirers pay venture-scale prices in every deal (Freight Farms cleared at $2.6M).

sources.title: The Outlier Problem: Understanding the Real Distribution of Venture Returns (Tiger VC Funds, citing Correlation Ventures)
sources.claims: Correlation Ventures' analysis of US venture: about 65% of investments failed to return 1x capital and only 4% returned 10x or more.
sources.claims_weakened: A 3x-5x base-case return assumption for a single Series A position; supports the failure and 1x bands in a probability-weighted exit.

sources.title: Monarch Tractor Secures $133M to Navigate Crisis (Tractor Trends)
sources.claims: Monarch Tractor's $133M Series C had been reported by 2025-02-28; the round was raised amid production delays and delivery challenges.
sources.claims_weakened: Its account of the lead investors (Lightrock and Energize Ventures) conflicts with Monarch's own press release (Astanor and HH-CTBC), so only the date and the distress context are used.

sources.title: District Court Rules Against Labor Department's Late 2025 Adverse Effect Wage Rate Changes (California Farm Bureau, 2026-08-28)
sources.claims: On 2026-08-26 a US district court in California held DOL's late-2025 AEWR interim final rule unlawful on multiple grounds and remanded it; the rule had cut California's rate from $19.97 to $16.90; employers may face backpay depending on the final determination; appeal undecided.
sources.claims_weakened: Adds legal uncertainty and backpay exposure to 2026 wage savings; a restoration toward $19.97 or higher is possible, so the 2026 cut may not hold.

sources.title: New H-2A AEWR Wage Rates Take Effect August 3, 2026 (VisaVerge)
sources.claims: DOL notice 91 FR 48946, effective 2026-08-03 (2026-08-17 in 17 states covered by Kansas v. DOL, including Florida), sets California Skill Level I AEWR at $16.45/hour and Skill Level II at $18.71, down $3.52 (-17.6%) from the old Farm Labor Survey rate of $19.97; national average AEWR for H-2A labor contractor surety bonds is $15.96/hour; the OEWS methodology came from the interim final rule at 90 FR 47914 published 2025-10-02; California housing adjustment has run up to $3.00/hour; the $16.90 California minimum governs the entry-level rate.
sources.claims_weakened: Contradicts the statement that the 2026-08-03 notice set California at $19.97/hour; $19.97 was the superseded 2025 Farm Labor Survey rate. Also weakens any claim that California's wage floor rose monotonically in 2026.

sources.title: H-2A Changes Could Reduce H-2A Wages by $100 Million in 2026 (ARE Update v29n4, 2026-05)
sources.claims: Employers spend $1,000-1,500 per worker before arrival and $25-30 a day to house and transport workers; California AEWRs are about $3/hour lower in 2026; estimated $100M wage reduction in California in 2026. Search snippet only; PDF itself was not readable.
sources.claims_weakened: Provides no season-specific all-in hand-pick cost per hour; the $25-30/day add-on is the only public cost input found, so the all-in estimate remains derived.

sources.title: H-2A rule change puts spotlight on work visa program (Ag Alert, 2026-06-03)
sources.claims: DOL's October 2025 H-2A rule cut California's AEWR from $19.97 to the $16.90 state minimum; about 70% of California H-2A employers had adjusted pay to $16.90 in the first six months; potential saving estimated at $100M; California farm labour costs about $18B a year including $655M of H-2A wages; H-2A is about 20% of the US farm workforce but 5% in California; AB 2646 passed the Assembly in May 2026.
sources.claims_weakened: Undercuts a 2026 rising-wage-floor narrative and shows the labour-cost relief reached most California H-2A employers; the demand tailwind paused rather than compounded in 2026.

sources.title: Federal Court Invalidates New H-2A Wage Methodology (Agricultural Law, 2026-09)
sources.claims: United Farm Workers v. U.S. Department of Labor (E.D. Cal.): the interim final rule's two-tier system, housing adjustment, OEWS reliance and greater-than-50% classification rule were arbitrary and capricious and procedurally defective under the APA; the court did not immediately vacate the rule, leaving the existing OEWS methodology temporarily operative while DOL develops a replacement; DOL was remanded.
sources.claims_weakened: Confirms the OEWS rates, not $19.97, remain in force for now; but the replacement methodology could raise rates and expose backpay.

sources.title: AB 2646: Employment: minimum wages: agricultural workers (California Legislature, 2025-2026)
sources.claims: AB 2646 requires a $19.75/hour minimum wage for an approved agricultural employee and a corresponding employee; from 2027-01-01 and each January thereafter the rate is adjusted by the Social Security cost-of-living adjustment; the Labor Commissioner enforces and collects unpaid wages; the bill was signed in 2026.
sources.claims_weakened: The $19.75 floor is not operative in 2026; it binds from 2027-01-01 and therefore does not offset the 2026 AEWR cut until then.

sources.title: TechCrunch: Monarch Tractor's collapse ends with an acquisition by Caterpillar
sources.claims: Monarch Tractor (Zimeno, Inc.) entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors in January 2026; its assets, including IP and hardware designs, were acquired by Caterpillar; the company had raised more than $240M and was valued above $500M before the collapse.
sources.claims_weakened: Treats Monarch as a live independent competitor or as a benchmark for a standalone ag-robot scale-up; the wind-down sets the base rate for hardware-heavy venture outcomes.

sources.title: TechCrunch: Following acquisition by Bowery, Traptic's strawberry-picking robotics move into vertical farming
sources.claims: Bowery Farming closed its acquisition of Traptic, a Mountain View, California developer of strawberry-picking robots, for an undisclosed sum in February 2022; Traptic's field robots were retired and the team moved to indoor farming.
sources.claims_weakened: The base rate that an independent strawberry-harvesting robot vendor can scale alone; supports acquisition as the modal outcome.

sources.title: RobotToday company profile: DailyRobotics Q2 strawberry harvester
sources.claims: DailyRobotics scheduled field trials through April 2026 and a first commercial deployment with a California customer from April 2026, with robotics-as-a-service as the primary business model and outright sales possible; the Q2 unit uses two arms with soft grippers and onboard grading.
sources.claims_weakened: Any reading of the April 2026 date as a confirmed deployment: the profile describes a schedule, and no unit count, price or contracted acreage is disclosed.

sources.title: Standard Norge (ISO catalogue) — ISO 18497-4:2024, Agricultural machinery and tractors: safety of partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous machinery, Part 4: verification methods and validation principles
sources.claims: ISO 18497-4:2024, published 2024-07-31, specifies principles for verification methods and validation principles for agricultural machinery and tractors with partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous functions; it assists in providing safety requirements, means of verification and information for use; it revises ISO 18497:2018 and excludes forestry and public-road operation.
sources.claims_weakened: Any reading that the Part 1 listing (S166) covers verification and validation: Part 4 is a separate document (its abstract also leaves applicability of design principles outside its scope). Being a published standard, it certifies no machine by itself and predates the current build.

scope.decision: Whether Meridian Capital Ventures should invest in Orrin Fieldworks' Series A, and on what terms; whether the company's numbers hold up against competitors and the market.

spines.spine: Growth-stage startup: unit economics, GTM repeatability, retention, margin, financing need
spines.must_answer: Can growth scale without destroying economics: does the $9,500 per robot-season RaaS contract earn a real margin once fleet depreciation, field service, transport, insurance and utilisation across a 7-month California or 3-month Florida season are fully loaded, and can Orrin go from 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 to 360 robots in 2027 without a capital or service-quality break?

spines.spine: Deep tech / hard tech: technical feasibility, validation evidence, manufacturing, capex, regulation
spines.must_answer: What has been proven, under what conditions, and what remains unproven: is the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime credible outside the 212 rows Orrin's own field team selected, and is the IP defensible given the Calder exclusive licence, the rejected gripper claims and the missed PCT national-phase deadline?

spines.spine: Industrial / hardware: BOM, supply chain, quality, installation/service economics, utilisation
spines.must_answer: Can the company produce and support at scale: can Orrin cut unit cost from $48,000 to $31,000-$33,000 through a contract manufacturer that is also a noteholder, customer, v4 manufacturer and board observer, and support 360 robots across California and Florida with nine field staff plus a related-party service contractor without warranty, bruising or utilisation problems?

research_plan.industry_map: Agricultural robotics for specialty crops. Value chain: genetics and inputs -> growers (about 50,000 US strawberry acres, concentrated in California's Central Coast and Florida's Plant City) -> harvest labour (hand crews, H-2A guest workers) -> harvest aids (carts, conveyors, picker-assist platforms) -> autonomous harvest robots -> coolers, packers and shippers -> retailers. Decisive bottleneck: the harvest-window labour gap and per-tray picking cost; a robot must beat hand-pick economics across a 7-month California season with bruising below roughly 5% and uptime above 90%, or growers do not convert pilots to paid seasons. Orrin's place: a turnkey robots-as-a-service provider that owns, insures and maintains a 64-robot fleet, sells per robot-season at $9,500 in 2026 and $16,500 list in 2027, depends on Tallis Agricultural Machinery for v4 contract manufacturing and on an exclusive Calder University licence for core perception IP.
research_plan.geo_lens: Material. Four geographies mapped: (1) revenue markets — California Central Coast (Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria) and Florida (Plant City), where the 7-month versus 3-4-month season changes robot utilisation and payback; (2) manufacturing and supplier base — Guadalajara, Mexico (Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, 7 staff) and the Tallis v4 build, exposed to USMCA origin and a 10% duty on non-qualifying goods from 2026-07-24; (3) competitor and comparable market — US, European greenhouse/tabletop robotics and Israeli/US field robotics; (4) capital and exit market — US venture capital and agricultural equipment OEMs. California and Florida labour-cost and immigration-policy differences drive adoption and pricing power; Florida is counter-season capacity, not a stand-alone market.
research_plan.policy_lens: Material and priced. US farm-labour policy sets the hand-pick cost the robot must beat: California's minimum wage is $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and agricultural overtime applies after 8 hours a day and 40 hours a week. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; DOL interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative California floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01; the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I $16.45 and Skill II $18.71; the E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left those rates in place with backpay possible; AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01. The reversal risk is live: the 2026 cut lowered hand-pick cost 15.4%, so cheaper hand labour could slow conversion; no scenario in the deck prices it. Trade policy sets a cost risk: a 10% duty on non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24 is $3,300 per $33,000 robot, about $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build, so a USMCA certification or CBP ruling is a closing condition. USDA SBIR Phase II ($650,000, 2024-2026) ends in 2026.

gates: Confirm company identity, legal entity, geography, stage, and business model.
Decide whether the geographic market context lens is material; if yes, map home, revenue, expansion, supplier, comparable-company, capital, exit markets and the investor perspective.
Decide whether the policy and geopolitics lens is material; if yes, map jurisdictions and perspective.
Complete the profile requirements before drafting.
Build the source register with source type, date, confidence, claims and a link or file/page reference.
Use visible source IDs such as [S1] as citations in the report.
Complete the evidence matrix for all material sections before drafting.
Run the pre-draft evidence gate and fix failures.
Draft the report from evidence, not from outline memory.
Run the red-team pass and rewrite weak sections.
research_plan.hypothesis: Wait for milestone. The problem is real and the RaaS model is the right shape for growers, but the evidence does not support leading an $18M Series A at a $72M pre-money: the 94% pick rate rests on 212 rows the company chose, 41% gross margin excludes $12,000 of fleet depreciation per robot-season, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and the plan needs $9.9M of the round to build robots whose $31,000-$33,000 cost is still a related-party quote. The recommendation is to wait for an independent harvest-level trial and a measured v4 unit cost, then invest at $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and licence assignment consent. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the case reverses and $72M is cheap.
research_plan.author: Lead Analyst

items: Use web and data tools for fresh facts whenever a company, market, price, policy, filing, funding, or executive fact may have changed.
For each major section, record targeted search strings, opened sources, source IDs, and why the selected sources are decision-grade rather than merely convenient.
Use the server's checks for deterministic QA, extraction, citation checks and the delivery folder; do not rely on a one-shot narrative draft.
Do not generate repeated filler paragraphs such as per-section original-document priority, citation-anchor blocks, or repeated metric-card copy; each section must contain content-specific analysis.
Before drafting, write a section distinctness plan: the unique decision question, mechanism, comparison set, counter-evidence, and best visual artifact for each section.
For each section, draft one final-report thesis sentence that directly analyzes the company; never copy internal plan labels or rubric language into the report.
Remove repeated visible scaffolds such as "Economic mechanism", "Comparison and benchmark", "Counter-evidence and risk" and "Investor implication"; keep the scaffold internal.
Use a verdict strip, compact decision cards, selected tables, and at most a few KPI strips; do not repeat the same card, grid or dashboard pattern in every section.
Before writing the executive briefing, summarize the non-consensus or consensus view and the exact evidence that changes the decision.
Treat OCR as a pipeline: inventory files, OCR scan- or slide-heavy material, and keep page, slide or table references for every extracted claim.
Check every page holding numbers, TAM, valuation, customers, clinical or regulatory claims, policy claims, financing terms or team credentials before relying on it.
Mark OCR-derived claims low confidence until checked or corroborated; use ranges for OCR-derived financial inputs.
Build a claim verification table for material company-provided claims: verified, partially verified, unverified, contradicted, or not publicly disclosed.
profile_requirements.evidence: Client deck read in full (15 pages, figures as of 2026-09-30); 199 sources registered including primary and near-primary records (USPTO, SEC comparables, DOL OFLA and California wage orders, USDA SBIR, Cal/OSHA, 21 CFR 112), independent trials and OEM transactions. Every section has a saved evidence block with targeted queries, source IDs and a passing gate; all fourteen sections carry claim-verification labels, with deck-only claims marked unverified company material. After review R1 (verdict revise, 4 Critical and 6 Important), each owner revised: cash figures are dated and rolled to 2026-10-31 ($3.29M gross, $1.79M usable, 4.4 usable months to the 2027-03-14 covenant); the H-2A line is dated across labour, risk and thesis; the repriced case is split between the full $18M round and a $12M-only cheque; exit routes rest on independent precedents with a probability-weighted $116.8M value; competitor claims carry verification status; CAC and a lost-deal register are in section 6; and the entity and licence gaps are labelled not disclosed. Section 11, section 14 (composite 4.1 from the weighted table) and the executive summary have been updated to the revised evidence; QA still routes two formatting checks on company_overview and team to their owner before version 2 is saved for the second review.
profile_requirements.author: Lead Analyst

rows.belief: Real in California and rising with the wage floor, but narrower than the deck implies: the customer is a strawberry grower renting capacity one season at a time, not a buyer of robots.
rows.evidence: California minimum wage rose to $16.90/hour on 2026-01-01 with $17.40 scheduled for 2027; agricultural overtime after 8 hours/day and 40 hours/week; the 2026 California H-2A AEWR is reported at $19.97/hour and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor (S141, S142, S143, S146). Orrin billed 75 paid robot-seasons at $9,500 in 2026 (S53, unverified).
rows.counter_evidence: H-2A supply may be elastic, so an expansion or an AEWR freeze lowers hand-pick cost and slows conversion (S145, S147); Florida's 120-day season buys less utilisation (S53); US noncitrus bearing acreage fell 2% in 2025 (S160).
rows.confidence: high on the labour-cost mechanism, medium on urgency
rows.change: An H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze, or NASS data showing California strawberry acreage falling faster than the wage floor rises.

rows.belief: A real night-picking machine with five paying growers, but no harvest-level performance proof: the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%.
rows.evidence: 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms at 5.6 s/berry; 86% uptime; 3.8% bruising (S53, unverified). Independent trials: 74% of ripe fruit at 20 s/berry (WSU 2025) and 83-87% of detected fruit (JFR 2025) (S56, S42, S57). At 85% detection and 3.8% bruising, ~75% of ripe fruit reaches a clamshell.
rows.counter_evidence: Grower E ended its Plant City pilot over bruising (S53); no strawberry-robot paper reports a bruise rate against a hand-picked control (S50); ISO 18497 verification and an incident record are not disclosed (S166, S162).
rows.confidence: medium-low
rows.change: An independent harvest-level trial above 85% of fruit on the plant, with bruising at or below a hand-picked control, on blocks Orrin did not select.

rows.belief: The labour-cost case is timely, but the strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price, so the $310M obtainable market is 132% of the entire US acreage base.
rows.evidence: 50,000 acres / 3.5 acres per robot x $16,500 = $235.7M; 15% adoption by 2031 gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at renewal (S53, derived). Arizona- and Florida-based competitors and OEM appetite confirm category interest: Harvest CROO's 2025-04 claim, Deere/Bear Flag $250M (S1, S92).
rows.counter_evidence: The base rate is failure or absorption: Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025 after a $25M Series B, Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in 2025-03 (S91, S114, S115).
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: NASS strawberry acreage by state and the California Strawberry Commission's grower data, plus a third-party trial; the market section files both as open data requests.

rows.belief: Traction is relationship-led and concentrated: two growers are 53% of 2026 paid seasons, one the COO's former employer, and 2027 is 44% contracted (110 robots plus 50 LOIs of 360).
rows.evidence: Marisol Ridge 24 of 75 paid seasons and Pajaro Bluff 16; four paying growers contracted 110 robots for 2027 and eight pilots signed LOIs for 50; four sales staff (S53, unverified). Five of 14 pilots converted to paid.
rows.counter_evidence: Related parties carry both sides: Vashti Harvest Services (COO-owned) was paid $310,000, and Tallis is customer, noteholder, manufacturer, observer and investor (S53, S144). The 200 uncontracted robots must be sold in one selling cycle.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: Third-party contracts at list price for 2027, and a renewal rate on the 110 contracted robots signed at $12,700 or more.

rows.belief: The unit loses money once the robot is depreciated: -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and $48,000 cost, -$650 at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost; only the unsold $16,500 list clears cost.
rows.evidence: 41% gross margin = $9,500 less $3,100 service and $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables; $12,000 depreciation over four seasons turns contribution to -85%; break-even at current service cost is $13,350 (S53, derived). Service at 33% of price and a 35% cost cut plus 74% price rise are all required at once.
rows.counter_evidence: Florida-to-California redeployment could produce two seasons per robot and halve depreciation per season, but no 2027 Florida commitment exists and the $2,500 transport line is not in the plan (S53).
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the inputs
rows.change: A measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, a signed renewal price at or above $14,000, and telemetry showing service cost below $2,500 a season.

rows.belief: Strong founder-market fit with a thin bench: the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, and 360 robots implies ~45 technicians against nine field staff.
rows.evidence: CEO Castellano wrote the licensed perception work at Calder (11 filings); COO Vashti ran harvest crews for 15 years; VP Engineering Hollander spent 11 years at Corvane Robotics; 64 robots built and serviced by 38 staff on $20.5M raised (S53, unverified).
rows.counter_evidence: No full-time CFO, no hiring plan, no manufacturing-scale record, and the departed co-founder retains 720,000 shares with no disclosed separation terms (S53).
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: A full-time CTO and CFO hired, a field-service staffing plan to 1:8, and reference checks that confirm the founders' operating records.

rows.belief: Not at $72M: 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS and 101.1x 2026 RaaS, with a $36.8M (40.9% of post) 1x preference stack; $48M-$55M pre-money or a tranched $12M is the investable structure.
rows.evidence: Post-money $90M on $2.6M FY2026E revenue, of which 46% is Tallis services and 13% grants; listed ag peers median 2.7x EV/Sales; CNH/Raven 6.0x sales (S53, S8, S12, S14, S95). At $50M pre, $12M buys 17.65% and returns 3.68x at a $250M exit; at $72M, 13.33% returns 2.78x.
rows.counter_evidence: OEM precedent supports a strategic exit: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag pre-scale (S96, S92). If 2027 lands, the price is cheap optionality.
rows.confidence: high
rows.change: A lead investor anchoring at $48M-$55M, or the company accepting milestone tranching that shifts $6M past the 2027 season.

rows.belief: An OEM trade sale in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M is the realistic route; an IPO fails on $13.2M of 2028E revenue and a $6.9M loss, and the Calder licence test on 2027-12-31 decides what a buyer is acquiring.
rows.evidence: Deere (Blue River, Bear Flag, GUSS), CNH (Raven at 6.0x sales), Kubota (Advanced Farm investor); the specialty-crop harvesting purchase AppHarvest/Root AI cleared at $60M in 2021 (S96, S92, S95, S93, S91).
rows.counter_evidence: The category has produced no disclosed venture-scale strawberry-harvesting exit; Tortuga sold assets, Advanced Farm closed, Abundant liquidated (S114, S115, S91). The licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms are not disclosed (S53).
rows.confidence: medium
rows.change: An OEM partnership or term sheet before 2029, or disclosure of licence assignment and change-of-control terms.

scenarios.driver: The v4 robot hits $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units, 360 robots are delivered for the April 2027 season, at least 250 sell at the $16,500 list, an independent trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the Calder licence clears its 100-robot test on 2027-12-31.
scenarios.evidence: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons already delivered; 110 contracted and 50 LOIs for 2027; Tallis has quoted the v4 BOM (S53, unverified). Deere paid $250M-$305M for pre-scale autonomy businesses (S178, S92, S96).
scenarios.outcome: $8M+ of ARR exiting 2027, an OEM partnership or Series B in 2028, and a trade sale at $300M-$400M in 2030-2031; Meridian returns 3.3x-4.4x before further dilution ($40M-$53M on $12M).
scenarios.implication: This is the case the $72M price already assumes; only a tranche that captures it at a lower entry makes it an investment.

scenarios.driver: The build lands late or short: 180-250 robots at the $12,700 renewal, $2-3M of RaaS in 2027, a flat or down Series B in 2028 once the $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack is visible, and an OEM trade sale at $150M-$250M in 2029-2031.
scenarios.evidence: 2027 is 44% covered (110 contracted plus 50 LOIs of 360); renewal is below the $13,350 break-even at current service cost; the $18M funds one season and leaves $1.5-3.5M at end-2027 (S53, derived). Agtech deal count fell about 20% in 2025 (S180), and the category base rate is failure or absorption (S91, S114, S115, S176).
scenarios.outcome: $150M-$250M sale in 2029-2031; Meridian returns 1.7x-2.8x at $72M, or 1.3x-2.2x after a 20% Series B dilution. At $50M pre-money a $12M-only cheque (19.35% of a $62M post) returns 2.4x-4.0x; 2.2x-3.7x holds only if the full $18M closes.
scenarios.implication: Reprice the entry or tranche; at $72M the base case is a thin venture return, not a loss.

scenarios.driver: One domino takes several symptoms: the round slips past Q1 2027, the v4 build misses the April 2027 season, the fleet stays below 100 robots, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, the Calder licence becomes non-exclusive on 2027-12-31, a second grower leaves over bruising, and cheaper hand labour after the 2025-10 H-2A wage cut slows conversion.
scenarios.evidence: $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31, about 4.4 months to the covenant; only $4.0M of the $18M is committed and a $12M close is $1.63M short before working capital; $1.6M of secured debt ranks ahead of the preferred; the gripper patent claims are rejected and the PCT national phase was not entered; the IP sits in the issuer while the fleet and grower contracts sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC (S53, S128, S130). The $19.97 AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; DOL 90 FR 47914 cut the operative California floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01, and AB 2646 restores $19.75 from 2027-01-01 (S190, S195). The covenant rests on the deck alone: no loan agreement or UCC-1 is registered.
scenarios.outcome: A secured-lender event or a distressed asset sale in 2027-2028; the entity split may prevent the licence and fleet from being sold together, so Meridian recovers $0-$12M (0-1.0x). If the facility has no minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round rather than a secured-lender event: bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, base rises to 53%, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions.
scenarios.implication: Do not lead without a Kestrel standstill signed with the term sheet, a licence assignment consent and a covenant waiver as closing conditions.

assumptions.assumption: Harvest-level recovery reaches 85% or more, with bruising at or below a hand-picked control, on blocks Orrin did not select
assumptions.disproof: An independent trial below 80% of ripe fruit harvested, or a second paying grower leaving over fruit quality
assumptions.impact: -40% enterprise value; the product becomes a harvest aid and the price ceiling falls
assumptions.early_warning: Further pilot exits after Grower E in Plant City; retail or grower quality audits on machine-picked fruit

assumptions.assumption: The v4 robot can be built at $31,000-$33,000 at 300 units (35% below the $48,000 v3 cost) by Tallis in Guadalajara
assumptions.disproof: A contract-manufacturing quote above $36,000, or the first 20-unit build costing more than $40,000
assumptions.impact: -25% to -35% enterprise value; the $12,700 renewal never clears break-even
assumptions.early_warning: v4 design freeze slips past 2027-01; Tallis re-quotes the BOM; gripper cost-down abandoned

assumptions.assumption: The 2027 book clears at $12,700 renewal or better, with 360 robots sold rather than 160
assumptions.disproof: Renewals signed at $9,500-$12,700, or fewer than 250 robots contracted by 2027-02
assumptions.impact: -30% value; the base case becomes a bridge round at a flat or down price
assumptions.early_warning: 110 contracted plus 50 LOIs unchanged through Q1 2027; a grower renegotiating after a bruising complaint

assumptions.assumption: The round closes at $18M by Q1 2027 with a Kestrel standstill, so the company reaches a Series B without breaching the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant
assumptions.disproof: A close after Q1 2027, a $16M rather than $18M raise, or a burn above $410,000 a month
assumptions.impact: -100% of the equity in a secured-lender event; if no minimum-cash test exists, a 25%-40% down round instead
assumptions.early_warning: Covenant reached around 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the round committed at 2026-10-31; no loan agreement or UCC-1 in the register

assumptions.assumption: The wage floor rebinds: AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01, and no H-2A expansion or AEWR freeze cuts the hand-pick cost advantage
assumptions.disproof: A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling, or grower surveys showing crews available
assumptions.impact: -15% to -20% value; adoption slows and the 2027 book prices lower
assumptions.early_warning: DOL rulemaking on H-2A eligibility or wage methodology; the California all-in hand-pick cost falling year on year

consensus.consensus: The pitch, and the way an ag-robotics Series A is usually framed, assumes the only autonomous open-field strawberry picker above 90% accuracy, a $310M obtainable market off a $3.1B serviceable one, a 41% gross margin and a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with large peer rounds such as Monarch's.
consensus.our_view: The labour problem is real and the machine sells seasons, but the price is not supported: the observable market is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M headline, unit contribution is negative at the price actually sold, and the technology moat is a conditional licence with a 2027 cliff. The thesis is non-consensus on valuation and on harvest-level performance, not on the existence of the problem. We would not lead at $72M; the investable structure is $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M tranched on 2027 milestones and a Kestrel standstill.
consensus.evidence: Section 3: 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 company-chosen rows, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent trials report 72%-87% and harvest-level recovery is about 75%-80% [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181]. Section 4: 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 caps the whole US strawberry robot-revenue pool at $235.7M, so $310M is 132% of the base; the 15%-by-2031 pool is $35.4M at list [S53]. Section 6: after $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit is -$8,100 a season at the 2026 price and -$650 at the renewal with the target cost [S53]. Section 7: 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding; 46% of FY2026E revenue is one related-party services contract ending 2027-06-30 [S53]. Section 8: $72M pre is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted robot revenue, and section 12's probability-weighted exit value is $116.8M, 1.41x at the current price [S53].
consensus.proof_event: An independent harvest-level trial above 85% with bruising no worse than a hand-picked control, 250 robots contracted for 2027 at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and a Kestrel standstill signed before the money is wired.

one_question.question: What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?
one_question.why: The 94% divides by detected ripe fruit and excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%, so it cannot tell an investor whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. At 75%-80% recovery with 3.8% bruising the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the same numbers become conservative and the 2027 plan is financeable. It is the one measurement that reprices every other assumption in the case.

modules.capital_efficiency: FY2026E revenue $2.6M against $38.5M of equity and notes raised, $0.24 of revenue per equity dollar (0.15 on FY2027E); burn multiple 7.0x FY2026 and 5.9x FY2027; $18M buys 300 robots at $33,000 but leaves $1.5-3.5M at end-2027.
modules.position_sizing: Zero at $72M pre-money; $6M at $48M-$55M with $6M released on 2027 milestones (independent harvest trial above 85% with clean bruising, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, measured v4 cost at or below $33,000, Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test). Maximum loss $12M; $6M reserved for a Series B. At $50M pre-money a $12M-only cheque buys 19.35% of the $62M post and returns 4.0x at a $250M exit; 17.65% and 3.68x need the full $18M.

answers.most_damaging_fact: Harvest-level recovery. The 94% (S53) divides berries picked by berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms the field team selected, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (S56) and 83-87% of detected fruit (S42, S57), which puts harvest recovery at about 75-80% after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks. Sections 3 and 5 build the harvest-aid conclusion on that. If the reverse is true and detection on commercial blocks is near 100%, the machine replaces crews, the $235.7M pool in section 4 understates the market, the 360-robot plan and the $310M obtainable market become conservative, and the recommendation to reprice to $48M-$55M rather than invest at $72M is a costly pass. It is also the only load-bearing claim with no independent test at all.
answers.company_only_claims: Almost every positive claim is company-provided (S53): the 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising, 86% uptime and 5.6 seconds a berry; 75 paid robot-seasons, five paying growers, 110 contracted robots and 50 LOIs; the $3.2M ARR definition; the $48,000 v3 unit cost and the $31,000-$33,000 v4 cost, which is a Tallis bill-of-materials quote from a related-party manufacturer; the $42B, $3.1B and $310M market layers; the 2.1-season payback; and the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant, which no loan agreement in evidence supports. Verification status is 'company-reported, unverified' throughout and sections 4, 6, 7 and 8 state it. One caveat for the register: S53 and S144 are the same 15-page deck filed twice, so apparent source diversity across sections is overstated.
answers.generic_section: Section 2 (team) is the weakest on evidence: its own check fails for missing career granularity, it adds no independent source on the founders' operating records, and the team claim ('founder-market fit with a thin bench') is load-bearing for the tranching decision. Section 12 (exit) is next: at 8,149 characters it is the thinnest, and it reuses the same five OEM comparables (S96, S92, S95, S93, S91) already carried in sections 5 and 8, with no disclosed valuation for any private peer. Section 4 is not generic but rests entirely on one unverified company input, the 50,000-acre base; its own open data requests (NASS acreage, California Strawberry Commission) are still outstanding.
answers.unpriced_risk: Two. First, the labour-policy reversal: the 2026 California floor is $16.90, 15.4% below the 2025 $19.97, and AB 2646's $19.75 from 2027-01-01 is still 1.1% below 2025, so the customer-pain pillar gets one cheaper season before a partial rebound. Section 10 prices this as a one-season delay (65%, -10% to -20% EV), not permanent relief, but the recommendation still carries no slower-conversion case. Second, the entity/asset split: the licence sits in the issuer, the fleet and grower contracts in Orrin Fleet Services LLC under a $1.6M secured facility, and no intercompany IP licence or parent guarantee is disclosed (S53, S128), so the pieces may not be sellable together. Section 10 prices this at -20% to -40% of recovery, but the thesis's 0-1.0x bear is still an optimistic reading.
answers.first_challenge: A skeptical investment committee partner would say: you are underwriting a covenant, not a crop. The company's own plan says a $12M minimum close funds $15.37M against $17.0M of uses, a $1.63M hole before working capital, and the $1.5M minimum-cash test binds on 2027-03-14 with $4.0M of $18M committed and 45 days to the target close. Then the challenge turns on the remedy: a reprice negotiation that takes three to six months consumes the runway it is meant to protect, and Kestrel's consent, waiver or estoppel is not a condition precedent in the current structure. The second challenge is that the 94% is a measurement definition, not a performance result, and no one has measured marketable berries in the clamshell per ripe berry on the plant on blocks the company did not choose.
answers.downside_survival: No, not as a recommendation to lead at $48M-$55M without conditions. Market 50% smaller: 25,000 acres gives a $117.9M pool at list and $17.7M at 15% adoption, which kills $72M but leaves $48M-$55M defensible. Revenue 30% lower: $3.9M instead of $5.6M, $0.87M less gross profit at a 52% RaaS margin, end-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M minimum — breached at the low end. CAC 2x: cannot be absorbed because the 200 uncontracted robots have one selling window, four sales staff and a 5-of-14 pilot conversion record. Financing six months late: $2.46M of extra burn leaves $1.24M of cash on 2027-06-15; if the minimum-cash test exists (company-reported, unverified), that is a secured-lender default from 2027-03-14; if the facility has no test, the same delay is a 25%-40% down round, not a wipe-out, and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions. The conclusion survives only as pass, or as invest with a Kestrel waiver and standstill as a condition precedent.
answers.ocr_claims: None. No OCR-derived source is registered or cited in this case, and the 15-page deck was read as a text PDF; the only borderline source is S152, a tariff aggregator, which is used for a duty rate and corroborated by S174 and S156.

rows.finding: Orrin asks $18M at a $72M pre-money (about $4.7145/share; $90M post-money; 19,090,116 fully diluted shares), with the pre-money already including 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares for the ~$7.77M of 2025 notes converting at 80% of the price and a pool top-up to 12% of post-money.
rows.mechanism: The headline pre-money is not the operating company's price: it bundles a 20% note discount ($1.95M of value at the round price) and a 1,210,805-share pool increase ($5.71M at the round price) into the pre-money, so founders, seed and option holders absorb both before the new money enters.
rows.benchmark: Precedent seed/Series A structures: 1x non-participating preferred with a 15-20% conversion discount on bridge notes and a post-money pool top-up are conventional, but the deck does not disclose the notes' original caps or discounts, so the bridge's effective price cannot be checked.
rows.weakens: If the notes had a valuation cap well below $72M, the A-1 block would be larger and the common dilution worse; the deck gives only the 80% price discount, not the cap or the note terms.
rows.implication: A lead should reprice the operating business rather than the headline: the effective pre-money for the operating company is about $64-66M before the bridge discount and pool are stripped out.
rows.confidence: high (deck arithmetic reconciles: 19,090,116 x $4.7145 = $90.0M; 15,272,108 pre-money shares x $4.7145 = $72.0M)
rows.follow_up: What are the 2025 notes' caps, maturity, security and change-of-control terms, and do they convert at the qualified-financing price or a cap?

rows.finding: At $72M pre the company is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue of $2.6M, 34.6x on the $90M post-money, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR, and 101.4x the $0.71M of actual 2026 RaaS revenue (75 robot-seasons x $9,500). On 2027E revenue of $5.6M it is 12.9x pre and 16.1x post; on 2028E revenue of $13.2M, 5.5x and 6.8x.
rows.mechanism: A revenue multiple is only comparable across companies if the revenue is recurring and cash-collected; Orrin's $3.2M 'ARR' is a forward construction ($1.4M contracted 2027 seasons + $1.2M Tallis engineering services ending 2027-06-30 + $0.6M letters of intent), so the denominator that matters today is $0.71M.
rows.benchmark: Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers trade at a median 2.7x EV/Sales (Deere 4.0x, Trimble 4.3x, AGCO 1.0x; median EV/EBITDA 15.6x) and CNH paid 6.0x sales for Raven's $348.4M revenue.
rows.weakens: Orrin is growing 2025-2028 revenue from $1.9M to a planned $13.2M (91% CAGR), so a forward multiple falls fast if the plan is delivered; the price is not expensive against its own 2028 plan at 6.8x post-money.
rows.implication: The multiple is defensible only if the 2027-2028 plan is treated as probability-weighted, not as a base case; at the current revenue base the price is a strategic option, not a revenue multiple investment.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; low on the 2027-2028 denominators, which are unaudited company projections
rows.follow_up: What share of the 2027 contracted $1.4M is signed with creditworthy growers, and what are the cancellation and deposit terms?

rows.finding: The comparable ag-robotics private set has absorbed far more capital than Orrin without any disclosed valuation: Carbon Robotics $232M across five rounds (latest $20M Series D in Oct 2025; $70M Series D in Oct 2024, total $157M then), Monarch Tractor $133M Series C in 2025 with over $220M raised, Advanced Farm $25M Series B in Sep 2021, Tortuga a reported $47.7M total, Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds since 2014.
rows.mechanism: In a capital-intensive hardware category the winners are the best-funded fleets; Orrin's $18M is 7.8% of Carbon's total and 8.2% of Monarch's, so Orrin is a sub-scale entrant whose price must be justified by a technology or licence edge rather than by fleet scale.
rows.benchmark: No comparable round discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre cannot be triangulated directly; the only hard comps are revenue multiples and the size of the capital pools.
rows.weakens: Smaller rounds at lower valuations are normal at Series A; Advanced Farm's $25M Series B shows a strawberry-robot leader raising a similar amount, which makes Orrin's $18M round size unremarkable even if its price is not.
rows.implication: The comp set supports the round size but not the price; a lead should underwrite Orrin as the smallest, least-funded player in a category where the leader has 13x the capital.
rows.confidence: medium: round amounts are disclosed, valuations are not; Tortuga and Harvest CROO figures are aggregator data
rows.follow_up: What post-money valuations did Carbon's and Monarch's last rounds clear at, and what revenue multiples are secondary buyers quoting for ag-robotics positions in 2026?

rows.finding: The round dilutes existing holders by 30.8%: founders fall from 47.0% to 33.3%, seed from 25.0% to 15.7%, granted options from 13.0% to 8.2%, and the unallocated pool rises from 9.0% to 12.0%; the 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.8M-$39.3M (Series A $18M + A-1 $7.77M + Seed $11.0M, plus the $2.5M pre-seed SAFEs if they converted into the Seed preference), equal to 41-44% of the $90M post-money.
rows.mechanism: A 1x non-participating preference converts only when the exit value per share exceeds the preference; with a $36.8M-$39.3M stack, common receives nothing below that value and the Series A receives only its money back until the exit clears about $90M, where conversion value equals its $18M preference.
rows.benchmark: The preference stack is 41-44% of post-money, high for a Series A because three preferred classes stack at 1x; the Kestrel equipment facility ($1.6M drawn at 11.5%, secured on the fleet, $1.5M minimum cash covenant) ranks ahead of the preferred on the fleet assets.
rows.weakens: 1x non-participating is the most company-favourable preference and is common at Series A, so the stack protects the investor's downside better than a participating structure would; the real problem is the entry price, not the preference.
rows.implication: At a $40M exit the common is wiped out and Meridian recovers roughly $12.1M (about 1.01x) on its $12M; the preference does not rescue a 1x return if the price is wrong.
rows.confidence: high on the cap table; medium on the seed preference because the pre-seed SAFE conversion terms are not in the deck
rows.follow_up: Do the $2.5M of 2022 SAFEs sit inside the $11.0M Series Seed preference, and is the preference senior to or pari passu with the Kestrel facility?

rows.finding: Meridian's $12M buys 2,545,339 Series A shares, 13.33% of the $90M post-money. At exit values of $150M, $250M, $300M and $500M in 2029-2031 it returns 1.67x, 2.78x, 3.33x and 5.56x with no further dilution, or 1.33x, 2.22x, 2.67x and 4.44x after a 20% Series B dilution.
rows.mechanism: Return depends on ownership at exit and exit equity value, both of which the entry price fixes: a 3x on $12M needs a $36M exit stake, which at 13.33% is a $270M company and at 10.67% (after 20% dilution) is $337.5M.
rows.benchmark: The plan's 2031 strawberry revenue ceiling is about $35.4M (15% of the company's $236M US strawberry robot market), so a $270M-$337.5M exit is 7.6x-9.5x that revenue, above CNH's 6.0x for Raven and far above the 2.7x listed median.
rows.weakens: A strategic buyer paying for the perception model, the Calder licence and the harvest dataset could pay $250M-$305M pre-scale, as Deere did for Blue River and Bear Flag; that is the one path that makes the current price work.
rows.implication: The round only earns a venture return through an OEM technology premium or revenue well beyond the 2031 plan; a 3x is not achievable on a 4x-sales exit of the planned business.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; low-medium on exit values, which are scenarios
rows.follow_up: What exit value does the company's own Series B model assume, and what ownership does it model for the Series A after the next round?

rows.finding: The terms are conventional on preference (1x non-participating, equal rank), anti-dilution (broad-based weighted average) and dividends (8% non-cumulative, if declared), but the board is 5 seats with only 1 independent, and the deck discloses no pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching, information rights or related-party approval protection for the lead.
rows.mechanism: Board control sits with the common and Seed bloc (2 common + 1 Seed + 1 independent agreed by both = 3 of 5 on most votes), so the Series A director cannot block budgets, debt, related-party contracts or a sale process without protective provisions; Tallis holds an observer seat while also being noteholder, $1.2M-a-year customer, v4 contract manufacturer and $1.0M investor.
rows.benchmark: Tallis's five roles and Vashti Harvest Services' $310,000 of related-party payments are exactly the transactions a lead's protective provisions and independent-director approval should cover.
rows.weakens: The deck is a summary, not the definitive documents; pro-rata and protective provisions may exist in the term sheet even if not listed.
rows.implication: Meridian should require a second board seat or a listed-veto package, a related-party approval majority including the Series A director, pro-rata and pay-to-play, monthly KPI information rights, and tranching tied to the 2027 season milestones.
rows.confidence: medium: terms are as disclosed in a summary deck; definitive documents not reviewed
rows.follow_up: What do the definitive documents say on pro-rata, drag-along, protective provisions, related-party approval and the Tallis manufacturing agreement's IP and tooling ownership?

rows.finding: The $18M is sized to a $9.9M robot build (300 robots at $33,000 average unit cost) plus $4.5M R&D and $3.6M sales and field operations; at the $12M minimum close the robot budget alone consumes 83% of the round, and the company's $3.7M cash at $410,000 monthly net burn runs to about 2027-06.
rows.mechanism: The 2027 season starts in April 2027 and needs 360 robots in service; a $12M close funds the fleet but not the service organization or the R&D that the v4 cost target depends on, so the round size and the plan are coupled.
rows.benchmark: Cash runway of about 9 months from 2026-09-30 against a target close of 2026-12-15 leaves roughly six months of buffer before the 2027 season; a missed close forces a bridge or a down round.
rows.weakens: A lower close might be paired with a slower build (fewer than 300 robots), which could still hit a smaller revenue base; the deck does not model that case.
rows.implication: The lead should size its check to the plan it believes, not to the $18M headline; $12M at a $72M pre funds a plan that needs $18M, so either the price falls or the plan shrinks.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the unit-cost quote, which is a Tallis bill-of-materials quote from Aug 2026
rows.follow_up: What is the minimum robot count for the 2027 season that keeps the Calder 100-robot test and the $8M ARR milestone in reach?

rows.finding: The failure base rate is real: Abundant Robotics raised $12M, ran commercial apple trials under a RaaS model with a claimed $100M+ pipeline, and sold its IP and assets in liquidation on 2021-06-29 after failing to raise another round; Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds since 2014 and remains at seed stage.
rows.mechanism: Harvesting robotics fails on market traction and follow-on capital, not only on technology: field trials and a pipeline did not convert into a fundable revenue base before the cash ran out.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's $2.6M of 2026E revenue and $3.2M company ARR are ahead of Abundant's at shutdown, but its $18M round and $72M pre assume a funding market that Abundant never reached.
rows.weakens: Abundant's apple market and 2017-2021 capital environment differ from 2026; Carbon's $232M and Monarch's $220M+ show the category leaders can still raise, so capital is available for leaders, not for the field.
rows.implication: A lead should price the downside as a liquidation or a flat-round recapitalization, not as a protected 1x; the preference only helps if there is an exit above $36.8M-$39.3M.
rows.confidence: high on the facts; medium on their transferability to Orrin
rows.follow_up: What is Orrin's liquidation waterfall if the 2027 season fails and the fleet is sold to a grower or a competitor?
