plan.decision_question: Is $72M pre-money defensible against comparable rounds and precedent transactions, and what must be true for a Series A investor to earn a venture return?
plan.thesis_sentence: At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x 2026E revenue and 101x its actual 2026 RaaS revenue, so the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M-$338M; the price asks the Series A investor to underwrite execution the company has not yet shown.
plan.why_different: This section prices the round: what the investor pays, how the cap table and preference stack convert that price into ownership, and what exit value the price therefore requires. It does not re-argue the technology or the market.
plan.mechanism: Price paid sets ownership; ownership plus exit equity value sets the return. A 27.7x forward-revenue entry with a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack leaves a 13.33% Series A stake needing a $270M exit for 3x, which is 7.6x the plan's 2031 revenue.
plan.comparison_set: Private ag-robotics rounds (Carbon $232M raised, Monarch $220M+, Advanced Farm $25M Series B, Harvest CROO $10M, Abundant $12M then liquidation); listed ag equipment and precision ag (Deere 4.0x, Trimble 4.3x, AGCO 1.0x EV/Sales, median 2.7x); strategic M&A (Raven 6.0x sales, Blue River $305M, Bear Flag $250M).
plan.counter_evidence: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag before scale; if Orrin's 2027 milestones land, a $72M pre is 9x the $8M ARR target and an OEM could pay $250M+, making the price look cheap. The 2027 plan itself ($5.6M revenue, $8M ARR) would put the post-money at 16.1x forward revenue, inside the range of venture-priced hardware growth rounds.
plan.visual: Valuation methods table (method, inputs, value, source) plus a peer-multiples table and a return-sensitivity table at $150M-$500M exits with and without 20% Series B dilution.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong team; well positioned; clear business model; fierce competition; risks are manageable; about; many; recently; internal tool, record or bot names; review or request IDs

Tested Company Analyst note N11 against S53 p.14 wording on the unallocated option pool
Tested Fundamentals Analyst note N14 against S53 p.10 and section 7's 5.4-month cash bridge
Recomputed the price on contracted 2027 RaaS ($1.4M) and the payback including the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line

rows.finding: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue ($2.6M), 34.6x post, 22.5x the company-defined $3.2M ARR, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.7125M of 2026 RaaS revenue.
rows.mechanism: The price capitalises services and letters of intent as if they were recurring robot revenue; 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, so the multiple on contracted robot revenue is more than twice the headline multiple.
rows.benchmark: Listed ag-equipment and precision-ag peers at a median 2.7x EV/Sales; CNH/Raven at 6.0x sales.
rows.weakens: If the 110 contracted robots renew at $12,700 and the 50 LOIs convert, 2027 RaaS reaches $5.9M and the pre-money falls to 12.2x revenue.
rows.implication: Price at or below $55M pre-money, or make the price contingent on 2027 contracted seasons at list pricing.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; the revenue is company-reported and unverified.
rows.follow_up: Will the 110 contracted 2027 seasons be repriced to the $16,500 list, and what are the renewal terms?

rows.finding: $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant leaves $2.2M usable; at $410,000 a month that is 5.4 months and the covenant is reached around 2027-03-14, not 9.0 months.
rows.mechanism: The secured lender's minimum-cash test converts a financing delay into a default event before the 2027 season's first collections.
rows.benchmark: Round target close 2026-12-15; 2027 California season begins April 2027.
rows.weakens: The $0.9M undrawn facility and any 2026 season collections could extend the date; the deck does not give the collection schedule.
rows.implication: Tranche the round and require a covenant waiver or amendment at close; a Q1 2027 slip is a default, not only dilution.
rows.confidence: high; derived from disclosed cash, covenant and burn.
rows.follow_up: What is the Kestrel covenant test frequency and cure period, and will the lender waive it through 2027?

rows.finding: The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M ($18.0M Series A + $7.77M A-1 + $11.0M Seed), 40.9% of the $90M post-money and pari passu with new money, or $39.27M (43.6%) if the 2022 SAFEs carry their own preference. Total option overhang is 20.2% (12.0% unallocated plus 8.2% granted).
rows.mechanism: A preference stack of 41-44% of the post-money means the new investor is flat until an exit of $36.8M-$39.3M and the common absorbs the first loss.
rows.benchmark: Series A preference stacks commonly run 25-40% of post-money for a round of this size.
rows.weakens: The $2.5M SAFE preference is not disclosed; if the SAFEs are common or already in the Seed, the stack is $36.8M and the common gets $3.2M at $40M.
rows.implication: Meridian is flat at 1.0x from a $36.8M to a $90M exit; the $40M sale returns $12.0M and the common $3.2M.
rows.confidence: high on the disclosed stack; medium on the SAFE treatment.
rows.follow_up: Do the 2022 SAFEs convert into Series Seed Preferred with their own 1x preference?

rows.finding: The named US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced a shutdown and an asset sale, not a disclosed venture exit: Advanced Farm Technologies ceased operations on 2025-07-08 and Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii on 2025-03-24; Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation in 2021.
rows.mechanism: The category's failure rate raises the discount rate on the 2027 plan and lowers the price a strategic will pay for a pre-scale asset.
rows.benchmark: Abundant Robotics liquidation 2021-06-29; Advanced Farm $25M Series B in 2021; Tortuga $47.7M raised.
rows.weakens: Carbon Robotics raised $232M and Monarch Tractor $133M in 2025, so capital is still available to category leaders.
rows.implication: Underwrite to an asset-sale floor and require the 2027 licence test to be cleared before a second tranche.
rows.confidence: high on the events; medium on the causes.
rows.follow_up: Did Advanced Farm's assets or IP sell, and at what value, or was the shutdown a pure liquidation?

rows.finding: The advertised 2.1-season payback assumes a $1,750 service cost and omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons at the $16,500 list price and 4.4 seasons at the $12,700 renewal with today's $3,100 service cost.
rows.mechanism: A longer grower payback slows adoption and the 360-robot plan, which is the revenue base the $90M post-money depends on.
rows.benchmark: Grower payback of 2 seasons or less is the deck's selling point; 4.4 seasons is beyond a typical seasonal contract.
rows.weakens: The v4 service cost target of $1,750 and a $31,000 unit cost would restore 2.5 seasons; both are unverified.
rows.implication: Discount the 2027 plan and test contracted seasons at list price, not LOIs.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; the cost line is company-reported.
rows.follow_up: What service cost and transport line have the five paying growers actually incurred per robot-season?

rows.finding: Meridian's $12M buys 13.33% at $72M pre-money: $150M returns 1.67x, $250M 2.78x, $300M 3.33x and $500M 5.56x; at a $50M pre-money it buys 17.65% and the same exits return 2.21x, 3.68x and 4.41x.
rows.mechanism: Entry price, not exit value, moves the MOIC; a 3x needs $270M of exit value at the current price and $204M at $50M pre.
rows.benchmark: Venture Series A target of 3x gross MOIC.
rows.weakens: A $300M OEM exit (Deere paid $305M for Blue River) delivers 3.33x even at $72M pre.
rows.implication: Reprice to $48M-$55M or tranche $6M against the 2027 season.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; exit range medium.
rows.follow_up: What exit value does the 2031 plan's $35.4M revenue ceiling support at 4-6x sales?

plan.decision_question: Is $72M pre-money defensible against comparable rounds and precedent transactions, and what must be true for a Series A investor to earn a venture return?
plan.thesis_sentence: $72M pre-money is not defensible: it is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS, and at a $12M cheque the probability-weighted return is about 1.4x, so Meridian should reprice to $48M-$55M or tranche $6M against the 2027 milestones.
plan.why_different: This section prices the round itself: the per-share price, the dilution, the preference stack and the return at each exit value. The product, market and financial sections test whether the plan can be delivered; this one tests what the investor pays for it.
plan.mechanism: The $72M pre-money bundles a note-conversion discount and a pool top-up, so part of the price is a transfer to existing holders; the $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack then absorbs the first exit proceeds, leaving Meridian flat until roughly $38.4M and wholly dependent on entry price for its multiple.
plan.comparison_set: Announced agricultural robotics rounds (Monarch Tractor, Carbon Robotics, Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm, Tortuga); listed ag-equipment and precision-ag multiples (Deere, CNH, AGCO, Trimble) at a 2.7x median EV/Sales; precedent M&A (Blue River $305M, Bear Flag $250M, CNH/Raven 6.0x sales).
plan.counter_evidence: The category's failure record (Advanced Farm shutdown 2025-07, Tortuga asset sale 2025-03, Abundant liquidation 2021), hardware multiples below software, 65% of venture investments returning under 1x, and the preference overhang that makes a $40M sale return only capital.
plan.visual: The repriced return table showing the $12M-only versus full $18M cases, and the funding-round table with sources.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, about/many/experienced, any mention of the report's process, bots, tools or internal records.

rows.implication: Condition the $12M on Kestrel estoppel and consent, an intercompany IP licence, and confirmation the lien covers only the fleet.
rows.confidence: medium — deck only, no registry or UCC record retrieved
rows.follow_up: Does Kestrel hold a blanket lien on Fleet's contracts and receivables, and does the facility have a change-of-control trigger?

rows.finding: The parent owns zero granted patents: of five applications, US 17/902,118 (gripper) had every claim rejected in a first office action (response filed 2026-05), US 18/655,430 awaits examination, and the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline (Europe, Mexico, Australia) was 2026-10-30 — one day before this analysis.
rows.mechanism: A licensed, partly rejected and time-limited IP estate raises the chance competitors copy the gripper and that the core perception licence becomes non-exclusive.
rows.benchmark: The Calder licence turns non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31; Orrin has 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026.
rows.weakens: Prior art exists in sensorised soft grippers (US20220134579A1, 2022) and slip-sensing grippers (US4605354A, 1986).
rows.implication: Price the round as a service business, not an IP monopoly; require a patent prosecution plan and a Calder licence amendment before close.
rows.confidence: medium-low — the deck discloses the rejection but USPTO records were not retrievable
rows.follow_up: Were the PCT national-phase fees paid by 2026-10-30, and can the Calder licence be made exclusive regardless of the 100-robot test?

rows.finding: Cap table: 12,000,000 fully diluted today, 19,090,116 after; $72M pre / $90M post at $4.7145 a share; 2025 notes of ~$7.77M convert at 80% ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares (10.8%); the pool top-up of 1,210,805 shares is charged to the pre-money.
rows.mechanism: New money buys exactly 20.0% and is not diluted by the note conversion or pool top-up; existing common and seed holders bear it.
rows.benchmark: The option pool is stated as 12% of post-money unallocated on top of 8.2% granted options — 20.2% total overhang versus a 10-15% Series A norm.
rows.weakens: The deck labels the 2,290,805 shares 'unallocated pool'; if 12% was meant as the total pool, the unallocated reserve should be 730,805, so the table overstates it by 1,560,000 shares.
rows.implication: Confirm the pool definition in the term sheet; a 20.2% overhang reduces future round capacity even though the lead's 20% is protected.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic, medium on interpretation
rows.follow_up: Is 12% the unallocated pool or the total pool, and what refresh is assumed before the Series B?

rows.finding: The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M at the deck's stated amounts ($18.0M Series A + $7.77M A-1 + $11.0M Seed), 40.9% of the $90M post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if the $2.5M of converted SAFEs carry their own preference the stack is up to $39.3M (43.6%).
rows.mechanism: The lead's $12M has no seniority over $18.8M of seed and note preference; at a $40M exit the preferred takes essentially all value and common is wiped.
rows.benchmark: Market lead terms usually give new money seniority or a stronger ratchet; broad-based weighted average anti-dilution is standard.
rows.weakens: Equal rank may be acceptable if the lead gets protective provisions and a board majority, neither of which is disclosed.
rows.implication: Negotiate seniority or a preference top-up, and price the $72M pre-money against a $36.8-39.3M preference.
rows.confidence: medium — deck terms only
rows.follow_up: What is the Seed liquidation preference, and what protective provisions attach to the Series A?

rows.finding: Governance after closing: five board seats — two common (Castellano as chair and CEO, Vashti), one Series Seed (Granary partner Hollis Arvidsson), one Series A and one independent agreed by both; founders plus Seed control three of five, Tallis has an observer seat, and the independent seat is vacant today.
rows.mechanism: The lead can be outvoted 3-1 on a four-seat board if the independent seat stays empty; a supplier/customer/noteholder observer sees board material.
rows.benchmark: Lead investors in $18M rounds typically hold a board seat plus protective provisions over budget, debt, related-party transactions and new share issues.
rows.weakens: A genuinely independent fifth director, agreed by the lead, would restore balance.
rows.implication: Require the independent seat to be filled at closing and protective provisions in the charter; otherwise the $12M buys influence, not control.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Who nominates and approves the independent director, and what is the protective-provision list?

rows.finding: Related-party cluster: Vashti Harvest Services LLC (wholly owned by the COO) received $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to date; Tallis is simultaneously $2.5M noteholder, $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer to 2027-06-30, v4 contract manufacturer, board observer and $1.0M Series A subscriber; Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, took 24 of 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 (32%).
rows.mechanism: The two largest 2026 customers account for 53% of paid robot-seasons, one is tied to the COO's career, and a related party supplies 37.5% of FY2026E revenue and the v4 bill of materials.
rows.benchmark: Related-party revenue above roughly 5-10% of revenue and customer concentration above 30% are diligence red flags in venture rounds.
rows.weakens: The board approved the Vashti contract and Tallis's roles are disclosed; at-market terms would mitigate.
rows.implication: Obtain the contracts, pricing and margin analysis; require recusal and an independent review; treat the 2027 revenue plan as dependent on a contract that ends 2027-06-30.
rows.confidence: medium-high — figures from the deck
rows.follow_up: What are Tallis's margins on the v4 BOM and services contract, and who owns the v4 design and tooling?

rows.finding: Cash and debt: $3.7M unrestricted cash at 2026-09-30 against $410,000 monthly net burn (9.0 months of runway) and a $1.5M minimum-cash covenant on the Kestrel facility, with $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5%.
rows.mechanism: A December 2026 close leaves roughly six months of buffer before the covenant and runway meet; a delayed close forces a bridge or cost cuts ahead of the 2027 build.
rows.benchmark: Series A companies typically target 12-18 months of runway at close; the 2027 plan spends $9.9M on robots alone.
rows.weakens: The $18M round would fund the plan; covenant headroom is 2.5x today.
rows.implication: Set a closing condition and a minimum-cash covenant test at the parent, not only at Fleet; consider a tranched close.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Does the Kestrel covenant apply to consolidated cash, and what is the default remedy?

rows.finding: No public registry record for the three entities, the five patent applications, the Calder licence or any litigation/UCC filing could be retrieved: Delaware and California portals and open-web fetches were blocked in this session, so good standing, registered agent, ownership and lien position are unverified.
rows.mechanism: Every legal-cleanliness conclusion depends on documents the deck does not include.
rows.benchmark: The evidence standard requires a user data request rather than a silent gap.
rows.weakens: All positive entity claims rest solely on company material.
rows.implication: Do not sign the Series A until the five registry, patent and litigation extracts are in the data room.
rows.confidence: high that the gap exists
rows.follow_up: Will the company provide certified registry extracts and authorise lender and licensor references?

plan.decision_question: Is Orrin a legally clean, properly capitalised Delaware parent that actually owns the fleet contracts and the IP, and what do the entities and cap table imply for a new lead investor?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, leaving the lead investor buying preferred stock in an IP holding company whose operating value is secured to a lender and whose core licence is performance-contingent.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that maps entities, ownership, cap table and governance; financials, valuation and risk treat Orrin as one operating company.
plan.mechanism: Asset location and the preference waterfall decide what $12M of Series A preferred can reach: IP at the parent, fleet and grower contracts at a pledged California LLC, and a 1x preference stack of at least $36.8M ahead of common.
plan.comparison_set: Monarch Tractor ($133M Series C, >$220M raised), Advanced Farm Technologies ($25M Series B, 2021-09), Harvest Croo (~$10M over 14 rounds), Abundant Robotics (shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021-06), and market-standard Series A terms (10-15% option overhang, senior lead preference).
plan.counter_evidence: A three-entity structure is ordinary; Kestrel's lien may be limited to the fleet; related-party contracts were board-approved; the cap-table arithmetic is internally correct; the 1% Mexican stake is a two-partner formality.
plan.visual: Legal-entity table, pre/post cap table and the KPI strip.
plan.prohibited: clean cap table, no red flags, standard structure, huge market, well positioned, strong team

rows.finding: The Mexican subsidiary's Registro Público de Comercio folio number, incorporation deed and partner register are not disclosed; the 99% parent / 1% Orrin Fleet Services ownership rests on deck p.12 alone, and a search of the Jalisco registry by entity name on 2026-10-31 returned no record.
rows.mechanism: Without a registry extract the subsidiary's legal existence, partner percentages and representative authority are unproven, so consolidated ownership of the Guadalajara assembly operation and its tooling cannot be confirmed at closing.
rows.benchmark: A Series A closing binder normally holds a constancia de existencia legal and partner register for each Mexican subsidiary, alongside Delaware and California good-standing certificates.
rows.weakens: The company may hold a valid deed; the registry search is not the registry itself, and a zero-result public search is not evidence the entity does not exist.

rows.follow_up: What is the folio number and deed date, and who is the legal representative with powers to pledge the subsidiary's assets?

rows.finding: The Calder licence term and duration are not disclosed. The deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, 2.5% royalty, $40,000 annual minimum and the 2027-12-31 100-robot exclusivity test, but not the term, renewal, termination or assignment and change-of-control clauses; the eleven university application numbers are not enumerated, only dockets CU-2017-031 (granted 2020) and CU-2019-114 (granted 2022).
rows.mechanism: The parent's core perception IP is licensed, not owned; if the licence can be terminated on a change of control or expires before an exit, the asset the Series A is priced on does not transfer to a buyer.
rows.benchmark: Licences of university IP typically run for the life of the licensed patents plus renewal terms; a Series A data room normally carries the executed agreement with its patent schedule.
rows.weakens: The company may have a standard long-dated licence; the exclusivity test is disclosed, which suggests the commercial terms are not being hidden.
rows.implication: Price and condition on the executed agreement: no lead should fund without term, assignment and patent-schedule review.
rows.confidence: High on what the deck omits; low on the licence's actual duration.
rows.follow_up: What is the licence expiry date, and does change of control trigger consent or termination?

rows.finding: Fully diluted shares go from 12,000,000 today to 15,272,108 pre-money and 19,090,116 post-money; at $4.7145 the pre-money is $72.0M and the post $90.0M; the $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares; the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money; new money buys exactly 20.0%.
rows.mechanism: The arithmetic is internally consistent: 18,000,000 / 4.7145 = 3,818,008 new shares, 20.0% of 19,090,116; the note conversion and pool top-up are priced before the new money, so the lead's percentage is not diluted by them.
rows.benchmark: A $18M round at $72M pre-money should give the new investor 20.0% post-money, before any side letters.
rows.weakens: The same share count supports a 12.0% unallocated pool on top of 8.2% granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm, and a $36.77M (40.9%) 1x preference stack ranked pari passu with the new Series A.
rows.implication: The price is arithmetically clean; the terms, not the maths, are where a lead loses protection.
rows.confidence: High: recalculated from deck p.14.
rows.follow_up: Does the 12% pool include the 1,560,000 granted options or sit on top of them, and do the $2.5M of SAFEs carry a preference?

rows.finding: The preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of the $90M post-money, ranking pari passu across Series A, Series A-1 and Series Seed; if the $2.5M of SAFEs carry their own preference the stack reaches $39.27M (43.6%). A $12M lead ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money in a liquidity event.
rows.mechanism: Pari passu 1x non-participating preferences share proceeds pro rata, so the new $12M does not get paid first; at a $40M sale the common receives $3.2M before the Kestrel debt of $1.6M is considered.
rows.benchmark: Series A preferences are normally senior to seed or at least structured with a senior series; pari passu stacking is a negotiated term, not a market default.
rows.weakens: A 1x non-participating preference is founder-friendly and the stack is only 40.9% of post-money, well below the 2-3x stacks seen in down markets.
rows.implication: Negotiate seniority or a multiple for the new money, or price the round lower.
rows.confidence: Medium-high: figures from deck p.14, but the SAFE terms are not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Do the Furrowline SAFEs convert into Series Seed with the same 1x preference?

rows.finding: The parent owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118 (soft gripper) had every claim rejected in a first office action, US 18/655,430 is awaiting examination, the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30, and the two later filings are unpublished; no USPTO record could be retrieved to check status, inventorship or assignments.
rows.mechanism: A pending, rejected or unpublished application is not an enforceable exclusion right; the operating moat at this stage is field data and the licence, not patents.
rows.benchmark: Deep-tech Series A companies typically hold at least one granted patent family in the core technology; peers such as Harvest CROO and Advanced Farm hold issued patents in their picking mechanisms.
rows.weakens: Patent prosecution often starts with a rejected first action; the company has five filings and a licensed granted family, so the estate is not empty.
rows.implication: Do not ascribe patent-protected defensibility to the $72M price; treat the IP as trade secret plus licence until a grant issues.
rows.confidence: High on the deck's own statements; no independent USPTO confirmation.
rows.follow_up: What is the current prosecution status of 17/902,118 and 18/655,430, and who are the named inventors?

plan.decision_question: Is Orrin a legally clean, properly capitalised Delaware parent that actually owns the fleet contracts and the IP, and what do the entities and cap table imply for a new lead investor?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin's structure is not exotic but it is unverified: the Series A issuer owns the IP while the fleet, grower contracts and the only secured debt sit in a pledged California subsidiary, and the missing registry, UCC and licence-term records are conditions a lead must convert into documents before closing.
plan.why_different: This section is the forensic identity: who the legal entities are, what each owns, and how the cap table allocates claims. It does not analyse revenue quality, market size or valuation, which belong to sections 6, 4 and 8.
plan.mechanism: Value created by the fleet and grower contracts accrues in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, which is pledged to Kestrel and is not the issuer; the parent's equity is therefore a claim on an IP holding company whose licence is performance-contingent. Registry and UCC records would show whether the lien reaches receivables and contracts and whether the parent's 100% ownership is valid.
plan.comparison_set: Series A norms: 10-15% option overhang, 1x non-participating preference, one independent director per lead seat; comparable ag-robotics capital positions (Monarch >$220M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest Croo ~$10M, Abundant shut 2021-06).
plan.counter_evidence: Subsidiaries commonly hold fleet assets and lenders commonly secure collateral; related-party terms may be at market; the round arithmetic is correct. Absence of a retrievable registry record is not evidence of a defect, only of non-verification.
plan.visual: Entity table plus cap table, with the KPI strip for valuation, runway, overhang and preference.
plan.prohibited: No 'legally clean' as a finding, no 'well positioned', no 'strong team', no vague counts, no claim that a registry record was checked.

rows.finding: Orrin reports a 94% pick rate on 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, defined as ripe berries picked divided by ripe berries detected, on rows chosen by its own field team and excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes over 4%.
rows.mechanism: Because the denominator is detected fruit, undetected ripe berries never enter the metric; harvest-level recovery is detection accuracy multiplied by pick success, so a 94% conditional rate is consistent with roughly 75-80% field recovery at the detection rates independent groups report.
rows.benchmark: WSU open-field harvester: 80% detection on average and 74% of ripe fruit picked (58% without leaf-blowing fans), 20 s per berry [S56]; modular system 87% of detected and 83% of pluckable [S42]; 50-97.1% first-attempt success depending on occlusion [S57].
rows.weakens: Sample was company-selected and excluded the growing systems (tunnels, wet ground, slopes) that cover a material share of California fresh-market acreage; no independent trial of this machine exists in the register.
rows.implication: Invest only against a harvest-level, randomly selected-block trial with an independent auditor; treat 94% as an upper bound, not a base case.
rows.confidence: high - the definition and exclusions are stated in the deck and the benchmark range is drawn from three peer-reviewed trials
rows.follow_up: What is the vision system's detection rate on the same 212 rows, and what share of California acreage is under tunnels or above 4% slope?

rows.finding: 3.8% of picked berries are bruised or punctured, 2.1% of picks are unripe, and one of the five paying growers - Grower E in Plant City, Florida - ended its pilot citing fruit bruising.
rows.mechanism: Bruising measured at the moment of picking misses latent damage that expresses over the following 24-72 hours in the cold chain; bruised tissue is the entry point for Botrytis, so the grower's loss appears as shrink and rejection at the cooler, not as a robot KPI.
rows.benchmark: No published strawberry-harvesting robot trial in the register reports a bruise rate at all [S42, S56, S57]; bruise severity is now quantified at pixel level by hyperspectral imaging [S50], and mechanical damage is a leading cause of loss along the fresh-fruit chain [S100].
rows.weakens: The deck gives no hand-pick comparator, so 3.8% sits on no scale; the Florida exit is direct in-deck counter-evidence against the fleet average.
rows.implication: Condition the investment on a simulated cold-chain trial (7-10 days) measuring marketable outturn against a hand-picked control on the same block.
rows.confidence: medium - the company figure is clear but unbenchmarked, and the contradicting exit is a single grower
rows.follow_up: How is bruising scored (visual, firmness, cut surface) and at what point after picking; what share of Grower E's fruit was downgraded?

rows.finding: Uptime is 86% of scheduled hours at about 20 hours a day, with one field technician supervising up to eight robots and 3.4 hours between operator interventions.
rows.mechanism: 14% downtime is 2.8 robot-hours a day lost per robot; eight robots generate 22.4 robot-hours of attention a day against a technician shift of 8-10 hours, so either downtime is largely unattended (idle capital) or the 1:8 ratio is aspirational. At $48,000 over four seasons the lost depreciation is about $1,680 a robot-season against $3,900 of gross profit.
rows.benchmark: Independent open-field harvester takes about 20 seconds to identify and pick a berry [S56] against Orrin's 5.6 seconds per arm, a 3.6x cycle-time gap that the deck does not explain.
rows.weakens: Scheduled hours may exclude charging, battery swaps and transport between farms, which would flatter the uptime figure.
rows.implication: Re-underwrite the service model at 70-75% uptime and 1:20 supervision; require 30 days of fleet telemetry logs.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on what the 86% measures
rows.follow_up: What counts as scheduled hours, and what is the mean time to repair by subsystem?

rows.finding: The gripper patent application US 17/902,118 has had every claim rejected in a first office action (response filed 2026-05); the core ripeness and stem-localisation patents are licensed from a university and become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31.
rows.mechanism: With no allowed gripper claim, the picking end-effector is unprotected; the perception that makes picking work is rented, and the exclusivity that makes it scarce is conditional on a fleet milestone 14 months after closing. A competitor can license the same families if the milestone is missed.
rows.benchmark: Slip-sensitive robot gripper art dates to 1986 [S130] and academic slip sensing is dense from 2020-2026 [S103, S104, S106, S107]; Harvest CROO holds 13 patents in strawberry harvesting [S1] and has held federal strawberry-harvesting SBIR awards since 2016 [S98].
rows.weakens: A first-action rejection of all claims is a common prosecution event and does not by itself predict a poor outcome; the file wrapper, which would show whether the rejections are prior-art or formality based, was not obtained.
rows.implication: Price the company as an operations business with a licensed technology base, not as an IP-protected platform; make the 100-robot milestone a board-level covenant.
rows.confidence: high on the facts, medium on legal significance without the file wrapper
rows.follow_up: What are the examiner's grounds, and does the licence survive if robots are in service but under 100 at year end?

rows.finding: The v4 bill of materials is quoted at $33,000 (Tallis, August 2026) against a $48,000 current build, a 31% reduction, for a design whose first units are planned for the 2027 season; the PCT national-phase deadline for the platform patent fell on 2026-10-30.
rows.mechanism: The cost-down is a paper quote from a supplier that is simultaneously a noteholder, a $1.0M investor in this round, a board observer and a $1.2M-a-year engineering-services customer, with no competitive bid disclosed; a late or over-budget build misses a season that cannot be recovered because revenue is tied to the April-October harvest window.
rows.benchmark: A comparable two-armed strawberry picker is listed at $120,000-$200,000 per unit [S125]; peers raised $25M (Advanced Farm) and $47.7M (Tortuga) and still failed to build a durable business [S116, S118].
rows.weakens: Volume economics genuinely reduce unit cost, so $31,000-$33,000 is not implausible at 500 units; the question is 300 units, one season, one supplier.
rows.implication: Require a competitive bid, a signed supply agreement with liquidated damages, and a 20-unit v4 pilot build before releasing the second tranche.
rows.confidence: medium - the quote is company-reported and the comparator listing is a low-confidence aggregator
rows.follow_up: What is the costed BOM delta by line item, and what did a second contract manufacturer quote?

rows.finding: At the 2026 contract price of $9,500 a robot-season, contribution after field service ($3,100) and transport, insurance and consumables ($2,500) is $3,900, while depreciation on a $48,000 robot over four seasons is $12,000 a season.
rows.mechanism: The reported 41% gross margin excludes fleet depreciation, which the deck books in operating expenses; on a capital-recovery basis each 2026 robot-season loses about $8,100, and four seasons return $15,600 against a $48,000 asset. The plan needs a 74% price increase, a 35% unit-cost cut and a 44% service-cost cut at the same time.
rows.benchmark: The deck's own 2.1-season payback at the 2027 price excludes the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; including it, payback is 2.5 seasons and four-season contribution at the $12,700 renewal price is $33,800 against a $31,000 robot.
rows.weakens: Robot prices of $16,500 may hold if the machine demonstrably saves more hand labour than it costs, which is untested because the deck discloses no hand-pick cost per acre.
rows.implication: Growth at today's price destroys capital; underwrite the plan on 2027 pricing and require evidence that growers renew at $12,700+.
rows.confidence: high - all inputs are the deck's own disclosed figures
rows.follow_up: What is the grower's hand-harvest cost per acre per season, and what price did the 2027 contracts actually sign at?

rows.finding: The two best-known open-field strawberry robotics companies exited within four months of each other: Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025 after a $25M Series B and a CNH minority investment; Tortuga AgTech's IP, assets and engineering team were acquired by Oishii in March 2025.
rows.mechanism: The binding constraint in this category has been operating cost and grower willingness to pay rather than picking accuracy, so technical credibility and named commercial growers have not predicted survival.
rows.benchmark: Three of the four leading harvest-robotics attempts in the register have exited or been absorbed since 2021, including Abundant Robotics in 2021 [S91].
rows.weakens: Orrin's RaaS model avoids the grower capex objection that equipment sales faced, which is a genuine difference from the two failures.
rows.implication: Price the round for the base rate: smaller cheque, milestone tranches, and a preference structure that survives a 12-month delay.
rows.confidence: high on the facts, medium on how far the failures generalise to a rental model
rows.follow_up: What did Advanced Farm's growers say about why they stopped, and what did Oishii pay for Tortuga's assets?

plan.decision_question: Has Orrin proved the picking technology under conditions that generalise to commercial strawberry fields, and is the IP strong enough to defend a $72M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin has a working night-time picker and five paying growers, but the evidence it presents measures a conditional success rate on rows its own field team chose, and the IP that would defend a $72M pre-money is rejected, unpursued or licensed, so the technology is a demonstrated service prototype rather than a proven platform.
plan.why_different: This section judges the machine and the patent estate on their own terms - mechanism, measurement definitions, trial conditions, claims - not the market size, the financials or the exit. It is the only place the 94% and 3.8% numbers are tested against how they were measured.
plan.mechanism: The deck's pick rate divides by detected ripe berries, so undetected fruit drops out of the denominator; harvest-level recovery is therefore the product of detection accuracy and pick success. Bruising is measured at pick time, not after cold-chain expression, so latent damage moves cost to the grower. Uptime and supervision ratio together set capital utilisation, and depreciation excluded from COGS turns a capital-destroying per-season contribution into a reported 41% gross margin.
plan.comparison_set: Independent field trials: WSU open-field harvester 74% of ripe fruit and 20 s per berry (2025); modular system 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% first-attempt by occlusion (JFR 2019). Commercial peers: Harvest CROO claiming human parity in a Florida commercial operation (2025); Advanced Farm, commercial since 2019, ceased operations 2025 after $25M; Tortuga IP sold to Oishii 2025.
plan.counter_evidence: A Florida grower in the deck's own customer table ended its pilot because of fruit bruising, contradicting the 3.8% headline; the moat rests on university-licensed perception patents that become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in service on 2027-12-31; the gripper application's claims were all rejected and slip-sensing art dates to 1986.
plan.visual: Technology comparison table plus the patent table, with the evidence component carrying the single claim that the 94% is a conditional rate.
plan.prohibited: No 'industry-leading', 'best-in-class', 'proprietary moat', 'strong IP', 'huge market', 'first-mover advantage'; no unqualified '94% pick rate' without its denominator; no claim that peers are behind without a dated source.

rows.finding: Orrin's 94% pick rate divides by berries the vision system classified as ripe, over 212 rows it selected at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%.
rows.mechanism: A denominator of detected fruit removes every missed berry, so the metric measures gripper accuracy given detection, not harvest recovery.
rows.benchmark: WSU 2025 picked 74% of ripe fruit at 20 s/berry with 80% detection; JFR 2025 harvested 87% of detected at 83% success; JFR 2019 spanned 50-97.1%.
rows.weakens: The exclusion list omits the tunnel and slope conditions that dominate California and Florida strawberry acreage, so the sample is not the commercial field.
rows.implication: Underwrite 75-80% harvest recovery and a supplement-to-crew role; do not price a labour-replacement multiple until detection rate is reported on the same rows.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the benchmark comparison because trial configurations differ.
rows.follow_up: What is the detection rate on the same 212 rows, and what share of the 2027 target acreage is in tunnels or on slopes above 4%?

rows.finding: Bruising is 3.8% at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, the independent trials reviewed report no bruise rate, and one paying grower in Plant City left its pilot citing fruit bruising.
rows.mechanism: Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould, so damage shows up as cull and shelf-life loss at the packer, where the grower bears the cost.
rows.benchmark: No published bruise rate exists for any strawberry harvesting robot; hand-picking is the implicit control and is not benchmarked in the deck.
rows.weakens: One grower exit is a single, small-volume observation and may reflect pack-out expectations that a robotic supplement cannot meet at any bruise level.
rows.implication: Make a cold-chain bruise trial against hand-picked fruit a condition before the Series B; the current 3.8% cannot be validated or priced.
rows.confidence: medium - the exit is company-disclosed and the literature is silent rather than contradictory.
rows.follow_up: What was Grower E's pack-out before and after the robot, and does Orrin hold bruise data at 72 hours?

rows.finding: The deck discloses no ISO 18497 conformity assessment, no CE or UKCA marking, no incident log and no liability-insurance terms; ISO 18497-1:2024 gives design principles and vocabulary and ISO 18497-4:2024 the verification methods.
rows.mechanism: The standards are voluntary and no US federal rule covers a ground-based harvest robot, so the machine's safety case is built only if a buyer, insurer or state regulator demands it.
rows.benchmark: Cal/OSHA has examined ISO 18497-type frameworks against an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230; EU sales would require CE marking under that regulation.
rows.weakens: No US peer holds a published conformity assessment either, so the gap does not yet lose Orrin a sale - but the first buyer that asks will have no answer.
rows.implication: Price the absence of a safety file as an unbudgeted cost and an unbounded liability rather than as neutral; condition the cheque on an incident log and insurance terms.
rows.confidence: high that nothing is disclosed; medium that no certification exists, because non-disclosure is not proof.
rows.follow_up: Has any pilot farm's insurer, retail buyer or Cal/OSHA inspector asked for a conformity or incident file, and what did Orrin supply?

rows.finding: The gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to maintain and clean harvest equipment on the grower, not on the machine's maker.
rows.mechanism: The compliance burden lands on the customer, so a machine that is hard to clean adds sanitation labour and audit risk to the grower's harvest and depresses adoption and price.
rows.benchmark: Best practice for produce harvesting equipment is routine cleaning and sanitation of food-contact surfaces and adjacent areas; no per-machine cleaning time is published for any picker.
rows.weakens: Growers already clean harvest bins, knives and clamshells, so a cleanable robot may add less marginal labour than the surface count suggests.
rows.implication: Treat tool-free tear-down and swab-clean surfaces as a product requirement, and read the v4 cost-down for the cleanability it trades away.
rows.confidence: high on the rule; low on the size of the added labour.
rows.follow_up: How many minutes per robot per shift does cleaning take, and have any of the five growers run an ATP swab or GAP audit on the machine?

rows.finding: 32 strawberry-related foodborne outbreaks sickened 933 people in the United States between 1997 and 2017, and strawberries are eaten raw.
rows.mechanism: A contamination event traced to harvest equipment reaches consumers directly, so the reputational and contractual consequence for a 64-robot vendor with five customers is disproportionate to the volume of fruit handled.
rows.benchmark: No outbreak has been attributed to a harvesting robot; the record establishes category risk, not a causal link.
rows.weakens: Hand crews and bins, not machines, dominate the historical record, so a robot may reduce contamination risk by removing hand contact.
rows.implication: Sanitation design is both an insurance cost and a sales asset with retail audits; ask for swab results before scaling to 360 robots.
rows.confidence: medium - the outbreak count is peer-reviewed, the link to robots is inferential.
rows.follow_up: Do retail buyers' GAP audits treat an autonomous picker as new food-contact equipment requiring a sanitation plan?

rows.finding: US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action with a May 2026 response, core perception is licensed from two university families, and exclusivity lapses on 2027-12-31 if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service.
rows.mechanism: A narrow or absent gripper claim plus licensed perception means a funded competitor can copy the machine's function while Orrin carries royalty, minimum and reversion risk on the part that is hardest to build.
rows.benchmark: Slip-sensitive gripper art dates to a 1986 US patent; the 100-robot test sits between 64 robots today and 360 planned for 2027.
rows.weakens: First-action rejections are routinely overcome, and trade secret plus field-service know-how can protect performance without a patent.
rows.implication: Do not pay a patent-defended multiple; condition on the office-action outcome, the PCT national-phase entry and renewal evidence on the licence.
rows.confidence: high on the rejection and the licence terms; medium on the prior-art breadth.
rows.follow_up: What did the May 2026 response amend, did the PCT enter Europe, Mexico and Australia by 2026-10-30, and what are the renewal and minimum-royalty terms?

rows.finding: The 2027 plan needs unit cost to fall from $48,000 to $31,000-$33,000 and service cost to $1,750 per robot-season while price rises 74% to $16,500.
rows.mechanism: At 1:8 technician coverage, 360 robots need roughly 45 technicians against 9 field staff today, so the cost plan depends on a service ratio and a design change that are both unproven.
rows.benchmark: No contract-manufacturing quote is in the deck; the peer set (Advanced Farm, Tortuga) did not reach 300-500 unit volumes before failing.
rows.weakens: A 300-500 unit order can genuinely cut a $48,000 BOM by a third, and v4 gripper tooling is aimed at exactly that.
rows.implication: Condition the round on a competitive contract-manufacturing bid and a named hire plan for field service, not on the modelled 60% margin.
rows.confidence: medium - the arithmetic follows from the disclosed figures, the quotes do not exist.
rows.follow_up: What quotes exist from contract manufacturers for 300-500 units, and what is the technician attrition assumption behind 1:8?

plan.decision_question: Has Orrin proved the picking technology under conditions that generalise to commercial fields, and is the patent estate plus the safety and sanitation file strong enough to defend a $72M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin's 94% is a conditional pick rate on rows it chose, with no independent trial, no conformity assessment and no allowed patent claim, so at $72M pre-money an investor is buying a service organisation and a compliance file that do not yet exist rather than a defensible picking technology.
plan.why_different: Section 3 judges whether the machine physically works and can be defended - performance net of exclusions, bruising against a hand-picked control, autonomous-machinery safety and food-contact sanitation, and patent enforceability. Section 4 sizes the market and section 5 judges competitors' commercial position, so this section compares peers only on measured performance and IP, not share.
plan.mechanism: A pick rate measured over detected fruit on vendor-chosen rows inflates harvest recovery; unmeasured bruising, an unbuilt ISO 18497 verification file and food-contact surfaces the grower must clean transfer loss and liability to the customer, which caps the price the RaaS model can charge and slows the fleet ramp its unit economics need.
plan.comparison_set: Independent strawberry-harvest trials (WSU 2025, Journal of Field Robotics 2025 and 2019), the commercial status of Harvest CROO, Advanced Farm and Tortuga, and ISO 18497-1/-4 with 21 CFR 112 as the compliance baseline every peer faces equally.
plan.counter_evidence: No peer publishes a bruise rate and Advanced Farm and Tortuga failed commercially before any certification requirement bound a buyer, so the compliance gap may be immaterial to the sale; a short ISO 18497-4 verification and a clean sanitation file would convert the gap into an advantage over crowdfunded rivals.
plan.visual: Standards-and-liability table (ISO 18497-1/-4, 21 CFR 112.123, Cal/OSHA review) plus the performance metrics table with its independent benchmark column.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, clear technology lead, best-in-class, well positioned, patent-protected, world-class gripper, about/many as counts, recently, cutting-edge

rows.finding: AGRIST (Shintomi, Miyazaki, founded 2019) rents rail-guided greenhouse harvest robots for bell peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives: JA Niikappu (pepper, 2026-06-29/30), Hokuren (cucumber, 2026-07-01 to 08-31) and JA Kitasorachi (cucumber, 2026-07-02 to 10-31). Vendor-stated 55% harvest rate; Series B announced 2025-09-17; six announced deployments, all in Japan; no strawberry or open-field product.
rows.mechanism: A rental model for harvest robots can exist without solving open-field perception, because rails remove navigation, weather and canopy variability; the paid-rental model is therefore not itself a moat.
rows.benchmark: Orrin: 94% of detected ripe fruit in open field, 64 robots, five paying growers; AGRIST: 55% harvest rate, rail-guided, greenhouse.
rows.weakens: Weakens any claim that paid harvest-robot rental is novel to Orrin; weakens the idea that a rental model proves field performance. No audited fleet size or revenue, and the performance figure is vendor-stated.
rows.implication: Value the picker on the open-field problem it solves, not on the rental contract form; a co-operative rental channel is replicable and already exists in another crop system.
rows.confidence: medium: deployment announcements and funding date are corroborated by co-operative notices; the 55% performance is vendor-stated.
rows.follow_up: Has AGRIST published any strawberry or open-field trial, and does it hold patents that read on soft-fruit end-effectors?

rows.finding: Four Growers (Pittsburgh, Y Combinator-backed) says on its own site that it is 'working closely with various greenhouse growers to develop a tomato harvesting robot'; two patents are described as filed, not granted; the design uses 8 stereo cameras. Tracxn puts funding at $15.1M across 63 active competitors.
rows.mechanism: Greenhouse tomato is the easiest commercial picking case - fixed rows, no rain, uniform fruit, no bruising-sensitive soft skin - and it is still pre-commercial after $15M, which sets the capital and time required for a harder open-field crop.
rows.benchmark: Orrin has raised $20.5M and runs 64 robots; Four Growers $15.1M and no disclosed paid fleet.
rows.weakens: Weakens a reading that picking robotics is about to commoditise: a narrower task, with more capital than Orrin has spent on hardware, remains in development. Also weakens any claim that filed patents signal an enforceable position.
rows.implication: Orrin's open-field paid fleet, if verified, is ahead of a comparable team; but the capital required to get a picking product to market is of the same order as this round, not an order smaller.
rows.confidence: medium on development stage (company's own current site); low on the $15.1M, which is an aggregator total.
rows.follow_up: Do Four Growers' two filings claim grasp or perception methods that Orrin's v4 gripper would need a licence for?

rows.finding: Carbon Robotics (Seattle, founded 2018) sells the LaserWeeder, an autonomous laser weeder with 30 lasers and a claimed 200,000 weeds an hour, to roughly 100 growers across three continents. Cumulative funding is reported as $157M at the 2024-10 Series D, $232M in one 2026 tracker and $276M in another.
rows.mechanism: Field robotics has reached commercial distribution where the end-effector never touches the crop and the value is chemical replacement; distribution to 100 growers took $157M-$276M, ten to seventeen times Orrin's total raise.
rows.benchmark: Orrin total raised $20.5M, 5 growers; Carbon Robotics $157M-$276M, ~100 growers.
rows.weakens: Weakens the manufacturing argument for a $16M round: even a non-contact tool needed an order of magnitude more capital to reach 100 customers, and the grower-count and throughput are company-sourced. The three funding totals disagree, so none is reliable.
rows.implication: Distribution, not invention, is the capital sink; an OEM or dealer channel is the cheaper route to 300-500 units, and a stand-alone fleet must be priced against that alternative.
rows.confidence: medium on the product and commercial status; low on grower count and funding total, which are company or aggregator figures.
rows.follow_up: Who manufactures the LaserWeeder at volume, and on what contract terms? That is the comparable for Orrin's 300-unit BOM and ramp.

rows.finding: None of the three screened entrants builds a soft-fruit end-effector: AGRIST runs rail-guided pepper and cucumber harvesters, Four Growers files in greenhouse tomato grasping, Carbon Robotics in laser weed control. The freedom-to-operate risk to Orrin's gripper comes from crowded legacy slip-sensing art (a 1986 US patent) and the university licences, not from these peers.
rows.mechanism: The competitive set that matters for price is broader than the set that matters for patent risk; a crowded gripper art field narrows any allowance without giving a competitor a blocking position.
rows.benchmark: US 17/902,118: every claim rejected in a first office action, response filed 2026-05.
rows.weakens: Weakens the case that Orrin's patents are the barrier; also weakens the fear that a well-funded entrant will take the strawberry field in the next 12 months, since none is close in this crop.
rows.implication: Underwrite operations and contracted acres, not the estate; and do not pay for IP defensibility that the register does not support.
rows.confidence: medium: the crop and product scope of each entrant is documented; the absence of soft-fruit work is an absence of evidence, not proof.
rows.follow_up: A freedom-to-operate search against Four Growers' two filings and the 1986 slip-sensing family before the v4 gripper is frozen.

rows.finding: Orrin reports a 94% pick rate over 212 company-selected rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding plastic tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%, on a denominator of detected ripe berries. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU 2025), 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit (JFR 2025) and 50-97.1% (JFR 2019).
rows.mechanism: Defining the denominator as detected fruit removes missed berries from the failure count; choosing the rows removes the hard canopy and terrain, so the metric measures the arm, not the harvest.
rows.benchmark: WSU 80% detection, 74% of ripe picked; JFR 83-87% of detected; harvest recovery at 85% detection is 80%, and 75% after bruising and unripe picks.
rows.weakens: Weakens the deck's comparison with human crews and any claim that the picker replaces them in year one.
rows.implication: Price the round on supplement-to-crew economics until an independent harvest-level trial clears 85% on blocks Orrin did not choose.
rows.confidence: high that the definition and exclusions are as stated (company documents); medium on the independent comparison, which is drawn from different cultivars and seasons.
rows.follow_up: What is the detection rate on the same 212 rows, and what share of those rows had slopes above 4%?

rows.finding: The 3.8% bruise rate is measured at picking with no hand-picked control, and no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate; mechanical damage is a leading loss driver after harvest. One of five paying growers (Plant City, Florida) ended its pilot citing bruising.
rows.mechanism: Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould, so a pick-time measurement understates the loss the retailer sees; the buyer's quality bar is hand-picked fruit.
rows.benchmark: Hand-picked fruit is the retail benchmark; no published robot bruise rate exists for comparison.
rows.weakens: Weakens the credibility of the 3.8% as a quality claim: without a control it cannot be shown to meet the grower's standard, and the one revealed commercial exit points the other way.
rows.implication: A bruise trial against hand-picked fruit is a closing condition; without it the quality risk is unpriced.
rows.confidence: high on the absence of a benchmark; medium on how far 3.8% sits from commercial thresholds.
rows.follow_up: What bruise rate, measured at 72 hours against hand-picked controls, did the Florida grower see before exiting?

rows.finding: Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, CE or UKCA marking, incident log or liability-insurance terms. ISO 18497-1:2024 and -4:2024 cover design and verification of autonomous farm machinery but are voluntary; no federal US rule covers a ground-based harvest robot, so a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability. 21 CFR 112.123 puts the harvest-equipment cleaning duty on the grower.
rows.mechanism: Absent a mandatory standard, the standard of care is set after an injury by a jury; the grower bears the food-safety duty, which makes cleanability a product requirement the vendor must design for and the buyer will audit.
rows.benchmark: ISO 18497 verification is the emerging norm for autonomous farm machinery; 32 strawberry outbreaks and 933 illnesses in the US, 1997-2017.
rows.weakens: Weakens the assumption that a cheaper v4 gripper is a pure cost win: cleanability and validation are where the 35% cost cut is most likely to be taken out.
rows.implication: Require an ISO 18497-4 verification report, an ATP swab record and the insurer's terms as closing conditions; one contamination or injury event is existential for a five-customer vendor.
rows.confidence: high on the rules; not disclosed on Orrin's compliance, which is an absence in the file, not proof of absence.
rows.follow_up: Has any grower's insurer or retail buyer asked for a conformity assessment or a cleaning validation record?

rows.mechanism: Detection recall and pick success multiply, so a conditional rate overstates harvest-level recovery; a commercial field mixes the excluded conditions into the same block.
rows.benchmark: Washington State University open-field harvester 2025: 80% detection, 74% of ripe fruit picked at 20 s per berry; Journal of Field Robotics 2025: 83-87% on detected fruit; JFR 2019: 50-97.1% across trials.
rows.weakens: Orrin's figure is company-reported and unverified; no independent trial has run the machine, and WSU's 74% suggests whole-farm recovery well below the headline.
rows.implication: Price the round on 75-80% recovery, not 94%; make an independent harvest-level trial a condition before Series B.
rows.confidence: medium: three independent trials agree in direction, Orrin's number is unverified
rows.follow_up: What is detection recall on rows Orrin did not choose, and what share of a commercial block falls in the excluded categories?

rows.finding: Bruising is 3.8% at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control; Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying 2026 growers, ended its pilot over bruising; no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate for comparison.
rows.mechanism: Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens fruit to grey mould, so damage at pick converts to cull at pack; without a hand-picked control the 3.8% cannot be priced against the 2-5% pack-out loss growers already absorb.
rows.benchmark: Hand-picking is the implicit control and is not reported; horticultural literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver but publishes no robot comparator.
rows.weakens: A single grower exit is a small sample and may reflect service or cost rather than bruising alone; Orrin's own measurement could be conservative or generous.
rows.implication: The bruise rate is the metric that decides repeat purchase; commission a paired bruise and shelf-life trial before the Series B.
rows.confidence: low-medium: one grower exit, no independent bruise measurement
rows.follow_up: What bruise rate and 7-day shelf life does hand-picked fruit from the same rows show, and what cull did Grower E actually see?

rows.finding: US 17/902,118 (soft gripper with slip sensing) had every claim rejected in a first office action with a response filed 2026-05; slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent; the two university families behind perception are licensed exclusively at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31; the PCT national-phase deadline was 2026-10-30 with entry undisclosed.
rows.mechanism: A patent estate that is rejected, licensed and time-limited transfers no exclusionary power, so the moat must sit in field service and labelled data rather than in claims.
rows.benchmark: Screened entrants: AGRIST rail-guided greenhouse (vendor-stated 55%), Four Growers greenhouse tomato in development, Carbon Robotics laser weeder that never contacts the crop; none holds a soft-fruit end-effector claim.
rows.weakens: A response is pending, so a narrow allowance is still possible; the university licences may be renewable on negotiated terms.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite a $72M pre-money on IP; condition the cheque on a surviving claim and a licence renewal at $12,700 or more per robot.
rows.confidence: medium-high: office action and licence terms are documented; PCT status unverified
rows.follow_up: What did the May 2026 response claim, did the PCT enter national phase, and what are the renewal terms above 100 robots?

rows.finding: No conformity assessment, CE or UKCA marking, incident log or insurance terms are disclosed; ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary (17 pp.) and ISO 18497-4:2024, published 2024-07-31, sets verification methods and validation principles; both are voluntary; 21 CFR 112.123 places the harvest-equipment cleaning duty on the grower.
rows.mechanism: With no federal rule for ground-based harvest robots, an injury is litigated as strict product liability and a jury sets the standard of care, so an unverified safety file becomes a tail risk carried by the grower and its insurer; food-contact cleanability is audited by the buyer, and the 35% cost cut lands on the gripper.
rows.benchmark: 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people 1997-2017; produce-safety audits already require cleanable harvest equipment.
rows.weakens: Standards are voluntary and a small fleet may simply not have been asked for a conformity file yet; absence of a record is not evidence of an unsafe machine.
rows.implication: Add a safety and sanitation diligence condition: ISO 18497-4 verification report, ATP swab record, incident log and insurer terms.
rows.confidence: medium: standards and regulation verified, Orrin's file not disclosed
rows.follow_up: Has any grower's insurer or retail buyer requested a conformity or sanitation file, and what did Orrin supply?

rows.finding: Unit economics do not recover the robot: $48,000 build cost against a $31,000-33,000 plan, $12,000 depreciation per robot-season, and a claimed $3,900 contribution that 14% lost utilisation cuts by $1,680; closing the gap needs +74% price ($16,500), -35% unit cost and -44% service cost simultaneously.
rows.mechanism: A capital-intensive machine rented by the season only works if price, build cost and service cost move together; at 1:8 a 360-robot fleet needs about 45 technicians against 9 field staff today.
rows.benchmark: Screened peers reached distribution only with an order of magnitude more capital (Carbon Robotics $157M at the 2024-10 Series D).
rows.weakens: Manufacturing at 300-500 units could cut BOM more than the plan assumes, and utilisation may rise with a second shift.
rows.implication: The 2027 plan is a manufacturing and service build, not a software ramp; fund against contract-manufacturing quotes, not the plan.
rows.confidence: medium: arithmetic follows from disclosed figures, cost path unverified
rows.follow_up: What contract-manufacturing quote exists at 300-500 units, and what service cost per robot does the 2026 fleet actually run at?

plan.decision_question: Has Orrin proved the picking technology under conditions that generalise to commercial fields, and is the IP strong enough to defend a $72M pre-money?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53].
plan.why_different: Section 3 tests the engineering and the IP record at claim level, not the market size or the unit economics: what the 94% denominator contains, what a bruise rate means at pack, what the office action and licences leave enforceable, and which standards a buyer will audit.
plan.mechanism: Detection recall multiplies pick success, so a conditional rate overstates harvest recovery; bruising converts to cull at pack; rejected claims and licensed perception transfer no exclusionary power, leaving field service as the only defensible asset.
plan.comparison_set: Independent strawberry-harvest trials (WSU 2025, JFR 2025, JFR 2019), hand-picking as the implicit control, and screened entrants AGRIST, Four Growers and Carbon Robotics.
plan.counter_evidence: A narrow patent allowance could still issue; the grower exit may reflect service or price rather than bruising; voluntary standards may never be requested by a small grower base; contract manufacturing could cut cost faster than the plan assumes.
plan.visual: Technology comparison table with a verification-status column, plus the patent table showing rejected, pending and licensed families.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, recently, about 5, many patents, experienced team

Arturo Benedetti, CPA, Head of Finance part-time since 2024-09: BS Accounting 1998 at Linden Valley College; fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners 2016-today.

rows.implication: Budget a full-time CFO/VP Finance and a second sales lead in the use of funds; test Achterberg's pipeline conversion outside the founder-linked accounts.
rows.confidence: medium — deck only
rows.follow_up: How many of the 2027 contracted robots were sold by Achterberg versus the founders, and who signs off on the Kestrel covenant reporting?

rows.finding: Headcount is 38 — 22 engineering, 9 field operations, 4 sales, 3 finance and administration, with 7 in Mexico — against a plan to go from 64 robots and 75 paid robot-seasons in 2026 to 360 robots in 2027, a 5.6x increase; at one technician per 8 robots the 2027 fleet implies about 45 technician-equivalents versus 9 field-operations staff today.
rows.mechanism: Service capacity, not robot demand, becomes the binding constraint: every robot-season needs transport, night supervision, maintenance and insurance, and the deck does not show the hiring or contractor plan that delivers it.
rows.benchmark: Monarch Tractor has raised $133M Series C and over $220M; Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B; Harvest Croo about $10M over 14 rounds; Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021-06.
rows.weakens: Remote supervision and the Vashti Harvest Services contractor could cover part of the gap, and one technician may supervise more than 8 robots with better software.
rows.implication: Treat the 2027 plan as operations-constrained: require a field-service hiring and contractor plan, with unit-cost assumptions, before leading the round.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic, medium on the operating assumption
rows.follow_up: How many field technicians and contractors will Orrin employ at 360 robots, and what is the fully loaded service cost per robot-season?

rows.finding: None of the five disclosed leaders has a prior venture exit, and the only founder departure is Abernathy's; Castellano and Vashti hold 29.5% combined after the round and Abernathy 3.8%, against preferred holders at 46.5% and an option overhang of 20.2%.
rows.mechanism: The team has raised about $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes and shipped 64 robots, but has not yet taken a hardware company through a scale-up or an exit; the founder equity base is thin relative to the capital still required.
rows.benchmark: Abundant Robotics failed and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021-08, so strategic exit paths exist but require fleet-scale proof.
rows.weakens: First-time founders are common in ag robotics, and the 64-robot fleet is real operating evidence that many seed teams lack.
rows.implication: Add an independent director or chair with hardware scale-up experience as a closing condition, and tie founder retention to the 2027 milestones.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: What vesting and retention terms apply to the founders after the Series A, and who on the board has scaled a hardware fleet?

rows.finding: No public record of any named individual's education, employment, patent inventorship or licensing status could be retrieved: university pages, patent databases and corporate registries were blocked or returned no records in this session, so every personal claim rests on the deck.

rows.weakens: All positive team claims are unverified.

rows.confidence: high that the gap exists

rows.finding: 2026 per-robot-season waterfall: $9,500 price - $3,100 field service (33%) - $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables (26%) = $3,900 reported gross profit (41%); a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so true contribution is -$8,100 (-85%) and cash payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life.
rows.mechanism: Depreciation is the cash cost of a four-season asset; excluding it from gross margin converts a capital-destroying contract into a 41% margin and hides that each robot-season consumes about a quarter of the robot's cost.
rows.benchmark: Reported 41% gross margin versus -85% fully loaded; the 2026 price covers 54% of the $17,600 fully loaded break-even price ($48,000/4 + $5,600).
rows.weakens: The four-season life is the company's own assumption; at six seasons depreciation falls to $8,000 and contribution is still -$4,100 per season.
rows.implication: The 2026 cohort cannot repay its robots at $9,500; do not underwrite the fleet on the reported gross margin, and price the round for a price or cost step-change that is not yet proven.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; medium on asset life and residual value.
rows.follow_up: What is the measured useful life, warranty cost and residual value of a v3 robot after four seasons?

rows.finding: At the $31,000 target v4 cost, the $12,700 renewal price gives $7,100 gross profit against $7,750 depreciation: -$650 contribution and 4.4-season payback, beyond the four-season life. At the $1,750 target service cost it turns to +$700 and 3.7 seasons; at the $16,500 list price it is +$3,150 and 2.8 seasons.
rows.mechanism: The renewal price sits below the $13,350 fully loaded break-even at current service cost; only the list price clears cost, so the 110 already-contracted 2027 renewals are structurally marginal while the pitch depends on new-customer pricing.
rows.benchmark: The deck claims a 2.1-season payback at $31,000, $16,500 and $1,750 service; recomputed with the omitted $2,500 transport line it is 2.5-2.8 seasons, and 4.4 seasons at the renewal price.
rows.weakens: If field service falls to $1,750 and transport/insurance fall with route density, the renewal cohort is marginally positive (+$700 per season, about 2.2% of robot cost).
rows.implication: Underwrite 2027 at $12,700, not $16,500; a renewal-heavy 2027 fleet does not earn its capital cost, and the list price is the single most important unproven commercial assumption.
rows.confidence: High.
rows.follow_up: How many 2027 contracts are at the $16,500 list versus the $12,700 renewal, and what service and transport cost per season is in the 2027 plan?

rows.finding: $3.2M 'ARR' = $1.4M contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots x $12,700 = $1.397M) + $1.2M Tallis engineering-services annual rate that ends 2027-06-30 + $0.6M signed LOIs. 56% ($1.8M) is non-recurring or non-binding; 2026 RaaS revenue is $0.71M.

plan.decision_question: Does the per-robot-season RaaS contract earn a positive contribution after fleet depreciation at any price the market will pay, and can the model scale?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin's RaaS contract loses about $8,100 per robot-season at its 2026 price once the fleet is depreciated, is only marginally positive at the 2027 renewal price and $31,000 target cost, and becomes attractive only at the unproven $16,500 list price, so this is a capital-intensive fleet rental whose economics depend on a price increase the company has not yet sold.
plan.why_different: Section 6 is the only place that rebuilds the contract-level cash flow and prices the fleet asset itself; the market section sizes demand, the technology section tests field performance, and the financial section aggregates the P&L.
plan.mechanism: Depreciation is a real cost of a four-season asset; excluding it from gross margin turns a negative contribution into a 41% margin and hides a 12-season payback against a four-season life. Price, unit cost and service cost jointly decide whether a robot-season creates or destroys cash.
plan.comparison_set: Orrin's own 2026 actuals, 2027 renewal and list prices and $31,000 target cost; peer capital raised (Monarch >$220M, Carbon $157M, Advanced Farm $25M, Harvest CROO ~$10M) and Abundant Robotics' 2021 shutdown.
plan.counter_evidence: If robots last six or more seasons, service cost falls to $1,750 and transport falls with route density, the renewal case turns positive (+$700 to +$2,800 per season) and the 2026 loss is a launch-price problem rather than a structural one.
plan.visual: Unit-economics sensitivity table (price x unit cost) plus the price-versus-break-even pricing table.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong team; high barriers to entry; clear business model; fierce competition; risks are manageable; well positioned; SaaS ARR language for non-recurring revenue.
