rows.finding: At $9,500 and a $48,000 v3 robot, contribution after $12,000 of four-season depreciation is -$8,100 a season (-85%) and cash payback is 12.3 seasons; at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 target cost it is -$650 and 4.4 seasons; only the $16,500 list at $31,000 cost turns positive at +$3,150 and 2.8 seasons.
rows.mechanism: Depreciation is a cash-equivalent cost of the fleet. Leaving it in opex turns a contract that covers 54% of its fully loaded cost at $9,500 into a reported 41% gross margin.
rows.benchmark: Deck's reported 41% gross margin and 2.1-season payback ($31,000/$14,750).
rows.weakens: A six-season asset life cuts depreciation to $8,000 and narrows the 2026 loss to -$4,100; Florida-to-California redeployment could double seasons per robot, which the deck does not claim.
rows.implication: The 110 contracted renewals are the weakest part of the book, not the strongest; a fleet built on them destroys capital unless the price moves to list.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; low on inputs, which are company-reported and unverified.
rows.follow_up: Obtain the v4 purchase order or fixed-price BOM and a four-season maintenance record; both decide whether the target case exists.

rows.finding: The fully loaded break-even price is $17,600 at current service cost, so the 2026 contract covers 54% and the renewal 95%; only the $16,500 list covers 124% and the target-service variant 138%.
rows.mechanism: Service intensity is set by robots per technician and the harvest calendar; the price only clears cost if service cost falls $1,350 a season, which is a 44% reduction in the largest direct-cost line.
rows.benchmark: Fully loaded break-even: $17,600 at 2026 service cost, $13,350 at the $12,700 renewal, $12,000 at target service cost.
rows.weakens: If remote supervision reaches 1:25, the target service cost could be reached; the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet show it.
rows.implication: The renewal price is 5% below break-even; a 2027 book at $12,700 cannot fund the fleet, and the plan's 52% RaaS margin assumes a service cost the organisation cannot yet deliver.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; medium on the service-cost target, which no field data supports.
rows.follow_up: Reconcile the $3,100 service line to the 9 field staff and the 1:8 technician ratio; at 360 robots the line implies 45 technicians.

rows.finding: 53% of 2026 paid seasons sit with Marisol Ridge (24) and Pajaro Bluff (16). Grower B cut from 22 to 14 robots (-36%) with no reason disclosed and is contracted for 20 in 2027; Grower E exited in 2026-06 over bruising, Grower D has no 2027 contract, 6 of 8 other pilots have no LOI and 9 of 14 pilot farms never paid.
rows.mechanism: With five paying growers, each relationship is 20% of the book; retention and expansion, not new logos, carry the plan, and a single non-renewal is material.
rows.benchmark: Five paying growers in 2026; four contracted for 2027; 110 contracted robots versus 64 rented by those four in 2026 (+72%).
rows.weakens: The Grower B cut could reflect acreage or planting rather than performance; the deck does not say.
rows.implication: The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four relationships, one of which just cut its fleet; a second Grower B would remove 20 of 110 contracted robots.
rows.confidence: High on the counts; low on the reasons, which the deck does not disclose.
rows.follow_up: Ask Grower B and Grower D for the reason for the cut and their 2027 intentions; obtain the 110 executed contracts and 50 LOIs.

rows.finding: CAC is not reported. Five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new paying growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted 2027 robot and $24,000-32,000 per robot added in 2026; LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal.
rows.mechanism: Pilots and a once-a-year buying window front-load selling cost before a four-season asset earns contribution, so acquisition cost has to be recovered within the same four seasons as the robot.
rows.benchmark: 3x LTV:CAC venture benchmark; $12,600 of four-season contribution per robot at the $16,500 list.
rows.weakens: Sales and marketing spend is not a reported line; the estimate rests on headcount and an assumed fully loaded cost.
rows.implication: CAC payback at list is 2.5-3.5 seasons on top of 2.8 seasons of hardware payback, beyond the four-season life; at renewal it never pays back.
rows.confidence: Low-to-medium; an estimate with stated assumptions, not a disclosed figure.
rows.follow_up: Request sales and marketing spend by year, pilot cost per farm and the sales-qualified opportunity count.

rows.finding: Overhead is $92,000 per paid robot-season in FY2026, $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027 and $14,700-19,000 in FY2028; gross profit per season is $3,900 at the 2026 price and $3,150 at list with target cost.
rows.mechanism: Operating leverage only works if revenue per season grows faster than the fixed field and engineering base; the plan grows the fleet 4.8x while opex grows 1.6x, which is the right direction but not enough.
rows.benchmark: Deere FY2024 17.5% operating margin and 22.8% ROIC; United Rentals fleet rental at scale.
rows.weakens: FY2028 is a projection; the 2027 opex line could be cut, but the field organisation needed for 360 robots is not in the deck.
rows.implication: Until opex per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger; the plan never reaches that crossover.
rows.confidence: Medium; the fleet-rental comparison is directionally right but Orrin is pre-scale.
rows.follow_up: Show the operating-expense build at 360 robots, including the 45 technicians implied by a 1:8 ratio.

rows.finding: The category has absorbed several hundred million dollars without a scaled commercial strawberry winner; two entrants shut down and one, Monarch, wound down in 2026 after raising over $220M.
rows.mechanism: Hardware fleets need capex, service density and a seasonal selling window; capital raised does not shorten the field-validation clock, so well-funded entrants still fail on unit economics.
rows.benchmark: Private ag-robotics: Monarch over $220M raised (S54), Carbon $157M at the 2024-10 Series D (S55), Advanced Farm ceased operations 2025 (S93, S114), Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds (S94), Abundant Robotics shut down 2021 (S91).
rows.weakens: Survivorship cuts both ways: Carbon and Monarch raised at large multiples, so a strategic buyer may still pay for the technology.
rows.implication: A $72M pre-money for a 64-robot fleet with $1.4M of contracted robot revenue is a pre-commercial price; the peer base rate supports a milestone-based entry, not a full-cycle bet.
rows.confidence: Medium; funding and shutdown facts are sourced, but the peer set is small and private.
rows.follow_up: Compare Orrin's capital intensity with Harvest CROO and Carbon on robots in service, not dollars raised.

plan.decision_question: Does the price the company actually sells at cover the full cost of a robot-season, and which unit-economics variable decides whether the fleet can scale?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin's robot-season loses $8,100 at the 2026 price once the fleet is depreciated, breaks even only at the $16,500 list price with the $31,000 target cost, and therefore has to reprice its 110 contracted renewals and its 2027 expansion before more robots add value rather than loss.

queries: Deere 10-K item 1 keywords autonomy, robotic, acquisition, precision

rows.finding: FY2025 revenue of $1.9M comprised $0.95M of engineering services (Tallis), $0.30M of USDA SBIR grants, $0.38M of RaaS and $0.27M of paid pilots; services and grants were 66% of revenue and both end by mid-2027 (services 2027-06-30, grants after FY2026).
rows.mechanism: Neither line scales with robots and neither is recurring in any useful sense, so the FY2027 plan requires revenue to be 82% RaaS in one season; the $3.2M ARR figure borrowed $1.2M from a contract that expires and $0.6M from letters of intent, so the contracted RaaS base is about $1.4M.
rows.benchmark: Peer strawberry-robotics companies were funded as hardware businesses, not services businesses: Advanced Farm $25M Series B, Tortuga $47.7M raised, Harvest CROO about $10M over 14 rounds; none converted services revenue into a rental fleet at scale.
rows.weakens: Pilot and services revenue funded the fleet and kept the team together, so the mix is rational at this stage rather than evidence of a broken model; but it cannot support a $72M pre-money on a revenue multiple.
rows.implication: Underwrite the round on the $1.4M contracted RaaS base and treat the rest as pipeline; require ARR to be reported as contracted robot-seasons only.
rows.confidence: high - the segment revenue and the ARR definition are both disclosed in the deck
rows.follow_up: What share of 2027 contracted robots has a signed contract with a price and a deposit, as opposed to a letter of intent?

rows.finding: The round is $18M at $72M pre-money, but committed capital is $4.0M (Granary $3.0M, Tallis $1.0M) and Meridian is asked for $12.0M, which totals $16.0M; the plan spends $9.9M building 300 robots, then forecasts a $7.9M loss in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028.
rows.mechanism: Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 with $410k monthly burn gives nine months of runway before the round; after the build and the FY2027 loss the company needs a Series B in 2028, while the equipment facility requires $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, so the covenant bites exactly when the build is heaviest.
rows.benchmark: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C and Carbon Robotics a $70M Series D to scale hardware fleets [S54, S55], against $16M-$18M here; the capital bar for fleet scale in ag robotics sits well above this round.
rows.weakens: The $7.9M FY2027 loss includes depreciation of the new fleet, which is non-cash, so operating cash burn is lower than the net loss by roughly $2.5M; that improves but does not close the gap.
rows.implication: Structure the cheque so a missed milestone does not hand the plan to the lender: tranche the $12M against build and pilot-rate evidence, and require the $2M gap to be committed before closing.
rows.confidence: high - all figures are disclosed and the arithmetic is simple
rows.follow_up: What is the cash balance forecast for 2027-12-31 under the base plan, and who fills the $2M gap?

rows.finding: The 2027 plan puts 360 robots in service, but the use of funds builds 300 and the field organisation is 9 people; at the stated supervision ratio of one technician per eight robots the fleet needs about 45 technicians, against a target service cost of $1,750 a robot-season, or $630,000 for the whole fleet.
rows.mechanism: 45 technicians at any plausible fully loaded cost exceed $2M, three times the service budget, so either the supervision ratio improves to about 1:25 through remote autonomy or the 52% gross margin in FY2027 is not reachable; service labour is the variable that decides whether RaaS scales.
rows.benchmark: The deck's own 2026 service cost is $3,100 a robot-season; the target of $1,750 implies a 44% cut while the supervised fleet grows 5.6x, which is the opposite of the usual direction of travel in the first year of scaling.
rows.weakens: Technicians are seasonal and could be shared across the California and Florida calendars, which lowers annual cost per robot; the ratio could also improve with the v4.
rows.implication: Make the demonstrated supervision ratio in paid 2026 deployments the gating metric for the second tranche, ahead of the pick-rate milestone.
rows.confidence: medium-high - the arithmetic is robust but the labour cost is an estimate the deck does not disclose
rows.follow_up: What is the actual robots-per-technician ratio in the 2026 paid deployments, and what does a technician cost per season?

rows.finding: 300 v4 robots must be built for the April 2027 season from a design not yet in production, assembled in Guadalajara by a subsidiary with 7 staff, at a unit cost quoted by Tallis in August 2026 and never achieved.
rows.mechanism: The build window is roughly six months and the output is tied to a fixed harvest calendar, so a two-month slip converts into a lost season rather than deferred revenue; seven assemblers imply about 28 hours of labour per robot at 50 units a month, leaving no slack for rework on a first build.
rows.benchmark: Advanced Farm built and sold commercial machines for six years before closing [S114, S116], which shows a build process is necessary but not sufficient; Harvest CROO needed 14 funding rounds to reach a commercial machine [S94].
rows.weakens: The company already built 64 v3 robots, so it has a build process; the question is a five-fold step-up in one season, which is a different problem.
rows.implication: Require a signed manufacturing agreement with capacity commitments and a 20-unit pre-season pilot build; a slip here is the most likely way the round is lost.
rows.confidence: medium - headcount and quote are disclosed, the labour-per-robot figure is an estimate
rows.follow_up: What is the build takt time on the v3 line today, and what is the longest-lead component?

rows.finding: Tallis Agricultural Machinery is simultaneously the engineering-services customer ($1.2M a year, 63% of FY2025 revenue), a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.0M investor in this round, the board observer and the quoted manufacturer of the v4; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026, and the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer.
rows.mechanism: Revenue quality, cost of goods and governance all pass through the same small set of related parties, so neither the revenue nor the bill of materials has been tested by an arm's-length market; the same counterparty also gains information rights over the plan it is pricing.
rows.benchmark: No peer in the register discloses a comparable concentration of supplier, lender, investor and customer roles in one counterparty; the closest analogue is CNH investing in a supplier relationship with Advanced Farm, which was arm's length by comparison [S117].
rows.weakens: Related-party arrangements are normal in a capital-scarce hardware company and the board approved them; Tallis taking equity alongside a supply role does align incentives.
rows.implication: Make an independent director, an arm's-length manufacturing bid and a related-party review closing conditions, not post-closing intentions.
rows.confidence: high - the relationships are disclosed in the deck
rows.follow_up: Was the v4 BOM put out to any manufacturer other than Tallis, and on what terms can Tallis terminate the services agreement?

rows.finding: The realistic strategic routes are an OEM partnership or an asset sale: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries, and Tortuga's IP and team went to Oishii in 2025.
rows.mechanism: Value in this category has accrued to OEMs buying perception and autonomy, and to founders selling IP and engineering teams, not to standalone rental fleets; Deere's own filing describes autonomy, machine learning and Solutions-as-a-Service as core to its small-agriculture and high-value crop strategy, which makes a berry picker a plausible tuck-in for a machinery OEM.
rows.benchmark: Four machinery acquisitions bracket the range: Deere-Bear Flag $250M (2021), Deere-Blue River $305M (2017), CNH-Raven $2.1B (2021) and Oishii's undisclosed purchase of Tortuga's assets (2025).
rows.weakens: The same OEM route did not save Advanced Farm, and an asset sale at Series A scale would likely return capital rather than a multiple; a licensing model would collide with the Calder licence, which is exclusive only for agricultural harvesting.
rows.implication: Shape the company for a strategic sale or OEM licence by keeping the perception and fleet-scheduling IP owned, and avoid contracts that make the fleet unassignable.
rows.confidence: medium - the precedents are solid but none is a strawberry RaaS fleet
rows.follow_up: Has any OEM signed an NDA or evaluation agreement, and does the Kestrel facility permit assignment of the fleet on a sale?

rows.finding: The 2027 plan asks for 5.6x more robots in service (64 to 360), 2.4x revenue growth, a 74% price increase and a 31% unit-cost reduction in a single season, with 110 robots contracted and 50 under letters of intent as of October 2026.
rows.mechanism: Every one of those step changes lands in the same twelve months and the same four-month build window, so they are not independent risks; the probability that all four hold is materially below the probability of any one, which is what a single-point plan assumes.
rows.benchmark: The closest peer, Advanced Farm, ran commercial machines for six years and never disclosed a fleet above the low hundreds before closing in 2025 [S114]; 360 robots in one season would already be an outlier in this category.
rows.weakens: The 64 existing robots plus 300 new ones approximately reaches 360, so the unit count is internally consistent with the use of funds.
rows.implication: Ask for a plan that shows what happens at 200 robots and a $12,700 renewal price; if that case is not cash-positive by 2028, the round needs a larger buffer.
rows.confidence: high on the ratios, medium on the demand read-through
rows.follow_up: What is the downside case in the board pack, and at what robot count does the fleet cover its own service cost?

plan.decision_question: Is the RaaS plus engineering-services plus grant revenue mix a coherent path to a Series B, and what must the 2027 plan deliver operationally for the next round to be financeable?
plan.thesis_sentence: The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business - engineering services and grants were two-thirds of FY2025 revenue and both end by mid-2027 - so the Series A is really a one-season bet that 360 robots can be built, serviced and repriced before the current cash runs out, and the capital, headcount and unit economics in the plan do not yet reconcile.
plan.why_different: This section tests the plan against resources and time - what must happen, by when, with whose money and people - while section 3 tests the machine and section 6 tests the market. It is the only place the 2027 operating plan, the round arithmetic and the exit routes are put on one timeline.
plan.mechanism: Engineering services and grants pay the bills while the robot fleet is sub-scale, but neither scales with robots; the Series A must convert a services business into a rental fleet within one season, and the fleet only earns its cost of capital at a price 74% above today's contract price with a unit cost 35% lower - three simultaneous step changes whose failure modes all land in the same four-month build window.
plan.comparison_set: Capital and exit precedents: Advanced Farm raised $25M and closed in 2025; Tortuga raised $47.7M and sold its IP to Oishii in 2025; Harvest CROO raised about $10M over 14 rounds and is still private; Monarch raised $133M Series C and Carbon Robotics $70M Series D to scale hardware, so the capital bar for fleet scale is well above $18M. OEM exits: Deere-Bear Flag $250M (2021), Deere-Blue River $305M (2017), CNH-Raven $2.1B (2021).
plan.counter_evidence: The rental model removes grower capex, which is a real difference from the equipment-sale peers that failed; and 110 contracted robots plus 50 letters of intent show demand exists. But the largest revenue line is a related-party engineering contract that expires 2027-06-30, the round is $2M short of its own $18M target, and service labour at the claimed 1:8 supervision ratio exceeds the target service cost several times over.
plan.visual: Milestone table with target dates and current status, plus the partner table showing that every counterparty with real leverage over the plan is also an investor, lender or related party.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong pipeline', 'well positioned for growth', 'clear path to profitability', 'strategic partnerships' without scope and dates, no 'Series B is achievable' without the conditions, no unqualified ARR figure without its composition.

rows.benchmark: Target close 2026-12-15; the 2027 California season's first collections fall after the covenant date.
rows.weakens: Weakens any presentation of runway as nine months: the usable figure is less than half the gross one, and the difference is the covenant, not a modelling choice.
rows.implication: A close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the secured fleet, not a dilution event; the runway must be quoted on one definition - gross to zero versus usable to covenant - in every section.
rows.confidence: high on the figures and arithmetic (company-reported cash, disclosed covenant); the covenant test definition is not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Is the covenant tested on a spot balance or a trailing average, and does an equity close cure a breach?

rows.finding: Carbon Robotics reached roughly 100 growers across three continents with a laser weeder on a claimed 200,000 weeds an hour, after $157M raised at its 2024-10 Series D, with 2026 trackers reporting $232M and $276M cumulatively.
rows.mechanism: Distribution to 100 field-robotics customers took ten to seventeen times Orrin's total capital, which makes a channel partner the cheaper route to scale.
rows.benchmark: Orrin: $20.5M raised, 5 growers, 64 robots.
rows.weakens: Weakens the assumption that $16M funds a 300-unit ramp to commercial distribution; also shows that the category's one scale success avoids contact with the crop.
rows.implication: A stand-alone fleet at 360 robots must be priced against an OEM or dealer route to the same 300-500 units.
rows.confidence: medium on the product and commercial status; low on the funding total and grower count, which are company or aggregator figures.
rows.follow_up: Which contract manufacturer builds the LaserWeeder at volume, and what does it charge per unit?

rows.finding: AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse harvest robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives in 2026 after a Series B announced 2025-09-17, on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six announced deployments.
rows.mechanism: Rail-guided greenhouse operation removes navigation and weather risk, which is why a rental harvest fleet exists there before it exists in open-field strawberries.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's plan: 360 robots rented to US growers, one paid season per robot.
rows.weakens: Weakens the claim that Orrin's RaaS model is itself differentiating; the differentiation has to be open-field performance.
rows.implication: The rental model is proven as a contract form but not as a route to 360 robots in one crop; a co-operative channel is the replicable part, not the technology.
rows.confidence: medium: deployments and funding date corroborated; performance vendor-stated.
rows.follow_up: Does the Japanese rental model produce positive unit economics, and does AGRIST publish any fleet size?

rows.finding: The exits in this category went to equipment makers, and the independent failures were absorbed or shut: Abundant Robotics in 2021, Advanced Farm in July 2025 and Tortuga in March 2025.
rows.mechanism: An equipment maker buys distribution and a validated crop workflow, not a rental fleet, so contract assignability and owned IP are what preserve the option value.
rows.benchmark: Blue River $305M (2017), Bear Flag $250M (2021), Raven $2.1B (2021); Advanced Farm ceased 2025 after a $25M Series B; Tortuga sold to Oishii 2025-03-24.
rows.weakens: Weakens the standalone-scale-up case: no peer reached independence at this capital level, and the closest comparable with a fleet claim (Harvest CROO) has disclosed no shipments.
rows.implication: The cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with fleet contracts assignable and the IP owned rather than licensed.
rows.confidence: high on the transactions; medium on the read-across to Orrin's value.
rows.follow_up: Which equipment maker has a berry or small-acreage autonomy programme that a 64-robot fleet would fit?

rows.finding: At one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and the $1,750 target service cost per robot-season is $630,000 for the whole fleet.
rows.mechanism: Service labour scales with the fleet while revenue per robot is capped by the seasonal price, so the margin is a labour-productivity bet, not a hardware bet.
rows.benchmark: One technician per eight robots is the company's own service ratio.
rows.weakens: Weakens the FY2027 margin plan and the headcount plan, which funds 9 field staff against 360 robots.
rows.implication: Either supervision reaches about 1:25 through remote operation or the 52% projected gross margin is unavailable; the technician ratio belongs in the Series B milestones.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; the technician ratio is company-reported.
rows.follow_up: What does remote supervision actually deliver in technician-hours per robot-season, measured in telemetry?

rows.finding: Three hundred v4 robots must be built for the April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, on a bill of materials quoted by Tallis, which is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer.
rows.mechanism: A seasonal calendar with one selling window converts a manufacturing slip into a full year of lost revenue, and a related-party quote removes the market test of the cost.
rows.benchmark: The company has built 64 robots in total; the plan needs 300 v4 units before April 2027.
rows.weakens: Weakens the $31,000-$33,000 unit-cost target: the only quote comes from a party with interests in the outcome.
rows.implication: An arm's-length bid and a fixed-price build contract should be closing conditions; a two-month slip is a lost season, not deferred revenue.
rows.confidence: medium: the quote and the schedule are company-reported; no purchase order is disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Will Tallis bid the 300-unit build on fixed-price terms with liquidated damages for a late season?

plan.decision_question: Is the RaaS plus engineering-services plus grant mix a coherent path to a Series B, and what strategic options exist if it is not?
plan.thesis_sentence: The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: services and grants fund the company until the fleet can pay for its own service organisation, and on the deck's own numbers the $16M round buys one season with 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a Series B.
plan.why_different: Section 9 tests whether the plan is fundable and executable - dates, headcount, capital and partners; section 6 tests the unit economics and section 7 the cash.
plan.mechanism: A seasonal rental business needs capital before revenue each year; a covenant on the fleet converts a financing delay into a default; services and grants carry the company until the fleet is large enough to pay for its own service organisation, and the 2027 plan requires four step changes in one build window.
plan.comparison_set: Precedent exits to equipment makers (Blue River $305M 2017, Bear Flag $250M 2021, Raven $2.1B 2021); failed and absorbed peers (Abundant 2021, Advanced Farm 2025, Tortuga 2025); scale comparison with Carbon Robotics (~100 growers, $157M-$276M) and AGRIST (co-operative FaaS rentals).
plan.counter_evidence: The 110 contracted robots and 50 LOIs could convert faster than the 44% coverage implies; a $12M close plus the Kestrel facility may be enough for a 110-robot season if the build is deferred; an OEM could sign before the 2027 season; service cost per robot-season may fall faster than modelled if remote supervision works; and Harvest CROO, the closest direct peer, has disclosed no fleet at all, so Orrin's position in the crop is still the strongest disclosed.
plan.visual: Milestone table with target dates and status at 2026-10-31, plus the partner table with signing dates.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, best-in-class, recently, about 5, nine months of runway

rows.finding: Reconstructed FY2023-FY2028 P&L: revenue $0.1M, $0.4M, $1.9M, $2.6M, $5.6M, $13.2M; gross profit $0.0M, $0.3M, $1.0M, $1.5M, $2.9M, $8.0M; operating loss -$2.6M, -$4.0M, -$5.2M, -$5.4M, -$7.9M, -$6.9M; the operating loss equals gross profit minus opex every year, with no interest, tax, capex or working-capital line.
rows.mechanism: The reported growth is services- and grant-led, not robot-led; the omission of interest and working capital understates cash need, and depreciation sits in opex so gross margin overstates product economics.
rows.benchmark: FY2026 mix is 27% RaaS, 13% paid pilots, 46% engineering services and 13% grants; FY2025 was 50% services and 16% grants.
rows.weakens: The projections are the company's own and are not commitments; the arithmetic is internally consistent, which makes the mix issue easy to miss.
rows.implication: Model revenue quality, not headline growth: the largest FY2026 line is a services contract that ends in June 2027, and the P&L omits the interest and working-capital costs of the fleet.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; low on verification, since there is no audit or public filing.
rows.follow_up: Will management provide FY2023-FY2025 statements and a Q3 2026 balance sheet, and is any of it audited?

rows.finding: The $3.2M ARR is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots x $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis engineering services at its annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed LOIs; 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services revenue will be recognised in FY2027 because the agreement ends at mid-year.
rows.mechanism: The definition converts a one-season order book, a related-party services contract and non-binding letters into 'recurring' revenue, inflating the revenue base used for valuation and milestone language.
rows.benchmark: 2026 RaaS run-rate $0.71M and contracted 2027 RaaS $1.4M versus the $3.2M headline; $72M pre-money is 22.5x headline ARR and 51x contracted RaaS.
rows.weakens: If the 110 contracts renew annually, the $1.4M becomes recurring in substance after one cycle; no renewal history beyond 2025-2026 is disclosed.
rows.implication: Use contracted RaaS, not company ARR, for pricing and for the 2027 milestone; the $8M 2027 ARR target cannot include Tallis after June 2027 and therefore depends on 2028 contracts that do not yet exist.
rows.confidence: High on composition; medium on renewal behaviour.
rows.follow_up: What are the termination, deposit and renewal terms of the 110 contracts and the 50 LOIs?

rows.finding: Cash of $3.7M at 2026-09-30 against $410k monthly net burn gives the advertised 9 months, but the Kestrel facility requires at least $1.5M of unrestricted cash at all times, so only $2.2M is usable, or 5.4 months to about 2027-03-15; the $2.5M facility has $1.6M drawn at 11.5%, is secured on the fleet, and $0.9M undrawn buys only 27 robots at $33,000.
rows.mechanism: The minimum-cash covenant converts the cash balance into a dated obligation; the secured fleet means a breach gives the lender control of the revenue-generating asset.
rows.benchmark: Claimed 9 months; usable cash of $2.2M at $410k a month is 5.4 months, and $184k of annual interest adds about $15k a month if not already in the burn.
rows.weakens: If burn falls below $410k or the lender waives the covenant, the runway is longer than 5.4 months.
rows.implication: A delayed round is a covenant event, not just dilution; require a covenant waiver or a closing condition and treat the effective runway as about five months.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; medium on whether the burn includes interest and maintenance capex.
rows.follow_up: Is the $410k burn net of interest, maintenance capex and working capital, and what are the facility's maturity and financial covenants beyond the minimum cash?

rows.finding: Sources of $18M plus about $2.5M of year-end 2026 cash and $0.9M undrawn facility = $21.4M; uses of $9.9M for 300 robots at $33,000, about $7.1M of cash operating loss (the $7.9M net loss less about $0.8M depreciation) and an estimated $1M-$2M of working capital leave roughly $1.5M-$3.5M at end-2027; at the $12M minimum close the same uses leave a $1.6M shortfall before working capital.
rows.mechanism: Robot capex is paid to Tallis in Q1 2027, months before the April-October season's collections; the round is a bridge across one season, not a plan to breakeven.
rows.benchmark: $18M full close leaves $1.5M-$3.5M at end-2027, of which $1.5M is the covenant; the $12M minimum close is about $1.6M short before working capital.
rows.weakens: If 2027 collections arrive earlier or opex is cut, the full round leaves more cash; the working-capital estimate is not company-disclosed.
rows.implication: The full $18M is the minimum viable amount for 300 robots, and even then a Series B must close in the first half of 2028; the $12M minimum close funds at most about 200 robots and requires a smaller plan.
rows.confidence: Medium; the cash loss and working-capital estimates are derived and not company-disclosed.
rows.follow_up: What is the Tallis prepayment schedule for 300 robots, and what payment terms have growers agreed for the 2027 season?

rows.finding: Burn multiple (cash burn divided by net new revenue) is about 7.0x in FY2026 ($4.9M burn / $0.7M net new revenue) and about 5.9x in FY2027 (($7.9M operating loss + $9.9M robot capex) / $3.0M net new revenue); cumulative revenue FY2023-FY2026E of $5.0M against $20.5M of equity raised is $0.24 per dollar, and FY2027E revenue of $5.6M against $38.5M raised is $0.15.
rows.mechanism: Each round buys capacity ahead of revenue; with a $9,500-$16,500 price and $30k of opex per robot-season in 2027, the revenue base cannot cover the capital and overhead it consumes.
rows.benchmark: No-source venture norm: a burn multiple above 3x is generally considered capital-inefficient; Orrin's plan is 5.9x-7.0x.
rows.weakens: Early-stage hardware companies often show high burn multiples before scale; a rapid 2028 revenue ramp would improve the ratio.
rows.implication: Capital efficiency is far below what a $72M pre-money and a 2028 Series B require; the investor is paying for a fleet build whose revenue per dollar raised falls as the company scales.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; medium on the comparability of a hardware fleet to software burn multiples.
rows.follow_up: What revenue and burn does management expect in 2028, and at what fleet size does opex per robot-season fall below gross profit per robot-season?

rows.finding: Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation divided by unit cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal price and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list price and $31,000 cost, all before sales, R&D and G&A; no balance sheet, audit, DSO, DIO, DPO, warranty accrual or revenue-recognition policy is disclosed, and finance is led part-time by a fractional CFO.
rows.mechanism: A fleet rental earns its return through asset utilisation and depreciation, not gross margin; without balance-sheet and working-capital disclosure the investor cannot see whether growth consumes cash before it produces it.
rows.benchmark: Deere earned a 17.5% operating margin in FY2024 and a 22.8% ROIC; Orrin's best fleet cash yield is 10.2% before $30k-a-season overhead.
rows.weakens: Deere's ROIC benefits from a different capital structure and financial-services mix, and Orrin's list-price case may be reached in 2027; the yielded returns are derived, not audited.
rows.implication: Returns sit below the cost of capital even in the target case, and the absence of a balance sheet and audit is a material diligence gap; make these documents conditions of investment.
rows.confidence: Medium; Orrin figures derived, Deere figures from its 10-K.
rows.follow_up: Will the company provide audited or reviewed statements, the grower contracts with payment terms, the Kestrel loan agreement, the Vashti contract and the Tallis agreements?

rows.finding: USDA SBIR grants contributed $0.07M, $0.08M, $0.30M and $0.35M in FY2023-FY2026E and are projected at zero from FY2027; removing them from FY2026 leaves $2.25M of revenue and a gross margin of about 51% rather than 58%.
rows.mechanism: Grants are non-dilutive but temporary and often carry little cost of revenue, so their end both removes revenue and lowers the reported margin quality of what remains.
rows.benchmark: Grants are 16% of FY2025 and 13.5% of FY2026E revenue and zero thereafter; stripping them cuts FY2026 gross margin from 58% to about 51%.
rows.weakens: Grants are small relative to the round and may have covered engineering that would otherwise be opex; their loss is a growth hole rather than a solvency event.
rows.implication: Normalise FY2026 revenue and margin for grants; the 2027 plan has to replace $0.35M of grant revenue and the $1.2M services contract with robot revenue at the same time.
rows.confidence: Medium; grant accounting and cost allocation are not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: How are grant costs and revenues recognised, and what happens to the engineering team when the Phase II grant ends in 2026?

plan.decision_question: Do the unit economics and the cash plan support a venture-scale outcome, and what does the reported revenue mix hide?
plan.thesis_sentence: The projections are consistent arithmetic but not a fundable plan: 46% of FY2026 revenue is related-party engineering services and 13% is grants, the $3.2M ARR is 56% non-recurring or non-binding, and even the full $18M round funds 300 robots only by leaving a Series B that must close in the first half of 2028.
plan.why_different: Section 7 is the only place that aggregates the P&L, tests the ARR definition, rebuilds the cash bridge and prices the covenant; section 6 works at contract level.
plan.mechanism: Revenue mix determines quality: services and grants end, LOIs are non-binding, and one-season contracts are not ARR. The $1.5M minimum-cash covenant converts the cash balance into a dated obligation, while robot capex is paid to the manufacturer months before the season's collections.
plan.comparison_set: Deere's FY2024 17.5% operating margin and 22.8% ROIC as the mature ag-equipment benchmark; peer capital raised; Orrin's own 2026 run-rate versus its FY2027-FY2028 plan and the $18M/$12M financing cases.
plan.counter_evidence: If the 50 LOIs convert and list pricing holds on 250 new 2027 robots, RaaS could reach $5.5M rather than $4.6M; if every robot serves both Florida and California seasons, 360 robots could produce about 720 seasons and support FY2028 revenue without new fleet capex.
plan.visual: FY2023-FY2028 P&L reconstruction table, the returns and working-capital table, and the deck claim-verification table.
plan.prohibited: huge market; strong team; high barriers to entry; clear business model; fierce competition; risks are manageable; well positioned; unaudited figures presented as verified.

rows.finding: Cash is $3.7M at 2026-09-30; one month of $410k burn gives $3.29M gross at 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable above the $1.5M minimum, or 4.4 months to the covenant on 2027-03-14; gross months to zero cash are 9.0 from 2026-09-30 and 8.0 from 2026-10-31.
rows.mechanism: A fixed monthly burn against a minimum-cash test dates the failure: the covenant binds before the 2027 California season's first collections, so the round must close by Q1 2027 or the lender event precedes any operating recovery.
rows.benchmark: Deck's stated 9-month runway (gross, from 2026-09-30, no covenant); minimum-cash test of $1.5M.
rows.weakens: The $1.5M test appears only on deck p.10; no facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement supports it, so the 4.4-month figure is a company-reported assumption.
rows.implication: Fund on a dated covenant calendar and a January 2027 close, or obtain a Kestrel standstill with the term sheet; a Q1 2027 slip is default, not dilution.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; medium on the covenant because only the deck states it.
rows.follow_up: Produce the Kestrel facility agreement (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, cure, waiver price), the UCC-1 and the September 2026 bank statement.

rows.finding: If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event; the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35% and a $48-55M pre-money structure becomes investable with conditions.
rows.mechanism: Without a covenant the company survives to a dilutive refinancing; equity keeps option value, so the probability of a zero falls even though the plan is still unfunded.
rows.benchmark: Base case 50% bear weight in the risk assessment; $72M pre-money Series A.
rows.weakens: This is a sensitivity, not a finding: the covenant is unverified in both directions and the loan agreement is absent from the register.
rows.implication: Price and structure should be set on the no-covenant basis, with tranches tied to contracted seasons and lender consent; the covenant case is the planning case, not the only case.
rows.confidence: Medium; depends entirely on a document the team does not have.
rows.follow_up: Confirm whether the $1.5M test is a financial covenant, a springing test or an unused-commitment condition.

rows.finding: $3.2M ARR = $1.4M contracted 2027 robot-seasons at $12,700 + $1.2M Tallis engineering services ending 2027-06-30 + $0.6M signed LOIs; 56% is non-recurring or non-binding and the $72M pre-money is 51x the $1.4M contracted robot revenue.
rows.mechanism: The headline blends a one-season rental book, a related-party services contract and non-binding letters, so it overstates revenue that recurs without re-selling.
rows.benchmark: 22.5x headline ARR versus 51x contracted robot revenue at $72M pre-money; SaaS rule-of-thumb revenue multiples.
rows.weakens: The $1.4M contracts are themselves unverified and are one-season, so even the 51x base may not recur.
rows.implication: Underwrite on contracted robot-seasons at list or renewal price, not on the $3.2M; a price above $50M needs the services line replaced by robot revenue.
rows.confidence: High on the split (deck arithmetic); low on contract enforceability.
rows.follow_up: Obtain the 110 executed 2027 grower contracts and the 50 LOIs with expiry and cancellation terms.

rows.finding: FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M is stated at the $16,500 list (782 robot-seasons, 5.5% of 50,000 acres) but the plan's FY2027 line ($4.6M/360 = $12,778) implies the $12,700 renewal, which needs 1,016 seasons, 7.1% of acreage, 422-656 new robots and $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex.
rows.mechanism: Mixing list and renewal prices changes the adoption share and the capex needed; the 2% adoption assumption in the deck is exceeded on either basis.
rows.benchmark: Deck's 2% 2028 adoption assumption; 3.5 acres per robot; 50,000 US strawberry acres.
rows.weakens: FY2028 is a projection with no contracted volume; both bases rely on unverified acreage and price assumptions.
rows.implication: Treat the 2028 plan as a capacity requirement, not a forecast; the round does not fund the fleet it implies.
rows.confidence: Medium; arithmetic high, inputs unverified.
rows.follow_up: State the price and adoption basis for every projection year and reconcile to the 2% assumption.

rows.finding: Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) with no reason disclosed, while contracting 20 for 2027; Grower E exited in 2026-06 over bruising, Grower D has no 2027 contract, 6 of 8 other pilots have no LOI and 9 of 14 pilot farms never paid.
rows.mechanism: The 2027 contracted book is an expansion bet on four relationships, one of which just cut its fleet; retention, not new logos, carries the plan.
rows.benchmark: Five paying growers in 2026; four contracted for 2027; 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 those four rented in 2026.
rows.weakens: The deck does not disclose why Grower B cut, so the cut could reflect acreage or planting rather than performance.
rows.implication: Diligence the reason for the cut and the renewal terms before pricing; a second Grower B would remove 20 of the 110 contracted robots.
rows.confidence: High on the counts; low on causation.
rows.follow_up: Ask Grower B and Grower D for the reason for the cut and their 2027 intentions; obtain the 2026 service logs.

rows.finding: CAC is not reported; an estimated $0.9-1.2M of sales cost (five sales staff at $180,000-240,000 fully loaded) over three new paying growers in 2026 is $300,000-400,000 a grower, $8,000-11,000 per contracted 2027 robot or $24,000-32,000 per robot added in 2026; LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal.
rows.mechanism: A field-sales model with pilots and a once-a-year buying window front-loads acquisition cost before a four-season asset earns contribution; at renewal prices there is no contribution to recover it.
rows.benchmark: 3x LTV:CAC venture benchmark; $12,600 of four-season contribution per robot at the $16,500 list.
rows.weakens: Sales and marketing spend, pilot costs and sales-cycle length are not disclosed, so the range rests on headcount and assumed fully loaded cost.
rows.implication: CAC must be cut or list price held; a renewal-priced book cannot pay back acquisition, which is why the 2027 plan needs list-price contracts.
rows.confidence: Low-to-medium; an estimate with stated assumptions, not a disclosed figure.
rows.follow_up: Request sales and marketing spend by year, pilot cost per farm and the number of sales-qualified opportunities.

plan.decision_question: Do the unit economics and the cash plan support a venture-scale outcome, and what does the reported revenue mix hide?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin is a grant- and related-party-funded pilot business whose robot-season loses money after depreciation and whose $18M round buys one season, not a Series B; the equity is a conditional option on a 2027 fleet contracted at list pricing and a v4 at target cost, with the covenant date and the no-covenant down-round case as the two ways to price it.
plan.why_different: Section 7 tests the statements, the dated cash position, the accounting quality and the financing plan; section 6 tests price and unit economics per robot-season.
plan.mechanism: Fleet capex is paid before the season, depreciation sits in opex, revenue is concentrated in a related-party services contract and grants that end, and a minimum-cash covenant converts a financing delay into a lender event.
plan.comparison_set: Deere FY2024 operating margin 17.5% and ROIC 22.8%; 3x burn multiple; private ag-robotics peers (Monarch, Carbon, Advanced Farm, Harvest CROO); the deck's own 2% 2028 adoption and 360-robot plan.
plan.counter_evidence: The no-covenant case leaves the company alive to a down round; 110 contracted robots and 50 LOIs are real demand evidence; the $18M case reaches end-2027 with $2.6-3.6M if the plan holds; list-price sales would turn contribution positive.
plan.visual: The six-year statements table, the returns and working-capital table, the deck claim-verification table and an info danger box on the dated covenant runway.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong team', 'huge market', 'high barriers to entry', 'well positioned', 'risks are manageable'; no unlabelled company claims; no invented figures; no internal review, request or bot identifiers.

rows.finding: Cash is $3.7M at 2026-09-30; one month of $410k burn gives $3.29M gross at 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable above the $1.5M minimum, or 4.4 months to the covenant on 2027-03-14; gross months to zero cash are 9.0 from 2026-09-30 and 8.0 from 2026-10-31.
rows.mechanism: A fixed monthly burn against a minimum-cash test dates the failure: the covenant binds before the 2027 California season's first collections, so the round must close by Q1 2027 or the lender event precedes any operating recovery.
rows.benchmark: Deck's stated 9-month runway (gross, from 2026-09-30, no covenant); minimum-cash test of $1.5M.
rows.weakens: The $1.5M test appears only on deck p.10; no facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement supports it, so the 4.4-month figure is a company-reported assumption.
rows.implication: Fund on a dated covenant calendar and a January 2027 close, or obtain a Kestrel standstill with the term sheet; a Q1 2027 slip is default, not dilution.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; medium on the covenant because only the deck states it.
rows.follow_up: Produce the Kestrel facility agreement (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, cure, waiver price), the UCC-1 and the September 2026 bank statement.

rows.finding: If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event; the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35% and a $48-55M pre-money structure becomes investable with conditions.
rows.mechanism: Without a covenant the company survives to a dilutive refinancing; equity keeps option value, so the probability of a zero falls even though the plan is still unfunded.
rows.benchmark: Base case 50% bear weight in the risk assessment; $72M pre-money Series A.
rows.weakens: This is a sensitivity, not a finding: the covenant is unverified in both directions and the loan agreement is absent from the register.
rows.implication: Price and structure should be set on the no-covenant basis, with tranches tied to contracted seasons and lender consent; the covenant case is the planning case, not the only case.
rows.confidence: Medium; depends entirely on a document the team does not have.
rows.follow_up: Confirm whether the $1.5M test is a financial covenant, a springing test or an unused-commitment condition.

rows.finding: $3.2M ARR = $1.4M contracted 2027 robot-seasons at $12,700 + $1.2M Tallis engineering services ending 2027-06-30 + $0.6M signed LOIs; 56% is non-recurring or non-binding and the $72M pre-money is 51x the $1.4M contracted robot revenue.
rows.mechanism: The headline blends a one-season rental book, a related-party services contract and non-binding letters, so it overstates revenue that recurs without re-selling.
rows.benchmark: 22.5x headline ARR versus 51x contracted robot revenue at $72M pre-money; SaaS rule-of-thumb revenue multiples.
rows.weakens: The $1.4M contracts are themselves unverified and are one-season, so even the 51x base may not recur.
rows.implication: Underwrite on contracted robot-seasons at list or renewal price, not on the $3.2M; a price above $50M needs the services line replaced by robot revenue.
rows.confidence: High on the split (deck arithmetic); low on contract enforceability.
rows.follow_up: Obtain the 110 executed 2027 grower contracts and the 50 LOIs with expiry and cancellation terms.

rows.finding: FY2028 RaaS of $12.9M is stated at the $16,500 list (782 robot-seasons, 5.5% of 50,000 acres) but the plan's FY2027 line ($4.6M/360 = $12,778) implies the $12,700 renewal, which needs 1,016 seasons, 7.1% of acreage, 422-656 new robots and $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex.
rows.mechanism: Mixing list and renewal prices changes the adoption share and the capex needed; the 2% adoption assumption in the deck is exceeded on either basis.
rows.benchmark: Deck's 2% 2028 adoption assumption; 3.5 acres per robot; 50,000 US strawberry acres.
rows.weakens: FY2028 is a projection with no contracted volume; both bases rely on unverified acreage and price assumptions.
rows.implication: Treat the 2028 plan as a capacity requirement, not a forecast; the round does not fund the fleet it implies.
rows.confidence: Medium; arithmetic high, inputs unverified.
rows.follow_up: State the price and adoption basis for every projection year and reconcile to the 2% assumption.

rows.finding: Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) with no reason disclosed, while contracting 20 for 2027; Grower E exited in 2026-06 over bruising, Grower D has no 2027 contract, 6 of 8 other pilots have no LOI and 9 of 14 pilot farms never paid.
rows.mechanism: The 2027 contracted book is an expansion bet on four relationships, one of which just cut its fleet; retention, not new logos, carries the plan.
rows.benchmark: Five paying growers in 2026; four contracted for 2027; 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 those four rented in 2026.
rows.weakens: The deck does not disclose why Grower B cut, so the cut could reflect acreage or planting rather than performance.
rows.implication: Diligence the reason for the cut and the renewal terms before pricing; a second Grower B would remove 20 of the 110 contracted robots.
rows.confidence: High on the counts; low on causation.
rows.follow_up: Ask Grower B and Grower D for the reason for the cut and their 2027 intentions; obtain the 2026 service logs.

rows.finding: CAC is not reported; an estimated $0.9-1.2M of sales cost (five sales staff at $180,000-240,000 fully loaded) over three new paying growers in 2026 is $300,000-400,000 a grower, $8,000-11,000 per contracted 2027 robot or $24,000-32,000 per robot added in 2026; LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal.
rows.mechanism: A field-sales model with pilots and a once-a-year buying window front-loads acquisition cost before a four-season asset earns contribution; at renewal prices there is no contribution to recover it.
rows.benchmark: 3x LTV:CAC venture benchmark; $12,600 of four-season contribution per robot at the $16,500 list.
rows.weakens: Sales and marketing spend, pilot costs and sales-cycle length are not disclosed, so the range rests on headcount and assumed fully loaded cost.
rows.implication: CAC must be cut or list price held; a renewal-priced book cannot pay back acquisition, which is why the 2027 plan needs list-price contracts.
rows.confidence: Low-to-medium; an estimate with stated assumptions, not a disclosed figure.
rows.follow_up: Request sales and marketing spend by year, pilot cost per farm and the number of sales-qualified opportunities.

rows.finding: Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the $9,500 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 per season of 2027 overhead.
rows.mechanism: Depreciation is a real cash-equivalent cost of the fleet; excluding it from gross margin turns a -85% contract at the 2026 price into a reported 41% margin.
rows.benchmark: Deere FY2024: 17.5% operating margin and 22.8% ROIC on a mature equipment book.
rows.weakens: The four-season life and $31,000 target cost are company assumptions; a six-season life raises the renewal yield toward zero, not to Deere's level.
rows.implication: Even the list-price case earns half of Deere's ROIC before overhead; the renewal book is below the cost of capital, so growth at renewal prices destroys value.
rows.confidence: High on arithmetic; medium on the Deere comparison because fleet rental and equipment sale are different models.
rows.follow_up: Get a four-season maintenance and residual-value record for the 64-robot fleet; the yield depends on life and resale.

plan.decision_question: Do the unit economics and the cash plan support a venture-scale outcome, and what does the reported revenue mix hide?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin is a grant- and related-party-funded pilot business whose robot-season loses money after depreciation and whose $18M round buys one season, not a Series B; the equity is a conditional option on a 2027 fleet contracted at list pricing and a v4 at target cost, with the covenant date and the no-covenant down-round case as the two ways to price it.
plan.why_different: Section 7 tests the statements, the dated cash position, the accounting quality and the financing plan; section 6 tests price and unit economics per robot-season.
plan.mechanism: Fleet capex is paid before the season, depreciation sits in opex, revenue is concentrated in a related-party services contract and grants that end, and a minimum-cash covenant converts a financing delay into a lender event.
plan.comparison_set: Deere FY2024 operating margin 17.5% and ROIC 22.8%; 3x burn multiple; private ag-robotics peers (Monarch, Carbon, Advanced Farm, Harvest CROO); the deck's own 2% 2028 adoption and 360-robot plan.
plan.counter_evidence: The no-covenant case leaves the company alive to a down round; 110 contracted robots and 50 LOIs are real demand evidence; the $18M case reaches end-2027 with $2.6-3.6M if the plan holds; list-price sales would turn contribution positive.
plan.visual: The six-year statements table, the returns and working-capital table, the deck claim-verification table and an info danger box on the dated covenant runway.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong team', 'huge market', 'high barriers to entry', 'well positioned', 'risks are manageable'; no unlabelled company claims; no invented figures; no internal review, request or bot identifiers.

exit.author: Valuation Analyst
queries: Deere Blue River Technology acquisition 305 million
Deere Bear Flag Robotics acquisition $250 million 2021
CNH Industrial Raven Industries acquisition $2.1 billion revenue multiple
Abundant Robotics shut down 2021 apple harvesting robot raised
Harvest CROO Robotics funding raised strawberry picking machine
Carbon Robotics Series D funding valuation agricultural robotics
Monarch Tractor Series C funding $133 million valuation

rows.finding: The only named buyers with a track record of paying for ag autonomy are Deere (Blue River $305M in September 2017; Bear Flag Robotics $250M in August 2021; GUSS listed in its FY2025 10-K business description), CNH (Raven Industries $2.1B EV, 6.0x sales, June 2021) and Kubota (a Series A investor in Advanced Farm Technologies, the strawberry-harvesting competitor).
rows.mechanism: OEMs buy autonomy assets to defend precision-ag share and to avoid a competitor owning the perception layer; a strawberry picker is a beachhead into specialty crops where Deere and CNH have limited harvesting automation.
rows.benchmark: Blue River $305M (2017) and Bear Flag $250M (2021) were pre-scale autonomy acquisitions; Raven $2.1B was a $348.4M-revenue platform at 6.0x sales.
rows.weakens: The precedents are row-crop and precision-ag deals, not strawberry harvesting; no precedent shows an OEM paying for a specialty-crop picking robot at scale.
rows.implication: The exit universe is narrow and OEM-led; an IPO is not a route, and a private-equity buyer is unlikely for a pre-profit fleet owner with $1.6M of secured debt.
rows.confidence: high on the transactions and prices; medium on transferability to a strawberry picker
rows.follow_up: Has Deere or CNH signed any letter of intent, evaluation agreement or minority investment with Orrin, and does the Calder licence survive a change of control?

rows.finding: Precedent exit values cluster at $250M-$305M for pre-scale autonomy and $2.1B for a scaled precision-ag platform; at a $150M-$300M exit Meridian's 13.33% stake is worth $20.0M-$40.0M before dilution, 1.67x-3.33x its $12M.
rows.mechanism: Exit value is set by the buyer's strategic alternative (build versus buy) and by the scarcity of the licence; with no revenue multiple on the target asset, the price is negotiated against the cost of building the capability.
rows.benchmark: CNH/Raven 6.0x EV/Sales; Deere paid $250M-$305M for pre-scale autonomy; Root AI $60M.
rows.weakens: The AppHarvest/Root AI $60M deal is the most recent harvesting-robot acquisition and it cleared far below $150M, which is the relevant low-end data point.
rows.implication: A $250M-$300M OEM exit is the outcome the current price requires; a $150M exit returns 1.67x, below the 3x a venture fund needs.
rows.confidence: high on figures; low-medium on the $150M-$300M range applied to Orrin
rows.follow_up: What revenue, robot count and licence status would a strategic buyer's diligence require before paying $250M?

rows.finding: The 2027-12-31 Calder licence test (100 robots in commercial service, or exclusivity is lost) and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on the fleet sit between the investor and an exit: the licence is the asset a strategic buyer would pay for, and the fleet lender must consent to any asset sale.
rows.mechanism: A buyer pays for exclusivity and for the right to use the patents; if the licence becomes non-exclusive, the strategic premium collapses to the value of the fleet and the team.
rows.benchmark: Total preference stack $36.8M-$39.3M against a $40M exit: common zero, Series A about 1.0x.
rows.weakens: The deck says the licence becomes non-exclusive only below 100 robots at 2027-12-31, and the plan is 360 robots, so the test is likely to be cleared if the plan is funded.
rows.implication: The exit is a binary licence outcome before it is a price outcome; if the 100-robot test fails, the buyer is buying a non-exclusive licence and the $250M-$300M scenario goes away.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the Calder licence permit assignment on a change of control, and does Kestrel have a change-of-control consent or prepayment penalty?

rows.finding: An IPO is not a credible route before 2030-2031: the 2028 plan reaches $13.2M of revenue with a $6.9M net loss, and the market backdrop is hostile to hardware listings, with the industrial sector ETF down 6.9% over three months against the S&P 500, the 10-year Treasury at 4.93% and the VIX at 19.42 (77th percentile of its one-year range).
rows.mechanism: Listings need scale, a growth story and a receptive sector tape; Orrin has none of the three in 2026-2028, so the buyer set is corporate.
rows.benchmark: 2028 plan: $13.2M revenue, $6.9M net loss; public ag-equipment median 2.7x EV/Sales; XLI -6.9% over three months vs SPY.
rows.weakens: A 2031 window could reopen if rates fall and the industrial sector re-rates; the VIX at 19.42 is elevated but not a crisis level.
rows.implication: The exit must be a trade sale; the investor should not underwrite an IPO and should negotiate drag-along and tag-along terms that make a trade sale executable.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What revenue and profitability would a Nasdaq listing require in 2030, and is a direct listing or a secondary sale a faster liquidity path for the Series A?

rows.finding: The failure case is a liquidation, not a slow exit: Abundant Robotics sold its IP and assets on 2021-06-29 after failing to raise, and Harvest CROO remains at seed stage after 14 rounds and $10M raised since 2014.
rows.mechanism: Harvesting robots carry little liquidation value because the fleet is custom, the IP is early-stage and the grower contracts are seasonal; the preference stack only matters if there is an enterprise value above it.
rows.benchmark: Abundant raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Harvest CROO has raised $10M since 2013; Orrin has raised $38.5M of equity and notes.
rows.weakens: Orrin has more revenue and a larger fleet than Abundant had at shutdown, so its floor is higher than zero.
rows.implication: A lead should underwrite a liquidation floor of well below the $12M check; the 1x preference does not protect against a sub-$36.8M asset sale.
rows.confidence: high on facts; medium on base-rate application
rows.follow_up: What is the recovery value of the 64-robot fleet and the patent portfolio if the 2027 season fails?

rows.finding: The entry price changes the exit math more than any term: at the $72M pre Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M; at a $50M pre its 17.65% returns 2.2x at $150M and 4.4x at $300M.
rows.mechanism: Ownership is the multiplier on every exit value; a 32% lower entry price buys 32% more of the company for the same check.
rows.benchmark: $72M pre: 13.33% for $12M; $50M pre: 17.65% for $12M in a $68M post.
rows.weakens: A lower price may not be available if the company has competing term sheets at $72M; the investor's leverage is the $14M gap and the 2026-12-15 close date.
rows.implication: Repricing to $48M-$55M or tranching the last $6M is the only structural change that makes the exit range produce a venture return.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic
rows.follow_up: Will existing holders accept a $48M-$55M pre, or is the round only available at $72M with a tranche?

plan.decision_question: Through which named exit, at what value and when, can a Series A investor realize a venture return, and what licence, debt and related-party tests block it?
plan.thesis_sentence: The realistic exit is a sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M, which at the $72M pre-money returns Meridian 1.7x-3.3x; the deal depends on the 2027 licence test and the first full season, not on an IPO, and the price should be set with that range in view.
plan.why_different: This section prices the way out: who buys, which asset they buy, when the asset becomes buyable, and what the Series A stake is worth at each exit value. It does not repeat the valuation methods or the operating plan.
plan.mechanism: An OEM buys the perception model, the exclusive Calder licence and the labelled harvest dataset to defend precision-ag share in specialty crops; the buyer's willingness to pay depends on the licence remaining exclusive and on the 2027 season proving the fleet, so the 2027-12-31 test and the first full commercial season set both the timing and the price.
plan.comparison_set: Strategic precedents: Deere/Blue River $305M (2017), Deere/Bear Flag $250M (2021), CNH/Raven $2.1B at 6.0x sales (2021), AppHarvest/Root AI $60M (2021); failure: Abundant Robotics liquidation 2021 after $12M raised, Harvest CROO $10M since 2013. Public market backdrop: XLI -6.9% over three months vs SPY, 10-year Treasury 4.93%, VIX 19.42.
plan.counter_evidence: Deere already has an in-house autonomy portfolio (Blue River, Bear Flag, GUSS) and may not need a strawberry picker; the Calder licence can go non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, which removes the asset a buyer would pay for; hardware exits trade below software and the current industrial tape is hostile to listings.
plan.visual: Exit-routes table (route, named buyer or venue, rationale, timing, likelihood, source) and a precedent-exits table (transaction, year, value, multiple, source), plus a small return-by-entry-price table.
plan.prohibited: IPO or M&A as a generic answer; huge market; well positioned; about; many; recently; internal tool, record or bot names; review or request IDs

rows.finding: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, both pre-scale autonomy platforms; CNH paid $2.1B (6.0x sales) for Raven. No precedent bought a harvesting robot.
rows.mechanism: OEMs buy autonomy technology and teams before scale to avoid building perception and controls in-house, but the price tracks strategic fit with their existing platform.
rows.benchmark: Deere/Blue River $305M (2017) and Deere/Bear Flag $250M (2021); CNH/Raven $2.1B at 6.0x sales.
rows.weakens: Blue River and Bear Flag were row-crop platforms that plugged into Deere's dealer network; a specialty-crop picker has no such channel.
rows.implication: A $250M-$300M trade sale is a plausible upper case but not the base case; set the entry price to a $150M-$300M range.
rows.confidence: high on the transactions; medium on the inference for Orrin.
rows.follow_up: Would Deere pay a strategic price for a harvesting dataset when its autonomy programme is row-crop focused?

rows.finding: The peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit: Advanced Farm ceased operations on 2025-07-08, Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii on 2025-03-24, and Abundant sold its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29.
rows.mechanism: Repeated failures reduce the buyer set and the price a strategic will pay, because the buyer can wait for a distressed asset.
rows.benchmark: Named US strawberry-harvesting peers: Advanced Farm ($25M Series B, 2021), Tortuga ($47.7M raised), Abundant ($12M raised).
rows.weakens: Carbon Robotics ($232M) and Monarch Tractor ($133M Series C) show capital still reaches category leaders.
rows.implication: Underwrite to an asset-sale floor and demand the 2027 licence test before a second tranche.
rows.confidence: high on the events; medium on the causes.
rows.follow_up: Did Advanced Farm sell any assets, or was the shutdown a pure liquidation?

rows.finding: The Calder licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31; its assignment and change-of-control terms are not in the deck.
rows.mechanism: Exclusivity is the asset a buyer pays for; without it the buyer is acquiring commodity hardware and a dataset it could license elsewhere.
rows.benchmark: Contract term: exclusive licence over two patent families, 2.5% net-revenue royalty, $40,000 annual minimum.
rows.weakens: If the licence is non-exclusive, the company can still sell the fleet and data, but at an asset value, not a strategic one.
rows.implication: The 2027 licence test is the gating event for any sale; a buyer will discount or walk if it is missed.
rows.confidence: high on the deck terms; assignment and change-of-control terms not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Does Calder consent to a change of control or an asset sale, and on what terms?

rows.finding: The $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, and the $1.6M Kestrel facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing.
rows.mechanism: Secured debt and a minimum-cash covenant turn a timing miss into a default, which can force a sale at the wrong point in the cycle.
rows.benchmark: Series A target close 2026-12-15; 2027 California season and first collections in April-July 2027.
rows.weakens: The company could cure with a small bridge or an equity cure if the covenant permits one; not disclosed.
rows.implication: A financing slip or a forced sale before the 2027 season hands the lender and noteholders the negotiating position.
rows.confidence: high; derived from disclosed cash, covenant and burn.
rows.follow_up: What are the Kestrel change-of-control and asset-sale consent terms and fees?

rows.finding: Kubota and Yamaha participated in Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in 2021 and CNH took a stake in 2022; the company ceased operations in July 2025, leaving both OEMs without the harvesting asset they backed.
rows.mechanism: A closed portfolio company is both a reason to buy the next asset and a reason to demand proof, so it shortens the buyer list without raising the price.
rows.benchmark: Kubota and CNH both invested in Advanced Farm Technologies, which ceased operations in July 2025.
rows.weakens: The OEMs may conclude the category is uninvestable and exit the buyer set entirely.
rows.implication: OEM appetite exists but comes with first-hand evidence of failure; expect a lower price or a milestone-structured deal.
rows.confidence: high on the investments and the shutdown; medium on buyer intent.
rows.follow_up: Are Kubota or CNH building an in-house strawberry programme, or looking for a replacement asset?

rows.finding: At $72M pre-money Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M, 2.78x at $250M and 3.33x at $300M; at $50M pre-money 17.65% returns 2.21x, 3.68x and 4.41x.
rows.mechanism: The entry multiple sets the MOIC; the preference stack means the first $36.8M of exit value goes to preferred, so the common and new money need a high exit to compound.
rows.benchmark: 3x gross MOIC Series A target; $150M-$300M exit range.
rows.weakens: A $300M strategic sale returns 3.33x even at $72M pre-money.
rows.implication: Reprice to $48M-$55M or tranche; the exit range alone does not produce a venture return at $72M.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic; medium on exit range.
rows.follow_up: What does the 2031 plan's $35.4M revenue ceiling support at 4-6x sales?

rows.finding: California's agricultural wage floor is $16.90/hour from 2026-01-01, with overtime at 1.5x after 8 hours/day and 40 hours/week since 2022 (26+ employees) or 2025 (25 or fewer) and double time after 12 hours; the 2026 California H-2A AEWR is reported at $19.97/hour and AB 2646 sets a $19.75/hour floor for non-resident agricultural employees.
rows.mechanism: Rising hourly floors and overtime make the hand crew more expensive per tray each season, widening the gap between hand-pick cost and Orrin's $9,500 robot-season price and pulling growers toward mechanisation.
rows.benchmark: 2026 general minimum $16.90 vs the $19.97 H-2A floor and $19.75 AB 2646 floor; 2027 minimum scheduled at $17.40.
rows.weakens: AEWR and AB 2646 figures come from secondary summaries, not the DOL table or chaptered bill; a freeze or cut in the AEWR would narrow the gap.
rows.implication: Demand tailwind is real and policy-driven; underwrite adoption as a function of the wage floor, not as a permanent moat.
rows.confidence: high on minimum and overtime (DIR), medium on AEWR and AB 2646 (secondary)
rows.follow_up: Obtain OFLC H-2A disclosure data and the 2026 AEWR table (request U9).

rows.finding: USMCA-qualifying Mexican goods enter the US at 0% duty, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24 on top of MFN; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content (transaction value) or 50% (net cost) and documented origin. Sources conflict on whether a 25% IEEPA surtax or a 10% Section 122 charge applies to non-qualifying goods.
rows.mechanism: If the Guadalajara-assembled robots or subassemblies fail origin, roughly 10% of the $33,000 v4 unit cost (about $3,300 a robot) lands on Orrin, against a 41% 2026 gross margin and a $9,500 selling price.
rows.benchmark: $33,000 average v4 unit cost in the deck's $9.9M robot budget; 10% duty equals about $3,300 per robot.
rows.weakens: Orrin may already qualify; a shift to US assembly removes the duty; the tariff stack itself is inconsistent across secondary sources and may change at the 2027 review.
rows.implication: Make a USMCA certification or CBP ruling a closing condition; do not underwrite Mexican assembly without it.
rows.confidence: low to medium: no primary customs notice could be opened in this run
rows.follow_up: Obtain Orrin's USMCA certification and the HTS 8433 product-specific rule (request U10).

rows.finding: No Orrin product-safety certification, recall or enforcement record is disclosed; the machine works at night around harvest crews, had 3.8% bruising and 2.1% mistaken unripe picks in 2025 pilots, and one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets the design-safety standard for autonomous agricultural machinery and Cal/OSHA has published a framework review of such standards; the FDA Produce Safety Rule imposes equipment and food-contact-surface sanitation on the grower.
rows.mechanism: An injury or a pathogen event traced to machine contact would trigger strict product liability, grower indemnity claims and reputational damage, and could force design changes or certification before fleet scale; bruising also raises decay and rejection risk that growers price into renewal.
rows.benchmark: ISO 18497-1:2024 as the design benchmark; 3.8% bruising vs the deck's own ~5% acceptability threshold; the Grower E exit as a realised quality failure.
rows.weakens: No California rule specifically mandates ISO 18497; the standard is voluntary; FDA requirements fall on growers, not directly on Orrin, and no incident is public.
rows.implication: Price product-liability exposure and make insurance limits, exclusions and incident logs diligence conditions.
rows.confidence: medium to high on the standards, low on Orrin's compliance because it is undisclosed
rows.follow_up: Obtain insurance certificates, autonomous-machinery exclusions, OSHA 300 logs and incident reports (request U11, U12).

rows.finding: Orrin's Mexican subsidiary has 7 staff and must comply with IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing; dismissal without cause costs at least three months' salary plus seniority premium.
rows.mechanism: The absolute cost is small at 7 employees, but PTU is a profit-linked liability, IMSS/INFONAVIT add mandatory payroll cost, and a subsidiary with its own payroll and profit-sharing obligations needs separate governance and transfer-pricing discipline.
rows.benchmark: 7 of 38 employees in Mexico (18%); $650,000 SBIR and $1.9M FY2025 revenue set the scale against which any labour liability is immaterial.
rows.weakens: No evidence of non-compliance; the subsidiary is an assembly operation, not a maquila shelter, so exposure is routine rather than structural.
rows.implication: Not a valuation driver, but a governance and reporting item; require Mexican payroll and PTU compliance evidence.
rows.confidence: medium: advisory summaries, not the statute text
rows.follow_up: Confirm IMSS/INFONAVIT registration and PTU provision in the data room.

rows.finding: The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award (2024-2026) brings Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference for products embodying subject inventions under 35 U.S.C. 204, and audit exposure; a recent executive order pushes agencies toward taking title and requiring domestic manufacturing.
rows.mechanism: If any Orrin invention was made under the award and is assembled in Guadalajara, the US-manufacturing preference could require a waiver or reshoring, and an audit or title dispute would cloud the IP that the Calder licence and the patent portfolio depend on.
rows.benchmark: Grant revenue $0.30M in FY2025, 16% of $1.9M revenue, and $0.35M projected for FY2026; the award ends in 2026.
rows.weakens: A waiver is available; the clause covers only subject inventions; Orrin may be able to show US assembly or that the robots do not embody award-funded inventions.
rows.implication: Require a Bayh-Dole compliance opinion and SBIR data-rights schedule before closing; treat grant revenue as ending in 2026.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Obtain the USDA SBIR award terms, invention disclosure and US-manufacturing plan.

rows.finding: Governance concentrates control and related-party flows: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025-2026; Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M/year customer, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor in this round; the independent board seat is vacant; two of five seats are common; the departed CTO retains 720,000 shares.

rows.benchmark: $310,000 related-party payments equal 16% of FY2025 revenue; $1.2M Tallis revenue equals 63% of FY2025 revenue; 5-seat board with 1 independent seat vacant.
rows.weakens: The board approved the Vashti contract and Tallis's roles are disclosed; the amounts are small in absolute terms and may be at market.
rows.implication: Make an independent director, a related-party approval committee and information rights conditions of the investment.
rows.confidence: high on the facts (company deck), unverified independently
rows.follow_up: Obtain the Vashti and Tallis contracts, board minutes and related-party approvals.
