plan.decision_question: Which regulations and policies materially change Orrin's ability to sell, price and operate in California, Florida and Mexico, and what ESG liabilities should an investor price?
plan.thesis_sentence: ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 before a statutory 2027 rebound, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around night crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor with little control.
plan.why_different: Other sections price demand, unit economics and technology; this section prices the rules that set the hand-pick cost, the tariff and safety regimes around the machine, and the related-party terms - exposures that survive a good product.
plan.mechanism: Wage floors set the hand-pick cost the robot replaces; the 2026 AEWR cut lowered it, and AB 2646 restores it in 2027. USMCA origin decides whether about 10% duty lands on the $33,000 unit cost; safety standards and liability set insurance and design cost; related-party contracts move cash and control away from new investors.
plan.comparison_set: California 2025 vs 2026 vs 2027 wage floors; H-2A vs state-minimum growers; California vs Florida AEWR cuts; USMCA-qualifying vs non-qualifying Mexican assembly; ISO 18497-certified vs uncertified machines; related-party intensity vs venture-stage norms.
plan.counter_evidence: The 2026 AEWR cut lowered California H-2A pay to $16.90 and Florida's to $12.47, easing labour scarcity; a replacement methodology could keep rates low; machine bruising (3.8%) and the Grower E exit; Orrin may already satisfy USMCA; no mandatory California robot standard.
plan.visual: Policy impact matrix with jurisdictions, dates, probability and mitigants, supported by the regulatory record and ESG issues tables.
plan.prohibited: No empty ESG language ('ESG is important', 'strong governance', 'risks are manageable'), no vague counts, no unlabelled company claims, no generic policy essay.

rows.finding: The deck's bottom-up is 50,000 US strawberry acres / 3.5 acres per robot = 14,286 robots x $16,500 list = $235.7M a year at 100% adoption. The claimed $310M obtainable market is 31% larger than that ceiling and requires 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, or 132% of the US base.
rows.mechanism: Robot revenue equals acres divided by acres per robot times price per robot-season; the deck's own adoption and pricing cannot produce its stated obtainable market from strawberries.
rows.benchmark: Management's 15%-by-2031 adoption: 7,500 acres, 2,143 robots, $35.4M at list or $27.2M at the $12,700 renewal price, 9-11% of the claimed $310M.
rows.weakens: The $3.1B serviceable market is a labour-spend figure (13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool), not a revenue number.
rows.implication: Underwrite a $27-35M 2031 revenue opportunity, not $310M; the $72M pre-money cannot be supported by the strawberry SOM alone.
rows.confidence: high on arithmetic, low on the 50,000-acre input
rows.follow_up: What NASS strawberry acreage by state has been for 2019-2025, and does the $3.1B include non-strawberry soft fruit?

rows.finding: The stated adoption glide path conflicts with the financial plan: 2% of 50,000 acres in 2028 is 1,000 acres or 286 robots, about $4.7M at list, but FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 1,016 robots, 3,556 acres and 7.1% adoption, 3.6x the stated 2%.
rows.mechanism: Either adoption is three times faster than stated, or realised price is far below list; the deck never reconciles the two.
rows.benchmark: Company plan of 360 robots for 2027 and 64 robots in the 2026 fleet.
rows.weakens: The 2%-to-15% glide path cannot be used to test the financial plan because the plan already assumes more than the glide path.
rows.implication: Ask management which number is the plan and price the round on the lower of the two.
rows.confidence: medium-high (derived from deck figures)
rows.follow_up: What average price and robot count underpin FY2028 RaaS revenue?

rows.finding: Price realisation is the margin lever and it is unproven: contracts sold at $9,500 in 2025-26, 2027 renewals average $12,700 (+34%) and the 2027 list is $16,500 (+74%). At $9,500 the gross profit is $3,900 per robot-season, 41%, before $12,000 a season of depreciation on a $48,000 v3 robot.
rows.mechanism: A 74% price rise with unchanged service cost would lift gross margin to about 66%; without it, contribution after depreciation is negative.
rows.benchmark: Deck's own 2026 contract price and its 60%+ at-scale margin projection.
rows.weakens: The claim that the business reaches 60% gross margin depends on a price no grower has yet paid.
rows.implication: Underwrite the renewal price, not the list price, and condition the round on realised renewal pricing.
rows.confidence: high (deck arithmetic)
rows.follow_up: How many of the 110 contracted 2027 robots are signed at $12,700 versus $16,500?

rows.finding: Season length sets robot utilisation: a 7-month California season (April-October) at 1.5 acres per 24 hours, 20 hours a day and 86% uptime covers about 226 acre-passes, roughly 64 passes over 3.5 acres, consistent with picking every three to four days. Florida's December-March window of about 120 days covers about 2.0-2.5 acres per robot, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre instead of $4,714.
rows.mechanism: Utilisation, not labour cost, determines the per-acre price of a robot-season; short-season Florida is a worse unit-economics market unless robots are redeployed to California.
rows.benchmark: One robot per 3.5 acres in California; 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each, one paid season per robot, so no cross-season redeployment is assumed.
rows.weakens: The Florida expansion case rests on counter-season utilisation that the financial plan does not use.
rows.implication: Value Florida as fleet-utilisation capacity, not as a stand-alone market, and test redeployment logistics.
rows.confidence: medium (derived with stated assumptions)
rows.follow_up: Can a robot serve Florida December-March and California April-October, and what does transport cost per move?

rows.mechanism: A shrinking acreage base reduces both the robot count and the serviceable market proportionally, and makes a 15% adoption target harder to reach.
rows.benchmark: Deck's ~50,000 US strawberry acres, company estimate, unverified.
rows.weakens: The deck's acreage figure and its assumption of a stable base.
rows.implication: Request NASS and California Strawberry Commission acreage before underwriting the TAM; a 10% acreage decline removes about $24M from the 100%-adoption ceiling.
rows.confidence: low (strawberry line not retrieved)
rows.follow_up: What is NASS strawberry bearing acreage for California and Florida in 2019-2025?

rows.finding: Labour-cost policy is the demand driver and it is reset annually: the H-2A adverse-effect wage rate for 2026 was published on 2026-08-03 and California's agricultural overtime rules raise the cost of peak-season hours; neither the H-2A position counts nor wage levels could be retrieved in this run.
rows.mechanism: A regulated wage floor plus overtime after long days raises the marginal cost of hand harvest, which is the budget the robot displaces.
rows.benchmark: Deck's claim that crews are smaller and older each year (grower interviews, 2025) is company-reported and unverified.
rows.weakens: The urgency claim rests on company interviews; if H-2A supply is elastic and wages flat, adoption slips.
rows.implication: Demand is organic, not subsidy-driven, but its timing depends on policy; watch the annual AEWR and H-2A certification volumes.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: How many H-2A positions were certified for California and Florida berry growers in FY2023-FY2026, and what is the California AEWR?

plan.decision_question: Is the strawberry harvest-labour problem large and urgent enough to support the company's claimed $3.1B serviceable and $310M obtainable market by 2031, and does the bottom-up robot math hold?
plan.thesis_sentence: The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: 100% of US strawberry acres is worth $235.7M of robot revenue at the 2027 list price, so the $310M obtainable market is 31% larger than the entire crop, and the wage floor fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute only in 2027, so urgency is dated rather than permanent.
plan.why_different: Sizes the opportunity and tests the deck's arithmetic against USDA, wage and trade records; the other sections test the machine, the price and the exit.
plan.mechanism: Robot revenue equals acres divided by acres per robot times price per robot-season; adoption is gated by harvest quality and season length, not by willingness to pay.
plan.comparison_set: 100% adoption ceiling vs claimed SOM; 15% adoption; FY2028 revenue-implied adoption; Florida vs California acres per robot; 2025 noncitrus acreage trend.
plan.counter_evidence: The 2026 H-2A cut and litigation lower the hand-labour floor; strawberry acreage may be shrinking; one Florida grower exited over bruising.
plan.visual: Market size table and regional market table
plan.prohibited: 'huge market', 'strong tailwind', 'frictionless adoption', 'recently', 'about', 'many growers'

Tortuga AgTech USAspending search (no federal awards)
SEC EDGAR full-text search for 'Root AI' (AppHarvest filings S81-S90) and 'strawberry harvesting robot' (no results)
Read Deere FY2025 10-K Item 1 with keywords strawberry, berry, robotic harvest (no mention)

Read registered peer sources in the shared case file: Harvest CROO press release S1, JFR modular strawberry robot S42, WSU hidden-fruit robot S56, Xiong et al. S57, Advanced Farm closure S114, Tortuga/Oishii S115, advanced Farm Series B S93 and CNH investment S117, Abundant Robotics S91, Deere/Bear Flag S92, Deere/Blue River S96, CNH/Raven S95, Monarch S54, Carbon Robotics S55 and S119

rows.finding: The 'only autonomous open-field picker above 90%' claim is a measurement definition, not a capability gap: 94% is berries picked divided by berries the vision system classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded and rows chosen by Orrin's field team. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected or pluckable fruit.
rows.mechanism: Conditioning the denominator on detected fruit and the sample on favourable rows inflates the reported rate; adjusted for detection, harvest recovery is around 80%, and about 75% after bruising and unripe picks.
rows.benchmark: WSU 2025 (74% of ripe, 20 s per berry); JFR 2025 (83-87% of detected/pluckable); JFR 2019 (50-97.1% across configurations).
rows.weakens: The company's claim of a unique 90%+ open-field capability.
rows.implication: Do not pay for a performance moat; ask for a third-party trial with detection rate and a hand-picked bruise control.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the detection rate on the same 212 rows, and what is the bruise rate against a hand-picked control after 72 hours?

rows.finding: Harvest CROO is the longest-funded direct competitor: NSF SBIR Phase I of $225,000 in 2016 and Phase II of $1,249,719 in 2018 ending 2023-09-30 to build 'a commercially viable robotic strawberry harvesting system', $10M raised over 14 rounds, 13 patents, and a 2025-04-24 claim of open-field Florida performance 'on par with human harvesting'. No paid fleet, price or shipment figures are disclosed.
rows.mechanism: A decade of public and private funding in the same crop and state means Orrin's lead is commercial execution, not technology access.
rows.benchmark: Orrin: 64 robots, 75 paid robot-seasons, about $21M raised.
rows.weakens: Any implication that Orrin is alone in claiming commercial readiness.
rows.implication: Price the round on service density and contracted acres, not on a technology lead.
rows.confidence: high on awards and funding; low on commercial status
rows.follow_up: How many Harvest CROO machines are in paid service, at what price, and with which Florida growers?

rows.finding: The category's base rate is failure or absorption: Advanced Farm Technologies, commercial in US strawberry harvesting from 2019, raised a $25M Series B and took a CNH investment, then ceased operations in July 2025; Tortuga AgTech's IP, assets and engineering team were acquired by Oishii on 2025-03-24; Abundant Robotics shut its fruit-harvesting business in 2021.
rows.mechanism: Strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner; capital and customer logos did not prevent failure.
rows.benchmark: Monarch Tractor over $220M raised; Carbon Robotics $232M across five rounds, both still private.
rows.weakens: The assumption that a $18M Series A is enough to build a national fleet.
rows.implication: Treat 2027 contracted acres as the gating milestone and plan for an OEM sale rather than independent scale.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Why did Advanced Farm fail after Driscoll's and California Giant deployments, and what happened to its fleet and contracts?

rows.finding: The exit route in agricultural robotics is acquisition by an equipment maker: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021, and CNH paid $2.1B for Raven Industries in 2021; Deere's FY2025 10-K business description mentions no berry or robotic harvesting product.
rows.mechanism: OEMs buy capability rather than build it, so a proven fleet and grower contracts are the saleable asset; the absence of an OEM product today means the threat is capital, not a current competitor.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's $72M pre-money against these transaction values.
rows.weakens: The idea that incumbents will not enter; it also supports a trade-sale path.
rows.implication: An OEM partnership or acquisition is the credible liquidity route; diligence whether Tallis or CNH has rights over the fleet or IP.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Does the Tallis manufacturing and board-observer relationship carry any option, right of first refusal or exclusivity?

rows.finding: The patents do not defend the position: the gripper application had every claim rejected in a first office action (response filed 2026-05), and the two perception families are licensed from a university and become non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31.
rows.mechanism: Without an enforceable estate, the defensible asset is the seasonal service organisation and grower contracts, which take years to replicate.
rows.benchmark: 64 robots in service today against the 100-robot license test in 14 months.
rows.weakens: The technology-moat narrative behind the valuation.
rows.implication: Condition the investment on the license threshold being met and on service cost per robot-season.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the prosecution status of US 17/902,118 after the May 2026 response, and will the 100-robot test be met?

rows.finding: The status quo is the share leader: hand crews pick nearly every US strawberry acre, harvest-aid platforms keep the crew and only make pickers faster, and the H-2A wage floor is reset annually (2026 rule published 2026-08-03) while California overtime rules raise peak-season cost.
rows.mechanism: A robot must beat a working labour system on quality before it beats it on cost; labour policy sets the pace of switching, not the direction.
rows.benchmark: Orrin's 75 paid robot-seasons against an addressable base of about 14,286 robot-equivalents at 3.5 acres each.
rows.weakens: The assumption that labour scarcity forces adoption on Orrin's timetable.
rows.implication: Track H-2A certification volumes and the annual AEWR; a looser labour market delays the adoption curve by a season or more.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: How many H-2A positions were certified for California and Florida berry growers in FY2023-FY2026?

rows.weakens: A well-funded entrant can now buy most of the software stack, so the lead is operational and time-limited.
rows.implication: Technology is not the moat; contracted acres and service density are.
rows.confidence: medium; estimate

Orrin deck pp.1-15 read for cash, covenant, entity structure, licence test, patent dates (client document)

rows.finding: $3.7M of cash less the $1.5M Kestrel minimum-cash balance leaves $2.2M, 5.4 months at $410,000 a month, putting the covenant around 2027-03-14; $4.0M of $18M was committed on 2026-10-31 against a 2026-12-15 target close (45 days); a $12M minimum close gives $15.37M of cash and facility against $17.0M of robots and 2027 cash operating loss, a $1.63M hole before working capital.
rows.mechanism: A minimum-cash covenant converts a financing delay into a secured-lender default; the lender's claim on the fleet ranks ahead of the preferred, so a delay destroys equity rather than diluting it. Negotiators who take longer to reprice consume the runway they are protecting.
rows.benchmark: Six-month delay adds $2.46M of burn; cash on 2027-06-15 would be $1.24M, below the $1.5M floor an entire quarter before the money arrives.
rows.weakens: A Kestrel waiver, standstill or insider bridge could remove the trigger; the loan agreement may define the covenant on a broader cash measure.
rows.implication: Make a signed Kestrel waiver and a close by 2027-01 conditions precedent; at $48M-$55M the same cash problem remains, so repricing alone does not fix it.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic; medium on the covenant terms, because the Kestrel loan agreement is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What is the Kestrel agreement's minimum-cash definition, cross-default clause and waiver price?

rows.finding: The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms chosen by the field team, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit, giving 75-80% harvest recovery after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks.
rows.mechanism: Removing undetected fruit from the denominator converts a detection failure into a picking success; harvest-level recovery is what decides whether a crew is replaced or supplemented, and therefore whether the price is a labour substitution or a harvest-aid rental.
rows.benchmark: Mechanical blueberry harvest shows severe bruising in 78% of fruit against 23% by hand (Brown et al. 1996); Orrin's 3.8% has no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale.
rows.weakens: If detection is near 100% on commercial blocks, harvest recovery approaches the reported 94% and the machine does replace crews.
rows.implication: -40% to -60% of enterprise value; at 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots rather than 360, and a reprice to $48M-$55M is not enough.
rows.confidence: medium-high that harvest recovery is 75-80%; low on the exact bruise differential
rows.follow_up: What is marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, on blocks the company did not select, against a hand-picked bruise control?

rows.finding: Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), a $2.5M noteholder, the quoted v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30; Vashti Harvest Services (COO-owned) was paid $310,000 inside the $3,100 service line; Marisol Ridge, the COO's employer to 2021, is 24 of 75 paid seasons.
rows.mechanism: One counterparty is simultaneously the largest revenue source, the only manufacturing route and a creditor, so its interests and the company's diverge exactly when the 2027 build needs capital; the related-party service contract sets the cost line that determines unit economics.
rows.benchmark: A second-source requirement is standard in contract manufacturing; four roles in one counterparty is not.
rows.weakens: Tallis may be a committed strategic partner whose interests genuinely align; the board approved the Vashti contract.
rows.implication: -35% to -50% of value if Tallis withdraws or re-quotes; require a fixed-price supply agreement, tooling ownership and a second source.
rows.confidence: high on the roles; medium on the amounts, which are unaudited
rows.follow_up: Will Tallis sign a fixed-price 300-unit supply agreement with tooling held by the issuer, and fund its $1.0M?

rows.finding: The Series A issuer holds the patent applications and the Calder licence; the 64-robot fleet, grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on that fleet sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC; no parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence or change-of-control term is disclosed. Every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05) and the platform PCT national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed.
rows.mechanism: Separating the licence from the revenue-generating assets means a buyer must take both entities or neither, and a break-up sale realises less than the sum of the parts; a secured lender inside the operating subsidiary ranks ahead of the parent's preferred.
rows.benchmark: Abundant Robotics and Tortuga AgTech both realised value by selling IP and assets separately, which this structure makes harder.
rows.weakens: The subsidiary is 100% owned, so a stock sale of the parent transfers everything at once; a parent guarantee may exist but be undisclosed.
rows.implication: -20% to -40% of recovery in a sale or insolvency; require an intercompany IP licence, a parent guarantee and Calder's consent to assignment.
rows.confidence: high on the structure and the rejection; low on the licence's assignment terms, which are not disclosed
rows.follow_up: Does the Calder licence permit assignment or change of control, how does it define commercial service, and was the PCT national phase entered on 2026-10-30?

rows.source_type: independent trade advisories plus a primary USTR notice
rows.finding: A 10% Section 301 duty applies to most Mexico-origin products from 2026-07-24 with USMCA-origin goods exempt; on a $33,000 robot that is $3,300, taking the v4 to $36,300 against a $36,000 milestone ceiling and a $31,000 target, and adding $825 a season of depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475. The USMCA joint review falls in 2027-07.
rows.mechanism: Electronics-heavy assembly in Guadalajara may fail USMCA regional value content, so the duty lands on landed cost; a $3,300 cost increase is 10% of unit cost against a 35% cost-reduction plan.
rows.benchmark: The company's own v4 target is $31,000; the milestone ceiling is $36,000. Duty alone consumes half the gap between them.
rows.weakens: If the robots qualify under USMCA rules of origin the duty is zero; component sourcing could be shifted.
rows.implication: -10% to -15% of value; require a USMCA origin opinion and a landed-cost bridge in the supply agreement.
rows.confidence: medium: the duty rate is documented, its application to these HTS lines is not
rows.follow_up: What is the USMCA regional value content of the v4 bill of materials, and what HTS line is used?

rows.finding: The US Department of Labor lowered the H-2A wage for many California jobs in 2025-10 and made dairy farms eligible in 2026-06, with California described as a candidate to become the largest H-2A employer; DailyRobotics reported a first California customer deployment from April 2026 at about 30 kg an hour, a ~4% bruise rate and one operator per eight robots.
rows.mechanism: Cheaper, more elastic hand labour lowers the grower's alternative cost and slows a purchase that can only be made once a year before planting; a second commercial vendor removes the exclusivity that supports list pricing.
rows.benchmark: Monarch Tractor raised over $240M, was valued above $500M, laid off its workforce and vacated its headquarters in 2026-03; farm-robotics venture funding fell 36% from Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below the year-earlier quarter.
rows.weakens: AEWR changes are annual and reversible, and one deployment is not a fleet; a wage cut slows conversion rather than stopping it.
rows.implication: -15% to -25% of value from 2028; price on fruit quality and hours, not on a rising wage floor.
rows.confidence: high on the policy facts and the competitor's stated plans; medium on whether DailyRobotics deployed at commercial scale
rows.follow_up: How many acres and robots did DailyRobotics actually deploy in California in the 2026 season?

plan.decision_question: Does Meridian lead at $48M-$55M with a Kestrel waiver, a Calder assignment consent and an independent harvest-level trial as conditions, or pass until the 2027 season produces them?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology: $2.2M of usable cash puts a secured-lender covenant around 2027-03-14, and the measurement that would justify any price has not been taken.
plan.why_different: The other sections price the business; this one prices the failure modes, orders them by probability and timing, and separates the dated, fatal covenant risk from the execution risks that only cost value.
plan.mechanism: A minimum-cash covenant converts a financing delay into a total loss of equity; a conditional university licence and a patent estate with no allowed claim cannot be sold separately from the fleet they operate, so recovery in a break-up falls below the preference stack; harvest-level recovery below 85% turns the product from a crew replacement into a harvest aid and reprices every figure in the plan.
plan.comparison_set: The category's base rate (Abundant 2021, Tortuga 2025, Advanced Farm 2025, Monarch 2026) is failure or absorption; the peer capital record (Monarch over $240M, Carbon $232M raised) shows scale of funding does not protect a vendor, and farm-robotics venture funding fell 57% year on year.
plan.counter_evidence: A Kestrel waiver or insider bridge removes the covenant trigger; if harvest recovery is genuinely above 90% on unselected blocks the machine replaces crews and $72M is cheap; the licence lapsing to non-exclusive does not stop Orrin operating.
plan.visual: risk-matrix with nine ranked risks plus a downside stress table (market -50%, revenue -30%, CAC 2x, financing +6 months) and a danger card for the thesis-breaking risk.
plan.prohibited: risks are manageable, well positioned, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, huge market, strong team, recently, about 5, any bot or record name, any sentence about how the report is written

rows.finding: Lely installed its 50,000th Astronaut robotic milking unit in 2024, 29 years after the first commercial unit in 1995, selling through dealer installation and after-sales service; 100 units were in use by 1997 and the installed base now milks about 3 million cows a day in 50 countries.
rows.mechanism: Capital-equipment robotics in agriculture is a decades-long replacement cycle sold with service, not a software-style land grab; the installed base compounds only as fast as dealers can install and support it.
rows.benchmark: Lely: 100 units after two commercial years, 50,000 after 29. Orrin: 64 robots after about four years, 360 planned for 2027.
rows.weakens: Orrin's 360-robot plan for one season assumes a ramp roughly six times its cumulative base in 12 months, faster than the category's most successful product scaled at any point.
rows.implication: Underwrite the 2027 plan as a stretch case, not a base case, and price the service capacity that the ramp requires.
rows.confidence: high on Lely's numbers; medium on the analogy because milking is a daily fixed route and strawberry picking is seasonal.
rows.follow_up: How many field technicians and dealer partners would Orrin need at 360 robots, and who installs and services them?

rows.finding: Deere paid $305 million for Blue River Technology in 2017, a 60-person pre-scale perception and spraying company, and $250 million for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021.
rows.mechanism: OEMs buy autonomy technology before revenue scale when it defends a core equipment franchise; the exit value is strategic, not a revenue multiple.
rows.benchmark: Blue River $305M; Bear Flag $250M; AppHarvest/Root AI $60M for a harvesting-specific team.
rows.weakens: A $150M-$300M exit is plausible only if an OEM sees the perception stack as franchise-defending; if the moat is a licensed university patent and rejected gripper claims, the strategic premium shrinks toward the $60M harvesting clearing price.
rows.implication: The exit case is real but binary on IP ownership and OEM appetite; size the position to the $60M-$150M end, not the $305M headline.
rows.confidence: high on the transactions; medium on applying them to Orrin.
rows.follow_up: Has any OEM signed an evaluation, partnership or term sheet with Orrin, and on what technology?

rows.finding: The category's failure record is now the base rate: Abundant Robotics raised about $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025 after a $25M Series B with Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025; Monarch Tractor raised about $217M including a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors reported in January 2026, and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026.
rows.mechanism: Harvest robotics has a 12-month cash cycle with no margin for a missed season; a technology that works in trials can still fail on unit economics, service cost and adoption speed.
rows.benchmark: Four of the five funded peers in the comparison set failed, liquidated or sold assets between 2021 and 2026; none reached a venture-scale IPO.
rows.weakens: The bull case that treats commercial deployments and OEM investment as proof of a durable business, and any probability of a $300M+ exit above 20%.
rows.implication: Set the bear case at or above 50% until an independent trial and a financed 2027 season exist; the burden of proof is on the company.
rows.confidence: high on the events; medium on Monarch because the source is a data aggregator.
rows.follow_up: What did Caterpillar pay for Monarch's assets, and which technology did it keep?

rows.finding: Harvest CROO markets a 16-arm autonomous strawberry harvester on a six-bed chassis as a harvesting service, claiming up to 8 berries a second, in the same Florida season Orrin targets.
rows.mechanism: A service model with a multi-arm harvester competes for the same grower relationship and the same harvest window; if its throughput claim holds, Orrin's 5.6 seconds a berry is an order of magnitude slower per machine.
rows.benchmark: Orrin 5.6 s/berry on 212 selected rows (company); Harvest CROO up to 8 berries/s (company). Neither is independently verified.
rows.weakens: The 'only autonomous open-field picker above 90%' positioning and any assumption that Orrin sets the service price.
rows.implication: Competitive diligence should benchmark throughput and cost per marketable berry, not pick accuracy on selected rows.
rows.confidence: low: both figures are company claims with no independent trial.
rows.follow_up: What does Harvest CROO charge per acre or per season, and how many machines are in commercial service in 2026?

rows.finding: A 2026 peer-reviewed berry-harvesting platform reported a 72% overall harvest success rate across 50 controlled indoor trials with synthetic fruit.
rows.mechanism: Selective harvesting is a perception, manipulation and occlusion problem; success rates fall as the environment moves from synthetic indoor fruit to commercial open field.
rows.benchmark: 72% in controlled indoor trials against Orrin's 94% of detected ripe fruit on selected rows and independent reports of 74%-87% of ripe or detected fruit.
rows.weakens: Any reading of 94% as a harvest-level or generalisable rate.
rows.implication: Demand an independent harvest-level trial before pricing the technology; the 94% cannot carry the valuation.
rows.confidence: medium: small trial, synthetic fruit, but peer-reviewed and independent.
rows.follow_up: What harvest-level recovery and bruise rate did the independent strawberry trials report on commercial blocks?

rows.finding: Agtech venture funding fell to $4.799 billion across 735 deals in 2025 from $5.099 billion across 913 deals in 2024, the lowest level in several years, with capital concentrating in robotics and AI.
rows.mechanism: A shrinking deal count makes a Series B in 2028 harder and lengthens the path to liquidity, which raises the cost of a missed 2027 season.
rows.benchmark: Deal count down about 20% year on year; Orrin's plan assumes a Series B after one funded season.
rows.weakens: The assumption that the 2028 Series B is available on plan; financing risk is systemic as well as company-specific.
rows.implication: Require a financing plan that does not depend on a 2028 Series B at a premium, or a tranche that preserves the option.
rows.confidence: medium: PitchBook data reported second-hand by an industry blog.
rows.follow_up: Which ag-robotics rounds closed in 2026 at what step-up, and who led them?

plan.decision_question: Should Meridian lead Orrin's $18M Series A at $72M pre-money, and if not at what price and on what conditions?
plan.thesis_sentence: The harvest-labour gap is real and Orrin's machine works well enough to sell seasons, but at $72M pre-money the investor is paying for a harvest-level proof and a 2027 build the evidence does not yet support; the case becomes investable at $48M-$55M pre-money with an independent trial, a measured v4 cost and a lender standstill.
plan.why_different: This section owns the go/no-go judgement, the probability-weighted returns and the price at which the case turns; it synthesises the analysts' evidence and adds only the analog and consensus research.
plan.mechanism: A seasonal service model with negative contribution per robot-season, a conditional university licence and a thin capital base cannot absorb a missed 2027 season; the value therefore depends on harvest-level recovery, unit cost and the financing path, not on the size of the labour problem.
plan.comparison_set: Lely Astronaut (successful slow adoption), Deere/Blue River and Bear Flag (OEM exit ceiling), Abundant, Advanced Farm, Tortuga and Monarch (failure and asset-sale base rate), Harvest CROO (direct competitor), listed ag peers at 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x.
plan.counter_evidence: If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with bruising at or below a hand-picked control, the machine replaces crews rather than supplementing them, the $235.7M pool understates the market and $72M is cheap; the reprice would then be an expensive pass.
plan.visual: Scenario table with probabilities and returns, plus the ranked key-assumptions table and the analog table.
plan.prohibited: No 'strong team', 'huge market', 'high barriers to entry', 'clear business model', 'fierce competition', 'risks are manageable', 'well positioned'; no vague counts; no sentences about how the report is written.

rows.finding: Private ag-robotics valuations are not reliably disclosed: CB Insights records Carbon Robotics at $213.65M raised across nine rounds with a 2023-12 valuation of $119M-$169M, while other trackers report $128M-$232M raised and a $548M 2025-10 valuation.
rows.mechanism: Without disclosed post-money values or revenue, a private peer multiple cannot be observed; the valuation dimension must be scored on the round's own revenue multiples and terms rather than on a peer benchmark.
rows.benchmark: Orrin at 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x sales.
rows.weakens: The company's implicit claim that $72M is in line with peer rounds; the peer data cannot support any multiple.
rows.implication: Score valuation at 2 of 10 and let the recommendation rest on observable revenue multiples and the preference stack.
rows.confidence: medium: trackers conflict, so the peer set is directional only.
rows.follow_up: What post-money valuations did 2024-2026 ag-robotics Series A and B rounds clear at, from PitchBook or Caplight?

rows.finding: Monarch Tractor raised a $133M Series C at a reported $518M post-money in July 2024 with CNH Industrial among its investors, then ceased operations, entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors reported in January 2026 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in April 2026.
rows.mechanism: A high private mark does not survive a missed commercial ramp; the equity can go to zero while the technology is bought out of an insolvency at an undisclosed price.
rows.benchmark: 21 months from a $518M post-money to an asset sale; Orrin is priced at $90M post on $2.6M of revenue.
rows.weakens: Any use of large peer rounds as evidence of value; it is evidence of capital intensity and failure risk.
rows.implication: Weight exit and financial survival heavily and cap the exit dimension at 4 of 10 despite the OEM precedent.
rows.confidence: medium: aggregator source, corroborated by its funding detail and the 2026 timeline.
rows.follow_up: What recovery did Monarch's preferred investors receive, and who bought the assets?

rows.finding: Agtech venture funding fell to $4.799 billion across 735 deals in 2025 from $5.099 billion across 913 deals in 2024, a roughly 20% drop in deal count.
rows.mechanism: A thinner financing market raises the cost of the 2028 Series B and lengthens time to liquidity, which lowers the score on financial durability and exit timing.
rows.benchmark: Deal count down 20%; Orrin needs $6M-$10M of Series B money in 2028 to protect the stake.
rows.weakens: The base case that assumes a flat or better Series B after the 2027 season.
rows.implication: Score financial durability and exit timing at 3 and 4 of 10, and require a financing plan that survives a closed 2028 market.
rows.confidence: medium: secondary reporting of PitchBook data.
rows.follow_up: Which agtech robotics rounds closed in 2026, at what step-up and with which lead investors?

rows.finding: Deere paid $305 million for Blue River in 2017 and $250 million for Bear Flag in 2021; AppHarvest paid $60 million for Root AI, a harvesting-specific team, in 2021.
rows.mechanism: OEM trade sales are the realistic exit for a proven autonomy stack, but the harvesting-specific clearing price is a fifth of the broad autonomy price.
rows.benchmark: $305M and $250M autonomy exits against a $60M harvesting exit; Orrin's base case assumes $150M-$250M.
rows.weakens: An exit score above 5: the $150M-$250M range requires the technology to be read as franchise-defending, not as one harvesting feature.
rows.implication: Score exit 4 of 10 and test the OEM partnership question in diligence.
rows.confidence: high on the transactions; medium on the mapping to Orrin.
rows.follow_up: Is any OEM evaluating Orrin's perception stack for its own equipment line?

rows.finding: Lely's Astronaut reached 50,000 installed units in 2024, 29 years after commercial launch, with dealer installation and after-sales service; 100 units were in use by 1997.
rows.mechanism: Successful farm robotics scales through service capacity and a long replacement cycle; adoption speed, not demand, sets the revenue curve.
rows.benchmark: Lely: 100 units in two commercial years and 50,000 in 29. Orrin: 64 units after about four years and 360 planned in 2027.
rows.weakens: The 2027 plan's ramp and the 15%-adoption-by-2031 market case as a base case.
rows.implication: Score market timing 6 of 10 and business model 3 of 10: the need is real, the delivery capacity is not yet proven.
rows.confidence: high on Lely; medium on the analogy.
rows.follow_up: What is Orrin's service technician ratio and installation cycle time at 360 robots?

rows.finding: The machine's performance is company-only: 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, 3.8% bruising, 86% uptime and 5.6 s/berry, while independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 s/berry, 83%-87% of detected fruit and 72% in controlled indoor trials.
rows.mechanism: The 94% denominator is already-detected ripe fruit on chosen rows; harvest-level recovery of about 75%-80% after bruising and unripe picks is the economically relevant number.
rows.benchmark: Independent 72%-87% against the company's 94%; hand-picking is the quality control the robot must match.
rows.weakens: The technology score: without an independent harvest-level trial the dimension cannot score above 5.
rows.implication: Score technology 5 of 10 and make an independent trial a condition of any investment.
rows.confidence: high that the 94% is conditional; medium on the 75%-80% range.
rows.follow_up: What is the harvest-level recovery and bruise rate against a hand-picked control on unselected commercial blocks?

plan.decision_question: What is Orrin worth on a weighted basis, at what check size, and what would have to be true to invest?
plan.thesis_sentence: Orrin scores 4.1 of 10 and is a wait-for-milestone at $72M pre-money: the technology, market and exit are real but unproven, while the unit economics, cash position and price are not investable as offered.
plan.why_different: This section converts the evidence into a weighted score, a position size and a sensitivity ranking; it is the only place where the composite and the check size are set.
plan.mechanism: The composite is driven by negative contribution per robot-season, a 5.4-month usable runway and a $72M price at 27.7x forward revenue; the strengths sit in a real labour need and an OEM exit precedent.
plan.comparison_set: Listed ag peers at 2.7x EV/Sales, CNH/Raven at 6.0x, Blue River $305M and Bear Flag $250M, Root AI $60M, and the failure record of Abundant, Advanced Farm, Tortuga and Monarch.
plan.counter_evidence: If an independent trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% and the v4 robot lands at $33,000, the technology and unit-economics scores rise and the composite moves above 6, which would justify leading at $48M-$55M.
plan.visual: Weighted score table, sensitivity table and takeaways.
plan.prohibited: No empty phrases, vague counts, internal names or sentences about how the report is written; every figure carries a source.

user_data_requests.why: Section 1 must clear liens and litigation and Section 2 must explain the CTO departure; a separation dispute, an IP ownership claim or a supplier lien would not appear in the deck and would change the price and conditions.
user_data_requests.how: Run name searches in each county superior court portal, Delaware CourtConnect/Chancery, and PACER; provide docket sheets and pleadings for any hits.

user_data_requests.database: PitchBook / Caplight private-round data
user_data_requests.query: Post-money valuations, round dates and disclosed revenue at the last round for Carbon Robotics, Monarch Tractor, Advanced Farm Technologies, Tortuga AgTech, Harvest CROO Robotics, Burro and Agrobot, 2023-2026.
user_data_requests.why: No ag-robotics comparable round in the public record discloses a post-money valuation, so the $72M pre-money can only be benchmarked against revenue multiples and round sizes. Post-money valuations would show whether Orrin's price is at, above or below the private market for the category and would change the recommendation from repricing to market.
user_data_requests.how: Pull the company profiles from a PitchBook or Caplight seat and export the round history (date, amount, post-money valuation, lead investor) for the seven companies; a screenshot or CSV is enough.

user_data_requests.database: Orrin data room (client-provided documents)
user_data_requests.query: Calder University exclusive licence agreement (assignment, change-of-control, sublicense and termination clauses) and the 2025 note purchase agreement and Kestrel equipment facility (caps, maturity, consent and change-of-control terms).
user_data_requests.why: The exit depends on whether the Calder licence survives a sale and whether the noteholders and Kestrel can block one; the deck discloses only the 100-robot exclusivity test and the $1.5M cash covenant. Without these documents the exit section cannot say whether a trade sale is executable or who must consent.
user_data_requests.how: Request the licence and the note and equipment-facility agreements from the company's data room, with the signature pages and any consent or assignment clauses unredacted.

user_data_requests.database: USPTO Patent Public Search / Patent Center file wrapper, and WIPO Patentscope
user_data_requests.query: Prosecution history for US application 17/902,118 (soft gripper with slip sensing): the first office action's grounds of rejection, the claims rejected, and the response filed 2026-05; plus the national-phase entry status for PCT/US2025/027761 in Europe, Mexico and Australia after the 2026-10-30 deadline, and the application numbers behind the two university-licensed families (dockets CU-2017-031 and CU-2019-114).
user_data_requests.why: Whether the gripper claim is rejected on prior art or on form decides if any enforceable end-effector protection exists; whether the platform PCT was entered decides if the machine is protected outside the US; and the licensed families' claim scope decides how much of the perception stack a competitor could license if exclusivity lapses at the 100-robot test on 2027-12-31. All three bear directly on whether $72M pre-money is defensible.
user_data_requests.how: Pull the file wrapper from USPTO Patent Public Search (ppubs.uspto.gov) or Patent Center for 17/902,118 and send the office action and response as PDFs; check Patentscope for PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase entries; obtain the two licence schedules from the company's data room with patent numbers.

user_data_requests.database: DOL Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC) H-2A disclosure data
user_data_requests.query: FY2025-FY2026 H-2A certifications for California and Florida, SOC 45-2092 (farmworkers and laborers, crop), with employers, positions certified, and the 2026 Adverse Effect Wage Rate by state; plus the 2026 AEWR Federal Register table (91 FR 48946).
user_data_requests.why: Settles whether the hand-pick wage floor is rising and how many H-2A positions California and Florida strawberry growers rely on; the 2026 California AEWR is only available here at secondary medium confidence ($19.97/hour), and this figure drives the demand case for Orrin's robots.
user_data_requests.how: Download the OFLC H-2A disclosure files at flag.dol.gov/performance-data and the 2026-08-03 Federal Register AEWR notice; send the California and Florida rows.

user_data_requests.database: US Customs and Border Protection / USITC HTSUS and USMCA rules of origin
user_data_requests.query: The USMCA product-specific rule of origin for HTS heading 8433 (harvesting machinery), the 2026 duty stack for Mexico-origin goods, and Orrin's USMCA certification or CBP ruling for robots and gripper/harness subassemblies made in Guadalajara.
user_data_requests.why: If the robots or subassemblies fail USMCA origin, a 10% Section 301-type duty applies to the $33,000 v4 unit cost, about $3,300 a robot and roughly 10% of the 2027 build budget; the source register carries conflicting accounts of the 2026 tariff stack, so the duty rate and origin test decide whether Mexican assembly is viable.
user_data_requests.how: Ask Orrin for its USMCA certification and customs broker's origin analysis; check HTSUS chapter 84 and the USMCA Chapter 4 product-specific rules; request a CBP binding ruling if no certification exists.

user_data_requests.database: Orrin Fieldworks data room — insurance and safety records
user_data_requests.query: Product liability and general liability insurance certificates for Orrin Fleet Services LLC and Orrin Fieldworks, Inc.: limits per occurrence and aggregate, autonomous-machinery exclusions, additional-insured status for growers, and Cal/OSHA Form 300 logs and incident reports for 2024-2026.
user_data_requests.why: Autonomous machines working at night around harvest crews create strict product-liability and premises-liability exposure; the deck says Orrin insures the fleet but discloses no limits or exclusions, and an autonomous-operation exclusion would leave the liability with the company or the grower.
user_data_requests.how: Request certificates of insurance, policy endorsements and loss runs from the data room, plus OSHA 300 logs and any incident reports.

user_data_requests.database: PACER, California Superior Court and Cal/OSHA enforcement databases
user_data_requests.query: Civil, product-liability and wage-and-hour litigation, judgments, liens and Cal/OSHA inspections or citations for Orrin Fieldworks, Inc., Orrin Fleet Services LLC and Vashti Harvest Services LLC, 2021-2026.
user_data_requests.why: The public record for a private company is thin; absence of enforcement in this research is not evidence of a clean record, and a single serious injury or wage claim would change the liability and governance assessment.
user_data_requests.how: Search PACER by entity name, the California Superior Courts' public case search in Monterey, Santa Cruz and San Diego counties, and Cal/OSHA's inspection database; send case numbers and dispositions.

user_data_requests.database: Orrin Fieldworks data room (access offered on request, deck p.15)
user_data_requests.query: Executed 2027 grower contracts for 110 robots and the 50 LOIs; Tallis engineering-services agreement and v4 BOM quote or purchase order; Vashti Harvest Services contract; grower payment terms and deposits.
user_data_requests.why: Section 6's $1.4M contracted revenue, $31,000 target unit cost and related-party service costs are unverified. The contracts decide whether 44% of the 2027 plan is binding, whether the $12,700 renewal price is market, and whether the $310,000 Vashti payments are at arm's length.
user_data_requests.how: Request executed contracts, LOI letters and the Tallis/Vashti agreements from management, with prices, volumes and payment terms unredacted.

user_data_requests.database: Orrin Fieldworks data room (access offered on request, deck p.15)
user_data_requests.query: Audited or reviewed financial statements FY2023-FY2025 and Q3 2026 management accounts; Kestrel Equipment Finance credit agreement (maturity, covenant schedule, security, permitted debt); grower receivables aging.
user_data_requests.why: Section 7's revenue, margin, cash, debt and 5.4-month effective runway are reconstructed from an unaudited deck. The loan agreement decides whether the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant is a hard default trigger, and the statements decide whether the $1.9M FY2025 revenue and $3.7M cash are real.
user_data_requests.how: Ask Orrin management to grant data-room access or send the documents directly; signed PDFs of the Kestrel agreement and FY2023-FY2025 statements are sufficient.

user_data_requests.database: UC Davis / UC Cooperative Extension crop cost studies
user_data_requests.query: Cost and return study for strawberries on the Central Coast (Santa Cruz-Watsonville and Santa Maria) for 2023-2025: harvest labour cost per acre, total cultural cost per acre, yield and price assumptions.
user_data_requests.why: The key willingness-to-pay test is the harvest-labour budget per acre a robot displaces; the deck discloses no hand-harvest cost, so the price ceiling is inferred from company productivity figures rather than a grower budget.
user_data_requests.how: Download the latest UC Davis Agricultural and Resource Economics cost-and-return study PDF for strawberries; the harvest-labour line per acre and the assumed wage rate are what is needed.

user_data_requests.database: California Strawberry Commission (industry data and annual acreage reports)
user_data_requests.query: California strawberry acreage by district (Salinas/Watsonville, Santa Maria, Oxnard), grower count, top-20 grower share of acreage, and season start/end dates for 2022-2026.
user_data_requests.why: The deck claims the top 20 growers farm over half of California acreage and a seven-month season; both shape buyer concentration and robot utilisation, and neither could be verified from public records in this run.
user_data_requests.how: Request the Commission's acreage and grower statistics page or its annual report; if the site needs a login, a PDF of the latest acreage report is sufficient.

user_data_requests.database: US Department of Labor OFLC H-2A disclosure data and FLAG Adverse Effect Wage Rates
user_data_requests.query: H-2A positions certified for California and Florida crop growers in FY2020-FY2026 (strawberries/berries where the crop field permits), and the California and Florida Adverse Effect Wage Rates for 2020-2026.
user_data_requests.why: Labour scarcity is the demand driver behind the 2027-2031 adoption case; without certification volumes and wage levels the urgency claim rests only on company interviews, and an elastic H-2A supply would delay adoption by a season or more.
user_data_requests.how: Download the OFLC H-2A disclosure files (flag.dol.gov/performance-data) and the AEWR table; a CSV of California/Florida certifications and the AEWR series is enough.

user_data_requests.database: USDA NASS, Noncitrus Fruits and Nuts 2025 Summary and Quick Stats
user_data_requests.query: Strawberry bearing acreage, area harvested, production and price by state (California, Florida, total US) for 2019-2025, from the Noncitrus Fruits and Nuts 2025 Summary (released 2026-05-01) and Quick Stats series STRAWBERRIES - AREA BEARING.
user_data_requests.why: The deck's ~50,000-acre US base and its 2%-to-15% adoption path drive the whole market sizing; the PDF could not be read and the strawberry-specific line was not retrieved, so the TAM and the $310M obtainable-market test rest on an unverified acreage figure.
user_data_requests.how: Download the Noncitrus Fruits and Nuts 2025 Summary PDF (release.nass.usda.gov/reports/ncit0526.pdf) and export the strawberry table, or query NASS Quick Stats for the series above; a CSV or a screenshot of the strawberry table is enough.

user_data_requests.database: Orrin Fieldworks data room — executed Calder University licence agreement
user_data_requests.query: The executed exclusive licence dated 2022-01-20: its term and duration (start, expiry, renewal), termination for cause/convenience, assignment and change-of-control clauses, the patent schedule listing all eleven university application numbers, and the definition of "commercial service" used in the 100-robot test on 2027-12-31.
user_data_requests.why: Section 1's legal-cleanliness judgement rests on whether the parent actually holds a licence that survives a change of control and long enough to reach an exit. The deck discloses the royalty (2.5%), the $40,000 minimum and the 100-robot exclusivity test but not the term, renewal, termination or assignment terms, and it does not enumerate the eleven university application numbers. Without the agreement the licence is an assertion, not a verified asset, and confidence in the IP half of the thesis stays low.
user_data_requests.how: Request the signed licence agreement with its patent schedule and amendments from the data room (access offered on deck p.15), unredacted as to term, termination and assignment; ask Calder University's technology-transfer office to confirm the licensor's executed copy.

user_data_requests.database: Orrin Fieldworks data room — Kestrel Equipment Finance facility, UCC-1 and bank records
user_data_requests.query: Executed $2.5M Kestrel Equipment Finance facility dated 2025-06-16, with the $1.5M minimum-cash definition, cross-default, cure period and waiver price; the UCC-1 financing statement naming Orrin Fleet Services LLC as debtor; and the September 2026 bank statement showing the $3.7M balance and $1.6M drawn.
user_data_requests.why: The $1.5M minimum-cash test is the difference between a 4.4-month runway to a lender default on 2027-03-14 and a no-covenant case in which a 25-40% down round is the failure mode; the bear weight moves from 50% to about 35% and a $48-55M structure becomes investable with conditions. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the source register, so the covenant rests only on deck p.10.
user_data_requests.how: Ask the company for the executed facility agreement with all amendments and any waiver or standstill terms, the California Secretary of State UCC-1 filing, and the September 2026 bank statement; account numbers can be redacted.

user_data_requests.database: Orrin Fieldworks grower records — Grower B (Santa Maria, CA) 2026 season file
user_data_requests.query: Grower B's 2026 season record: contracted versus delivered robot count (22 in 2025 to 14 in 2026), acres harvested per robot, yield and bruising rate, uptime, the price or discount paid, and any written reason for the reduction (acreage, price, performance or bruising).
user_data_requests.why: A 36% cut at a reference customer in its second paid season is the single best test of whether the 110-robot 2027 renewal book is an expansion or a churn signal; an acreage or price cause leaves the renewal case intact, a performance or bruising cause contradicts it and would lower the 2027 base case.
user_data_requests.how: Ask management for the Grower B service agreement, the 2026 season report (harvest logs, bruise/quality inspection, uptime) and the 2027 order; or obtain the grower's own confirmation under NDA.

1.name: Completeness sweep
1.notes: Sections read: all fifteen, version 1. Depth floors met everywhere (7,896-8,991 characters, 6+ paragraphs, 8+ figures, 4+ source IDs, source columns in every table); executive summary 6,311 characters with all four components. Check findings: team (granularity), market (granularity), competition (N3); report-level rewrite-plan line is the three section items. Evidence matrix: every section's own gate passed, 5-12 queries and 6-8 rows each, so no section is unsourced. Structure and disclosure are above the usual standard for a private round: the entity split, the preference stack, the rejected gripper claims, the PCT deadline of 2026-10-30 and the related-party map are all in the text with the correct 'not disclosed' language. What is missing is verification, not description. The three user-facing claims I could not close from the register: any primary filing of any kind (there is none — the whole report rests on one 15-page deck), any registry extract, and any audited or management account. The 18 open data requests are named in the sections and every resulting gap is labelled unverified, so N10 is satisfied; the reviewer's concern is that the report's own confidence language is right while several of its headline numbers are not yet dated or reconciled.

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: Verification summary. Independently supported in the register and correctly used: listed peer multiples (S8, S12, S14, S9, S95 CNH/Raven 6.0x); USDA ERS noncitrus bearing acreage down 2% (S160); ISO 18497-1:2024 and -4:2024 (S166); 21 CFR 112.123 (S163); California wage and overtime rules (S141, S142); 2026 AEWR publication and the $19.97 rate (S145, flagged in the ESG table as 'primary table not read'); Deere/Blue River $305M and Bear Flag $250M (S92, S178); Advanced Farm's closure, Tortuga's sale to Oishii, Abundant's liquidation (S114, S115, S91); Carbon and Monarch capital (S55, S175, S176). Company-only with no independent support, correctly labelled unverified but load-bearing: 94% pick rate, 3.8% bruising, 86% uptime, 5.6 s per berry; 64 robots, 75 paid seasons, 110 contracted, 50 LOIs; the $48,000 v3 and $31,000-$33,000 v4 costs, where the only quote is a related-party BOM; the $3.2M ARR definition; the $42B, $3.1B and $310M market layers; the 50,000-acre base; the 1.9M labelled images; the 2.1-season payback; the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant; and the 11 Calder filings. Contradicted or over-stated: ARR as recurring (56% non-recurring or non-binding, correctly contradicted in section 7); payback 2.1 seasons (correctly recomputed); 'only open-field picker above 90%' (flagged Critical); DailyRobotics 'first California customer deployment from April 2026' (S170 is dated 2025-11 and describes a planned 2026 launch — handled in pass 3). Staleness: S172-S173 (2024) and S168/S171 (2025-10/11) are the oldest independent sources used for live claims; none is more than about two years old and each is tagged with its date, so no stale-source item is raised beyond Monarch.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: Missing-competitor screen, section by section. Geographic: Japan and Korea are the blind spot — Agrist has sold strawberry-harvesting robots commercially and neither the competition table nor the market's Europe/Asia row mentions Japan; Mexico is treated only as a cost base, which is right, but no Latin American grower-side competitor is screened. Adjacent giants: Deere, CNH, Kubota, Yamaha and AGCO are covered as acquirers and dismissed as current competitors on the strength of Deere's FY2025 10-K language (S8), which is a fair test; Carbon Robotics is the gap, because it is capital-rich, in-field and one crop away. Substitutes: the hand crew is handled better than in most reports — cost per picker-day, H-2A floor, retail quality bar and the fact that a crew costs nothing when idle are all in the text — and 'do nothing' is effectively the same row. Open source: not addressed anywhere (pass 3 minor). Academic: WSU and the Journal of Field Robotics work is used as independent performance evidence, which is the right use; the gap is that no university spin-out is screened as a future competitor in open-field berries. Greenhouse/tabletop vendors (Tortuga, Agrobot, MetoMotion, Dogtooth) are correctly classed as non-comparable. Net: one Critical omission (DailyRobotics plus the unchecked Japanese entrant) and one base-rate omission (Traptic); the rest of the map is sound and better sourced than the category norm.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: Product/market-fit questions and where the report stands. (1) Hardest thing about selling: quality, not price — a hand crew meets the retail bruise bar and costs nothing when idle, and the report says so with the Grower E evidence; this is the report's strongest PMF passage. Unanswered: whether the bruise objection is fixable in v4 or intrinsic to a gripper that grips at 5.6 s a berry. (2) Budget owner: the harvest manager is named as the budget owner and the buyer as the owner or head of harvest, but no deal is evidenced by a named signature, so the authority question rests on the deck. Ask for one signed 2026 order form and the approval chain. (3) Sales cycle: one selling window a year, agreed before planting, is a mechanism, not a measured cycle; no contract dates exist to show how long a pilot-to-paid conversion actually takes. (4) Why adoption is not faster: five of fourteen pilots converted and four sales staff cover the whole book, which is answered; what is missing is the cost of the nine failures. (5) Lost deals: only Grower E is documented, and the Grower B downgrade is undocumented (item above). Two further questions for the owners: does the grower insist on a second robot vendor before committing a material acreage, and does Orrin's RaaS contract carry a minimum-season guarantee that would move the grower's seasonal risk onto Orrin?

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Stress-test arithmetic, each key number checked and then run 30% worse. (1) US acreage base 50,000 → 35,000: pool $165.0M (10,000 robots at $16,500); 15% adoption gives 428.6 robots and $7.1M at list, so the $310M obtainable market becomes 188% of the base and dies outright; the thesis survives only as a reprice or a pass, which is the report's own conclusion. (2) Harvest recovery 75%-80% → 52%-56%: a fifth to a half of ripe fruit left on the plant, the machine is strictly a harvest aid, the 360-robot plan needs 500+ robots for the same acres, and enterprise value falls 40%-60%; thesis survives as Pass only. (3) v4 unit cost $31,000 → $40,300: renewal contribution goes to -$2,975 a robot-season from -$650; the report's $36,000 ceiling and $40,000 trigger cover the direction but never publishes the -$2,975 number. (4) 2027 contracted 110 robots → 77: RaaS falls from $1.4M to $0.98M and FY2027 revenue from $5.6M to about $5.1M; the 44% cover becomes 31%; thesis survives, the valuation does not. (5) Contract price $12,700 → $8,890: contribution -$4,460; the report prices a $12,700 renewal but not a rollback toward the 2026 $9,500, which is the more likely response to a soft season. (6) Burn $410,000 → $533,000 a month: usable cash of $1.79M reaches the covenant about 2027-02-10, four weeks before the reported date; not in the report. (7) Harvest 94% → 66%: unenforceable gripper, licence test missed, exit value 0-1.0x. Verified and correct: 14,286 robots and $235.7M at 100% adoption; $35.4M at 15% adoption and $27.2M at renewal; 18,788 robots and 132% of the base for $310M; -$8,100 and -$650 contribution; $13,350 break-even; 5.4 months from the 2026-09-30 balance; burn multiples 7.0x and 5.9x; fleet yields -16.9%, -2.1% and +10.2%; all multiples of revenue (27.7x, 34.6x, 22.5x, 51.4x, 101.1x, 12.9x, 6.8x); preference stack $36.77M and 40.9% of post; the share count of 19,090,116 and the $4.7145 price; 1.67x, 2.78x, 3.33x, 5.56x at $72M pre; and the composite score of 4.1 from the weights. Only the $50M repriced case fails, and only on the post-money assumption (item above). Thesis survival test: at $72M the recommendation holds under every 30% case; at $48M-$55M it holds only with the tranche, the standstill and a measured v4 cost, which the report already proposes.

1.name: Completeness sweep
1.notes: All 14 sections' checks pass: no rule, depth, citation or report-level finding; all evidence gates pass. Every section is 6,961-8,994 characters, so the depth floor is met and none is near the 9,000 ceiling. Executive summary components (verdict, briefing, efficiency, one-question, takeaways) present; team, competition, risk, thesis, scoring, exit, esg carry their required components and tables. R1 Criticals: competition N3 statuses now sit at each claim, including the quad; team now has a month-level career table with dated achievements and three named CV checks that returned nothing, with Abernathy's 2023-08-31 separation and undisclosed IP assignment stated; the cash clock is dated in all seven sections that use it, with usable and gross months separated; technology_product cites ISO 18497-1:2024 (S166) and ISO 18497-4:2024 (S199, 2024-07-31) separately. R1 Importants: lost-deal register and CAC ($300,000-$400,000 a grower) are in business_model; Traptic and the open-source route are in the base rate; the Mexican entity and Calder term are labelled not disclosed; exit route likelihoods rest on independent records with a probability-weighted table. Three earlier Importants survive in narrowed form: round size, Monarch in business_model, and the H-2A line in market (pass 2).

2.name: Claim verification
2.notes: R1 claim-verification items closed: the three CV lines (Calder University, Marisol Ridge Farms, Corvane Robotics) were checked by institution and role on 2026-10-31 and returned no record, and the section states that plainly; the licensed families' dockets (CU-2017-031, CU-2019-114) are given with the nine unlicensed filings flagged; Abernathy's separation date and the undisclosed IP assignment are stated; the Delaware, California, Mexican, USPTO and court gaps are labelled as unobtainable rather than skipped. Company-only claims elsewhere carry a status (competition's \"only open-field picker above 90%\" and \"only disclosed paid fleet\", the quad, the 94%, Grower E's exit, the 2027 contracted book). Source independence remains the report's structural weakness: S53 is the deck and carries most operating figures, so the text correctly says so rather than implying corroboration. Net cash, $3.29M at 2026-10-31 and $1.69M after the $1.6M drawn, reconciles to the dated balance.

4.name: Product/market fit
4.notes: The selling mechanism is now on the page and it is the right one: the budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting with one selling window a year (April-October in California, December-March in Florida), so a missed season costs twelve months and the product is bought on a dated calendar, not a budget cycle. Sales cycle: 14 farms piloted since 2024, 5 converted to paid in 2026, 9 never paid - a 5-of-14 conversion against four sales staff and an estimated $300,000-$400,000 a grower to acquire, $8,000-$11,000 per contracted robot. Why adoption is not faster is answered with mechanism rather than adjectives: price at $9,500 is 54% of fully loaded cost to the company but only 1.2-5.9% of the picker-days it displaces, so willingness to pay is not the constraint; the gate is bruise-free harvest-level recovery, one Florida exit over bruising, and a technician ratio of 1:8 against 45 needed. Lost deals are now registered (Grower E, Grower D, Grower B, 6 of 8 other pilots, 9 of 14 never paid), which is the register R1 asked for. The residual gap is the reason behind Grower B's cut, which the deck does not give and which the report cannot infer.

3.name: Missing competitors
3.notes: The R1 competitor gap is closed and the treatment is now the strongest evidence work in the report. DailyRobotics is in the table with the correct status (Q2 unit, announced 2025-11 for a first California deployment from 2026-04, unconfirmed at 2026-10-31), so the risk section's reference and the competition section's record agree. AGRIST, Four Growers and Carbon Robotics are screened with the reason none competes in open-field strawberries (rail-guided greenhouse, greenhouse tomato in development, a laser weeder that never touches the crop) and with capital raised, and the same screen appears in technology_product. Harvest CROO's human-parity claim is statused. Substitutes are covered where they matter: hand crews and H-2A as the 100%-share incumbent, harvest aids, tabletop systems, and the open-source ROS 2 route with 6-9 months off a 24-month estimate and the service organisation it cannot supply. Adjacent giants are priced as capital and acquisition appetite rather than as competitors, which is the right read given Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot. Geographic blind spots: Mexico is treated as a cost base, Europe as unentered with ISO 18497 and CE marking as the gate; no named European entrant (MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot) is analysed beyond a one-line note, which is acceptable while Europe is not entered. No new competitor item is raised in round 2.

5.name: Number stress-test
5.notes: Re-derived every key number from stated inputs. Checks: revenue build $0.71+$0.34+$1.20+$0.35 = $2.60M; gross margin ex-grants (1.51-0.35)/(2.6-0.35) = 51.1%; contribution $9,500-$3,100-$2,500-$12,000 = -$8,100 and 54% of a $17,600 fully loaded cost; break-even $5,600+$7,750 = $13,350; renewal at target service $12,700-$4,250-$7,750 = +$700; list at target service +$4,500, payback 2.5-2.8 seasons; ARR decomposition 1.4+1.2+0.6 = $3.2M with 56% non-recurring or non-binding; 2027 price $4.6M/360 = $12,778; $72M/$2.6M = 27.7x, /$1.4M = 51.4x, /$0.7125M = 101.1x, /$3.2M = 22.5x, $90M/$2.6M = 34.6x; burn multiple $4.9M/$0.7M = 7.0x; cash $3.7M-$0.41M = $3.29M, usable $1.79M/$410k = 4.4 months to 2027-03-14, gross $3.29M/$410k = 8.0 months; bridge $18M+$2.68M+$0.9M-$9.9M-$7.1M-$1.5M leaves $2.6-3.6M; $7.0M-$7.77M at $3.7716 = 2,061,303 A-1 shares; price $4.7145, $12M = 2,545,339 shares = 13.33% of 19,090,116; preference $36.8M/$90M = 40.9%; pool $235.7M, 15% adoption $35.4M/$27.2M, $310M = 132% of the pool; CAC $0.9-1.2M/3 new growers = $300,000-$400,000, LTV $12,600 over four seasons = 1.1-1.6x; weighted exit 0.30x10+0.25x75+0.25x150+0.15x250+0.05x400 = $116.8M; composite 0.20x5+0.15x6+0.15x5+0.15x3+0.10x3+0.15x2+0.10x4 = 4.05, rounds to 4.1 as stated. 30%-worse stress: exit values 30% lower give a weighted $81.8M, i.e. 1.13x at $72M and 1.60x on the $50M/$12M case - the recommendation (do not lead at $72M) survives, and $48M-$55M still clears 1x; burn 30% higher ($533k) brings the covenant forward to about 2027-02-13, which the six-months-late case already covers; revenue 30% lower and CAC doubled are both addressed. final_memo:
# Orrin Fieldworks: Investment research report
Rating: Wait for milestone
Composite score: 4.1
Data as of: 2026-10-31

## Executive Briefing

Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 20 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, a $35.4M pool at the claimed 15% share rather than $310M, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 2.78x at $250M and 1.30x on the $116.8M weighted value. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What it sells | 64 robots, 75 paid seasons and five paying growers at $9,500 a season in 2026 (company-reported, unverified); 110 robots contracted and 50 letters of intent for a 360-robot 2027 plan | S53 unverified |
| Performance | 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 selected rows with 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime (company); independent trials report 72%-87%, putting harvest-level recovery near 75%-80% | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350; a grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. If the trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the right answer reverses and $72M is cheap [S53 unverified].

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| FY2026E revenue | $2.6M, 46% Tallis engineering services and 13% grants | S53 unverified |
| 2026 RaaS revenue | $0.71M | S53 unverified |
| Gross margin | 41% as reported; -85% after fleet depreciation | S53 unverified |
| Contribution per robot-season | -$8,100 at $9,500; -$650 at $12,700 with $31,000 cost | S53 unverified |
| Net burn and runway | $410,000 a month; 4.4 usable months to covenant at 2026-10-31 | S53 unverified |
